en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the *Petavatthu* in the *Khuddakanikāya*.
Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Lord of Great Compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known, and who teaches through methods that are skillful, profound, and diverse.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, by which people are led out from the world;
to that one who is perfected in virtues such as morality and is established in the paths and their fruits.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has been generated through this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be everywhere free from obstacles.
Whatever karma was performed by those who became ghosts in previous births,
each of which brought about their state as ghosts— since their fruits differ—
the teachings of the Buddhas, especially their specific instructions, clearly reveal this.
Producing a sense of spiritual urgency and making the fruits of karma directly manifest,
this work titled *Petavatthu*, whose subject matter is thoroughly understood,
was compiled among the *Khuddakanikāya* by the great seers.
Having correctly grasped the method of the ancient commentaries,
and specifically elucidating the introductory narratives (nidāna) here and there,
[I shall provide] a very pure, unconfused, and subtle determination of the meaning.
"I shall provide a beautiful commentary on the meaning according to my ability, following the tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins without deviation.
Listen attentively, O virtuous ones, as I speak it."
In this context, "stories of the departed" (*petavatthu*) refers to the karma that serves as the cause for the state of being a departed spirit (*petabhāva*) for various beings,
such as the merchant’s son; however, it is the Dhamma of the scriptures— such as the passage beginning "The Arahants are like a field"— which proceeds by way of illustrating that [karma],
that is intended here by the term "stories of the departed."
By whom was this *Petavatthu* spoken, where was it spoken, when was it spoken, and for what reason was it spoken? It is said:
This *Petavatthu* occurs in two ways—by way of an occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and by way of questions and answers (*pucchāvissajjana*).
Of these, that which occurs by way of an occasion was spoken by the Blessed One; the other was spoken by the Elder Nārada and others.
These were spoken by various hungry ghosts when questioned by them.

However, because the Teacher—having made each respective occasion for instruction (*aṭṭhuppatti*) upon the reports given by the Elder Nārada and others during those various question-and-answer sessions—taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude, all of these *Petavatthu* passages came to be known as "spoken by the Teacher" himself. This occurred after the Wheel of the Sublime Dhamma had been set in motion.

For indeed, while the Teacher was dwelling here and there in places such as Rājagaha, for the most part through various introductory occasions (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and by way of questions and answers, those various *petavatthu* stories were brought into the teaching in order to make beings directly perceive the results of their own karma.
This, then, is the general answer to the phrases beginning with "By whom was it spoken? Now, as for the specific [answers]:
However, the explanation of the meaning of each respective subject matter will follow later.
Furthermore, this *Petavatthu* is included within the Sutta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas— the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—
specifically within the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, and the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

The *Khuddakanikāya* refers to that which is included within the *Khuddakanikāya* among the five *nikāyas*, and among the nine factors of the teaching (*sāsanaṅga*), it is the collection of verses consisting of *sutta*,
*geyya*, *veyyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, *jātaka*, *abbhutadhamma*, and *vedalla*.
“I received eighty-two [verses] from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks.”
“There are eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma that have been proclaimed by me.
Thus, when the Custodian of the Dhamma had thus declared the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma, [the following] was a compilation of a few of those sections:

in terms of recitation portions (*bhāṇavāra*), it consists of about four recitation portions; in terms of chapters (*vagga*), they are the Uraga-vagga, the Ubbari-vagga, the Cūḷa-vagga, and the Mahā-vagga.

It comprises four chapters (*vagga*). Among them, there are twelve topics (*vatthu*) in the first chapter, thirteen topics in the second chapter, ten topics in the third chapter, and sixteen topics in the fourth chapter;
thus, it is adorned with fifty-one topics in total. Within its chapters, the *Uragavagga* (The Chapter on Snakes) is the first;
among the topics, the *Khettūpama-peta-vatthu* (The Topic of the Ghost Simile of the Field) is the first; and of that too, the "Simile of the Field" (*Khettūpamā*)...
The verse beginning with “The Arahants” is the first.
1. The Chapter on Snakes (Uragavagga). 1. Explanation of the Story of the Simile of the Field (Khettūpama-petavatthu-vaṇṇanā).
The Blessed One, while dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, spoke this account concerning a certain deceased son of a merchant.

It is said that in Rājagaha there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with abundant assets and provisions, and a store of many tens of millions of coins. Because of his possession of such great wealth—
Thus he became known by the name “Mahādhanaseṭṭhi. He had an only son, who was dear and beloved.

When the boy reached the age of discretion, his parents thought: “Even if we were to provide our son with a daily allowance of a thousand pieces of money every day, this accumulation of wealth would not be exhausted even in a hundred years.”
"What is the use of this exhaustion from learning a craft? Let him enjoy his wealth as he pleases, with body and mind unwearied," they said, and so they did not have him train in a craft.

When he reached maturity, they brought home for him a maiden endowed with noble lineage, beauty, youth, and charm—one who was intent on sensual pleasures and averse to the perception of the Dhamma. While he was taking delight with her, even the slightest thought of the Dhamma [did not arise].
Having failed to produce [merit], being disrespectful toward ascetics, brahmins, and elders, surrounded by a crowd of profligates, he spent his time intoxicated,
delighting in and greedy for the five strands of sensual pleasure; blinded by delusion, after his parents had passed away,
he squandered his wealth by giving whatever they desired to actors, dancers, singers, and the like, and before long he fell into destitution.
Having offered [the property] and lived by taking up a debt, he was unable to repay that debt as well;

being pressed by his creditors, he gave them his own fields, lands, house, and so forth. Then, wandering for alms with an alms-bowl in hand and eating what he received, he lived in a hall for the destitute in that very city.
Then one day, some thieves gathered together and said to him: "O man, what is the use of this wretched life for you?
You are young and endowed with strength, speed, and power; why do you sit here like one whose hands and feet have been cut off?
Come, take the property of others by theft along with us and make a living in comfort. He replied, "I will not commit theft..."
“I know how to do it,” he said. The thieves replied, “We shall teach you; you simply must follow our instructions.
He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and went along with them.
Then those thieves, having given him a large club in his hand and having broken through the wall, placed him at the entrance of the breach as they entered the house.
They said, "If anyone else comes here, strike him with this club and kill him in a single blow.
That foolish man, not knowing what was beneficial or harmful, stood there watching for the arrival of others.
Meanwhile, the thieves, having entered the house and seized the goods that were ready to be taken, were recognized by the householders as soon as they had done so.

They fled hither and thither. The householders, having risen up, ran very swiftly, looking here and there, and seeing that man standing at the junction of the doorways, cried out, "Seize the wicked thieves!
They seized him, beat his hands and feet with clubs and other weapons, and presented him to the king, saying, "Sire, this thief has been caught while breaking into a house. The king—
“Have his head cut off! he commanded the city guard.

“Very well, Your Majesty,” the city guard replied, and having seized him, had his arms bound tightly behind his back, placed a garland of red flowers around his neck, and smeared his head with brick-dust.
Then, with the drum of execution being beaten to announce the path, he led him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads.
Having paraded him through the crossroads and beating him with whips, they led him toward the place of execution.
A great clamor arose: "This plundering thief has been caught in this city!
At that time, in that city, a beautiful woman named Sulasā was standing on her palace, looking out through the window.
Seeing him being led away in that manner, she— who had previously been acquainted with him— thought, "This man,
having enjoyed great prosperity in this very city, has now fallen into such misfortune and ruin.
Feeling compassion for him, she sent four sweetmeats and some water, and she also informed the city watchman.
—"May the noble one wait until this man has eaten these sweetmeats and drunk water.
Then, in that interval, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, surveying with his divine eye, saw the man's impending calamity;
his heart stirred with compassion, he thought: "This man has not performed merit but has committed evil; therefore, he will [fall] into hell."
"He will be reborn there; however, when I have gone, he will give sweetmeats and drinking water and arise among the earth-deities.
What if I were to become his support? Having thought this, as the drinking water and sweetmeats were being brought forward, he appeared before that man.
Seeing the Elder, with a mind full of serene faith, he said: "What is it to me now with these..."

Thinking, "While he is being executed, let him eat these sweetmeats; this shall serve as his provisions for the journey to the next world," he had the Elder provided with sweetmeats and drinking water.
For the sake of increasing the man's faith, the Elder sat down in such a place while the man was looking on, ate the sweetmeats, and drank the water.

Having risen from his seat, he departed. As for that man, although he had been led by the executioners to the place of execution and was about to have his head cut off, he was destined to be reborn in a sublime heavenly world due to the merit he had performed for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna—that unsurpassed field of merit.
Nevertheless, at the time of death, because of the affection felt for Sulasā, thinking, "It was through Sulasā that I obtained this object of charity," [he spoke].
His mind was defiled; therefore, being reborn in a lowly state, he was born as a tree deity in a great banyan tree that possessed dense shade and grew within a mountain thicket.
It is said that had he exerted himself in establishing his family lineage during his first stage of life, he would have become a merchant chief in that very city.
In his first stage of life he would have been foremost, in his middle stage middlemost, and in his final stage last.
Had he gone forth in his first stage of life, he would have become an Arhat; in his middle stage, a Once-returner or a Non-returner;
and in his final stage, a Stream-enterer. However, through association with evil friends, he was a libertine after women and a libertine after liquor.
They say that, being devoted to misconduct and becoming disrespectful, he gradually fell away from all his prosperity and met with great calamity.
Then, on another occasion, seeing Sulasā gone to the pleasure garden, lust for her arose within him;
creating darkness, he led her to his own abode and lived in union with her for seven days, and he revealed himself to her.
Not seeing her, her mother wandered here and there weeping.
Seeing this, the great crowd said, "The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is of great psychic power and great majesty; he might know her whereabouts. You should approach him and ask.
She replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and approached the Elder, asking about the matter. The Elder said, "Seven days from now..."
“Today, at the Veḷuvana Mahāvihāra, you will see me at the edge of the assembly while the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma,” he said.
Then Sulasā spoke to that deva-son: “It is improper for me to remain in your abode;
today is the seventh day, and my mother, not seeing me, will have fallen into lamentation and grief. It would be well if you—”
“Your Majesty, lead her right there. He led her to the Bamboo Grove and, having placed her at the edge of the assembly while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, he stood there invisible.
Then the great multitude, seeing Sulasā, said: “Mother Sulasā, where have you been for all these days?”
“Your mother, not seeing you, has fallen into lamentation and grief; she has become as if she has reached the state of madness.
She related this occurrence to the great multitude. When the great multitude asked, “How can that man, addicted to such evil and having performed no wholesome deeds, obtain rebirth among the gods?
Sulasā replied, “In the sweetmeats and drinking water provided by me for the noble Elder Mahāmoggallāna...”
“By that merit, one obtains rebirth among the devas,” he said. Upon hearing this, the great multitude was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement:
“The Arahants are indeed the unsurpassed field of merit for the world, for even a small service rendered to them brings beings to rebirth among the devas.
Thus they experienced sublime joy and gladness. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
They reported this. Then, on account of this incident, the Blessed One said:
“The Arahants are like a field; the donors are like farmers;
The gift to be given is like the seed; from this, the fruit is produced.”
“This is the seed, this is the plowing, and this is the field for both the departed and the donor.
The departed partake of it, while the donor prospers through merit.
Having performed wholesome deeds right here and having honored the departed,”
"Having performed auspicious karma, one goes to heaven, the place of rest"—thus he spoke these verses. 1.
Regarding that, "like a field" (*khettūpamā*): a field (*khetta*) is so called because it protects (*tāyati*) the sown seed by causing it to yield great fruit;
it is the place where rice seeds and the like grow. Those [deeds] for which this is the simile are "like a field," meaning they are similar to a plowed field.

The meaning [of the term] is as follows: "Arahants" refers to those whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. They are called "Arahants" because they have destroyed the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*) and the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra;
because they are remote (*āraka*) from those very things; because they are worthy (*araha*) of requisites and so forth; and because they lack the opportunity (*raha*) to commit evil deeds.
In this regard, just as rice, free from defects such as chaff and weeds, when sown with its own prepared seed and endowed with other conditions such as soil and water...

Just as the harvest of a farmer is of great fruit, so too, when the seed of the gift to be given—which has been prepared by one whose mental continuum is free from the taints (āsava) and devoid of faults such as greed—is sown, it becomes of great fruit for the donor provided there are other conditions such as the proper time.

Therefore the Blessed One said: "The Arahants are like a field. This is a description of the highest type, since even those who are still in training (sekha) and others are excluded from being considered a "field" in this specific sense.
“Givers” (*dāyaka*) means those who give the requisites such as robes and so forth, those who relinquish them;

by that relinquishment, they are those who relinquish greed and other defilements within their own mental continuum, or those who cut them off, or rather, those who cleanse and protect their own continuum—this is the meaning.
“Like farmers” (*kassakūpamā*) means similar to farmers. Just as a farmer, having plowed rice fields and the like, [at the] appropriate time...

Just as one who is diligent in watering, weeding, removing water, and protecting the stored crops obtains an abundant and extensive harvest of grain and fruit, so too the donor, being diligent in the relinquishing of goods to be given and in service toward the Arahants, obtains an abundant and extensive fruit of giving. Therefore it is said: "Donors are like farmers."
The phrase "the gift is like a seed" is stated with a change of grammatical gender; the meaning is that the object to be given is similar to a seed.
This is the name for the ten kinds of things to be given, such as food, drink, and so forth.
"From this the fruit is produced" means that from this—namely, the donor, the recipient, and the relinquishing of the object to be given—the fruit of giving is both produced and arises.

And the meaning is that it proceeds by way of a very long continuity. And here, because the existence of the object—such as food and drink—is conditioned by the volition of relinquishment (*pariccāga-cetanā*), and not that of anything else, the term "thing to be given" (*deyyadhamma*) is employed in the phrase "the thing to be given is like a seed.
By means of this designation of the "thing to be given," the status of being a seed belongs specifically to the volition of relinquishment directed toward the object that is the thing to be given.

It should be understood as such; for it is that which produces the fruit—distinguished by its types such as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and so forth, and by its types such as the support (nissaya) and the object (ārammaṇa)—but it is not itself the thing to be given. 2.
"This is the seed, this is the field and the cultivation": the seed as previously described, and the field as previously described, of that seed...
"In that field" means cultivation, which consists of the practice of sowing. To the question "For whom is this triad desired?", he says:
"For the departed and for the donor. If the donor gives a gift dedicated to the departed, it is [the seed, the cultivation, and the field] for both the departed and the donor;
if he does not give the gift dedicated to the departed, it is the seed, the cultivation, and the field for the donor alone.
The intended meaning is that it serves as a benefit. Now, in order to demonstrate that benefit, it is said: "The departed ones enjoy it, and the donor prospers through merit.

In this context, "the departed ones enjoy it" means that when a gift is given by a donor specifically for the sake of the departed, whatever is beneficial to them arises through the excellence of the field, the seed, and the harvest, as well as through the act of rejoicing (anumodanā).

The hungry ghosts (petas) enjoy that fruit of giving. "The giver prospers through merit" means that the giver, by reason of his own merit consisting of giving, prospers among gods and humans through the fruit of merit such as the excellence of wealth and so forth.
For even the fruit of merit is called "merit" in such passages as: "Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states that this merit thus increases."

3. "Having performed wholesome deeds right here" means that by accumulating merit consisting of giving dedicated to the departed (*petas*)—in the sense of producing blameless and pleasant results—one does so "right here," in this very current existence.

And "having honored the departed" means having gratified the departed with gifts dedicated to them, thereby liberating them from the suffering they are currently experiencing. For when a gift is given dedicated to the departed...
Giving to them is indeed called "worship. Therefore, he said: "Worship has been performed for us," and "Noble worship has been performed for the departed.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the departed" (*pete ca*), [he refers to] such benefits pertaining to the present life as: "He becomes dear and pleasing; he becomes approachable and trustworthy;
he becomes one to be cultivated and honored; he becomes praiseworthy and fit to be extolled by the wise."
One embraces the benefits of giving. And one goes to the heavenly state, having performed auspicious karma— having performed wholesome,

skillful karma— one goes to, that is, approaches by way of rebirth, the world of the devas, the place of birth for those who have made merit, which is named "heaven" because it is preeminent in ten respects such as celestial lifespan.

And here, after saying "having performed what is wholesome," the subsequent statement "having performed a meritorious deed" should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that the relinquishment of the dharma of giving—by way of the transfer of merit (*pattidāna*)—is indeed a wholesome deed consisting of giving, just like the relinquishment of the object to be given.
Some, however, say here that "the departed ones" (*petā*) refers to the Arahants; that is merely their own opinion.
“Peta” [is used here] because there is no place for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsavā) to go to;
because the state of being a seed and so forth is as inappropriate for them as it is for the donor; and because it is appropriate for those belonging to the peta realm.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings, beginning with the young deva Sūlaseyyaka, attained realization of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the *Khetūpama-peta-vatthu* is finished.
2. The commentary on the *Sūkaramukha-peta-vatthu*:
“Your body is entirely of gold”—this was [spoken] by the Teacher while staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
This was spoken while dwelling [in the Saṅghārāma] concerning a certain *sūkaramukha* (pig-faced) *peta*.
It is said that in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was a certain monk who was restrained in body but unrestrained in speech; he reviled and abused the other monks.
Having passed away, he was reborn in hell, and after being cooked there for the duration of one *buddhantara*, having passed away from there, in this [present time]...

During the time of a Buddha's appearance, near Rājagaha at the foot of Mount Gijjhakūṭa, due to the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he was reborn as a hungry ghost (peta) overcome by hunger and thirst. His body was golden-colored, but his face resembled the face of a pig.
Then, while dwelling on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, the Venerable Nārada, having performed his bodily care early in the morning, took up his bowl and robe.
While going for alms toward Rājagaha, seeing that peta on the way, he asked about the deed performed by him:
"Your body is entirely of gold and all the quarters shine with its light;
yet your face is like that of a pig—what deed did you do in the past?"
He spoke this verse. Regarding it: "Your body is entirely of gold" means that your body, your physical frame, is entirely the color of gold, resembling refined, molten gold.
"All directions shine" means that by its radiance, all directions all around shine and gleam. Alternatively, this phrase "obhāsate" (it shines) contains within it the sense of the verb;
thus [the full meaning is]: "Your body is entirely of gold; it shines and gleams in all directions."
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Your face is like that of a pig" means that your face is indeed like a pig's; the sense is that your face resembles the face of a pig.
"What deed did you do in the past?"—this asks, "What kind of karma did you perform previously in a former birth?
Thus, being questioned by the Elder regarding the deed he had committed, the peta replied with a verse:
“I was restrained in body, but I was unrestrained in speech;
therefore, my complexion is such as you see me, O Nārada,” he said.
Therein, “I was restrained in body” means I was restrained by bodily restraint, by the control pertaining to the door of the body.
"I was restrained. "I was unrestrained in speech" means I was unrestrained in speech, possessed of lack of restraint regarding verbal conduct.
"By that" means by both that restraint and that lack of restraint. "Mine" means my own. "Such a form" means of such a kind;
just as you, Nārada, see it directly, it was of such a nature: human in shape with a body of golden hue.
The construction is: "He has a face like that of a pig. For here, the word *vaṇṇa* should be understood as referring both to the skin and to the shape.
Thus, having been questioned by the Elder, the peta explained the matter and, making that very reason his basis, gave the Elder this advice:
"I tell you this, Nārada: this was seen by you with your own eyes."
"Do not commit evil with your mouth; do not become like a pig-faced one"—thus he spoke this verse.
In it, "tasmā" (therefore) means for that reason. "Tyāham" (I to you) means I to them. "Nārada" is how he addresses the Elder.
"Brūmi" means I speak. "Sāmaṃ" means by oneself. "Idaṃ" refers to his own body. This is the meaning here.

“Venerable Nārada, since you have seen with your own eyes that this body of mine is human in form from the neck downwards, but above that it is the shape of a pig, therefore I speak to you by way of advice. And what is that?
He said: “Do not commit evil with your mouth; do not become a pig-faced one. In this context, *mā* is used in the sense of prohibition.
*Nipāto* (is a particle). *Mukhasā* means by the mouth. *Kho* is used for emphasis: "Do not commit an evil deed with your speech;
do not do it. "Mā kho sūkaramukho ahū" means: "May you certainly not become pig-faced like me.
However, if you were to become talkative and commit evil through your speech, you would inevitably become pig-faced; therefore, do not do so by way of the mouth.
By way of negating the fruit, he also negates the cause itself.

Then the Venerable Nārada, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround after the meal, reported that matter to the Teacher as he was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
The Teacher said, "Nārada, that teacher was already seen by me long ago."
Having spoken thus, he taught the Dhamma, revealing the danger associated with various forms of verbal misconduct and the benefits connected with verbal good conduct.
That teaching was fruitful for the assembled assembly.
The commentary on the *Sūkaramukha-peta-vatthu* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Story of the Foul-Mouthed Ghost (*Pūtimukhapetavatthu*).
"He bore a divine, beautiful, radiant complexion"—this was spoken concerning a certain foul-mouthed ghost while the Teacher was dwelling at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground in Veḷuvana.
It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, two...
Having gone forth in his teaching, certain sons of good family—endowed with virtue and conduct, living a life of austerity—dwelt in harmonious community at a certain village monastery.
Then, a certain monk of evil disposition, who delighted in slander, approached their dwelling place.
The elders exchanged greetings with him, gave him a place to stay, and on the following day...

Taking him with them, they entered the village for alms. When the people saw them, they showed those elders the highest possible reverence and honored them with rice porridge, food, and other offerings.
Having entered the monastery, he thought: "Truly beautiful is this village for alms;
the people are faithful and confident, and they give most excellent alms-food. And as for this monastery..."
"It is well-provided with shade and water; I can live here in comfort. But if these bhikkhus dwell here, there will be no peaceful dwelling for me;
it will be like living under the tutelage of a pupil. Come now, I shall cause them to break with one another so that they will not dwell here again."
Then one day, after the Great Elder had given exhortation to both [of them] and entered his own dwelling place,
a slanderous monk waited for some time, approached the Great Elder, and having paid homage, was asked by the Elder,
“Why have you come at an improper time, friend? He replied, “Yes, venerable sir, there is something that must be said,” and added, “Speak.”

Permitted by the elder with the words, “Friend,” he said: “Venerable sir, this elder who was your companion shows himself as a friend when face-to-face, but when behind your back, he reviles you like an enemy. When asked, “What is he saying? he replied:
“Listen, venerable sir: ‘This great elder is deceitful, fraudulent, crafty, and maintains his livelihood through wrong means.’”
“He is speaking of your faults,” he said. “Friend, do not speak thus; that bhikkhu will not disparage me in such a way.
From the time we were householders, he has known my true nature: ‘He is amiable and of virtuous character.
“Venerable sir, if you think this because of the purity of your own mind, that is indeed worthy of you; but for me—”
"But there is no enmity with him; why then do I say that he has said what was not said? Let it be;

in due course you will know for yourselves," he said. The Elder, his mind wavering due to the fault of being an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), became apprehensive, thinking, "It might be so," and his confidence became somewhat slackened. That fool first...
Having caused a schism with the Mahāthera, he likewise caused a schism with the other elder in the same manner.

Then, on the following day, those two elders, without speaking to one another, took their bowls and robes, went into the village for alms, and having received the alms-food, ate it right there at their respective dwellings; yet that day they did not perform even the slightest act of mutual courtesy.
When night had dawned, they departed for whatever place was convenient without having informed one another.
However, when people saw the slanderer monk entering the village for alms with his desires fulfilled, they asked, "Venerable sir, where have the elders gone?
He replied, "After quarreling with one another all night long..."
"Even though I said to them, 'Do not quarrel; be in harmony. Quarrel indeed brings about harm, produces suffering in the future, and leads to unwholesome states;
even those of old fell away from great welfare because of quarreling,' they departed without heeding my words.
Then the people said, "Let the elders go for now, but you..."
“Out of compassion for us, please dwell right here without longing for elsewhere,” they entreated him.

He consented, saying, “Very well,” and while dwelling right there, after a few days he thought: “Because of greed for a residence, I have caused monks who were virtuous and of noble character to fall into division;
alas, I have committed much evil karma! Overwhelmed by powerful remorse, he was seized by a surge of grief.
Having fallen ill, he passed away before long and was reborn in the Avīci hell.
The other two companion elders, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, met at a certain monastery;
after exchanging greetings with one another, they informed each other of the divisive words spoken by that monk and [realized] their false nature.
Having learned this, they became reconciled and gradually returned to that very same monastery.
When the people saw the two elders, they were joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness; they attended upon them with the four requisites.
The elders, dwelling right there, their minds composed through obtaining suitable food, increased their insight and before long attained Arahatship.

The monk Pesuṇika, having been boiled in hell for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha as a "putrid-mouthed" hungry ghost (pūtimukhapeta) not far from Rājagaha.
His body was golden-colored, but from his mouth worms emerged and devoured him here and there; even at a great distance, a foul stench pervaded the space.
He was blowing [on it]. Then the Venerable Nārada, descending from Mount Gijjhakūṭa, saw him and said:
“You bear a divine, beautiful complexion; you stand in the sky, suspended in mid-air.
Yet worms are devouring your mouth, which reeks with a foul stench. What deed did you do in the past?”
With this verse, he asked about the deed performed. Therein, "divine" (*dibba*) means that which is found in the heavens (*divi*), comprised within the state of being a deity.
However, here it is "divine" because it is like the divine. "Beautiful" (*subha*) means splendid or the state of being lovely.
"Complexion-element" (*vaṇṇadhātu*) means the color of the skin. "You bear" (*dhāresi*) means you carry. "In the air" (*vehāyasaṃ*) means in the sky, known as the atmosphere.
"You stand. However, some, reading the text as "vihāyasaṃ tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe," explain the meaning by supplying the words:
"You stand in the sky, illuminating the atmosphere. "Pūtigandhaṃ" means the stench of a corpse;
the sense is "foul-smelling. "What deed did you do in the past? [is asked because] worms are devouring your mouth, which is extremely foul-smelling, and your body...
"Golden-hued one, what kind of karma was it that served as the cause for such a physical form? What did you do in the past?
Thus questioned by the Elder regarding the deed he himself had committed, the peta answered this matter:
"I was a monk of evil and wicked speech, appearing like an ascetic yet unrestrained in my mouth."
"And having obtained that element of beauty through my darkness, my mouth has been made foul by slander"—thus he spoke this verse.
In that regard, "I was a wretched ascetic" means: I was a base ascetic, a wicked bhikkhu.
"One of exceedingly foul speech" means: one whose speech is extremely foul; one who speaks by overstepping and leaping over others; one whose words destroy the virtues of others.
The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, the reading is “*atidukkhavāco*,” meaning one who speaks excessively harsh words, being devoted to verbal misconduct such as lying and slander.
“*Tapassirūpo*” means one who merely has the appearance of an ascetic (*samaṇa*). “*Mukhasā*” means by means of the mouth. “*Laddhā*” means obtained.

The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction. “*Me*” means by me. “*Tapasā*” means by the holy life (*brahmacariya*). “*Pesuṇiyena*” means by way of slanderous speech. “*Putī*” means having a putrid odor.
Thus, having explained the deed he himself had committed, that peta now gave this exhortation to the Elder:
“O Nārada, you have seen for yourself this very thing;
those who are compassionate and skilled would speak thus.”
"Do not speak slander, nor do speak falsehood;
you shall become a *yakkha* who indulges in his desires"—this is the concluding verse he spoke.
Therein, "this here" (*tad idam*) refers to this form of mine. "Those who are compassionate and skilled would say" means...

The intention is this: "Whatever those who are compassionate by nature, merciful, skilled and adept in acting for the welfare of others—such as the Buddhas and the rest—should say, that very thing I say.
Now, in order to show that advice, he said: "Do not speak slander, nor do speak falsehood;
otherwise you will become a *yakkha* who craves his own desires. The meaning of this is: do not speak slander (*pesuṇa*), which is malicious speech, nor falsehood (*musā*).
He said: "Do not speak thus. For if you were to abandon false speech and malicious speech and become restrained in speech, you would become either a *yakkha*, a god, or some other deity.
Having obtained whatever sublime divine success you desire, you would be one who enjoys it there, delighting at will by indulging the sense-faculties."
Having heard this, the Elder went from there to Rājagaha; after walking for alms and returning from his meal, he reported that matter to the Teacher.
The Teacher made that the occasion for a teaching and preached the Dhamma.
That teaching was fruitful for the assembled assembly.
The commentary on the *Pūtimukha-peta-vatthu* is finished.
4. The commentary on the *Piṭṭhadhītalika-peta-vatthu*:
"Whatever object one makes [the basis for meditation]"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana in Sāvatthī concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.

He spoke concerning the gift of the householder. It is said that the nurse of the granddaughter of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika gave her a clay doll, saying, "This is your daughter; take this and play with her.
She conceived the perception of it as a daughter. Then one day, while she was playing with it, through negligence it fell—
It broke. Then the girl wept, crying, "My daughter is dead! None of the household members were able to console her as she wept.
At that time, the Teacher was seated on a prepared seat in the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, and the great merchant was seated near the Blessed One. A nurse took the girl...
She went into the presence of the merchant. When the merchant saw her, he asked, "Why is this girl weeping?
The nurse reported the matter to the merchant. The merchant, having seated the girl on his lap and reassured her by saying, "I shall provide for your daughter's marriage," informed the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, my granddaughter, Piṭṭhadhītalikā..."
“Desiring to give a gift intended for you, may you together with five hundred bhikkhus accept my invitation for tomorrow.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then, on the following day, the Blessed One went to the merchant’s house together with five hundred bhikkhus; having finished his meal, he gave a blessing of thanksgiving:
“Whatever object one makes the basis for giving, if one gives without stinginess—
whether directed toward the departed ancestors or toward the deities of the site;
or toward the four Great Kings, the illustrious guardians of the world;”
Kuvera, Dhatarattha, Virūpakkha, and Virūḷhaka—
these are indeed honored, and the donors are not without fruit.
For neither weeping nor sorrow, nor any other lamentation, [averts death].
“This does not benefit the deceased; thus do kinsmen stand [in grief].
But this offering given, well-established in the Saṅgha, will be of immediate benefit and for his long-term welfare.”—he spoke these verses.

10. In this context, "having made anything whatsoever the object" means having taken as a basis or directed toward any one among the auspicious signs (*maṅgala*) and so forth. "One should give" (*dajjā*) means one should bestow.

"Non-avaricious" (*amaccharī*) means one who is non-avaricious due to the absence of avarice (*macchariya*), which is characterized by the inability to endure sharing one's own prosperity with others;
such a person is disposed toward relinquishment and has cast far away the mental stains of avarice, greed, and the like.
The intention is: "Having made [the offering], one should give. "And for the departed ancestors" means: having in mind even those who have passed away in the past.
"For the deities of the site" is to be construed as: having in mind the deities residing in the house-site and so forth.
Alternatively, by the word "or," he shows that one may give a gift having in mind anyone else whatsoever, such as gods, humans, and so on.
11. Therein, first among the devas, having pointed out certain manifest devas by saying "the four Great Kings," he then mentions them by name, beginning with "Kuvera.

Therein, "Kuvera" refers to Vessavaṇa. "Dhataraṭṭha" and so forth are the names of the remaining three World-Protectors. And they are honored; that is, those Great Kings are the deities of the ancestral spirits (pubbapeta).
And they become the recipients for the act of dedication. Furthermore, donors do not go without fruit:
those who give gifts do not go without fruit merely by the act of dedicating them to others; rather, they indeed partake in the fruit of their own giving. 12.
Now, as for those who weep, lament, grieve, and mourn at the death of their own kinsmen, that [mourning] is useless for them.
In order to show that it is "merely self-mortification," he spoke the verse beginning with "for weeping...
(*na hi ruṇṇaṃ*). Therein, "weeping" (*ruṇṇaṃ*) means crying or shedding tears; the ellipsis of the sentence is "should not be done.

"Sorrow" (*soko*) means grieving or mental anguish; the meaning is "internal brooding. And "whatever other lamentation" (*yā caññā paridevanā*) refers to that lamentation other than weeping and sorrow—the verbal outburst such as "Where is my only son? and so forth.
The meaning is that even that [crying] should not be done. In all instances, the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative.

"That is not for the sake of the peta" means that since neither crying, nor sorrow, nor lamentation—indeed, all of these—are of no benefit or assistance to the peta who has passed away, therefore they should not be performed;
nevertheless, the relatives remain thus, being ignorant—this is the intended meaning.

13. Having thus shown the pointlessness of weeping and so forth, he now speaks the verse beginning with “And this offering,” demonstrating the meaningfulness of the alms-offering (dakkhiṇā) given to the Saṅgha by a donor on behalf of deceased relatives and others.
Therein, the word “this” (ayaṃ) refers to that gift given by the donor, speaking of it as something directly perceived. The particle “and” (ca) has the sense of contrast (byatireka).
Just as weeping and so forth for the deceased serves no purpose for anyone, this is not so;
rather, it illuminates the very distinction that is about to be stated: "But this offering (dakkhiṇā) leads to his welfare for a long time. The word *kho* is used for emphasis.
*Dakkhiṇā* means a gift. *Suppaṭṭhitā saṅghamhi* means well-established in the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
“For his long-term welfare” means for the benefit and advantage of that peta over a long period of time.
“It is effective immediately” means it comes to fruition at that very moment and not at some other time. For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) therein:
when a gift is given in dedication to petas, if the petas rejoice in it, they are liberated by its fruit at that very instant.
Having thus taught the Dhamma and caused the great multitude to set their minds on giving for the sake of the departed spirits, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed.
On the following day, the merchant’s wife and the remaining kinsmen, following the merchant’s example, continued to offer this great almsgiving for about three months.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One and asked, “Why...?”
“Venerable sir, why have the bhikkhus not come to my house for a month? he asked.
When the Teacher explained the reason for this, the king, following the lead of the treasurer, offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Seeing that, the citizens followed the king’s example and offered a great almsgiving for a month. Thus, for two months—
“They set forth a great almsgiving with flour and *dhītalika* radishes.
The commentary on the *Piṭṭhadhītalika-peta-vatthu* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Tirokuṭṭa-peta-vatthu*.
“They stand at the door-posts” refers to what the Teacher spoke concerning many *peta*s while dwelling in Rājagaha.
Herein is the detailed account: Ninety-two aeons ago, there was a city named Kāsī.
There, a king named Jayasena reigned. His queen was named Sirimā. Into her womb was conceived the Bodhisatta named Phussa.

Having been reborn, he gradually attained supreme perfect enlightenment. King Jayasena, having conceived the sense of ownership, thinking, "My son has gone forth on the Great Renunciation and become a Buddha;
the Buddha is mine alone, the Dhamma is mine, and the Saṅgha is mine," attended upon him personally at all times and gave no opportunity to others.
The three uterine half-brothers of the Blessed One thought to themselves:
“Buddhas indeed arise for the welfare of the entire world, not for the sake of a single person alone. Yet our father gives no opportunity to others.
How might we obtain the chance to attend upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus? To them—
It occurred to him: "Come now, let us employ some stratagem. They caused the border region to be made as if it were in rebellion.
Then the king, hearing that "the border is in revolt," sent his three sons to pacify the border.
Having gone and pacified it, they returned. The king, being pleased, granted them a boon, saying: "Take whatever you desire."
They said, "We wish to attend upon the Blessed One. The king said, "Set this one aside and take another.
They replied, "We have no need for anyone else. He said, "In that case, take him after making a fixed term.
They requested seven years; the king did not grant it. Likewise they requested six, five, four, three, two, and one year.
Having said, "Seven months, six, five, four," they requested it down to three months. Then the king, saying, "Take them," gave his consent.
They approached the Blessed One and said, "Venerable sir, we wish to attend upon the Blessed One for three months;
may the Blessed One, venerable sir, accept our invitation for this three-month rains retreat. He consented.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Those three sent a letter to an official in their own country, saying:
"During these three months, the Blessed One must be attended upon by us; starting with the monastery, prepare all the requisites for the Blessed One’s attendance.
Having prepared everything, he sent it back. They, dressed in saffron-colored robes, together with a thousand men...
While serving the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with great care, they led them to the countryside, presented them with a monastery, and had them spend the rains retreat there.
Among them was a treasurer’s son, a householder, who together with his wife was faithful and possessed of serene confidence. He [served] the community headed by the Buddha...
He respectfully gave the duty of almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
A man appointed to the countryside took that [gift] and, together with eleven thousand men from the countryside, caused the gift to be distributed with due respect.
Therein, some of those from the countryside had hostile minds; they created an obstacle to the gift and [seized] the articles to be given.
They ate [the food] themselves and set fire to the dining hall.
Having been invited, the princes paid homage to the Blessed One and, placing him at their head, returned to their father’s presence. Upon arriving there, the Blessed One attained final nibbāna.
The princes, the official appointed over the countryside, and the treasurer then proceeded by stages.
Having passed away, those with favorable minds were reborn together with their retinue in heaven, while those with obstructed minds were reborn in hell.
Thus, as these two groups of people were passing from heaven to heaven and from hell to hell, ninety-two eons elapsed.
Then, in this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, those people with obstructed minds were reborn among the hungry ghosts (petas).
Then, when people gave gifts for the sake of their deceased relatives and dedicated them, saying, "May this be for our relatives," those relatives obtained prosperity.
When these other spirits saw this, they approached the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa, and asked: "Venerable sir, might we too obtain such prosperity?"
The Blessed One said: “You shall not receive it now; however, in the future there will be a Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama.
At the time of that Blessed One, there will be a king named Bimbisāra, who was your kinsman ninety-two aeons ago.
He will give a gift to the Buddha and dedicate it for your sake; at that time you shall receive it. Thus [he spoke].
When those words were spoken to the hungry ghosts, it was as if they had been told, "You shall receive them tomorrow.
Then, after the interval of one Buddha-period had passed, our Blessed One appeared in the world.
Those three princes, together with a thousand men, descended from the heavenly realm and were reborn in brahmin families in the kingdom of Magadha; eventually, they went forth as ascetics.
Having gone forth at Gayāsīsa, three became matted-hair ascetics; in the countryside, Niyuttakapuruṣa became King Bimbisāra;
the treasurer’s son named Visākha became a merchant, and his wife was the merchant’s daughter named Dhammadinnā;
as for the rest of the assembly, they were reborn as the king’s own retinue.
After the Blessed One had arisen in our world as well, having passed seven weeks, he gradually arrived at Bārāṇasī and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

Beginning with the group of five monks, and after training the three matted-hair ascetics together with their thousand followers, he went to Rājagaha. And there, on that very day, to King Bimbisāra who was approaching him—
He established eleven myriads of brahmins and householders dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha in the fruit of stream-entry. Then,
having accepted an invitation for a meal on the following day from the king, on that second day,
with Sakka, lord of the devas, going before him in the guise of a young brahmin—
“The Tamed One, together with the tamed, the ancient matted-hair ascetics;
the Liberated One, together with the liberated—the Blessed One, with the color of refined gold, entered Rājagaha.
While being thus extolled with these and other verses, he entered Rājagaha and accepted a great almsgiving at the king’s residence.
Those hungry ghosts stood surrounding him with the hope, "Now the king will dedicate the gift to us; now he will dedicate it.
But after giving the gift, the king thought only of a place for the Blessed One to dwell, wondering, "Where might the Blessed One stay?
He did not dedicate that gift to anyone. Failing to receive that gift, the hungry ghosts were left with their hopes shattered, and during the night...
In the king’s residence, they raised an exceedingly terrifying outcry. The king, overcome by fear, terror, and agitation, said as the night was turning to dawn:
"I heard such a sound; what, venerable sir, will come to pass for me?
The Blessed One replied: "Do not fear, great king; nothing evil shall befall you. However—"
“Indeed, there are those former kinsmen of yours who have been reborn among the *petas*.
Having waited for you for an entire interval between Buddhas, thinking, ‘When he has given a gift to the Buddha, he will dedicate it to us,’ they were wandering about;
but because you did not dedicate the gift given by you yesterday, they became disappointed and raised such a great outcry,” he said. “Is this still the case now, venerable sir?”
“Would they receive them if they were given? “Yes, Great King. “In that case, venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my gift for today;
I shall dedicate it to them. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
The king went to his residence, had a great almsgiving prepared, and announced the time to the Blessed One. The Blessed One—
Having gone to the royal palace, he sat down upon the prepared seat together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Those hungry ghosts, thinking, "Perhaps we might receive something today," went and stood behind walls and other such places. The Blessed One acted in such a way that they all came within the king's line of sight.
As the king was offering the water of dedication, he dedicated it, saying, "May this be for my kinsmen."
At that very moment, lotus ponds covered with *kamala* and *kuvalaya* lilies appeared for the *petas*.
Having bathed and drunk there, their distress, fatigue, and thirst were allayed, and they became golden-hued. The king gave them rice gruel, hard food, and soft food, dedicating it to them;
at that very instant, divine rice gruel, hard food, and soft food appeared for them. Having partaken of these, they—
Their faculties became plump. Then, having given them dwellings and lodgings, he assigned them. For them, divine garments, palaces, bedspreads, couches, and various ornaments appeared.
And the Blessed One resolved that all of their prosperity should be manifest to the king.
When the king saw this, he was exceedingly delighted. Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal and being invited to do so...
For the sake of King Bimbisāra’s expression of gratitude, he recited the *Tirokuṭṭa-petavatthu*:
“They stand beyond the walls, at crossroads and junctions;
they stand by the doorposts, having come back to their own homes.”
“Though abundant food and drink, and various kinds of solid and soft foods are provided,
no one remembers them because of the condition of the beings’ own karma.
Thus do those who are compassionate give to their relatives.”
"Pure, excellent, timely, and permissible food and drink:
'May this be for your relatives; may the relatives be happy.
And having gathered there, those departed relatives who have assembled—"
When there is an abundance of food and drink, they express their appreciation with sincere thanks:
“May our kinsmen live long, for whose sake we receive this;
the honor has been rendered to us, and the donors shall not be without fruit.”
“For there is no plowing there, nor is cattle-herding found;
there is no such trade as buying and selling with coin.
The deceased spirits who have passed away there subsist on what is given from here.”
“Just as water that has rained upon a height flows down to the lowlands,
even so what is given from here benefits the departed.
Or just as rivers full of water fill the ocean,”
In the same way, what is given from here benefits the departed spirits.
“He gave to me, he did for me— my kinsmen, friends, and companions—
let one give a sacrificial gift for the departed, recollecting what was done in the past.”
“Neither weeping nor sorrow, nor any other lamentation, brings any benefit to the departed; thus do kinsmen remain.
But this offering, when well-established in the Saṅgha, [brings great fruit].”
"For his long-term welfare, it is immediately beneficial.
"Thus has this duty toward kinsmen been demonstrated, and a sublime offering has been made to the departed;
strength has been bestowed upon the monks, and by you, abundant and no small merit has been produced."
14. Therein, “through walls” (*tirokuṭṭesu*) means on the outer sides of walls. “Standing” (*tiṭṭhanti*) is a term for maintaining a standing posture, by way of excluding sitting and so forth;

the meaning is that they stand outside the doors of the house-walls and enclosures. “And at junctions and crossroads” (*sandhisiṅghāṭakesu ca*) means both at junctions (*sandhi*) and at crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*).
A “junction” (*sandhi*) refers to a four-way intersection, as well as the junction of houses, the junction of walls, and the junction of light-entrances.
They are called *siṅghāṭaka*, which means three-way junctions. "Standing at the door-posts" means they stand leaning against the door-posts of city gates or house doors.
Regarding "having come to their own home": a "home" (*sakagharan*) refers both to the house of former kinsmen and to a house one has lived in as its master;
since they approach both of these with the perception that it is their own home, [they are said to do so].
Therefore he said, "Having come to my own home.
Thus the Blessed One, although the residence of Bimbisāra had never been inhabited by him before, came to it with the perception that it was his own home because it was the house of a former kinsman;
and he beheld those standing beyond the walls and other places experiencing the fruit of envy and stinginess.

Having shown many ghosts to the king by means of the verse, “They stand beyond the walls,” which displays hideous, deformed, and terrifying sights, he then spoke the second verse, beginning with “Though there was abundant food and drink,” in order to demonstrate the dreadful nature of the karma performed by those beings.
In this context, *pahūte* means not small but much; that is to say, as much as desired. For here, the letter *pa* is substituted for the letter *ba*.
As in such passages as “The Lord, being present, does not partake,” and so forth. Some, however, read “bahuke” (many), but that is a careless reading.
“In food and drink” means in both solid food (*anna*) and liquid (*pāna*). “Chewable and edible” means in both chewables (*khajja*) and edibles (*bhojja*).

By this, he shows the fourfold nutriment according to the categories of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. “Upaṭṭhite” means having approached and stood [ready], prepared; the sense is “set out.”
"No one remembers those beings": for those beings who have arisen in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), no one—whether mother, father, son, or grandson—remembers them. For what reason?

Because of the condition of karma; that is, because of the state of their own miserly karma, consisting of such acts as failing to give or obstructing the giving of others. Indeed, that karma does not allow those relatives to remember [them].

16. Thus, having shown that even when abundant food, drink, and other necessities are available, there is an absence of even the mere recollection by relatives on behalf of deceased relatives who are longing for them due to the ripening of their own kamma, the Blessed One now spoke the third verse,
“In this way they give for their relatives,” praising the gift bestowed by the king on behalf of his relatives reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).

In this context, “evam” (thus) is a word used for comparison. Its connection is twofold: first, that among those beings, even though some do not reciprocate due to the condition of their own karma, some give to their relatives;
and second, O Great King, they give to their relatives pure, excellent, timely, and permissible food and drink, just as it was given by you, being thus compassionate.
"And those who are compassionate. In this context, "they give" means they bestow, assign, and hand over.
"To kinsmen" means to those related through the mother’s side and the father’s side. "Whoever" refers to sons and others. "Are" means they exist.
"Compassionate" means those who desire welfare and seek the good. "Pure" means clean, heart-pleasing, and righteous. "Exquisite" means sublime. "At the proper time" means...
"At the time suitable for the enjoyment of those worthy of offerings," or "at the time when deceased relatives have come and stood beyond the walls and so forth.
"Appropriate" means suitable, fitting, and worthy of the enjoyment of the Noble Ones. "Drink and food" refers to both drink and food;
by way of this, he speaks here of all things that may be given as a gift.
17. Now, demonstrating the manner in which what is given becomes truly "given" to those hungry ghosts (petas), he spoke the first half of the fourth verse:
"May this be for your kinsmen; may the kinsmen be happy. This is to be connected with the first half of the third verse:
"Thus do those who are compassionate give to their kinsmen..."
"May this belong to your relatives; may your relatives be happy.

By the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the sense of manner—namely, "they give in such a manner as 'may this belong to your relatives,' and not otherwise"—the demonstration of the manner in which it should be given is effected.
Therein, *idaṃ* (this) is the demonstration of the object to be given. *Vo* (to you) is a mere particle, as in [phrases] such as "by whom, for you, O Noble Ones," and so forth.
"May it be for kinsmen" means may it be for those kinsmen who have arisen in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).

They also read "no ñātīnaṃ," which has the meaning "for our kinsmen. "May kinsmen be happy" means that those kinsmen reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, while experiencing this fruit, may they be happy and attain happiness.
Because even when it is said, "Let this be for your relatives," an action performed by one does not yield fruit for another;
rather, that object being given specifically for their sake becomes a condition for the wholesome kamma of the deceased relatives.
Therefore, just as in that very object at that very moment, there arises for them a wholesome kamma that produces its fruit.
Showing that this is so, he says: “And they, being there,” and so forth.
Therein, “they” refers to the deceased relatives (*ñātipeta*). “There” means where the gift is being given.
“Having assembled” means having gathered there for the purpose of giving thanks, thinking: “These are our relatives; they are dedicating the gift for our benefit. In abundance...
“Regarding food and drink” means with respect to that object being given for one’s own sake. “They express appreciation respectfully” means that,
having full faith in the fruit of karma, not abandoning their sense of esteem, and with undistracted minds,
they rejoice and express appreciation, saying, “May this gift of ours lead to welfare and happiness,” becoming filled with joy and gladness.
18. "May they live long" means may those who live long have a long lifespan. "Our kinsmen" refers to our relatives.
"For whose sake" means for the cause of whom, depending upon whom. "We obtain" means we acquire such prosperity as this.
This indeed is a demonstration of the manner of praising one's own kinsmen—the *petas*—who are experiencing the prosperity obtained through the act of dedication (*uddisana*).

For the offering of the petas becomes productive of fruit at that very moment through three factors: by means of one’s own rejoicing (anumodana), by designating it for the donors (uddisana), and by the attainment of what was to be discarded (ukkhiṇeyya-sampatti). In this regard, the donors are the specific cause; therefore he said, "for whose sake we receive.
And as for the phrase "the worship performed for us," it refers to those who designate it thus: "May this be for your relatives."

The donors have performed an act of worship for us, and those donors have not been without fruit, because the karma consisting of the act of relinquishment produced within their mental continuum yields its fruit right there. Here it may be asked:

"Do only relatives reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts obtain such success of causes, or others as well? We need not state anything on this point, for the Blessed One has already declared it so. For this was said:
“Master Gotama, we brahmins give gifts and perform meritorious deeds, thinking:
‘May this gift benefit our deceased relatives and kin; may our deceased relatives and kin enjoy this gift.
Does that gift, Master Gotama, actually benefit those deceased relatives and kin? Do those deceased relatives and kin [enjoy it]?”
“Do they enjoy that gift? “In some cases, brahmin, it is appropriate; in other cases, it is not.
“But what, Master Gotama, is the appropriate case, and what is the inappropriate case? “In this case, brahmin, someone is a destroyer of life...
[as above] ...and holds wrong view; with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in hell. Whoever—”

The nutriment of beings in hell is such that by it they are sustained there, and by it they remain there. This, brahmin, is the case where, for one who stands [in such a state], that gift does not benefit them.
But here, brahmin, someone is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...he holds wrong view; he, with the breakup of the body...
After death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation among the animal womb. There, he subsists on whatever food is the sustenance of beings in the animal womb;
there, he persists by means of that. This too, brahmin, is an impossible situation where, for one situated therein, that gift does not provide benefit.
“But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life... [and so on] ... possesses right view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of human beings... or he is reborn in the company of devas.
Whatever is the food of the devas, by that he subsists there, by that he persists there. This too...”
“Brahmin, it is impossible that for one standing in such a state, that gift would be of benefit.
On the other hand, Brahmin, suppose someone here is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...up to: he holds wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya). Whatever food belongs to the beings in the realm of hungry ghosts, by that [gift]...”
He sustains himself there by that; thus he remains there by means of it. Or else, friends or companions, kinsmen or blood relations, send him provisions from here;
he sustains himself there by that, and thus he remains there by means of it.
This, brahmin, is the situation in which, for one who stands therein, that gift is of benefit.”
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased relative has not been reborn in that place, who then enjoys that gift?
“Brahmin, there are other deceased relatives of his who have been reborn in that place;
they enjoy that gift.”
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased relative has not been reborn in that place,
and other deceased relatives of his have also not been reborn in that place, who then partakes of that gift?
“Brahmin, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that such a place would remain empty throughout this long period of time.”
"That is to say, by their kinsmen and blood relations who have become *petas*; moreover, O Brahmin, the donor also is not without fruit.

19. Now, in order to show that for those reborn in the realm of *petas*, there is no other means of obtaining prosperity there—such as agriculture or cattle-rearing—and that they subsist on what is given from here, the passage beginning with "For there" (*na hi*) was spoken.
Therein, "for there is no agriculture" (*na hi tattha kasi atthi*) means that in that realm of *petas*, there is indeed no agriculture, depending upon which [they might live].
"May the departed live in happiness. Regarding the phrase "there is no cattle-rearing here":

in this realm of the *petas*, not only is there no agriculture, but furthermore, cattle-rearing does not exist, which they might rely upon to live in happiness. Regarding the phrase "there is no such trade":
even trade of that kind does not exist, which could serve as a cause for them to obtain prosperity.
They do not buy or sell with gold; there is nothing of that kind there which could serve as a cause for their obtaining prosperity.
"They subsist on what is given from here"—that is, they maintain themselves and sustain their existence solely by means of what is given from here by kinsmen or friends and colleagues.
"Pettā" refers to beings reborn in the realm of the *petas*. "Kālagatā" means those who have passed away.
They departed at the time of their own death. Alternatively, the reading is *kālakatā*, meaning those whose time has come, who have performed their [appointed] time, who have met with death.
*Tahiṃ* means in that realm of the hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*). 20–21.
Now, in order to illustrate the aforementioned matter through similes, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Water rained upon a height."

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as water rained down by clouds upon a high ground or elevated place flows toward the lowlands—reaching that portion of the earth which is sloping and inclined—so too does a gift given from here benefit the departed (petas) and is applied toward the production of its fruit.
For the world of the departed is like a low-lying place where water naturally flows.
For the sake of making that gift effective. As it is said: "This, brahmin, is the place where, for one who stands there, that gift becomes effective.

And just as the great rivers, filled by water flowing down from mountain clefts, gullies, branches, sub-branches, small pools, and great pools, eventually fill the ocean, so too the gift given from here [in this world] fills the ocean of merit in the past.
It is beneficial for the departed (petas) in the manner already described.

22. Since the departed—overcome by the longing, "May we receive something from here"—are unable, even when they come to the house of their relatives, to say, "Give us this or that," therefore one who recollects these bases for recollection for them...
A clansman, intending to give a gift, spoke this verse, saying, "He gave to me.
Its meaning is as follows: "He gave me such-and-such wealth or grain;
he performed for me such-and-such a service, undertaking the effort himself; 'such-and-such a person is my relative by descent from my mother's side or my father's side'—out of affection..."
Recalling all this—thinking, "He was my friend because he was capable of providing protection;

such-and-such a person was my companion and playmate from our childhood"—one should give a gift to the *petas* and dedicate that gift to them. Alternatively, the reading is "dakkhiṇā dajjā": a gift (*dakkhiṇā*) should be given to the *petas*;
by this, it is meant that one should give while recollecting in the manner described by "he gave to me," and so forth, what was done in the past.
For this is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. 23–24.

However, as for those beings who, upon the death of a relative, remain merely overcome by weeping, sorrow, and so forth, and do not give anything for their sake—their weeping, sorrow, and so on, result only in self-mortification; that does not benefit the departed.
Showing that it accomplishes some purpose, he spoke the verse beginning with “For weeping does not...”;

then, in order to demonstrate the beneficial nature of the sacrificial gift (dakkhiṇā) given by the King of Magadha, he spoke the verse beginning with “And this indeed...”. Their meaning has already been stated above. 25.
Now, since this sacrificial gift was given by the king through performing the duties that kinsmen ought to perform for their kin...
The duty toward kinsmen has been demonstrated and made manifest to the multitude;

the illustration has been made clear by the words, "In this very same way, you too must fulfill the duty toward kinsmen. And by enabling those departed spirits to attain celestial excellence, a sublime honor was rendered to the dead;
and by satisfying the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with food, drink, and other necessities, [great merit was gained].
Having bestowed strength upon the bhikkhus and having generated no small amount of merit by producing an intention of generosity accompanied by qualities such as compassion,
the Blessed One, gladdening the king with these qualities as they truly are,
spoke the concluding verse: "That is the duty toward kinsmen."
In this context, "the duty toward kinsmen" (*ñātidhamma*) refers to that which ought to be done for kinsmen by their kinsmen.
"Exalted" means prosperous and successful. "Strength" refers to physical strength. "Accumulated" means built up.

And here, with the words "Thus this duty toward kinsmen has been illustrated," the Blessed One instructed the king with a discourse on the Dhamma; for in this instance, the demonstration of the duty toward kinsmen constitutes the instruction.
With the words, “And a sublime offering was made to the *petas*,” he encouraged them. Here, “sublime” (*uḷārā*) is a praise intended to incite them toward performing offerings again and again.

With the words, “And strength was bestowed upon the monks,” he inspired them. Here, the bestowing of strength upon the monks is an inspiration achieved by increasing their enthusiasm for the bestowing of such strength. “By you... [the rest of the sentence follows].
He comforted him with the words, “Your merit is abundant and not small.
Here, the description of the flow of merit is to be understood as a form of consolation by way of praising his qualities exactly as they are.

And at the conclusion of the teaching, for those whose hearts were moved by the description of the danger of rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) and so forth, [the Buddha taught] the methodical...
Upon the mere touch of his foot, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.
On the second day as well, he taught this same "Tirokuṭṭa" discourse to gods and humans. In this manner, for seven days, there was a similar realization of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the *Tirokuṭṭa-petavatthu* is concluded.
6. Explanation of the Story of the *Peta* Who Ate Her Five Sons " Naked and of ugly form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a *peta* who ate her five sons.
It is said that in a village not far from Sāvatthī, the wife of a certain householder was barren.
It came to pass that his kinsmen said to him, “Your wife is barren; let us bring you another maiden.
Out of affection for his wife, he did not wish to do so. Then his wife, having heard of this matter, spoke thus to her husband:
“Husband, I am barren; another maiden should be brought, lest our family lineage be cut off.”
Thus, being pressured by her, he brought another maiden. At a later time, she became pregnant.
The barren wife, overcome with jealousy—thinking, "Once this woman has obtained a son, she will become the mistress of this house"—sought a means to cause her miscarriage.
She won over a certain female wanderer with food, drink, and other gifts, and had her induce an abortion for her.
She caused [it] to be done. When her pregnancy had miscarried, she informed her mother; the mother, having assembled her own kinsmen, reported the matter to them.
They said this to the barren woman: “Did you cause this woman’s pregnancy to miscarry? “I did not cause it to miscarry.
“If you did not cause the pregnancy to miscarry, take an oath. “If I have caused the pregnancy to miscarry, may I be destined for an evil rebirth.”
"Overcome by hunger and thirst, having given birth to five sons each evening and morning, I would eat them and yet never reach satiety;
I would be constantly foul-smelling and swarmed by flies. Having spoken thus, she made a solemn oath.
Before long, she passed away and was reborn as a hideous-looking *petī* not far from that very village.
At that time, eight elder monks who had completed their rains retreat in the countryside were traveling toward Sāvatthī to see the Teacher;
they took up residence in a forest spot near that village, well-provided with shade and water.
Then that female spirit revealed herself to the elders. Among them, the senior of the Saṅgha addressed that female spirit:
“Naked, you are ill-favored in form; foul-smelling, you breathe putridity;
swarmed by flies, who are you that stand here?”—with this verse he questioned her.
Therein, “naked” means unclothed. “Ill-favored in form” means of ugly appearance, exceedingly repulsive in form.
"You are possessed [of these things]. 'Foul-smelling' means having an undesirable odor. 'You stink of putridity' means you emit the smell of a corpse from your body.
'Surrounded by flies' means swarmed on all sides by blue flies. 'Who are you standing here?
means who indeed are you, one such as this, standing in this place? The meaning is that you are wandering here and there."
Then that female ghost, being thus questioned by the Great Elder, revealing herself and inspiring a sense of spiritual urgency in beings, said:
“Venerable sir, I am a female ghost, miserable, belonging to the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of ghosts.”
“Five sons at one time, and five more in the evening—
having given birth to them, I devour them, yet even they are not enough for me.
My heart burns and smokes with hunger.”
"I do not obtain water to drink; behold me fallen into calamity."—He spoke these three verses. 27.
Therein, "Venerable Sir" (*bhadante*) is an address to the Elder with respect. "Doomed" (*duggatā*) means having gone to a miserable destination. "Belonging to the world of Yama" (*yamalokikā*)...
“Yamaloka”: they are known as being included within that world of hungry ghosts (petaloka) which bears that name.
“Gone from here” means gone from this human world to the world of hungry ghosts by way of rebirth; the sense is that they have been reborn there.
“At the time” means at the time when the night has dawned. This instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. “Five sons” refers to...
"Five sons. This is stated with a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa).
The construction is: "In the evening, furthermore, five others"—meaning, in the evening time, I eat five other sons. "Having given birth" means having given birth to ten sons each day.
"Those too were not enough for me" means that even those ten sons, on a single day, were not sufficient for me to counteract my hunger.
They have not been mastered. Here, for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukha*), it is stated with the long vowel "nā" instead of "na.

29. "My heart is burning and smoking with hunger": when I am oppressed by hunger—that is, by the pangs of starvation—my region of the heart burns all around and smokes due to the digestive fire; it is tormented. Water...
"Overcome by thirst, I do not find anything to drink; though I wander here and there, I do not obtain even water to drink.

Behold me fallen into calamity!"—thus she made known to the Elder the suffering she was experiencing herself, saying, "Venerable sir, behold me who have entered upon such a calamity, both common to those reborn as *petas* and unique to myself."
Having heard that, the Elder, questioning her about the deed she had committed, said:
"What evil deed was done by you through body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what karma do you eat the flesh of your own son?"
He spoke this verse. In that context, *dukkata* means misconduct (*duccarita*). "As the result of what kind of kamma?

means as the result of what sort of kamma; does it mean as the result of killing living beings, or rather of one among [the other misdeeds] such as taking what is not given? Some read, "By the ripening of what kamma?
Then that female ghost, explaining to the Elder the kamma she herself had committed, said:
“My co-wife was pregnant; I conceived an evil thought toward her.
With a corrupted mind, I brought about an abortion.
Her two-month-old fetus merely flowed out as blood.”
Then her mother became angry and summoned my kinsmen;
she made me take an oath and caused me to be reviled.
"I, having uttered that terrible oath, spoke a falsehood."
“I eat the flesh of my own sons, if that was done by me.
“Through the ripening of that karma, and of both [the acts] of false speech,
I eat the flesh of my own sons, smeared with pus and blood.”— thus he spoke these verses.
31–32. In this context, "a co-wife" (*sapatī*) refers to a woman who has the same husband. "Intending evil against her" means she intended evil—that is, a cruel deed—against that co-wife.
"With a corrupted mind" (*paduṭṭhamanā*) means with a corrupted heart, or by means of a corrupted mind.
"Two months old" means having been born for two months; having reached that stage, he was two months old. "Only blood flowed" means that as he passed away, only blood flowed out.
It flowed out as blood alone. Her mother, becoming angry, thought, "She has brought my kinsmen together," and then her rival’s mother, being enraged, assembled her own relatives.
