Alternatively, the reading is *tatassā*; the analysis of the words is *tato assā*. 33–34. *Sapathaṃ* means an oath.
*Paribhāsāpayī* means she caused [her] to be threatened with fear. *Sapathaṃ* refers to false speech.
Thinking, "If this were done by me, it would be like this," she uttered a false oath—a lie—presenting as accomplished a sin that had not been committed, saying:
"I eat the flesh of my own offspring; if this were done by me.
This was a demonstration of the manner in which the oath was made at that time: "If this sin of causing an abortion were committed by me..."
The meaning is: "In the future, regarding the production of renewed existence, he would eat only the flesh of my own sons.
"Of that karma" means of that act of taking life committed by causing an abortion. "And of false speech" means of the karma of lying.
"Both" refers to both types of karma and their respective results. [The word *ubhaya* is used] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).

For this is a personal pronoun (*paccattavacana*). "Smeared with pus and blood" means being smeared with both pus and blood due to the process of discharging and the process of bursting open; the construction is: "I eat the flesh of my own sons.
Having thus made known the ripening of her own karma, that female ghost (petī) spoke further to the elders: "Venerable sirs, in this very [place]..."
“In a certain village, the wife of a householder became possessed by jealousy, committed an evil deed, and was thus reborn in this state of existence as a peta.
It would be well, venerable sir, if you would go to that householder’s home; he will give alms to you, and you should dedicate that offering to me.
In this way, my liberation from this world of petas will come to pass.”
When the elders heard this, out of compassion for him and being established in a nature inclined toward uplifting others, they entered the house of that householder to beg for alms.

Upon seeing the elders, the householder was filled with faith; he went out to meet them, took their bowls, seated them on seats, and began to feed them with choice food. The elders [informed] the householder of this occurrence.

Having announced that gift, they dedicated it for the sake of that peta. At that very moment, the peta departed from that suffering and, having attained magnificent prosperity, appeared before the householder during the night.
Then the elders, traveling by stages to Sāvatthī, reported this matter to the Blessed One. And the Blessed One [expounded] that matter as the occasion arose (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

Having done so, he taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude. At the conclusion of the teaching, the great crowd, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), refrained from envy and stinginess.
Thus, that teaching became beneficial for the multitude.
The commentary on the story of the hungry ghost who ate his five sons is finished.
7. The Explanation of the Story of the Ghost Who Ate Seven Sons " Naked and of ugly form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a ghost who had devoured seven sons.
It is said that not far from Sāvatthī, in a certain village, there was a certain lay follower...
He had two sons who were in the prime of their youth, endowed with beauty and possessed of virtuous conduct.
Their mother, thinking "I am one who has borne sons," began to treat her husband with contempt on account of her sons' strength.
Being thus insulted by his wife, he became despondent in mind and brought home another maiden. Before long, she became pregnant. Then his senior wife, overcome by jealousy—
Having bribed a certain physician with material goods, she had him cause her three-month-old pregnancy to miscarry.
Then, when questioned by her kinsmen and husband, "Did you cause this woman's pregnancy to miscarry?
she spoke a lie, saying, "I did not cause it to miscarry. When they did not believe her and said, "Take an oath," she replied, "Day and night, seven sons each..."
"Having given birth, I shall eat the flesh of my own children; may I always be foul-smelling and swarmed by flies," she swore this oath.
Later, having passed away, as a result of that very act of causing an abortion and that false speech, she was reborn in the womb of a peta.
Eating the flesh of her children according to the manner of a mother, she wandered not far from that same village. By him—
Now at that time, a number of elder monks who had completed the rains retreat while living in a village monastery were traveling to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One;
they took up residence for the night in a certain place not far from that village.
Then that female spirit revealed herself to those elders. The Great Elder questioned her with a verse:
“Naked, of ugly form, foul-smelling and emitting a stench,
surrounded by flies— what are you standing here for?
Being thus questioned by the Elder, she gave her reply in three verses:
“Venerable sir, I am a female peta, miserable and belonging to the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the realm of petas.
At dawn seven sons, and again seven others at evening—”
“Having eaten them, I still do not have enough.
My heart burns and smokes with hunger;
I find no relief, like one scorched by fire in the heat.”

38. Therein, "extinguishment" (*nibbāna*) means the subsiding of the suffering of hunger and thirst. "I do not attain" means I do not obtain it. "As if scorched by fire in the heat" is to be construed as: "I do not attain extinguishment, as if being burned by fire in the extreme heat of the sun.
Having heard this, the Great Elder, inquiring into the deed she had committed, asked:
"What evil deed has been done by body, speech, or mind? ... [text continues]"
“By the karmic result of kissing, you eat the flesh of your own sons,” he said, speaking this verse.
Then that female ghost (petī), explaining her own rebirth in the world of ghosts and the reason for eating her sons’ flesh, said:
“I had two sons, both in the full bloom of youth.”
Endowed with the strength of my sons, I held my husband in contempt.
Thereupon my husband, being enraged, brought home a co-wife for me;
she conceived a child, and I harbored evil thoughts toward her.
“With a corrupted mind, I caused an abortion;
that three-month-old fetus fell out as putrid blood.
Then her mother, being angry, summoned my kinsmen.”
He made me take an oath and caused me to be reviled:
“I myself uttered that terrible oath and a falsehood, saying:
‘I eat my own son’s flesh, if it was prepared by me.’”
“By the ripening of that karma, of both false speech and [the other], I eat the flesh of my own sons, smeared with pus and blood.”—these verses he spoke.
(40–45) In this context, “endowed with the strength of her sons” means endowed with the strength derived from her sons; she obtained strength by virtue of her sons. “They despised her”...
"Having transgressed, I thought too highly [of myself] and despised others. "The putrid blood falls away" means that the fetus, having become putrid blood, falls out.
Everything else is exactly the same as in the preceding [case]. In that [preceding case] there were eight elders, here there are many.
In that [preceding case] there were five sons, here there are seven—this alone is the distinction.
The commentary on the story of the hungry ghost who ate his own seven sons is finished.
8. Commentary on the Story of the Ox Hungry Ghost:
"Why do you wander about like one mad?"—this [verse] was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain householder whose father had died.
He spoke concerning this. It is said that in Sāvatthī, the father of a certain householder passed away.
With his heart seared by grief at his father’s death, weeping and wandering like one insane, he asked everyone he saw, "Have you seen my father? No one was able to dispel his sorrow.
In his heart, however, the proximate cause for the fruit of stream-entry was burning like a lamp within a jar.
At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw that proximate cause for the fruit of stream-entry and thought,
"It is fitting to bring forth this man's past history, pacify his grief, and grant him the fruit of stream-entry."
On the following day, after his meal, having returned from his almsround and not taking a junior monk as an attendant, he went to that man’s house.

Hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," the man went out to meet him, led the Teacher into the house, and when the Teacher was seated on the prepared seat, he himself paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. He asked, "Venerable sir, why..."
“Know the place where my father has gone,” he said. Then the Teacher asked him, “Lay follower, do you ask about your father in this present life, or in the past?
Upon hearing those words, [the man thought], “It seems there have been many fathers of mine.
His grief subsided, and he attained a degree of equanimity. Then the Teacher gave him a discourse on the Dhamma for the dispelling of sorrow.

Having dispelled his grief and knowing his mind to be ready, he established him in the fruit of stream-entry through a discourse on the Dhamma that was uniquely his own, and then departed for the monastery.
Then, in the Hall of Truth, the bhikkhus raised this discussion: “Behold, friends, the majesty of the Buddha!”
“Likewise, a lay follower who had fallen into grief and lamentation was disciplined by the Blessed One in the fruit of stream-entry in a mere moment.
Having gone there, the Teacher sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared and asked, “Bhikkhus, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
The bhikkhus reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, no...”
"Just now I have removed his sorrow, but in the past, too, it was removed," he said; and being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, the father of a certain householder passed away.
Overcome by grief and lamentation due to his father's death, with tearful face and bloodshot eyes, he wept as he circumambulated the funeral pyre. His son, named Sujāta—
The prince, wise, capable, and endowed with intelligence, reflecting on a means to dispel his father’s grief, one day saw a dead ox outside the city.
Having brought grass and water and placed them before it, he stood there saying, “Eat, eat!
Drink, drink! Those who came along and saw him asked, “Friend Sujāta, have you gone mad?”
"Do you offer grass and water to a dead ox? they asked. He did not say anything in reply.
The people went to his father and said, "Your son has become insane; he is giving grass and water to a dead ox.
Upon hearing this, the grief that had been weighing upon the householder's father subsided. He thought, "My..."
Thinking, "It seems a madman has been born as my son," he was seized with a sense of urgency and went in haste, rebuking him:
"Are you not, dear Sujāta, wise, competent, and endowed with intelligence? Why do you give grass and water to a dead ox? And he said:
"Why indeed, appearing like one who is mad, do you gather and carry away green grass?"
"You keep crying out, 'Eat! Eat! to this old bull whose life has departed.
For a dead ox will not rise up again by means of food and drink.
You are a fool and dull-witted, just like that very same one who is so wicked."
He spoke two verses. Therein, "kiṃ nu" is a word of inquiry. "Ummattarūpova" means as if having the nature of a madman, as if having fallen into a state of mental derangement.
"Lāyitvā" means having cut. "Haritaṃ tiṇaṃ" means fresh grass. "Lapasi" means you lament. "Gatasattaṃ" means lifeless.
"Jaraggavaṃ" means an old ox, a worn-out bull. "Annena pānena" means by you [with food and drink].
"By means of the green grass or the water that was given"—even if a dead ox were to rise up, a cow that has passed away would not indeed come back to life.

"You are foolish and dull-witted": you are foolish because of your association with folly, and you are dull-witted because of the absence of wisdom (paññā), which is synonymous with intelligence (medhā).
"Just as another who is likewise of poor intellect": just as any other person who is devoid of wisdom.
“Vippalapeyya” means you would prattle on thus in vain. “Yathā” is merely a particle.
Having heard that, Sujāta, wishing to convince his father, revealed his own intention:
“These are the feet, this is the head, and this body with its tail;”
“The tendons remain just as they were; this ox has arisen.
The master’s hands, feet, body, and head are visible;
weeping at the clay stupa, are you not yourself the one who is foolish?”
He spoke these two verses. Their meaning is as follows: “Of this ox, these are the four feet, this is the head;
together with the tail, it functions—thus this body is ‘with-tail. And these nostrils and eyes remain with their original shape unaltered, just as they were before death.
For this reason, this ox stands up. This ox [stands] because of this cause.
“May it rise up, may it stand up”—this would be my thought. Some read, “I think the ox will rise up”;
by that reason, I would think, “May this ox suddenly raise its body,” such would be the intention of my conceiving.
But as for my grandfather, my father’s father, his hands and feet...
"The body and head are visible, but it is merely a brick stupa constructed by inserting his bones.
Weeping a hundredfold or a thousandfold, my dear, you alone are foolish and witless;
conditioned phenomena are subject to disintegration and they do disintegrate—what lamentation can there be for those who understand this? Thus he spoke the Dhamma to his father.
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta’s father thought, “My son, being wise and liberated, has performed this deed to convince me.
Then, praising his son, he said: “Dear Sujāta, it is well known that ‘all beings are subject to death. From now on I shall not grieve;
one must indeed be as wise as you are, for such wisdom is capable of removing sorrow.”
“While I was burning, like a fire fed with ghee, you have sprinkled me with water and extinguished every dart.
You have indeed pulled out the arrow that was lodged in my heart; you have removed the grief that dwelt within.”
“You who have dispelled the grief for my father in me, who was overcome by sorrow—
‘Now I am one whose arrow has been pulled out, I have become cool and attained Nibbāna;
I do not grieve nor do I weep, having heard you, young man.’”
“Thus do the wise act, those who are compassionate;
they turn one away from sorrow, just as Sujāta did for his father.”—These four verses he spoke.
Therein, “blazing” (*āditta*) means set ablaze and burning with the fire of sorrow. “Calm” (*santa*) means peaceful.
"Pāvakam" means fire. "As if sprinkling with water" means as if dousing it with water.
"He extinguished all my distress" means he extinguished all the fever of my mind. "Abbahi vata" means indeed extracted. "The dart" refers to the dart of sorrow.
"Residing in the heart" means existing as a dart dependent upon the mind. "Of one overcome by sorrow" means of one who is overwhelmed by grief.
"Grief for my father" means the sorrow that arose concerning his father. "He dispelled" means he removed it.
"Having heard you, O youth"—O young man, having heard your words, I no longer grieve nor do I weep. "Just as this well-born one [dispelled grief] for his father":
just as this Sujāta turned his father away from sorrow, so too should others who are compassionate and of a helpful nature.
They are wise; the meaning is that they act in this way by performing services for their parents and others.

Having heard the young man’s words, the father became free from grief, bathed his head, ate, engaged in his work, and after passing away, was destined for heaven. The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching to them...
He proclaimed the Truths to the bhikkhus, and at the conclusion of the Truths, many were established in the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages.
At that time, Sujāta was the Lord of the World.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Goṇa-peta-vatthu*.
9. Explanation of the Story of the Great Weaver-Peta "Excrement, urine, blood, and pus"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a certain female weaver-peta.
It is said that twelve monks were [practicing] a meditation subject in the presence of the Teacher...

Taking their robes, they searched for a suitable place to dwell; as the time for the commencement of the rains approached, they saw a delightful forest region well-provided with shade and water, and a village for alms-seeking not too far and not too near.
Having stayed there for one night, on the second day they entered the village for alms. There, eleven weavers were residing.

Seeing those monks, they became filled with joy; leading them each to their own homes, they served them with excellent food and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going? "We shall go wherever it is comfortable for us.
"If that is so, venerable sirs, you must stay right here," they said, and requested that the monks enter the rains retreat. The monks—
They accepted [the offer]. The lay followers had forest huts built for them there and gave them to the monks.
The monks entered the rains retreat there.
There, the chief weaver attended to two monks with the four requisites with great care, while the others [attended] to one each.
They attended upon the bhikkhus. The wife of the chief weaver was faithless, lacking confidence, held wrong views, and was stingy;
she did not attend upon the bhikkhus with proper respect. When the husband saw this, he brought his younger sister to him and entrusted the authority over his household to her.
She became faithful and confident, and she attended upon the bhikkhus with proper respect.
She looked after them. When all those weavers had completed their rains retreat, they each gave a robe to every single monk.
Thereupon, the eldest weaver’s wife, being stingy and with a corrupted mind, reviled her husband:
"As for that gift of food and drink you have given to the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, it will become excrement and urine for you in the next world."
"Let it arise as pus and blood, and let the garments become blazing iron bands.
Thereupon, at a later time, the chief smith passed away and was reborn in the Vindhya forest as a tree deity endowed with great power.
His stingy wife, however, after passing away, [was reborn] in that very place where he lived...
Not far away, she was reborn as a female peta. Naked, hideous in form, and overcome by hunger and thirst, she went to that terrestrial deity and said:
"Master, I wander about naked and exceedingly overcome by hunger and thirst;
give me clothing, food, and drink. He offered her sublime, divine food and drink.
As soon as she grasps it, that very thing turns into excrement, urine, pus, and blood;
and the cloth given to her, when she puts it on, becomes a glowing iron band. Experiencing great suffering, she abandons it and wanders about wailing.
At that time, a certain bhikkhu who had completed the rains retreat was traveling to pay homage to the Teacher with a large [retinue].
He set out for the Viñjhā forest together with the caravan. Having traveled by night, the members of the caravan saw during the day a place in the forest endowed with abundant shade and water;

they unyoked their vehicles and rested for a moment. But the bhikkhu, desiring solitude, moved a short distance away and spread his outer robe at the foot of a certain tree that was well-shaded and concealed by a dense thicket of forest.
Having made this arrangement, he lay down and, his body exhausted by the fatigue of traveling the road during the night, fell asleep.
The porters rested and set out on the path, but that monk did not wake up.
Then, rising at evening time and not seeing them, he took a certain wrong path and eventually [reached] that deity’s...

She arrived at the place where he was staying. Then that son of the gods, seeing her, approached her in human form, exchanged greetings, led her into his own celestial mansion, and sat attending to her while providing oil for massaging her feet and other comforts.
At that moment, the female peta arrived and said, "Master, give me food, drink, and clothing. He gave those things to her.
She gave them to him. As soon as she had taken them, they became nothing but glowing iron slabs of excrement, urine, pus, and blood.
When the bhikkhu saw this, he was struck with a sense of spiritual urgency and said to that young deva:
“Excrement, urine, blood, and pus—what is the karmic result for one who consumes these?”
“What deed did this woman perform, that she always feeds upon blood and pus?
New garments, beautiful, soft, pure, and hairy, once given, become mixed with filth— what deed did this woman perform?”
He questioned him with two verses. Therein, "Of what is this the result? means:
of what kind of karma is this the result, which she is now experiencing? "What deed did this woman do? means:
what indeed did this woman do in the past? "She who at all times eats blood and pus" means: she who at every time eats only blood and pus.
He eats and consumes. "New" means they have just appeared, being of high value. "Beautiful" means lovely and pleasing to behold.
"Soft" means pleasant to the touch. "Pure" means of perfectly clean color. "Furry" means having hair on them that is pleasant to the touch;
the meaning is that they are beautiful. "Given as mixed with *kitaka*" means they are like the thorns of the *kitaka* plant.
They become like iron bands. Alternatively, there is the reading “they become *kīṭaka*,” which means they take on the appearance of biting insects.
Thus, when questioned by that bhikkhu, the devaputta, revealing the deed he had committed in that previous birth, said:
“O Venerable Sir, this woman was my wife; she was non-giving, stingy, and miserly.”
While I was giving [alms] to ascetics and brahmins, she reviled and abused me, saying:
“Eat excrement, urine, blood, and pus—impurity of every kind—for all time!
Let this be yours in the world beyond, and let your clothes be like rags!”
“Having practiced such misconduct, she has come here to be devoured for a long time”—thus he spoke these two verses.
In this context, *adāyikā* means one whose nature is not to give anything to anyone. *Maccharinī kadariyā* means:
first, she is stingy by the very nature of the stain of stinginess (*macchera-mala*); and furthermore, through repeated practice, she is one who is stubbornly stingy.
The construction is: "She was stingy by her nature. Now, demonstrating that very stinginess of hers, he said, "While I was giving," and so forth.
Therein, "having practiced such as this" means having practiced such things as the aforementioned verbal misconduct.

"Come here" means come to this world of ghosts (*petaloka*), having entered into the state of a ghost (*petattabhāva*). "She eats for a long time" means she eats only excrement and the like for a long duration.

For indeed, even though the fruit occurs in the very same manner as the abuse was inflicted, it falls upon oneself like a thunderbolt striking the head of one who is walking on the earth elsewhere than where the abuse was directed.
Thus that son of the gods, having related the deed previously committed by her, spoke again to that bhikkhu: "But there is..."
“Venerable sir, is there some means by which she might be released from this world of ghosts? When he replied, “There is,” [the king] said, “Tell me, venerable sir.

“If a gift is given to the Blessed One, to the Noble Saṅgha, or even to a single bhikkhu, and it is dedicated for her sake, and she herself rejoices in that, then she will be liberated from this suffering. Having heard this, the son of the gods—
Having given exquisite food and drink to that bhikkhu, he dedicated that offering to that peta.
At that very moment, the peta became well-satiated, her faculties refreshed, and she was filled with divine food.
Again, having placed a pair of divine garments in the hands of that same bhikkhu and offered them to the Blessed One, he dedicated that offering to the peta. At that very moment—
And she, clothed in celestial garments and adorned with celestial ornaments, was like a celestial nymph, perfected in every desire. And that bhikkhu,
having reached Sāvatthī on that very day through the supernatural power of that young god,
entered Jetavana, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, gave him the pair of robes, and related the incident.
He reported this. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the Story of the Great Weaver Ghost.
10. The Exposition of the Story of the Bald-Pated Female Ghost (*Khallāṭiyapetivatthu-vaṇṇanā*).
"Who is this within the celestial mansion?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while staying at Sāvatthī concerning a certain bald-pated female ghost.
It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a certain woman who lived by her beauty, who was lovely and fair to behold.
She was serene, endowed with supreme beauty of complexion, and possessed an exceedingly captivating mass of hair.
For her hair was blue-black, long, fine, soft, glossy, and curled at the tips;
reaching two spans in length, it fell in luxuriant tresses down as far as her waist-belt. Upon seeing the splendor of her hair, most young people became infatuated with her.
It came to pass that some women, unable to endure her beauty of hair and overcome by envy, consulted together.
They bribed a maidservant who was that woman’s attendant, and through her, they had a medicinal preparation for removing hair applied to her.
That maidservant, it is said, mixed that medicine with bathing powder and, at the time of bathing in the river Ganges—
He gave it to her. She soaked her hair roots with it and plunged into the water;

at the mere moment of plunging, her hair fell out by the roots, and her head became like a bitter gourd. Then, with her hair entirely shorn and her scalp raw from being plucked, she became as ugly as a female dove;
unable to enter the city out of shame, she wrapped her head with a cloth.
Living in a certain place outside the city, after a few days she lost her sense of shame;
turning back from there, she made her living by pressing sesame seeds for oil and trading in liquor.
One day, when two or three men had become intoxicated with liquor and had fallen into a deep sleep, she stole their loose-fitting garments as they lay there.
Then one day, having seen an elder whose taints were exhausted wandering for alms, she, with a heart full of faith, led him to her own home.
Having seated him on a prepared seat, she gave him a handful of oil-soaked linseed cake from a winnowing basket.
Out of compassion for her, he accepted and consumed it. With a mind full of faith, she held a parasol over him.
He stood there. The elder, gladdening her heart, offered a blessing of thanks and departed. At the very moment of that blessing, the woman made this aspiration:
"May my hair be long, fine, glossy, soft, and with curled tips.
Later, having passed away, as the fruit of that mixed karma, she was reborn in a golden palace in the midst of the ocean.
Having become solitary, she was reborn. Her hair appeared exactly as she had desired. However, because people had stolen her clothes, she remained naked.
Reappearing again and again in that golden mansion, she passed an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara) in a state of nakedness.
Then, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma...
Gradually, while [the Buddha] was dwelling at Sāvatthī, seven hundred merchants residing in Sāvatthī set out upon the great ocean by ship toward Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
Their ship, having set sail, was tossed about by the force of turbulent winds and, wandering hither and thither, came to that place.
Then that *vimāna*-petī, together with her celestial mansion, revealed herself to them.
She appeared. Seeing her, the elder merchant asked:
"Who is it that stands within the celestial mansion but does not come forth?
Come forth, O blessed lady; let us see you standing outside."
He spoke this verse. Therein, “Who indeed stands within the celestial mansion? means: who are you standing inside, within the interior of the mansion?
Is it a human woman or a non-human woman? He asks this. “Has she not come forth? means she has not emerged from the mansion.
“Come forth, blessed lady; let us see you standing outside,” means: O blessed lady, we [wish to see you].
“We wish to see you standing outside; therefore, please come out from your celestial mansion.
Or there is the reading, “Come forth, O Blessed One,” which means, “May it be well with you.
Then, demonstrating her own inability to go outside herself, she said:
“I am ashamed and abashed to go outside naked;
my hair is but scantily covered, for little merit have I performed.
Thus she spoke this verse. In it, *aṭṭiyāmi* means: being naked, I am distressed and pained to go outside. *Harāyāmi* means: [I am ashamed].
"I am ashamed. Why am I covered with hair? means: "I am concealed by my hair, my body being veiled. "Little merit has been done by me" means:
"A small, limited wholesome deed was performed by me," the intention being that it was merely the gift of a needle.
Then the merchant, wishing to give her his own upper garment—
“I give you this upper garment; put on this cloth.
Having put on this cloth, come forth, O beautiful one!
Come out, O blessed lady; let us see you standing outside.”
He spoke this verse. In it: *handā* means "take. *Uttarīyaṃ* refers to the upper garment; the meaning is "upper cloth" (*uttarisāṭaka*).
*Dadāmi te* means "I give to you. *Idaṃ dussaṃ nivāsayā* means "wear this cloth," that is, "you should wear this upper cloth of mine.
*Sobhane* means "in a beautiful form."
Having spoken thus, she offered her own upper garment to her. Demonstrating both the unsuitability of what was being given to her and how that which was being given would be suitable, she said:
"What you have given with hand to hand is not suitable for me;
here there is a faithful lay follower, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One."
“Having covered this [wound], give me my right [hand];
thus shall I be happy, with all my desires fulfilled. She spoke these two verses.
Therein, [he replied]: “What has been given by you from hand to hand does not serve me, O Noble One.”
"From your hand into my hand: what has been given by you does not serve me, it is not put to use; it is not fit for enjoyment—this is the meaning.

"There is a lay follower here who is faithful": this means that there is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) here in this assembly of people who, by virtue of having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and being endowed with faith in the results of kamma, is faithful (*saddho*). This...
"Having clothed me, dedicate this gift to me"— that is to say, having had that lay follower put on the garment being given to me,
dedicate that gift to me by giving the merit; "in such a way may they be happy"—
when it is done thus, I shall be happy, clothed in celestial garments and attained to bliss.
Having heard that, the merchants bathed the lay follower, anointed him, and clothed him in a pair of garments. To illustrate this matter, the compilers of the collection said:
"And having bathed him, and having anointed him, the merchants, having clothed him in garments, dedicated the gift to her."
“Immediately after it was recited, the result arose:
food, clothing, and drink—this is the fruit of that offering.
Then, pure and dressed in clean garments, wearing the finest cloth from Kāsī,”
"Laughing, she emerged from her celestial mansion; this is the fruit of giving to the South."—thus they spoke these three verses.
63. Therein, "taṃ" refers to that lay follower (*upāsaka*). The word "ca" is a mere particle. "Teti" is to be construed as "those merchants. "Vilimpetvāna" means...
"Having anointed her with the finest perfume. "Having clothed her in garments" means:

having fed her with food endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor, along with various condiments, they clothed her in two garments—a lower robe and an upper robe—the meaning being that they gave her two pieces of clothing.
"They dedicated the offering to her" means: they dedicated that offering to that peta.
64. *Samanantarānuddiṭṭhe*: here, *anu* is merely a particle; it means "immediately after that offering had been dedicated.
*Vipāko udapajjatha*: the result—that is, the fruit of that offering—arose for that peta.
When asked what kind [of result], the peta said: "Food, clothing, and drink. This refers to food resembling divine food of various kinds, and [clothing] resplendent with various colors and hues.
The construction is as follows: "By means of this kind of gift—clothing such as divine garments and various kinds of drinks—such a fruit arose. 65.
"From that" (tato) means after the obtaining of the aforementioned food and so forth. "Pure" (suddhā) means having a body purified by bathing.
“Wearing fine garments” means she was clothed in perfectly pure clothes. “Wearing the finest Kāsika” means she wore garments even superior to those made of Kāsika cotton.
“Smiling” means she emerged from her celestial mansion smiling by way of making this declaration: “Behold, now, the specific excellence of the fruit of your almsgiving!”
Then those merchants, having thus seen the fruit of merit before their very eyes, were filled with a sense of wonder and amazement;
conceiving deep reverence and esteem for that lay follower, they waited upon him with palms joined in salutation.
He, in turn, further inspired them with a discourse on the Dhamma and established them in the Refuges and the Precepts. They [then asked] about the deed performed by that *vimāna*-petī—
“Your celestial mansion shines forth, beautiful in form and lovely;
O deity, being asked, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?”—with this verse they questioned her.
Therein, “beautiful in form” means by way of elephants, horses, women, men, and so forth.
And it is a mental form well-fashioned by means of flower-garland making, creeper-work, and so forth. "Rucira" means delightful and beautiful to behold.
"Of what kind of action is this the fruit? means: of what sort of action—whether consisting of giving (*dānamaya*) or consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*)—is this the fruit? This is the meaning.

Being questioned thus by them, she explained both matters, saying: "This is the fruit of even that small wholesome deed performed by me; as for unwholesome deeds, such will be the result in the future in hell. She said:
"When the monk was wandering, I gave him a measure of rice-scum;
To him who was upright in being, I gave with a mind full of serene confidence."
“The ripening of that wholesome deed, after a long interval, I am experiencing here in this celestial mansion; yet now it has become limited.
In four months’ time from now, my passing away will take place.”
I shall fall into a terrible hell, utterly and exclusively bitter.
It has four corners and four gates, well-proportioned and measured out in sections;
it is surrounded by iron walls and covered over with iron.
“An iron ground, blazing and filled with heat,
stands there at all times, pervading a hundred leagues on every side.
There, for a long duration, I shall experience painful sensations.”
"And the fruit of evil karma—therefore I grieve intensely," he spoke in these verses.
(67) Therein, "of a bhikkhu wandering" means of a certain bhikkhu who has destroyed the defilements (*kilesa*) as he goes on his alms round.
"A bowl-scouring" refers to oil-cake from which oil is dripping. "Of one who has become upright" [refers to one] regarding those things that cause crookedness, curvature, and deviousness of mind...
"Of one who has attained uprightness through the absence of defilements. "With a serene mind" means with a mind that is thoroughly clarified by faith in the results of kamma.
68–69. "A long interval": the letter *m* is used here for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*);
"long interval" means a long period of time. "And now that is small": and now that fruit of merit, because the kamma has already matured its result, is small and only a slight remnant remains.
The meaning is: "I shall pass away from here before long. Therefore he said, "In four months, the passing away will occur.
This shows that after four months—that is, beyond four months, in the fifth month—my passing away will take place.
"Entirely bitter" means entirely painful because of its nature as an undesirable sphere of contact.
*Attha* means purpose. *Ghora* means dreadful. *Niraya* refers to hell, which has received the name "niraya" because there is no pleasure (*ayo*) here;
having considered that there is no happiness, it is called "niraya. *Papatissaṃ* means "I shall fall. 70.
And since "niraya" here intends the Great Niraya of Avīci, he said "four-cornered," etc., in order to show its specific nature.
In this context, "four-cornered" means having four corners. "Four-doored" means provided with four doors in the four directions.
"Well-proportioned" means well-divided.

"By its parts" means according to its divisions. "Measured" means weighed out. "Enclosed by an iron rampart" means surrounded by a wall made of iron. "Covered over with iron" means closed above by an iron lid.
71–72. Endowed with splendor, they are filled on all sides with a great mass of flames that has arisen; they are possessed of a continuous network of fire.
"A hundred yojanas all around" means thus, on the outside in every direction for a hundred yojanas—a hundred yojanas in each direction.
"At all times" means at all seasons. "Pervading and remaining" means spreading out and remaining. "Therein" means in that Great Niraya hell.
"I shall know; I will know; I shall experience. Regarding "the fruit of evil karma": the meaning is that such an experience of suffering is indeed the fruit of the evil deed committed in this way.
Thus, when the fruit of the deeds she herself had done and the future terror of hell were made manifest to her, that lay follower, his mind impelled by compassion—
Thinking, “May I become a support for him,” she said: “O deity, you were born endowed with the excellence of prosperity, having all your desires fulfilled through giving to me alone;
but now, by giving this gift to these lay followers and recollecting the virtues of the Teacher, you will be released from rebirth in hell. Delighted and joyful, that female spirit said, “Excellent!”

Having spoken thus, she satisfied them with divine food and drink, gave them various celestial garments and jewels, and placing a pair of divine cloths in their hands for the sake of the Blessed One, said:
"Venerable Sir, a certain *vimāna*-petī bows her head at the feet of the Blessed One; go to Sāvatthī and [inform] the Teacher in my name."
He sent word saying, "Pay homage," and by the power of his own supernormal might, he brought that ship to the very port they desired on that very day.
Then those merchants, proceeding gradually from that port, reached Sāvatthī, entered the Jeta Grove, and [approached] the Teacher.
Having presented that pair of robes and offered their salutations, they reported the entire matter to the Blessed One from the beginning.
The Teacher, taking that event as the occasion for a discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled company;
that teaching became fruitful for the great multitude. On the following day, those lay disciples [approached] the community headed by the Buddha...
Having given a great alms-offering to the community of monks, they dedicated the merit of that gift to her.
She, passing away from that world of ghosts, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven—a realm resplendent with various jewels—in a golden celestial mansion, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Khallāṭiyā-petivatthu*.
11. Commentary on the Story of the Nāga-Peta.
"An elephant goes first with white [trunk]"—this was spoken concerning two brahmin-petas while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana.
It is said that the Venerable Saṅkicca, having attained Arahantship at the very moment of his tonsure when he was seven years old, remained on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera).
Staying in a forest region together with about thirty bhikkhus, he warded off even death at the hands of those five hundred bandits for the sake of those bhikkhus;
having subdued those bandits and caused them to go forth, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma to those bhikkhus, and at the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus—

They attained arahantship. Then the Venerable Saṅkicca, having completed his full years of training and received full ordination, went with those five hundred bhikkhus to Bārāṇasī and dwelt at Isipatana.
People approached the Elder, and having heard the Dhamma, with hearts full of faith, they gathered in groups along the streets and offered gifts to guests.
They gave. There, a certain lay follower encouraged people to provide regular meals; they established regular meals according to their means.
At that time, in Bārāṇasī, a certain brahmin of wrong view had two sons and one daughter.
Among them, the eldest son was a friend of that lay follower. He took him [with him]...
He went into the presence of the Venerable Saṅkicca. The Venerable Saṅkicca taught him the Dhamma, and his mind became softened.
Then that lay follower said to him, “Give a regular meal to one bhikkhu.
“It is not customary for us brahmins to give a regular meal to ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan son; therefore, I will not give one.”
“Will you not give me food as well? he asked. “How could I not give it? he replied.
“If that is so, then give to one bhikkhu whatever you give to me. Having consented with “Very well,” on the following day at dawn, he went to the monastery, brought a bhikkhu back, and fed him.

As time passed in this way, having observed the practice of the bhikkhus and heard the Dhamma, his younger brother and sister became deeply devoted to the Teaching and delighted in performing meritorious deeds.
Thus, those three people, according to their means, gave gifts and honored, respected, esteemed, and worshipped recluses and brahmins. Their parents...
However, they became faithless, lacking confidence, disrespectful toward recluses and brahmins, indifferent to the performance of meritorious deeds, and devoid of desire for them.
Their kinsmen sought a young girl as a wife for their nephew.
But he, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Venerable Saṅkicca, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; he went forth into homelessness and constantly resided at his mother’s house.
He went to eat. His mother seduced him with her own nephew’s daughter. Because of this, he became distressed;
having approached his preceptor, he said, “Venerable sir, I shall renounce the homeless life; please grant me permission.
Seeing his excellence of spiritual potential (*upanissaya-sampatti*), the preceptor said, “Novice, wait for just one month.”
Saying, "Very well," he gave his consent. When a month had passed, he reported [the matter] in the same way.
The preceptor said again, "Wait for another half-month. When half a month had passed, when he was told the same thing again, [the preceptor] said, "Wait for seven days.
He replied, "Very well. Then, within those seven days, the roof of the novice's maternal aunt's house collapsed.
An old, dilapidated house, battered by wind and rain, collapsed. Therein, the brahmin, the brahmin woman, their two sons, and their daughter were overwhelmed by the falling debris and died.
Among them, the brahmin and the brahmin woman were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), while the two sons and the daughter were reborn among the earth-deities (bhummadevas).
Among those [deities], an elephant-vehicle manifested for the eldest son, and for the youngest...
A chariot drawn by mules, and for his daughter, a golden palanquin. Then the brahmin and the brahmin woman, each seizing a massive iron mallet, strike one another;
at the points where they are struck, great boils the size of jars arise, which in a mere moment become inflamed and burst open. They then tear at each other’s boils.
Overcome by anger and devoid of compassion, they tormented him with harsh words and drank his pus and blood, yet they found no satisfaction.
Then the novice, overcome by homesickness, approached his preceptor and said, "Venerable sir, the days for which I promised have passed;
I shall go home, please grant me permission. Thereupon the preceptor said to him, "When the sun has set..."
Having said, "Come on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight when it occurs," he walked a short distance along the back of the Isipatana monastery and stood there.
At that time, those two sons of gods were traveling along that same path with their sister to attend the assembly of yakkhas; meanwhile, their parents stood with mallets in their hands.
Those of harsh speech— black in form, with masses of disheveled, coarse hair falling about them, resembling palm trunks scorched by fire, dripping with pus and blood,
their limbs contorted— followed after him, appearing utterly loathsome and terrifying to behold.
Then the Venerable Saṅkicca performed such a feat of psychic power that the novice saw all of them as they went along.
Having made this arrangement, he said to the novice: "Novice, do you see these people going?
"Yes, venerable sir, I see them. "In that case, ask them about the deed they have done. He then questioned those traveling by elephant-vehicle and so forth in succession.
They said to him: "Ask those deceased ones who are coming from behind."
The novice addressed those departed ones with verses:
“Before him goes a white elephant, and in the middle a chariot drawn by mules;
behind, a maiden is being led in a palanquin, illuminating all ten directions.”
“But you, with clubs in hand, weeping-faced, with limbs cut and mangled—being human beings, what evil did you do that you drink each other’s blood?
Therein, *purato* means first of all. *Setena* means white. *Paleti* means goes. *Majjhe pana* means however, in the middle.
"Between one mounted on an elephant and one mounted on a palanquin. Regarding "with a chariot drawn by mules":
the construction is that he fled by means of a chariot yoked with mules. "Is led away" means he is carried off. "Illuminating all ten directions in every way":

illuminating and shining forth in every direction—that is, all around—the ten directions with the radiance of her own body as well as the radiance of her garments, ornaments, and so forth. "With clubs in their hands."
Those whose hands (pāṇi) hold clubs (muggara) are "those with clubs in hand.
Since the term *pāṇi* is applicable to the hands in contexts such as "smoothing the ground," the word *hasta* (hand) is used here specifically to qualify *pāṇi*.
"With limbs cut and shattered" means their bodies were cut and shattered here and there by the blows of the clubs. "Drink! means "drink."
Thus questioned by the novice,
those petas replied with all that account in four verses:
“He who goes ahead on a white elephant, a noble tusker with four tusks;”
Our eldest son was he who, having given gifts, now rejoices in happiness.
He who was our middle son, traveling in the midst on a chariot drawn by four well-trained mules, shines forth as a generous master of giving, free from stinginess. Our middle son was he.
“She who was later carried away in a palanquin, a wise woman with eyes like a deer’s—she was our youngest daughter;
sharing half a portion [of the merit], she rejoices in happiness.
And these gifts they gave in the past, with hearts full of faith, to ascetics and brahmins.”
"But we were miserly, revilers of recluses and brahmins;
while they give and enjoy themselves, we shall wither away like a cut reed.
(75) Therein, "he who goes ahead" means he who goes in front of these as they walk. "He who [goes] ahead..."
Alternatively, there is the reading “gacchati,” which means “he who goes before.
“By elephant” (kuñjarena) means by the one named “elephant” (kuñjara), because he wears out the earth (kuṃ pathaviṃ jīrayati), or because he delights in or moves among forest thickets (kuñjesu).

“By the Nāga” (nāgena): it is called a “Nāga” because there is nothing that is not to be approached or not to be overcome by him; thus, “by that Nāga. “In a fourfold gait” (catukkamena) means with four feet. “The eldest” (jeṭṭhaka) means the one born first.
76–77. *Catubbhi*: by means of four mules. *Suvaggitena*: with a beautiful gait, that is, with a graceful movement. *Migamaṇḍalocanā*:
having eyes like those of a doe, with glances as gentle as a female deer’s. *Bhāgaḍḍhabhāgena*: by means of half a portion;

that is, by the giving of half a share from the portion she herself had received, acting as the cause. *Sukhī*: happy (feminine). This is stated using a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).

78. "Abusers" means those who revile. "Sporting" means they cause their own faculties to move hither and thither at will among the divine strands of sensual pleasure, or they cause their attendants to provide service for them through the natural outflow of their own merit.
"And we shall wither like a cut reed" means that we, however, shall be like a reed cut down and cast into the sun.
“We shall wither away; let us become parched and utterly dried up by hunger and thirst, and by the blows of one another’s sticks.
Having thus confessed their own evil deeds, they declared, “We are your maternal uncles and aunts.
Upon hearing this, the novice, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency, thought: “How indeed can these evildoers eat?”
Asking, "Are you attaining success?", he said:
"What is your food, what is your bed, and how do you subsist, O you of most evil nature?
Having abandoned the happiness found in abundant and inexhaustible wealth, you have now fallen into suffering."
He spoke this verse. In it, "What is your food? means what kind of food do you have?
"What is your bed? means what kind of bed? Some read "kiṃ sayānā," which means what kind of beds, or in what kind of beds do you sleep?
"And how do you subsist? means in what manner do you subsist; there is also the reading "kathaṃ vo yāpetha," meaning how do you maintain yourselves?
The meaning is: "you shall live. *Supāpadhammino* means those whose nature is exceedingly and utterly evil.
*Pahūtabhogesu* means while there exist abundant and magnificent enjoyments that are limitless. *Anappakesu* means not few, but many.
*Sukhaṃ virādhāya* means having failed and missed out on happiness by not performing the merit that is the cause of happiness. [The phrase] "by the failure of happiness" (*sukhassa virādhenā*)...
Some read it thus: "Dukkhajja pattā" means "having today, now, arrived at this suffering included within the realm of the hungry ghosts.
Thus, being questioned by the novice, the hungry ghosts, answering the matter asked about, said:
"Having slaughtered one another, we drink pus and blood; ... [the rest of the verse]"
“Though we have acquired much, we are not its owners, nor do we enjoy it.
Thus do mortals lament, those who, having died, stand before Yama as non-givers— those who,
having understood and acquired wealth, neither enjoy it nor perform meritorious deeds.
“Having arrived at another world overcome by hunger and thirst, they later burn for a long time as they meditate [on their past].
Having performed deeds that were difficult to endure, they experience suffering with bitter fruits.
For wealth and grain are transient, and life here is transient.”
“Having understood the impermanent as impermanent, a wise person should make an island for themselves.
Those people who understand this, being skilled in the Dhamma,
do not neglect giving after hearing the words of the Arahants.”
They spoke five verses.
(80–81) Therein, “we are not sated” means we are not satisfied or satiated.
“We do not desire it” means we do not find pleasure in it, we do not produce a liking for it; the meaning is that we will not drink it by our own choice. “In this very way” means exactly so.
"Deathless beings lament" means that like us, other humans who have committed evil deeds also lament and wail.

"Non-givers" means those of a stingy nature, lacking the habit of giving. "Those who abide in Yama's realm" means those whose nature it is to dwell in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), which is known as the realm of Yama.
"Those who, having known and acquired wealth" refers to those things which provide various forms of happiness both in the present and in the future.
"Having enjoyed and obtained enjoyments"—they do not consume them, nor do they perform meritorious deeds;
like us, they themselves do not eat, and by giving to others, they do not even perform the merit consisting of generosity.
82. "They have arrived at hunger and thirst in the other world"—those beings, in the other world, in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), are overcome by hunger and thirst.

"Having sacrificed. "They meditate while burning" means they burn—meaning they lament—while being consumed by the fire of suffering caused by hunger and the like, and by the fire of remorse consisting of such thoughts as, "Alas, we have not done what is wholesome;
we have done evil. "Yielding bitter fruit" means having painful karmic results. "They experience suffering" means they undergo the pain.
Having performed evil kamma that yields undesirable results, they experience suffering for a long time—the suffering of the woeful states.
83–84. *Ittara* means not lasting for a long time; it is impermanent and subject to change.
"Life here is short" means that even the life of beings here in this human world is short, limited, and meager. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Whoever..."

“He lives long, for a hundred years or even more. “Knowing the limited as limited” means that, having investigated with wisdom, one understands that the requisites such as wealth and grain, as well as the life of human beings, are limited, scant, momentary, and do not last long.
“A wise man should make an island” means that a person possessed of wisdom should create an island—a firm footing for himself and a basis for welfare and happiness in the world beyond.
One should act thus. "Those who understand in this way" refers to those people who know, as it truly is, the transitory nature of human wealth and life;

they never neglect giving. "Having heard the word of the Arahants" means having heard the speech of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others; the sense is "because it has been heard. The rest is self-evident.
Thus, when questioned by the novice, those ghosts explained the matter to him and declared, "We are your maternal uncle and his wife.
Upon hearing this, the novice was moved with a sense of urgency;
he dispelled his weariness and, prostrating himself at the feet of his preceptor, spoke thus: "Venerable sir, that which ought to be done out of compassion—out of compassion..."
“Having relied on you, this has been done for me by you; indeed, I have been protected from a great calamity.
Now I have no further need for the household life; I shall delight in living the holy life. Then the Venerable Saṅkicca explained a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable to his disposition.
As he devoted himself to that meditation subject, in no long time he attained Arahantship. The Venerable...
Then Saṅkicca reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. The Teacher, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled company;
that teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Nāgapeta-vatthu*.

12. The Commentary on the Story of the Snake-Peta (*Uragapetavatthu*) "Like a snake casting off its old skin"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*).
It is said that in Sāvatthī, the son of a certain lay follower passed away. On account of his son's death, he...
Overcome by lamentation and grief, he went outside but, unable to perform any work, remained right there at home.
Then, at the hour of dawn, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw that lay follower.
Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he went to that man’s house.
He stood at the gate. The lay follower, hearing that the Teacher had arrived, rose quickly, went out, and met him halfway.
Taking the bowl from his hand, he led him into the house, prepared a seat, and offered it.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The lay follower, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. The Blessed One asked him: “What...?”
“Lay follower, you appear as if overcome by grief,” he said. “Yes, Blessed One, my beloved son has died;
that is why I am grieving. Then the Blessed One, dispelling his sorrow, related the Uragajātaka.
It is said that in the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in Bārāṇasī, there was a brahmin family named Dhammapāla. There lived a brahmin...
The Brahmin’s son, daughter, daughter-in-law, and slave-girl—all of them became devoted to the cultivation of the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*).
Whenever one among them departed from the house, he would depart without looking back, after having exhorted the remaining people.
Then one day, the Brahmin went out from the house with his son, went to the field, and was plowing. The son [gathered] dry grass, leaves, and wood.
He smeared [the ground]. There, a certain black snake, emerging from the hollow of a tree out of fear of the heat, bit this son of the brahmin.
Overwhelmed by the force of the poison, he fell right there and died, reborn as Sakka, the king of the devas.
Seeing his son dead, the brahmin saw a man passing by near his field of labor.
He spoke thus: "Friend, go to my house and say to the brahmin lady:
'Having bathed and dressed in clean clothes, take food for one person along with garlands, perfumes, and so forth, and come quickly.
He went there and delivered the message accordingly; the members of the household also did as instructed. Having bathed, eaten, anointed himself, and being surrounded by his attendants, the brahmin—

Having placed his son’s body upon the funeral pyre and applied the fire, he stood there free from grief and free from anguish, reflecting on the perception of impermanence as if burning a mere log of wood.
Then the Brahmin’s son was reborn as Sakka; he was none other than our Bodhisatta. He [Sakka], his own...
Reflecting upon his former birth and the merit he had performed, and out of compassion for his father and kinsmen, he came there in the guise of a brahmin.
Seeing that his kinsmen were not grieving, he said, "Ho! Burn this deer and give us its meat; I am hungry.
They replied, "This is no deer, brahmins; it is a human being. He asked, "Is he an enemy of yours?"
“He is no enemy, but a son born of your own breast, full of great virtues, your young child,” he said.
“For what reason do you not grieve for such a virtuous young son who has died? Hearing this, the brahmin spoke the reason for his lack of grief:
“Just as a snake casts off its worn-out skin and goes on, so does he leave his body behind.”
Thus, when the body is lifeless, deceased, and dead:
“Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore I do not weep for him, for he has gone to whatever destination is his.”
He spoke two verses (85–86).
Therein, "uraga" means one who moves by the belly; this is a designation for a snake.
"Tacaṃ jiṇṇaṃ" means his own old, worn-out, and ancient skin, the slough. "Hitvā gacchati saṃ tanuṃ" means that he goes away, casting it off, just as...
Just as a snake, like one shedding its old skin from between the trees,
between logs, between roots, or between rocks, casts it off from its body, abandons it, and discards it, then goes wherever it pleases; even so,
a being wandering through saṃsāra, because of the exhaustion of former karma, [discards] that which has become worn out.
"Having abandoned his own body, he goes"—the meaning is that he goes according to his karma; he is reborn by way of renewed existence (*punabbhava*).

He said "thus" while showing the son's burning body. "When the body has become devoid of enjoyment"—just as with him, so too when the bodies of others have likewise become useless, being bereft of enjoyment.
"A ghost (*peta*)"—one from whom life-force (*āyu*), heat (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have departed.
"Kālakate sati" means when the conviction that [he] has died has arisen. "Therefore" (*tasmā*):

because the burning body, due to the departure of consciousness, does not perceive even the weeping and lamentation of relatives—just as it does not feel the pain of the burning—therefore, making this my son the cause, I do not weep.
"He has gone to his destination" (*gato so tassa yā gati*): if deceased beings are not annihilated, then for one who has died and has made room [for rebirth],...
By the power of his karma, he has gone to whatever destination was to be expected immediately after death;

he does not look back for the sake of the weeping and lamentation of his former relatives, nor is there generally any accomplishment of purpose through the weeping of former relatives—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, when the Brahmin had stated the reason for his own lack of sorrow and had demonstrated his skill in the method of mental attention, the one in the form of a Brahmin...
Sakka said to the brahmin woman, “Mother, what does he mean to you when he is dead?
“He was my son, master,” she replied, “whom I carried in my womb for ten months, who I suckled with my own milk, and whom I raised by forming his hands and feet.
“If that is so, let the father at least not weep, being a man; but the heart of a mother is tender—why do you not weep?”
Having heard that, she spoke of the reason for her weeping:
“He came from there uninvited, and he departed from here without permission;
as he came, so he went—what cause for lamentation is there in that?”
“Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore I do not weep for him, for he has gone to whatever destination belongs to him.
He spoke these two verses. Therein, *anabbhito* means uninvited, [as in the thought]: “Come, enter into the state of being my son.”
"Thus summoned": from "there," meaning from that other world where he previously resided; "came" means he arrived. "Not permitted" means not authorized;
it means he was not dismissed by us with the words, "Go, dear one, to the other world.
"From here" means from this world; "gone" means departed. "In the manner he came" means in whatever way he arrived—that is, he arrived precisely without being bid farewell by us.
"Tathāgata" means gone in that very same manner. Just as he came by his own karma, so too has he gone by his own karma;

by this, he demonstrates the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā*). In that regard, what lamentation? He shows that when the process of saṃsāra is thus devoid of mastery, what kind of lamentation could there be concerning death? It is improper for a wise person and should not be performed.
Having heard these words of the brahmin woman, he asked her sister, "Mother, what is he to you?
"He is my brother, master," she replied. "Mother, sisters indeed feel affection for their brothers; why then do you not weep?
She too, explaining the reason for her lack of tears, said:
“If I were to weep, for whom would it be? What fruit would there be for me in that?
My kinsmen, friends, and companions would only feel greater distress.
One who is burning with grief does not perceive the lamentations of their kin.”
"Therefore, I do not weep for this; he has gone to whatever destination is his. Thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "If I were to weep, I would become thin"—if I were to weep, I would become emaciated with a parched body.
"What fruit would there be for me in that?"—what benefit would there be for me in weeping on account of my brother's death?

What fruit or what benefit would there be? The intention is: "My brother would not have come back because of that, nor would he have gone to a happy destination because of it. Regarding the words "there would be even more distress for our kinsmen, friends, and dear ones":
through my grieving, there would be even greater distress and sorrow for our relatives, friends, and dear companions than the suffering caused by my brother’s death.
Having heard these words of his sister, he asked her husband, "What is he to you? "He is my husband, master," she replied.
"My dear lady, women are indeed full of affection for their husbands; when he has died, they become widows and destitute.
Why then do you not weep? She too, explaining the reason for her lack of tears, said:
“Just as a child cries out after the moon as it moves away,
so too is he who grieves for the deceased. Burning with grief,
he does not perceive the lamentations of his kinsmen.”
"Therefore, I do not weep for this, for he has gone to whatever destination is his"—thus he spoke these two verses.
Therein, "the child" refers to a young boy. "The moon" refers to the lunar disc. "Going" means rising up into the sky.
"He weeps after it" means he cries out, "Take my chariot wheel and give it to me! "In this very manner" refers to that which is thus accomplished.

He grieves for the dead; this grieving of his is of such a nature and of such a kind as the desire of one traveling through the sky to seize the moon—it is the intention that it is a longing for an unattainable object.
Having thus heard the words of his wife, he asked the slave-girl: "Mother, what is he to you? "My lord..."

“Master, [he did]. “If that is so, then he must have beaten you and made you perform services; therefore, I suppose you do not weep thinking, ‘I am well rid of him’? “Master, do not speak thus to me. This is not fitting;
my noble son is exceedingly endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, and speaks what is appropriate—he is like a son raised upon my breast.”
...as it were. Then, [asked] “Why do you not weep? she too, explaining the reason for her not weeping, said:
“Just as a water-pot, O Brahmā, that is broken cannot be rejoined, even so is this for one who grieves for a deceased person.”
“Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives;
therefore I do not weep for him, for he has gone to whatever destination is his. He spoke these two verses.
Therein, “Just as a water-bubble, O Brahmin, when burst, is without reconnection”—thus [he spoke]. To the Brahmin:
Just as a water jar, once broken by a blow from a mallet or similar cause, cannot return to its original state without being reassembled;
the rest here is of plain meaning because it follows the method already explained.
Having heard their words, Sakka, with a mind full of faith, said: "Truly, you have cultivated mindfulness of death correctly. From this..."
"From this day forward, you have no need for the work of plowing and so forth. Having thus filled their house with the seven kinds of jewels, he exhorted them, saying, "Be diligent;

give alms, observe moral discipline, and perform the Uposatha rites," and having entrusted himself to them, he returned to his own place. Those brahmins and others [then practiced] meritorious deeds such as giving.
Having lived out their full lifespan while performing these deeds, they were reborn in the world of the gods.

The Teacher, having related this Jātaka, extracted the dart of sorrow from that lay follower and proclaimed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The commentary on the Uraga Petavatthu is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the first chapter,
the Uraga-vagga, adorned with twelve stories,
within the Petavatthu of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā.
2. Ubbarivagga 1.
Saṃsāramocakapetivatthu-vaṇṇanā: "Naked and of ugly form...
This was spoken while the Teacher was dwelling at Veḷuvana in the kingdom of Magadha, at the place named Iṭṭhakavati.
This was spoken with reference to a certain peta in a village. It is said that in the kingdom of Magadha there were two villages named Iṭṭhakavatī and Dīgharājī;
there, many proponents of the "Liberation from Saṃsāra" (saṃsāramocaka) who held wrong views resided.
And in times past, at the end of five hundred years, a certain woman [died] right there in Iṭṭhakavatī.

Having been reborn in a family of those who liberate [animals] from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-mocaka*), she deprived many insects and moths of life through wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) and was reborn among the hungry ghosts (*peta*).

After experiencing the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth for five hundred years, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, she eventually came to reside at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha. Furthermore...
Having been reborn right there in Iṭṭhakavati in a certain family of Saṃsāramocakas,
when she reached the age of seven or eight years and was capable of playing with other girls in the street, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera—
residing at that very time in the Aruṇavatī Monastery, depending on that same village— was one day [accompanied] by twelve bhikkhus.
He passed along the road near the gate of that village.

At that moment, many village girls who had come out from the village and were playing near the gate, their minds filled with faith, rushed forward upon seeing the conduct of their parents and paid homage to the Elder and the other monks by prostrating themselves on their five limbs. Now, this [event occurred] in a family lacking in faith...
For a long time, due to her lack of familiarity with wholesome qualities, she remained like one devoid of the conduct of the virtuous, disrespectful, and unfortunate.
The Elder, seeing her past conduct, her current birth in a family that liberates beings from *saṃsāra*, and her future destiny to be reborn in hell, thought:
"If she pays homage to me, she will not be reborn in hell, but among the *petas*."
Knowing that even after being reborn she would obtain prosperity only by relying on him,
his mind was stirred by compassion and he said to those girls, "You all pay homage to the bhikkhus, but this girl stands here as if she were unfortunate.
Then those girls took her by both hands, pulled her forward, and made her forcibly prostrate at the feet of the Elder.
At a later time, having reached maturity, she was given in marriage to a certain youth from a family of long-standing *saṃsāra*-liberators.
When her pregnancy was fully developed, she died and was reborn among the *petas*.
Wandering about naked, hideous in form, overcome by hunger and thirst, and exceedingly loathsome to behold, she showed herself to the Venerable Elder Sāriputta one night.
She stood to one side. Seeing her, the Elder said:
“You are naked, ill-favored in form, emaciated, with veins showing all over;
you are pale and thin—what are you doing standing here?”
He asked with a verse. In that context, "covered with veins" means having limbs spread over with networks of veins due to the absence of flesh and blood.
"Upphāsulikā" means those whose buttocks are prominent. "Kisikā" means those with emaciated bodies.

Although she was already called "emaciated" (*kisa*) previously, the repetition of the word "emaciated" (*kisikā*) is stated for the purpose of showing an extreme degree of emaciation, such that her body consists of nothing but bones, skin, and sinews. That...
Having heard this, the female spirit, making herself known, spoke this verse:
"I am a female spirit, venerable sir, miserable, belonging to the world of Yama;
having performed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of spirits. After she had spoken thus, the Elder [replied]:
“What evil have you done by body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what karma have you gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts?

Being thus questioned about the deed she had committed, she spoke three verses, showing that having been stingy and lacking the habit of giving, she had been reborn in the womb of a hungry ghost and was now experiencing such great suffering:
“Bhante, there were none who had compassion for me— not my father, nor my mother,
nor even my kinsmen— who might have urged me, ‘Give this gift with a clear heart to the recluses and brahmins.
For five hundred years from now, I shall wander about naked in such a manner.”
“Devouring by hunger and thirst, this is the fruit of my evil deed.
‘I bow to you, noble sir, with a clear heart; have compassion for me, O hero of great power!
Grant me whatever you can and instruct me; deliver me from the miserable states, O Blessed One.’”
98. In this context, "compassionate" (*anukampaka*) means those who favor one with regard to the welfare of the future life. "Wandering about" (*bhanta*) is an address to the Elder.

"Those who would urge me" (*ye maṃ niyojeyyuṃ*): whether it be mother, father, or kinsmen, such compassionate ones who, having become clear-minded, would urge me, saying, "Give alms to the recluses and brahmins"—the construction is that there were no such compassionate ones for me.

99. "For five hundred years from now, since I wander about naked in such a state"—this the female ghost (petī) said with the intention that, having recollected her own existence as a ghost during her third previous birth, she was wandering in that same way even now for five hundred years.
In this context, "since" (*yata*) means because; she is a naked ghost of such a kind because she failed to perform meritorious deeds such as giving.
The construction is: "Having sacrificed [this], from now on I shall wander for five hundred years. "By craving" means by thirst;
"being devoured" means being consumed, which is to say, being afflicted.
"I revere you, noble sir, with a serene mind": O noble sir, having become one whose mind is serene, I revere you—only this much [is meant].
He shows that he is now able to perform a meritorious deed. "Have compassion for me" means: show favor toward me; have pity on my account.
And after giving, "point out to me whatever [there may be]" means:
having given some small gift to ascetics and brahmins, point out that merit to me, with the intention that by means of it there will be liberation for me from this state of existence as a peta.
He speaks. For this very reason he said, "Release me from an evil destiny, O Venerable One.
When the female ghost had spoken thus, the compilers of the collection uttered three verses to show how that elder acted in response:
"Having promised 'So be it,' the compassionate Sāriputta..."
Having given a morsel of food to the bhikkhus, a cloth the size of a hand,
and water from his bowl, he dedicated the merit to her:
"Immediately after the dedication was made, the result arose."
“Food, clothing, and drink— this is the fruit of a donation. “Thereupon,
pure and dressed in clean garments, wearing the finest Kāsī cloth,
adorned with variegated raiment and ornaments, she approached Sāriputta.”
101–103. Regarding the phrase "there, to the monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ*): this is stated with a grammatical shift (vacanavipallāsa) for the singular "to a monk" (*bhikkhuno*).
Some read, "having given a mouthful to a monk. "Mouthful" (*ālopa*) means a morsel; the meaning is a meal consisting of only a single mouthful.
"And a cloth the size of a hand" means a piece of cloth measuring one hand. "And water in a bowl" means just enough to fill a single bowl.
[The offering was] water. The rest is exactly as described in the *Khallāṭiya-petavatthu*.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, seeing that peta standing near him with his faculties refreshed, his complexion pure, adorned with celestial garments and ornaments, and illuminating the surroundings with his own radiance, [perceived it] directly.
Desiring to make clear the fruit of that karma, he spoke three verses:
“O deity, you who stand there with such surpassing beauty,
illuminating all directions like a medicinal herb among the stars.”
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those riches arise for you that are dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you become so radiant in power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
(104) In this context, *abhikkantena* means “by that which is exceedingly pleasing,” the sense being “by that which is beautiful. *Vaṇṇena* means “by the color of the skin.
*Obhāsentī disā sabbā* means illuminating all ten directions, making them bright and creating a single expanse of light. To explain how this is so, he said: [as follows].

“Like a medicinal herb among the stars. Just as a star, having received the name “medicinal herb” (osadhī) because its abundant radiance is sustained by it, or because it provides support to medicinal herbs, remains making light all around;
even so, you illuminate all directions—this is the meaning.
105. *Kenā* is the word *kiṃ* used in the sense of a question. This instrumental case is used here in the sense of a cause; thus, the meaning is "by what cause. *Te* means "your.
*Etādiso* means "of such a kind," which is to say, "just as it is seen now. *Kena te idha mijjhati* means:
by what specific merit does that fruit of good conduct, which is being obtained by you right now in this place, succeed?

It comes to fruition. "Arise" means they are produced. "Wealth" refers to specific possessions such as clothing, ornaments, and so forth, which have received the name "wealth" in the sense of being objects for enjoyment. "Whatever there may be" includes all wealth without exception;
for this expression is all-encompassing, just like the phrase "whatever formations there may be. "Dear to the mind" means [dear] by the mind...
"Piyāyitabbā" means "to be cherished," that is, "beloved.
"Pucchāmi" means "I ask"; the sense is "I desire to know. "Taṃ" means "you. "Devī" refers to one who possesses a divine state; thus she is called "devi.
Therefore he said, "O lady of great power (mahānubhāve). "Manussabhūtā" means born among humans and having attained the human state.
This was said because, for the most part, beings established in the human state perform meritorious deeds.
This is the meaning of these verses in brief; however, it should be understood in detail according to the method explained in the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Vimānavatthu*.
Thus questioned again by the Elder, the female spirit, explaining the cause for her attainment of that state,
spoke the remaining verses: “Emaciated, wasted, hungry, naked, with skin fallen away—
the compassionate Sage in the world saw me there, so miserable.”
“Having given a mouthful of food to the bhikkhus, a mere handful of cloth, and water for the bowl, he dedicated this gift to me.
Behold the fruit of that single mouthful: for one thousand years, he enjoyed a meal.”
"I eat at will, enjoying many kinds of flavors and sauces.
Behold the kind of result that comes from a mere handful of cloth:
it covers as much as all the royal garments found within the realm of King Nanda."
“Even more numerous than those, O Bhante,
were my garments for clothing— silk, wool, linen, and cotton.
Vast and of great value, they hung suspended in the air.”
I burn that which is dear to the mind.
Behold the kind of ripening that comes from water in a shallow bowl:
