deep, four-cornered, and well-fashioned lotus ponds.
“With clear water, well-established, cool, and free from foul odors;
covered with lotuses and water-lilies, and filled with the pollen of the water-flowers.
Therein I delight, sport, and rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.”
“Venerable sir, we have come to pay homage to the Sage, the compassionate one in the world.
(107) In this context: *uppaṇḍukin* means one who has become pale. *Chāta* means hungry, overcome by hunger.
*Sampatitacchavin* means one whose skin on the body is torn and broken. *Loke*—this refers to the compassion mentioned here in the word “compassionate.”
"Beholding the object": "to me who am such"—that is, to me who, according to the method already stated, am exclusively a fit object for compassion.
"Faring ill" means having gone to a miserable state of existence (*duggati*). 108–109.
"Having given a mouthful of food to the bhikkhus," etc., is the Elder’s demonstration of the manner in which he acted out of compassion. In this regard:
“Food” (*bhatta*) means rice (*odana*); the meaning is “divine food. “A hundred years and ten” (*vassasataṃ dasa*) means ten hundred years; thus, “a thousand years” is what is intended.

This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). “I eat, being one who desires her at will, with many-flavored condiments” (*bhuñjāmi kāmakāminī anekarasabyañjanaṃ*):
the construction is, “I eat food with many-flavored condiments, endowed with other desirable objects of desire as well.”
110. "Coḷassa" (of the cloth): by means of this term for the object to be given, he shows specifically the merit consisting of giving pertaining to that [object].
"See what kind of ripening" means: see, venerable sir, the fruit reckoned as the ripening of that gift of cloth.
As to what kind—that is, of what nature—it is, he said: "As great as was [the merit] of King Nanda," and so forth.

In this regard, who was this one named King Nanda? It is said that in the past, when the lifespan of humans was ten thousand years, a certain householder living in Bārāṇasī, while wandering for exercise in the forest, saw a certain Paccekabuddha in a forest clearing.
That Paccekabuddha, while performing work on his robe there, folded it up because the wind was not blowing.
He began to set it aside. When the householder saw him, he asked, "Venerable sir, what are you doing?
Although the Paccekabuddha said nothing because of his fewness of desires, the householder understood from the context that there was not enough cloth for a robe.
He placed his own upper robe at the feet of the Paccekabuddha and departed. The Paccekabuddha took it and, while ascending the windward slope, fashioned it into a robe.
He donned it. At the end of his life, that householder passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
there, having enjoyed celestial prosperity for the duration of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in a minister’s family in a certain village a yojana away from Bārāṇasī.
When he reached the age of maturity, a festival was proclaimed in that village.
He said to his mother, "Mother, give me a garment; I shall play at the festival. She brought out a well-washed cloth and gave it to him.
"Mother, this is too coarse," he said. She brought out another and gave it to him, but he rejected that as well. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son..."
"In such a house as we were born into, there is no merit for us to obtain clothing finer than this.
"I shall go to a place where gain is possible, mother. "Go, my son; I desire for you the attainment of the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day.
Saying, "Very well, mother," he paid homage to his mother and circumambulated her.
He said, "I am going, mother. "Go, dear son," she replied. It was thought by her: "Where will he go?

He will sit here or there in the house. But urged on by the force of his merit, he departed from the village, went to Bārāṇasī, and lay down with his head covered upon the auspicious stone slab. And that king of Bārāṇasī...
It was the seventh day after the king had passed away.
Having performed the funeral rites for the king, the ministers and the chaplain sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated:
"The king has one daughter but no son; a kingdom without a king does not endure. Let us dispatch the chariot of Phussa."

Having yoked those four horses, white as white water-lilies, and having placed the fivefold royal regalia—headed by the white parasol—right upon the chariot, they released the chariot and had musical instruments played behind it.
The chariot went out through the eastern gate and headed toward the pleasure garden. "He is going toward the garden because of his familiarity with it."
"Let us turn back," some said. The chaplain said, "Do not turn back. The chariot, having circumambulated the prince and being ready for him to mount, stood still;
the chaplain, pulling back the corner of his upper garment and gazing at the soles of the prince's feet, thought, "May this island remain [for him];
may he exercise sole sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands."
Having said, "It is joined," he had the musical instruments struck three times, saying, "Play! Play again!
Then the prince opened his mouth, looked out, and asked, "For what purpose have you come, dear ones?
"Your Majesty, the kingdom has come to you. "Where is your king? "He has passed away, sire. "How many..."
“Have the days passed? “Today is the seventh day. “Do you have no son or daughter?
“I have a daughter, Your Majesty, but no son. “In that case, I shall rule the kingdom.
They immediately prepared a consecration pavilion, adorned the princess with all her ornaments, brought her to the park, and performed the consecration for the prince.
Then, when he had been consecrated, they presented him with a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
He asked, "What is this, dear sirs? "It is a lower garment, Your Majesty. "Is it not, dear sirs, too thick?
"There is nothing finer than this among garments used by humans, Your Majesty. "Does your king wear such a garment? "Yes, Your Majesty."
“I do not think your king is meritorious; bring a golden pitcher, and you shall obtain a robe.
They brought a golden pitcher. He rose, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, took water in his hand, and sprinkled it toward the eastern direction.
Then, having split the solid earth, eight wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) emerged.
They sprang up. Again, taking water, they sprinkled it in the four directions—south, west, north, and east.
In all directions, thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) sprang up, eight in each direction.
Some say that sixty-four work-trees (*kammarukkha*) sprang up, sixteen in each direction. He [took] one divine cloth...
Having dressed himself and put on one robe, he said, "Let the drums be beaten throughout King Nanda’s realm, proclaiming that no women shall spin thread. Then,
raising his parasol and adorned with finery, he mounted the back of a noble elephant,
entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.
As time passed in this manner, one day the queen, seeing the king’s prosperity, showed an expression of compassion, saying, "Oh, what an ascetic [this is].
When asked, "What is this, O Queen?", she replied, "Your majesty, your prosperity is indeed very great. In the past you did not perform wholesome deeds;
now you do not perform wholesome deeds for the sake of the future. [The king asked: "To whom shall we give?"
“There are no virtuous ones,” he said. “Your Majesty, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants;
you should simply prepare the alms-offering, and I shall find the Arahants,” she replied. On the following day, the king had a magnificent almsgiving prepared.
The queen made this resolve: “If there are Arahants in this direction, let them come here and accept our alms.”
She lay down on her chest, facing the northern direction.
As soon as the queen had lain down, Mahāpaduma Paccekabuddha—the eldest of five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were sons of Padumavatī living in the Himālayas—addressed his younger brothers:
"Friends, King Nanda invites you; please accept his invitation. Having accepted, they departed.
At that very moment, they arrived through the air and descended at the northern gate. People informed the king, "Your Majesty, five hundred paccekabuddhas have arrived.
The king, together with his queen, went out, paid homage, took their bowls, and had the paccekabuddhas ascend the palace.
There he gave them alms; at the conclusion of the meal, the king [addressed] the senior of the Saṅgha.
The queen prostrated herself at the feet of the new members of the Saṅgha and made this request: “Noble ones, may you not be burdened by the requisites;
may we not be diminished in our merit. Grant us your promise to dwell here. Having obtained their promise, she had residences built in the park for them.
She attended upon the Paccekabuddhas for as long as she lived, and when they had attained final Nibbāna, she celebrated the festival of the relics.

Having had the funeral rites for the body performed with fragrant wood and other materials, and having taken the relics and established a cetiya, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking:
"If even such great and powerful noble ladies must die, how much more so those like me?
He then installed his eldest son on the throne and himself went forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller. The queen as well—

Thinking, “What shall I do now that the king has gone forth? she went forth as well. Both of them, while dwelling in the pleasure groves, developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and spent their time in the bliss of those absorptions;
at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Brahma-world.
It is said that King Nanda was none other than our Teacher’s great disciple, the Elder Mahākassapa, and his chief queen was named Bhaddā Kāpilānī.
Furthermore, this King Nanda, for ten thousand years, wearing celestial garments himself and making his entire realm resemble Uttarakuru, gave celestial robes to every person who came to him.
It was with reference to this abundance of celestial garments that the peta said: "As far as [the extent] of King Nanda’s realm..."
“Coverings. In this context, “in the conquered realm” means in the kingdom. “Coverings” refers to garments;
for they are called “coverings” because one covers oneself with them. 111.
Now, that female ghost (petī), demonstrating that her own prosperity at present was even more abundant than the prosperity of King Nanda, said:
“Venerable sir, my garments and coverings are far more numerous than those,” he said, beginning with these words.
In this context, “than those” means that my garments and coverings are more numerous even than the garments belonging to the possession of King Nanda.
“Garments and coverings” refers both to lower garments (*nivāsana*) and upper robes (*pārupana*). “Silken and woolen” refers to silks (*koseyya*) and woollen cloths (*kambala*).
"Khomakappāsikāni" means both garments made of *khoma* (linen) and garments made of cotton (*kappāsa*).
"Vipulā" means extensive in length and breadth. "Mahagghā" means great and costly by virtue of their high value.
"Ākāsevalambare" means they remain suspended right in the sky. "Yaṃ yaṃ hi manaso piyaṃ" means whatever is dear to the mind.
The construction is: "Whatever was dear to my mind, taking each of those, I burn them and I wear them.

(113) Regarding the water in the bowl: "Behold the result of what kind it is"—showing that one should behold how great is the result of even the water given and for which gratitude was expressed, being merely enough to fill a bowl—she says: "Deep and square..."
And so he spoke these words, beginning with “deep,” and so forth. Therein, “deep” means bottomless. “Quadrangular” means having a square shape.
“Lotus ponds” means lotus pools (*pokkharaṇī*). “Well-constructed” means well-fashioned by the very power of karma.
“With white water” means having white water and being surrounded by white sand. “With beautiful landing-stairs” means having excellent bathing places. “Cool.”
"Cool water" means water that is cool. "Free from offensive odors" means devoid of repulsive smells and possessing a fragrant scent.
"Filled with lotus filaments" means completely full of water covered by the filaments of lotuses, water-lilies, and so forth.
115. "I" refers to myself. "I delight" means I experience pleasure. "I sport" means I cause my sense faculties to frolic. "I rejoice" means...
"I am delighted by the perfection of my enjoyments. 'Fearless from any quarter' means that, with no fear arising from anywhere, I dwell in happiness and self-mastery.
'Venerable sir, I have come to pay homage' means, venerable sir, I have approached and come here to pay homage to you, who were the cause for the attainment of this divine excellence.
As for whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning, it has already been explained in its respective place."
When the peta had spoken thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, while the inhabitants of the two villages of Iṭṭhakavatī and Dīgharājī were approaching him, explained this matter in detail.
Having stirred them with a sense of urgency and liberated them from the evil karma that binds one to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), he established them in the status of lay followers (upāsaka).
This account became well known among the monks. The monks [reported it to the Blessed One].
They reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company;
that teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the story of the *saṃsāramocaka* peta.
2. Commentary on the Story of the Petī Who Was the Mother of the Elder Sāriputta.

"Exposed, of ugly form"—this was spoken concerning the petī who had been the mother of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta five births prior to this, while the Teacher was dwelling at Veḷuvana. One day, the Venerable Sāriputta...
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Anuruddha, and the Venerable Kappina were dwelling in a certain forest retreat not far from Rājagaha.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin in Bārāṇasī who was wealthy,
possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, serving as a fountain for ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wretched, and beggars.

He gives food, drink, clothing, bedding, and so forth. While giving, he attends to all that is to be offered—beginning with water for the feet and ointment for the feet—to those who arrive at the appropriate time and in a fitting manner;
and before the meal, he respectfully serves the bhikkhus with food, drink, and other necessities.
When he was about to travel to another region, he said to his wife: "Lady, do not neglect this established method of giving."
“Attend upon him with due respect. Having assented with “Very well,” as soon as he had departed, she abolished the method of giving established for the monks.
However, to those travelers who had arrived seeking a place to stay, she showed an old shed discarded behind her house and said, “Stay here.
When the travelers [arrived] there for the sake of food, drink, and so forth—
When they arrived, she spoke harshly, addressing them by name with whatever impure and loathsome things there were, saying: "Eat excrement! Drink urine! Drink blood! Eat the brain of your mother!
Later, having passed away, she was cast into the womb of a peta by the power of her karma and was reborn there. Her own...

Experiencing suffering in accordance with her own verbal misconduct, she recalled her connection to a previous birth and, desiring to approach the Venerable Sāriputta, reached the door of his dwelling. The deities guarding the door of that dwelling prevented her from entering.
It is said that five births prior to this one, she had previously been the Elder’s mother.
Therefore she spoke thus: "I am the mother of the noble Elder Sāriputta from five births ago;
grant me entrance so that I may see the Elder. Having heard this, the deities permitted her entrance.
Having entered and stood at the end of the walking path, she revealed herself to the Elder. Upon seeing her, the Elder, out of compassion—
With his mind thus stirred, he said:
“You are naked, ill-favored in form, emaciated, with veins showing all over;
you are so haggard and so thin—what are you doing standing here?”
She questioned him with a verse. Being thus questioned by the Elder, she gave this reply:
"In former births, I was your mother, O Sakyan;
now reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, I am afflicted by hunger and thirst."
Spit and snot cast away, mucus and rheum;
The blood of those being burned, and the blood of those giving birth;
And the blood of those with wounds, and the blood of those whose noses and heads have been cut off.
“Devoted to God, I eat what depends on the man I desire.
‘I shall eat the pus and blood of cattle and humans;
homeless and houseless, I am devoted to my dark bed.’”
“Give me alms, my dear son;
having given them, dedicate them to me, so that perhaps I may be released from this feeding on pus and blood. Thus she spoke these five verses.
Regarding the phrase “I am your Sakyan mother”: because I was your progenitor, I am your Sakyan mother. Previously, among others...
"Though she was his mother in previous births, it was not in this birth; rather, it was in other previous births—this should be understood as 'five births prior to this.
She has been reborn in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya),' meaning she has entered the world of the *petas* by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
'Overcome by hunger and thirst' means she is overwhelmed by hunger and thirst; the sense is that she is being continuously oppressed by hunger and thirst."
118–119. "Discarded" (*chaḍḍita*) means that which is vomited; this is the meaning. "Spittle" (*khipita*) refers to the impurity that has emerged from the mouth along with what was spat out.
"Saliva" (*kheḷa*) refers to spittle. "Nasal mucus" (*siṅghāṇika*) refers to the impurity that flows from the brain and issues forth through the nostrils.
"Phlegm" (*silesuma*) refers to *semha*. And "fat of those being cremated" refers to the fat of those being burned upon the funeral pyre.
And the fat and oil from corpses; "the blood of those who have given birth" refers to the blood of women who have recently delivered, and by the word "and," it includes the impurities of the womb.
"Of those with wounds" means of those on whom sores have arisen. "Which" connects to "that blood.
"Of those whose noses or heads are severed" means the blood of those whose noses have been cut off or whose heads have been cut off—"that I eat."

The construction [of the compound] is as follows: the phrase “those whose noses have been cut off” (*ghānasīsacchinnānaṃ*) is merely a heading for the teaching, because I consume the blood even of those whose hands, feet, and so forth have been severed.
Likewise, it should be understood that by the term “of the wound-exuding” (*vaṇikānaṃ*), the blood of those [others] is also included.

“Overcome by hunger” (*khudāparetā*) means having been overcome by starvation. “Dependent upon the bodies of women and men” (*itthipurisanissitaṃ*) means dependent upon the physical forms of women and men.
This shows that one makes use of the aforementioned skin, flesh, sinews, pus, and so forth, as well as other such things.
(120–121) "Beasts" (*pasū*) refers to goats, cattle, buffalo, and the like. "Without shelter" (*aleṇā*) means without refuge. "Homeless" (*anagārā*) means without a dwelling.

"Destined for the blue bed" (*nīlamañcaparāyaṇā*) means those whose beds are the filthy couches discarded in the charnel ground. Alternatively, "blue" (*nīla*) refers to the cemetery ground abounding in ashes and charcoal.
The meaning is: "lie upon that very same couch. "Dedicate it for me" means: "dedicate the merit so that the gift given may be beneficial to me;
give the transfer of merit (pattidāna) accordingly. "Perhaps I might be released from this feeding on pus and blood" means:
"by dedicating [the merit] to you, perhaps I might even be released from this mode of existence as a peta, which consists of feeding on pus and blood."
Having heard that, on the following day, the Venerable Elder Sāriputta addressed three elders, beginning with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;
walking for alms together with them in Rājagaha, he went to the residence of King Bimbisāra.
Upon seeing the elders, the king paid homage and asked the reason for their visit: "Venerable sirs, why have you come? The Venerable...
Mahāmoggallāna reported this matter to the king. The king, saying, “Understood, venerable sir,” dismissed the elders and summoned the minister in charge of all affairs, commanding him:
“Have four huts built in a secluded place not far from the city, well-provided with shade and water.
He then divided the inner palace into three sections according to their respective requirements.
He had four huts constructed, and having gone there himself, he performed whatever was necessary to be done.

When the huts were finished, he had all the offerings prepared and provided food, drink, clothing, and all suitable requisites for the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters headed by the Buddha; then, [he addressed] the Venerable Elder Sāriputta...
He offered all of that to him. Then the Elder gave all of it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters, headed by the Buddha, for the sake of that peta.
Having expressed her appreciation for that, the peta was reborn in the world of the gods;
being endowed with the fulfillment of all desires, she approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna on the following day and paid homage to him.
She stood there. The Elder questioned her, and she related in detail her own rebirth as a peta and her subsequent rebirth as a deva.
Thus it is said:
“Having heard his mother’s words, the compassionate Upatissa...”
He addressed Moggallāna, Anuruddha, and Kappina:
“Having built four huts, he gave them to the Saṅgha of the four quarters;
the huts and food and drink, he dedicated as an offering for his mother.”
“Immediately after it was dedicated, the fruit of that offering arose:
food, drink, and clothing—this is the fruit of the gift.
Then, pure and dressed in clean garments, wearing the finest cloth from Kāsi,”
“Wearing various garments and ornaments, she approached a householder.

(123) Therein, “she gave to the Saṅgha of the four quarters” means she gave to the Saṅgha belonging to the four quarters; the sense is that she dedicated it to them. The rest has already been explained.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna [addressed] that peta—
“O deity, with such exquisite beauty as you stand here,
illuminating all directions like the star-herb at night—
by what cause is your complexion so radiant, that it shines forth here?”
"And those riches arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind.
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty?"
"And your radiance illuminates all directions," he asked.
Then she replied, "I am the mother of Sāriputta," and so forth. The rest has already been explained.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the basis for an occasion [of teaching], said:
He taught the Dhamma to the assembled company, and that teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the story of the mother of the Elder Sāriputta is finished.
3. The commentary on the story of the intoxicated woman.
"Naked and of ugly form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a peta named Mattā.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain householder who was faithful and devout.
His wife, however, was faithless, lacking devotion, irascible, and barren; her name was Mattā. Then, out of fear that his family lineage would be cut off, that householder...
From a family of equal status, he brought home another maiden named Tissā. She was endowed with faith and confidence, dear and pleasing to her husband;
before long she became pregnant, and after the lapse of ten months, she gave birth to a son, who was given the name Bhūta.
Having become the mistress of the household, she served four bhikkhus with great care, while the barren wife envied her.
On one day, both of them stood with their hair still wet after bathing;
the householder, bound by affection for her because of her virtues, stood conversing with her at length with a pleasant heart.
Unable to endure this, the intoxicated woman, overcome by jealousy, swept the house and threw the rubbish she had set aside over her head. She [the householder], after a short while...
Having died at that time and been reborn in the womb of a peta, she experienced five kinds of suffering through the power of her own karma.
That suffering is understood from the scripture itself.
Then one day, when twilight had passed, as Tissā was bathing on the back of the house, that peta woman showed herself to her. Upon seeing her, Tissā—
“You are naked, of ugly appearance, emaciated, with veins showing;
you are haggard and thin—what are you doing standing here?
Thus he questioned her with this verse. The other replied:
“I was Mattā, you were Tissā; you had me as your co-wife in the past.
Having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts.

With this verse she gave her reply. Therein, “I was Mattā, you were Tissā” means: I was named Mattā, and you were named Tissā. “In the past” means in a previous existence. “Of you” means you had me as your co-wife (*sapattī*); the sense is that I was so. Again, “of her”—
“What evil deed was committed by body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what karma have you gone from here to the world of hungry ghosts?”—with this verse she asked about the deed performed. Then the other one said:
“I was fierce and harsh, envious, stingy, and deceitful;
having spoken such evil words to her, I have gone from here to the world of the *petas*.
With this verse she explained the deed she herself had committed. In that context, “fierce” (*caṇḍī*) means prone to anger; “harsh” (*pharusā*) means one who uses harsh speech.
“Āsinti” means “I was. “Tāhanti” means “that I. “Duruttaṃ” means ill-spoken, useless speech.
From this point on, the verses proceed by way of their questions and answers:
“I know everything, just as you were fierce;”
"And I ask you another thing: by what means have you become so covered in dust?
'You had bathed your head, dressed in clean clothes, and adorned;
and I, moreover, was even more richly adorned than you.'"
"While I was looking on, my husband made his choice;
then great envy arose in me, and anger was born within me.
Then, taking up some dust, I indeed sprinkled it over him."
“By the ripening of that kamma, I am covered in dust.
‘I know all of this: you have sprinkled me with dust;
but I ask you something else: by what are you afflicted with this itch?’”
“Both of us went to the edge of the forest to gather medicine;
you gathered medicinal herbs, while I gathered *kapikacchu*.
While she was unaware of this, I scattered it upon her bed.”
“By the ripening of that kamma, I am tormented by this itch.
‘I know all of it as well; you have treated me as an equal in bed.
But I ask you another thing: for what reason are you naked?’”
“There was a gathering of companions, a meeting of kinsmen;
you were invited there, but I was not, for I am with my husband. Without my knowledge, you sent me this garment.”
“By the ripening of that kamma, for that reason I am naked.
“I know all of this as well—that you drove away my robe;
but I ask you something else: by what means have you come to smell of excrement?”
“Your perfume, your garland, and your most precious unguent—I cast them into a cesspool;
that evil was committed by me. Through the ripening of that kamma, because of it, I am one who smells of excrement.”
“I know all that evil deed committed by you;
yet I ask you this other thing: why are you so miserable?
Whatever wealth was found in the house belonged equally to both of us.”
"While there were gifts to be given among the virtuous, I did not make an island for myself;
through the ripening of that kamma, I have therefore become one who has fared ill.
"For that very reason, you said to me: 'You are practicing an evil deed.'"
For a happy destination is not easily attained through evil deeds.
"You roast me from the left, and yet you envy me;
behold what kind of ripening comes from evil deeds."
“Those houses and those maidservants, and these very ornaments—others now enjoy them; possessions are not eternal.
Now the father of this being will come home from the marketplace.”
“Even if I were to give you something, do not go away from here yet.
“I am naked, ill-favored in form, emaciated, and covered with veins;
this is a shameful exposure for women—let not my father-in-law see me.”
“Come now, what shall I give you, or what service shall I do for you,
so that you may be happy and successful in all your desires?
[I shall provide] four monks from the Saṅgha, and four individuals.”
“Having fed eight bhikkhus, dedicate the merit to me;
then I shall be happy, with all my desires fulfilled.
Having agreed, saying “So be it,” she fed the eight bhikkhus.
Having covered her with garments, he dedicated the offering to her.
Immediately after the dedication was made, the result arose:
food, clothing, and drink—this is the fruit of that offering.
“Then, pure and dressed in clean garments, wearing exquisite Kāsī cloth,
adorned with variegated robes and ornaments, she approached her co-wife. ‘O goddess,
you who stand there with such transcendent beauty— ’”
Illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs:
“By what means do you have such a complexion? By what means is it found here for you?
And how do those enjoyments arise that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?
“In my former life, I was your rival, Tissa; I was your co-wife.”
Having committed evil deeds, we have gone from here to the world of the departed.
"Through the gift given by you, I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter;
live long, sister, together with all your kinsmen."
“The stainless, dustless state, the abode of those who have mastery.
Having practiced the Dhamma here, having given gifts, O beautiful one,
and having eradicated the stain of stinginess along with its root, go blamelessly to the heavenly realm.”
138. "In this regard, I too know all that you said when you spoke thus: 'You were fierce and harsh,' meaning, 'You were both violent and cruel.
I too know all that you were—fierce, wrathful, harsh in speech, envious, stingy, and deceitful. Furthermore, I ask you another thing; I now ask you yet another."
"By whom have you been covered in dust? means: by what action have you become completely enveloped in the dust of refuse, with your entire body strewn over?
(139–40) "Washed head" means washed including the head. "Exceedingly" means more than usual. "Thoroughly and excessively adorned" means properly and pre-eminently decorated.
Alternatively, there is the reading *adhimattā*; this means excessively intoxicated by pride and intoxication, that is, dependent on conceit.
The meaning [of *attha*] is "you. *Tayā* means "by you," that is, by the lady (*bhavati*). *Sāmikena samantayī* means she conversed with her husband, speaking in a manner free from hesitation.
142–144. *Khajjasi kacchuyā* means you are being eaten by the disease of scabies; the sense is that you are afflicted by it.
*Bhesajjahārī* refers to those who carry medicine, namely, female herb-gatherers. *Ubho* means two; the sense is "both you and I. *Vanantaṃ*... [end of fragment].
"To the forest. "And you brought medicine" means that you brought the medicine prescribed by physicians which was beneficial to yourself.
"And I [brought] *kapikacchu*" means that I, however, brought *kapikacchu* fruits—fruits that cause itching—or alternatively, *kapikacchu* is called "self-arisen";
therefore, the meaning is that I brought the leaves and fruits of the self-arisen plant.
"Seyyaṃ tyāhaṃ samokirin" means: "I scattered over your bed on all sides with the leaves of the *kapikacchu* fruit.
(146–147) "Sahāyānaṃ" means of friends. "Samayo" means a gathering. "Ñātīnaṃ" means of kinsmen. "Samiti" means an assembly.
"Āmantitā" means invited for the purpose of performing auspicious rites. "Sasāminī" means together with her husband; that is, accompanied by her husband.
*Attho*: "No ca kho haṃ" means "Indeed, I was not invited"; this is the construction. *Dussaṃ tyāhaṃ* means "I [gave] cloth to you.
*Apānudiṃ* means "I took away by theft" or "I seized.
149. *Paccagghaṃ* means "new" or "of great value. *Atāresiṃ* means "I threw. *Gūthagandhinī* means "having the smell of feces," that is, one who wears excrement as clothing.
151. "Whatever wealth exists in the house" means whatever wealth is found in the house;
that was equal and identical for both of us, belonging neither to you nor to me. "While [wealth] exists" means while it is present. "Lamp" means a support;
he speaks with reference to meritorious action (*puññakamma*).

152. Thus that female ghost (petī), having explained the matter asked of her, spoke again the words beginning with "That very same [person] as me" (*tadeva maṃ tvaṃ*), revealing the offense she herself had committed because she had not previously acted upon her words.
Therein, *tadeva* means "at that very time," that is, while I was still in my human existence. Alternatively, the reading is *tatheva*, meaning "just as it has now occurred."
The meaning is: "He spoke thus. *Maṃ* refers to himself; *tvaṃ* is for her. *Avaca* means he spoke.
To show how he spoke, the passage beginning with "evil deeds" (*pāpakamma*) was stated. The Pāli reads "pāpakammāni. [The sense is:
"You perform only evil deeds; however, through evil deeds, a happy destination is not easily obtained, but rather an unhappy destination alone is easily obtained."
"Exactly as you previously spoke to and instructed me, so it is," she said.
Having heard that, Tissa spoke three verses beginning with "You answer me from the left. Therein, "You answer me from the left" means you approach me in a contrary manner;
you act as one who brings about the opposite of what is beneficial for you.
"Having done so, you take hold of me. 'You envy me' means you envy me; you harbor ill will toward me.
Behold what kind of result there is for evil deeds!"—he says this, meaning: "Behold directly for yourself that very nature of the result of so-called evil deeds, which is indeed most terrible."

154. "Others enjoy them" means that these female slaves and ornaments in the house, which were previously possessed by you, are now enjoyed—that is, used—by others. The word "these" (*ime*) is stated with a change of grammatical gender.
"Wealth is not eternal" means that these riches are not permanent; they are unstable, temporary, and subject to being taken away by others. Therefore...
The intention is that, for that purpose, envy, stinginess, and so forth should not be practiced.
155. Now, regarding "the father of my son who has been born": at this very moment, the father of my son who has been born is a householder.
"From the shop": he will come to this house from the shop. "Perhaps he might give you something": when the householder has arrived at the house...
"Perhaps he might give some gift suitable for you, something worthy of being given. Do not go away from here yet;
do not depart from this house just now," she said out of compassion for him.
Having heard that, the peta, revealing her own inner disposition, spoke the verse: "I am naked and of ugly form."
In this context, "this is a private part of women" means that because it must be concealed, this state of nakedness, ugliness,
and so forth is a private part (*kopīna*) of women that ought to be covered. "Lest my father, who is a living being,
see me" means she speaks out of shame, thinking, "May my father— the head of the household— do not see me."
157. Having heard that, compassion arose in her, and she spoke this verse, saying, "Come now, what shall I give you?
In this context, *handā* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. "What shall I give you? means: "What shall I give you?
Shall I give you a garment, or rather food? "Or what service can we do for you here? means: "Or what other assistance can we perform for you here at this time?"
158. Having heard that, the female spirit (petī) spoke this verse: “Four bhikkhus from the Saṅgha.
Therein, “four bhikkhus from the Saṅgha” means four bhikkhus by way of the Saṅgha and four bhikkhus by way of individuals;
thus, having fed eight bhikkhus according to one’s wish, dedicate that merit to me.
"Give me the gift of your merit. The meaning is: "When you dedicate the offering to me, I shall then be happy;
I shall become happy, attained to bliss, and successful in all my desires.
Having heard this, she informed her husband of the matter, and on the following day, eight bhikkhus—
Having fed her, he dedicated the merit to her; she, having immediately attained divine success, returned once more to his presence.
To illustrate this matter, the compilers of the collection placed three verses beginning with: "She, having assented, saying 'So be it'."
162–167. When she had approached and stood before her, Tissa questioned her with three verses beginning with, “With such exquisite beauty...

The other [Sujātā] identified herself with the verse, “I am intoxicated...,” offered her a blessing with the verse, “May you live long...,” and gave her this exhortation with the verse, “Having practiced the Dhamma here.... In that regard, your...

"By that which was given" means by what was bestowed by her. "The sorrowless, dustless state" (*asokaṃ virajaṃ ṭhānaṃ*): it is "sorrowless" (*asoka*) due to the absence of grief, and "dustless" (*viraja*) due to the absence of sweat and grime;
he says this with reference to the entire world of the gods (*devaloka*), which is a divine station (*dibbaṭṭhāna*).

"Abode" (*āvāsa*) means a place. "Of those who exercise mastery" (*vasavattīnaṃ*) means of those who bring themselves under their own control through divine sovereignty. "With its roots" (*samūlaṃ*)...
"Free from the fault of greed. For the fault of greed is indeed the root of stinginess. "Blameless" means unreviled and praiseworthy. "Attain the state called heaven":
because it is preeminent among the objects of the senses such as form and so forth, it is given the name "heaven";
attain that divine station—meaning, be destined for a happy rebirth. The rest is self-evident.
Then she reported that occurrence to the householder; the householder reported it to the monks;
the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for a teaching, taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude.

Having heard it, the great multitude was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and having removed the defilements of stinginess and so forth, they became devoted to generosity, virtue, and other such qualities.
"He became one whose ultimate destination is a happy rebirth.
The commentary on the story of Mattāpeti is finished.
4. The commentary on the story of Nandāpeti.
"Kālī was ugly in form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a peta named Nanda.
It is said that not far from Sāvatthī, in a certain village, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) named Nandisena who was faithful and confident.
His wife, however, named Nandā, was faithless, lacking confidence, stingy, fierce, and harsh in speech.
Lacking respect for her husband and showing no deference toward him, she reviled and insulted her mother-in-law, calling her a thief.
Later, having passed away and been reborn in the womb of a peta, she wandered not far from that very village.
One day, as the lay follower Nandisena was leaving the village, she showed herself near him. Seeing her, he—
“You are black and ill-favored in form, harsh and terrifying to behold;
you are tawny and speckled—I do not think you are a human being.
Thus he addressed her with this verse. Therein, “black” (kāḷī) means she was of a dark complexion, for her color was like that of burnt charcoal.
“Harsh” means having rough limbs. “Terrifying to behold” means having a frightening appearance, a form that inspires dread.
Alternatively, the reading is “bhārudassanā,” meaning “of dreadful aspect”; the sense is that she is unpleasant to look upon due to her ugliness and other such traits.
“Tawny” means having tawny eyes. “Spotted” means having spotted teeth. “I do not consider her human” means: I do not consider her to be human; I consider her to be a pet (peta).
And the intention is: "I think that [is you]. Having heard this, the female ghost (petī), revealing herself, said:
"I was Nandā, O Nandisena, your wife in the past;
having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of ghosts."
He spoke this verse. Regarding that: "I am Nandā, Nandisena," [he said], "O Master Nandisena, I am named Nandā. 'Your wife in the past' means I was your wife in a previous birth. Following this:
"What indeed was done by body, speech, or mind as an evil deed?
By the ripening of what karma have you gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts (petaloka)?"
The lay follower’s question:
Then she said to him, “I was fierce and harsh, and I lacked respect for you;
having spoken such ill words to you, I have gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts.”
He dismissed him. Then he said:
“I will give you an upper garment; put on this cloth.
Having put on this cloth, come; I will take you to my home.”
“Clothing and food and drink you shall receive when you have gone home;
you shall see your sons and you shall behold your daughters-in-law. To him she replied:
“What was given by hand into your hand does not benefit me.”
“Bhikkhus who are endowed with virtue, free from passion, and learned—
satisfy them with food and drink, and dedicate my offering to them;
then I shall be happy, having all my desires fulfilled.”
He spoke two verses.
Then, having replied, “Very well,” he distributed a vast amount of alms:
food, drink, hard foods, as well as clothing and lodgings.
An umbrella, perfumes, garlands, and various kinds of sandals—
having satisfied with food and drink monks who were endowed with virtue, free from passion, and learned,
he dedicated the merit of that gift to her.
“Immediately after it was recited, the result arose:
food, clothing, and drink—this is the fruit of that offering.
Then, pure and dressed in clean garments, wearing the finest Kāsika cloth;”
“Adorned with various garments and ornaments, she approached her husband.”—These four verses were spoken by the compilers of the collection. Following that:
“O deity, you who stand there with such exceeding beauty;”
Illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs, [he asked:
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?
“O Nandisena, I was your wife in the past, named Nandā.”
Having committed evil deeds, we have gone from here to the world of the departed.
"Through the gift given by you, I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter;
live long, householder, together with all your kinsmen."
“Unto that sorrowless, stainless, secure abode of the Lord of Power—
having practiced the Dhamma here and given gifts, O householder,
having eradicated the stain of stinginess along with its root— may you, blameless, go to the heavenly realm.”
The verses of dialogue between the lay follower and the female spirit.

176. Therein, “He scattered a vast gift” means that he offered a great almsgiving, as if scattering the seed of meritorious things upon a field ready for harvest. The remainder is exactly like the immediately preceding story.
Thus, having revealed her own divine prosperity and its cause to Nandisena, she returned to her own dwelling place.
She departed. The lay follower reported this matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the story of Nandāpeti.
5. Commentary on the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Petavatthu:
"Adorned with polished earrings"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the deva-son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.
Whatever is to be said regarding this matter has been explained in the commentary on the Vimānavatthu in the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
This has already been stated in the commentary on the *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī-vimānavatthu*; therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.

Furthermore, although the story of the divine son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī is included in the *Vimānavatthu* collection because he attained the state of a deity in a celestial mansion (*vimāna*), that divine son [was once] at a charnel ground due to grief over the death of his son, a brahmin who had not previously given anything.

Having gone to the cremation ground and circumambulated it, in order to dispel the grief of one who was weeping, he withdrew his own celestial form and manifested himself as a peta, overwhelmed by suffering, like one wailing with arms outstretched and glowing with yellow sandalwood.
Because he had departed from the human state, the designation "peta" (departed) is indeed applicable to him; thus, this account is found even in the *Petavatthu-pāḷi*.
It should be understood that [the text] has been included in the compendium.
The commentary on the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Petavatthu is finished.
6. Commentary on the Kaṇha Petavatthu.
"Arise, Kaṇha! What remains?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lay follower whose son had died.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, the son of a certain lay follower passed away;
overcome by the arrow of grief, he neither bathed nor ate, nor did he attend to his business, nor did he go to wait upon the Buddha.
He went along, merely lamenting, "Dear beloved son, having abandoned me, where have you gone first? and so forth.
At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw that he possessed the necessary conditions for the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

On the following day, surrounded by the community of monks, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī, and having finished his meal, [The Teacher]... [proceeded]. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.)
Having dismissed the bhikkhus, he went to the householder’s door with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk.

They informed the lay devotee that the Teacher had arrived. Then the householder’s family prepared a seat at the door of the house, and having seated the Teacher, they escorted the lay devotee, who was being received, into the presence of the Teacher. As he sat to one side, [the Teacher spoke to him:]

Having seen him, he asked, "Lay follower, why do you grieve? When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, in the past, ancient wise men did not grieve for their dead sons after hearing the discourse of the wise. Being requested by him, he related a story of the past:
In the city of Dvāravatī in the past, there were ten brothers who were kings—Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Candadeva, Sūriyadeva, and so forth.
Aggideva, Varuṇadeva, Ajjuna, Pajjuna, Ghaṭapaṇḍita, and Aṅkura. Among them, the beloved son of the great king Vāsudeva passed away.
Overcome by grief, the king abandoned all his duties and lay down grasping the foot of his bed, lamenting.
At that time, Ghaṭapaṇḍita thought: "Apart from me, no one else..."
"There is no one capable of dispelling my brother's grief; I shall remove his sorrow by means of a stratagem.
Adopting the guise of a madman, he wandered through the entire city looking up at the sky and crying out, "Give me a hare! Give me a hare!
The whole city was thrown into agitation, saying, "The wise Ghaṭa has gone mad."
At that time, a minister named Rohiṇeyya went into the presence of King Vāsudeva and, engaging him in conversation, said:
"Arise, Kaṇha! Why do you lie there? What is the use of your sleeping?
For he who is your own brother is your heart and your right eye."
“His winds grow violent, and his hair stands on end”—this verse he spoke.
(207) Therein, “Kaṇha” he addresses Vāsudeva by his clan name. “What is the use of your sleeping? means: what kind of benefit indeed comes to you from sleeping?
“Sako bhātā” means a brother born of the same womb. “Hadayaṃ cakkhu ca dakkhiṇaṃ” means with the heart... [and] with the right eye.
The meaning is that he is similar to [the moon] by means of his right eye.
"His winds grow strong" means that the winds of madness arising repeatedly within him become powerful, increase, and overwhelm him. "He prattles 'Sasaṃ'" means he stammers, saying, "Give me sasaṃ.
Regarding "Kesava": it is said that because he possessed beautiful hair (*kesa*), he was called "Kesava."
It is so called in common usage. By that name he addresses him.
Having heard his words, the Teacher, having attained full enlightenment, pointing out the fact that [Kesava] had risen from his bed, said:
“Having heard those words of Rohineyya, Kesava...”
He rose up in the form of one who was being rescued, distressed by grief for his brother.
Having spoken this verse, the king rose quickly, descended from the palace, went to the presence of Ghaṭapaṇḍita, and grasping him firmly with both hands, spoke to him while conversing:
“Why indeed do you appear like one mad, [standing] alone at this gateway?”
“You cry out, ‘Hare! Hare! What kind of hare do you desire?
“I shall have a hare made for you, fashioned from gold, from jewels, from iron, or from silver; or made of conch, stone, or coral.”
“There are other hares as well, whose range is the forest and the woods;
I shall bring those too. What kind of hare do you desire?”—with these words he spoke three verses.
209–211. Therein, "like one who is mad" means as if he were insane. "Entirely" means in its entirety.
"Wandering about the city of Dvāraka" means wandering through the city of Dvāravatī. "'Sasa, sasa,' you prattle" means you lament, "Sasa, sasa.
"Made of gold" means made of gold. "Made of copper" means made of bronze. "Made of silver" means made of silver. "Tell me whatever you wish; then..."
"Why do you grieve? There are other hares who roam the forest in the wilderness; I shall bring them to you.
Speak, gentle sir, what kind of hare do you desire? Thus, with the intention that "he has need of a hare," he invited him with the word "hare.
Having heard this, the wise Ghaṭa—
“I do not desire these hares that dwell upon the earth;
I desire the hare from the moon—bring that down for me, O Keśava,” he said, reciting this verse.
Therein, *ohara* means “bring down. Having heard this, the king, overcome with dejection, thought, “Without a doubt, my brother has gone mad.”
“Therefore, O sweet kinsman, you will surely abandon life;
you desire what should not be desired, you wish for the moon’s hare. Thus he spoke this verse.

Therein, “kinsman” (ñāti) is an address to his younger brother. This is the meaning here: “I think you will abandon my dear kinsman’s very sweet life, you who desire that which ought not to be desired.”
Having heard the king’s words, Ghaṭapaṇḍita stood motionless and, illustrating this point— “Brother,
knowing that one who prays for a hare from the moon will meet his death if he does not obtain it, why do you grieve for a son who is dead?”— said:
“If you understand this, O Kaṇha, just as you instruct others, why do you still grieve today for a son who died long ago?”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “If you understand this, O Kaṇha,” means: “O brother, Great King named Kaṇha, [you know that] an unobtainable thing...”
"If you know this, then one's own self should not be craved. "Just as you instruct others"—meaning, having known this, do not act otherwise than how you instruct others.
"Why [grieve] for a son dead long ago?"—that is to say, why do you still grieve even today for a son who died only four months ago?
Standing right there in the middle of the street, he said, “I pray for such a thing as this being known to the world, yet you grieve for one who is unknown. Then, teaching him the Dhamma, he spoke:
“That which cannot be obtained by a human being, nor even by a non-human being—‘May my son who has been born not die’—how could that which is unobtainable ever be obtained?”

“Neither by spells nor by root-medicines, nor by herbs, nor by wealth, O Kaṇha, can he be brought back whom you, as a human being or a deva, grieve for as a departed one. Thus he spoke these two verses.
Regarding the word *yaṃ* therein: “O brother, that [person] for whom a human being or a deva thinks, ‘May my son, thus born, not die’...”
Or else, that which cannot be obtained—that which is impossible to obtain—is what you desire. But from where could such a thing be obtained?
For what reason would it be possible to obtain it? Because it is an unobtainable thing, a matter that simply cannot be acquired;
this is the meaning. 216. *Mantā* means by the application of spells. *Mūlabhesajjā* means by means of root medicines. *Osadhehi* means by various kinds of herbs.
"By medicines," or "by wealth," that is, by wealth numbering even hundreds of millions. This is what is meant:
"That which you lament for as a deceased person cannot be brought back even by these applications of mantras and so forth.
Again, the wise Ghaṭa, demonstrating that "this thing called death cannot be warded off by wealth, nor by birth, nor by knowledge, nor by virtue, nor by meditation," said:
“Those who possess great wealth and vast enjoyments, even the kṣatriyas who rule over kingdoms,
and those with abundant riches and grain— even they are not exempt from old age and death.
Kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas— ”
These and others by birth— none of them are free from aging and death.
Those who recite the mantra consisting of six factors, as conceived by Brahmā,
these and others by their knowledge— none of them are free from aging and death.
“Even those seers who are self-restrained and ascetic, those practitioners of austerity,
they too at the proper time abandon their bodies.
The Arahants, having developed themselves, have done what was to be done and are free from taints.”
“They cast off this body when merit and evil are exhausted.
With these five verses he taught the Dhamma to the king.
217. In that context, “of great wealth” means possessing abundant riches due to the existence of a vast amount of wealth stored away as a hoard. “Of great possessions” means...
They were endowed with a great abundance of wealth and enjoyments comparable to those of the gods. "Possessing a kingdom" means possessing an entire kingdom.

"With abundant wealth and grain" means having limitless wealth and grain by way of the constant provisions that must be stored away for the sake of three or four years. "Even they are not exempt from old age and death."
The meaning is that even those such as Mandhātu and Mahāsudassana, who possessed such great wealth, were not free from old age and death; rather, they have all entered the very jaws of death.

(218) "These" refers to the aforementioned kṣatriyas and others. "Others" refers to certain individuals of this same nature, such as Ambaṭṭha and others. "By birth" means that for the sake of their own birth-status, they were not free from old age and death; this is the meaning.
219. "They recite" means they repeat [the Veda] and teach it. Alternatively, "they revolve" means that while revolving the Veda, they perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) and mutter prayers.
"Six-limbed" means endowed with the six limbs known as phonetics (sikkhā), ritual codes (kappa), etymology (nirutti), grammar (byākaraṇa), astronomy (jotisattha), and metrics (chandovicitī).
"Contemplated by Brahmā" means thought out and spoken for the sake of the brahmins by Brahmā.
"By means of knowledge" (vijjāya) means being endowed with knowledge similar to that of the Brahmās;

the meaning is that even they are not subject to aging and death. (220–221) "Sages" (isayo): they are sages in the sense of seeking (esana) through restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth, as well as through perceptions of repulsiveness (paṭikūlasaññā) and the like.

"Peaceful" (santā): they are of a peaceful nature in body and speech. "Self-restrained" (saññatattā): their minds are restrained by the restraint of passion and other defilements. [The term] "bodily austerity" (kāyatapana) refers to...
"Ascetics" (*tapassino*) means those who possess austerity (*tapa*). Again, "ascetics" refers to those who practice restraint (*saṃvara*).
By this, he shows that having thus become dependent on austerity, even those who desire to attain liberation through the body—namely, the practitioners of restraint—eventually cast off the body.
Alternatively, "seers" (*isayo*) are so called in the sense of seeking (*esanatthena*) the training in higher virtue and so forth; for that purpose, [they abandon] their opposites...
They are "peaceful" (santā) through the subsiding of evil qualities; they are "restrained" (saññatā) due to the restraint of the mind upon a single object;

they are "ascetics" (tapassino) through the heat of energy resulting from the application of right effort; and they are "ascetics" (tapassino) because they are "associated with the practice" (sappayogā) through the burning away of lust and other defilements—thus it should be construed.
They are "of developed self" (bhāvitattā) because their minds have been developed through the meditation on the four noble truths.
When the wise Ghaṭa had thus spoken on the Dhamma, the king, having heard it, was freed from the dart of sorrow and, with a serene mind, praised the wise Ghaṭa:
"Just as one might sprinkle water upon a blazing fire fed with ghee,
so have you extinguished all my burning anguish by pouring forth the rain of the Dhamma."
“Truly, you have pulled out for me the arrow that was lodged in my heart;
you have dispelled the grief for my son from me who was overcome by sorrow.
Now that the arrow has been pulled out, I am cooled and extinguished.”
“I do not grieve, nor do I weep, having heard this from you, brother.
Those who possess wisdom and are compassionate act in this way:
they turn one back from sorrow, just as Ghaṭa did for his elder brother.”
“For one who has such ministers and attendants as these, they follow after his well-spoken words, just as Ghaṭa followed his eldest brother.”—with these words he recited the remaining verses. 225.
Therein, “just as Ghaṭa [followed] his eldest brother” means that just as the wise Ghaṭa followed his own eldest brother when he was overcome by grief for his deceased son.
By means of his own skill in means and through a discourse on the Dhamma, he turned him away from that grief for his son;
thus, the meaning is that other wise ones who are compassionate likewise provide assistance to their kinsmen. 226.
"In whom these [qualities] exist" refers to this verse of the Fully Enlightened One. Its meaning is as follows: by whatever cause...
The wise Ghaṭa sought out King Vāsudeva, who was overcome with grief for his son, by means of well-spoken words for the purpose of removing that sorrow.
If even another person were to obtain such wise ministers as these, how could there be any sorrow for him?
The remaining verses have their meaning explained below.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "In this way, lay follower, the ancient wise ones, having heard the words of the wise, removed their grief for their sons.
Having thus spoken, he proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The commentary on the *Kaṇhapeta-vatthu* is finished.
7. The commentary on the *Dhanapāla-seṭṭhi-peta-vatthu*:
"Naked and of ugly form..."—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the peta Dhanapāla.
It is said that before the Buddha had arisen, there was a merchant named Dhanapālaka in the city of Erakaccha in Pañcāla.
He was faithless, lacking confidence, miserly, and held nihilistic views. His deeds are known from the canonical texts themselves.
Having passed away, he was reborn as a peta in the desert wilderness of Marukaṇṭaka. His body was the size of a palm tree trunk, and his skin was completely bare.
He was harsh, with disfigured hair, terrifying, ugly, exceedingly deformed, and hideous to behold.
For fifty-five years, having received neither a morsel of food nor a drop of water, his throat, lips, and tongue were completely parched;
overcome by hunger and thirst, he wandered here and there.
Then, while our Blessed One had appeared in the world and, having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, was dwelling in succession at Sāvatthī,
about five hundred merchants residing in Sāvatthī filled their wagons with merchandise and went to the Northern Road.
Having sold their goods and loaded the merchandise they had acquired onto the wagons, they were returning in the evening.
Having reached a certain dry river, they unyoked their carriage there and took up residence for the night.
Then that peta, overcome by thirst, came for the sake of water;
but finding not even a single drop of water there, he fell down like a palm tree whose roots have been severed or whose base has been cut away, his hopes vanished. Seeing him, the merchants—
“You are naked, of ugly appearance, emaciated, with veins showing all over;
you are gaunt and haggard—what indeed are you, O venerable sir?
With this verse they questioned him. Then the peta—
“Venerable sirs, I am a peta, gone to the miserable world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the realm of petas.
Having thus revealed himself, he was questioned by them again:
“What evil deed was committed by body, speech, or mind;
by the ripening of what karma have you gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts?”—
Thus questioned regarding his past actions, he showed them his own history— past, present, and future— beginning from the place where he had previously been reborn, and gave them this exhortation:
“There was a city renowned as Erakaccha;
there I lived formerly as a merchant, known by the name Dhanapāla.
I possessed eighty wagon-loads of gold.”
"I have abundant gold, and many pearls and beryl gems.
Yet, despite such vast wealth, nothing was dear to me enough to give away;
I kept my doors shut and lived on, lest beggars should come to me."
“I was faithless and stingy, miserly and abusive;
I would stop many people who were giving and doing meritorious deeds.
‘There is no result from giving—how could there be a fruit for self-restraint?’”
I destroyed lotus ponds and wells, groves, and planted trees;
I demolished causeways and built bridges across difficult terrain.
Thus, having failed to perform wholesome deeds and having committed evil, when I passed away from that state—
I was reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Since I passed away [from the human world] fifty-five years ago,
I do not recall having eaten anything, nor even having drunk a drop of water.
“That which is restraint is destruction; that which is destruction is restraint.
For it is said that the departed spirits know: ‘That which is restraint is destruction.
Had I restrained myself in the past, I would not have failed to acquire much wealth.”
While there were gifts to be given among the virtuous, I did not make an island for myself;
therefore, now that I have come under the power of the fruit of my own actions, I am filled with remorse.
"In four months' time, my passing away will take place."
I shall fall into a terrible hell, utterly and exclusively bitter.
It has four corners and four gates, well-proportioned and measured out in its divisions;
it is surrounded by iron walls and closed in with iron.
“His ground is made of iron, ablaze and filled with heat;
it stands pervading a hundred yojanas on all sides at all times.
There, for a long duration, I shall experience painful sensation.”
This is the fruit of evil karma; therefore, I grieve intensely.
"I say this to you for your welfare, all you who have gathered here:
Do not commit an evil deed, whether openly or in secret."
“If you will do, or have done, that evil deed,
there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly up and flee.
Be filial toward your mother, be filial toward your father, and honor those who are senior in the family.”
“Be samaṇas, be brahmins; thus you shall go to heaven.”—He spoke these verses.
230–231. Therein, “of the Paṇṇās” refers to the kings of the kingdom of Paṇṇāsa who were so named. “Erakaccha” means...
The name of that city. *Tattha* means in that city. *Pure* means formerly, in past existences.
*Dhanapālo ti maṃ vidū* means "they know me as the merchant Dhanapāla. Showing that this name was indeed appropriate for me at that time, he spoke the verse beginning with "Asīti.
Therein, *asīti sakaṭavāhānaṃ* refers to a load of twenty *khāris*. A load...
"Caravan" is what is said [there]. The construction is: "I had eighty loads of gold for those caravan-leaders, and likewise of *kahāpaṇa* coins.
"I had abundant gold" means that even the gold was abundant, measuring many loads; this is the connection. 232–233.
"Giving was not dear to me" means that giving a gift was not pleasing to me. "May the supplicants not find me" [means they did not find me].
Thinking, "May beggars not see me," I close the door of my house and eat. *Kadariyo* means one who is stubbornly stingy.
*Paribhāsako* means one who, seeing someone giving a gift, intimidates them out of fear. *Dadantānaṃ karontānaṃ* is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative;
it refers to those giving gifts and performing meritorious deeds. *Bahū jane* means many beings. Or, [it may refer to] those who are giving.
I would have prevented—or did prevent—a great multitude of people who were engaged in meritorious deeds from doing so.
(234–236) “There is no ripening for giving,” and so forth, is the statement of the reasons for preventing [others] from giving and other such acts.
In that context, “there is no ripening for giving” means that there is no fruit for the kamma of giving; it is merely the destruction of wealth, thinking, “merit, merit.”
Thus he illuminates [the point]. "Of restraint" means of restraint through virtue (*sīla*). "From where would there be fruit?"—the intention is: "How indeed could fruit be obtained?
The guarding of virtue is utterly useless. "Gardens" means groves and parks. "Steep places" means water-sheds (*pānīyasālā*).
"Difficult passages" refers to places hard to traverse due to water and mud. "Bridges" means causeways.
“Passed away from there” means passed away from that world of humans. “Fifty-five” means fifty-five. “Since I died” means since the time I passed away;
from that point onward. “I do not recall” means that during all this time, I do not remember having eaten or drunk anything at all.

237–38. "That which is restraint is destruction": the withholding from anyone of anything due to greed and other such motives is called the "destruction" of these beings, because it serves as the cause for the great calamity of those who have been reborn in the realm of the *petas*.
By the statement, "That which is destruction is restraint," he expresses the absolute certainty of the meaning already stated. For the *petas*...
Regarding the phrase "it seems they know": here, the word *hi* functions as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), while the word *kira* indicates lack of approval (*arucisūcane*).

[The meaning is: "It seems that only the *petas*—and not humans—know this fact, namely that 'restraint is the non-giving away of what is to be given because it is a cause of destruction,' since they experience it directly through their own perception.
This is not correct, for even humans, like the *petas*, are overcome by hunger, thirst, and so forth.
Because they are visible [to them]. However, because the results of the karma performed in their previous existence are manifest, the departed ones (petas) know that matter even more clearly.
Therefore he said: “In former times I was self-restrained,” and so forth.
In this context, “I was self-restrained” means that I myself practiced restraint and contraction from meritorious deeds such as giving. “When there was much wealth” means when great wealth existed.

243. *Tanti* means "therefore. *Vo* means "you. *Bhaddaṃ vo* means "may there be welfare for you"—the remainder of the sentence being that it may be auspicious, excellent, beautiful, and lovely for you.
*Yāvantettha samāgatā* means "as many as have assembled here";
the intention is: "all of you who have gathered here, listen to my words. *Āvi* means "openly," by way of making it manifest to others. *Raho* means "in secret."
"In public" means by way of manifest acts such as killing living beings or false speech through body and speech; or "in private" means by way of covetousness and so forth.
"Do not do evil, low, unwholesome karma"—do not perform it.
(244) "If you do that evil karma"—if, moreover, you will perform that evil karma in the future, [then] now...

Or even if you do so, there is no liberation from suffering—which is the fruit of that [kamma]—in the four states of misery beginning with hell, nor among humans by way of short lifespans and the like.
The meaning of "even having flown up" (*uppacca*) is that there is no liberation even for those who have leaped up and are traveling through the air;
the reading *upecca* also exists, meaning: "Even as you flee here or there, he will pursue you."
The meaning is this: even if you were to flee intentionally after having approached [the enemy] with such intent, there would be no escape for you from that;
however, when other conditions such as the time of death and the destination (*gati*) come together, it will certainly ripen. And this is the meaning:
"Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains..."
“There is no place in the world where one, while remaining there, could be released from evil karma”—this is what is illustrated by this verse. 245.

“Matteyyā” means being filial toward one’s mother. “Hotha” means you should perform services for them and so forth. It should be understood that the same applies to “petteyyā” (being filial toward one’s father).
"Those who honor the elders in the family" means those who show respect to the seniors within the family. "Those who honor recluses" means those who worship ascetics.

Likewise, "those who honor Brahmins" means those who worship those who have banished evil—this is the meaning. "In this way you will go to heaven" means that by performing meritorious deeds according to the method I have described, you will be reborn in the world of the devas. As for that which has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning:
This should be understood according to the method already explained below in the *Khallāṭiya-petavatthu* and other such texts.
Having heard his words, those merchants were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; out of compassion for him, they took water in vessels, laid him down, and poured it into his mouth.
Then, after the great multitude had poured much water upon him for a long time, that water reached the peta.
“Because of the power of my evil deeds, water has not flowed down into my throat; how then shall I quench my thirst? They asked him, “Have you obtained even a measure of comfort?

He said, “If, while so many people have been pouring water into me for such a long time, even a single drop has flowed down and entered [my throat], may there be no liberation from this state of existence as a peta! Then...
Having heard that, those merchants were overcome with extreme spiritual urgency and asked, "Is there any means for the allaying of our thirst?
He said, "When this evil karma is exhausted, if a gift is given to the Tathāgata or to the disciples of the Tathāgata, my gift will be dedicated;
then I shall be released from this state of being a peta. Having heard this, the merchants [went] to Sāvatthī...
Having gone and approached the Blessed One, they reported that occurrence;
having taken the refuges and the precepts, and having given alms for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, they dedicated the merit to that peta.
The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion, taught the Dhamma to the four assemblies. The great multitude—
And having abandoned the stain of stinginess such as greed, he became devoted to the merit of giving and other virtues.
The commentary on the *Dhanapāla-seṭṭhi-peta-vatthu* is finished.
8. The commentary on the *Cūḷa-seṭṭhi-peta-vatthu*.
"You have gone forth, venerable sir, naked and emaciated"—this was said by the Teacher while staying at the Veḷuvana regarding the Cūḷaseṭṭhi-peta.

It is said that in Bārāṇasī there was a householder named Cūḷaseṭṭhi who was faithless, lacking confidence, stingy, miserly, and indifferent toward the performance of meritorious deeds. Having died, he was reborn among the petas. Regarding him:
His body was devoid of flesh and blood, consisting merely of bones, sinews, and skin; he was shaven-headed and stripped of clothing.
Meanwhile, his daughter Anulā, living in the house of her husband in Andhakavinda, prepared rice and other offerings for almsgiving, desiring to feed brahmins on behalf of her father.
Knowing this, the peta traveled through the air out of hope and arrived at Rājagaha.
And at that time, King Ajātasattu, having been incited by Devadatta, had deprived his father of life;

being unable to fall asleep due to the remorse and a bad dream, he was walking back and forth on the upper terrace of the palace when he saw that peta traveling through the air and questioned him with this verse:
“Bhante, you have gone forth naked and emaciated; where do you go at night and for what reason?
Tell me that, so that we might provide you with all the wealth possible.
In this context, “one who has gone forth” (pabbajita) means a recluse (samaṇa). It is said that because of his nakedness and shaven head, the king thought, “This is a naked recluse.”
Out of perception, he said, "You are naked, emaciated, and have gone forth," and so on. "For what reason" (*kissahetu*) means for what cause.
"I would provide you with wealth in its entirety" (*sabbena vittaṃ paṭipādaye tvan*):

I would provide or accomplish for you wealth that serves as a requisite for prosperity, in accordance with your desire, by means of all my resources, or indeed with all my effort. May we perhaps be able to do so.
"Therefore, explain that to me; tell me the reason for your coming here"—this is the meaning.
Thus questioned by the king, the peta spoke three verses while recounting his own history:
"Bārāṇasī is a city renowned far and wide; there I was once a wealthy householder, yet I became wretched."
A non-giver whose mind is greedy for material things, having fallen into the realm of Yama due to his immorality,
is tormented by those very needles. Therefore,
I go among my kinsmen for the sake of some small material gift.
Lacking the habit of giving, they do not have faith,
thinking, "There is no fruit of giving in the world beyond.
Yet my daughter constantly pleads, "I will give alms to my fathers and grandfathers."
"The brahmins serve him what has been prepared; I am going to Andhakavinda to eat.
(247) In this context, *dūraghuṭṭhaṃ* means proclaimed from afar by way of praising his virtues; the meaning is that he is renowned and well-known everywhere.
*Aḍḍha* means wealthy and of great fortune. *Dīna* means one who is low-minded and lacks the inclination to give. Thus he said.
“*Adātā*”: one whose mind is greedy for material things—that is, whose mind is attached to the bait of sensual pleasures and has fallen into greed.
“*By my own misconduct I have reached the realm of Yama*”: by the unwholesome karma I myself committed, I have reached the realm of Yama, the world of the departed (*petaloka*).
248. “*I am tormented by a needle*”: I am [tormented] by that which, because it resembles a needle in the sense of piercing, is given the name “needle.”
“Constantly tormented and oppressed by hunger”—or rather, the reading is “kilamatho” (exhausted).
“By those” means by the evil kamma described as “miserable” and so forth, acting as the cause.
For that peta, as he recollected those evil deeds, an extreme state of dejection arose; therefore, he spoke thus. “By that very” means by that very suffering of hunger.
"Among kinsmen, I go"—I go, I approach, to the presence of my relatives. "For the sake of some material thing"—for the purpose of some material object;

the meaning is: desiring some material gift. "Those of a non-giving nature do not believe"—just as I do, so too other people of a non-giving nature do not believe that "there is a fruit of giving in the next world. [They think: "The fruit of giving is certainly..."
They do not believe that [beings] exist in the other world; the intention is that, like me, they too have become *petas* and are experiencing great suffering.
249. *Lapati* means speaks. *Abhikkhaṇaṃ* means repeatedly, many times. As to what he says as he speaks, it is said:
"I will give a gift for my parents, for my grandfathers. In this context, "parents" (*pitūnaṃ*) refers to mother and father, or to the maternal grandfather and paternal grandfather.
“Pitāmahānaṃ” means of the grandfathers and great-grandfathers. “Upakkhaṭaṃ” means prepared. “Parivisantī” means they feed.
“Andhakavindaṃ” is a city of that name. “Bhuttaṃ” means to eat. Following this, it was said by the compilers of the collection:
“The king said to him: ‘Having experienced even that...’”
"Come quickly, I too shall perform an offering.
Tell me that if there is a reason;
we listen to words of reason with faith."
Having said, “So be it,” he went there; they ate the meal, yet those worthy of offerings received nothing.
He returned again to Rājagaha and appeared once more before the lord of men.
Seeing that peta had come yet again, the king said, “What shall I give?”
"Tell me that, if there is a cause, by which you might be satisfied for a longer time. "O King,
having served the Buddha and the Saṅgha with food, drink, and robes—
point out that merit to me for my benefit, so that I may be satisfied for a longer time."
Then the king, having prostrated himself and immediately given incomparable gifts with his own hands to the Saṅgha,
announced what he had done to the Tathāgata, who then dedicated the merit to that peta.
Honored and appearing exceedingly radiant, he manifested himself before the lord of men.
“I am a *yakkha* who has attained supreme psychic power; among humans, there is none equal to me.

Behold this immeasurable majesty of mine: having given you an incomparable gift for the Saṅgha, and being constantly and perpetually satisfied by many [offerings], I go forth happy as a god among men.”
