250. "There, the King said to him": having spoken thus, King Ajātasattu spoke to that deceased one who remained there.
"Having experienced even that": having experienced that gift prepared for your daughter. "You would come": you might come. "What?
means "I shall do it. "Tell me that, if there is a reason": if there is some cause, tell me that cause.
"Tell me," means explain to me. "To be believed" means it is to be trusted. "A statement with a reason" means a speech endowed with a cause;
the meaning is that he speaks a reasoned statement such as, "When a gift was given in such-and-such a place by such-and-such a person in such-and-such a manner, it was beneficial to me.
251. "Having said 'So be it'" means having said "Very well. "Therein" means in that place of distribution of alms at Andhakavinda.

“They ate the meal, yet they were not worthy of the offering” means that the brahmins who ate the meal were immoral and thus not worthy of the offering, whereas those who were virtuous did not eat it.
“Once again” means once more, on another occasion, he returned to Rājagaha.

“What shall I give?”—the king asked the ghost, “What kind of gift shall I give you? “For which reason you”—that is, by what cause you. “For a very long time”—for a long period. “Be satisfied”—you would be satiated; tell me that, is the meaning.
253. “Having served” means having fed him. “The king” addresses Ajātasattu. “For my benefit” means for the sake of my welfare, namely, for liberation from the state of being a peta.
254. “From there” means because of those words, or from that palace. “Having descended” means having come out.
“At that very moment” means at that very time, at the hour of sunrise. It refers to the moment when the peta, having returned, showed himself to the king.
He gave the gift right before the meal. "With his own hand" means with his own hand. "Incomparable" means immeasurable, sublime, and excellent.
"Having given to the Saṅgha" means having given to the Saṅgha. "He reported what had been prepared for the Tathāgata" means:
"Venerable Sir, this gift has been prepared for a certain deceased person"; he thus reported that matter to the Blessed One. And having reported it, as...
That gift is beneficial to him; thus did he designate the offering for that peta. 255. "He" refers to that peta.
"Honored" means honored by the giving of the offering. "Shining exceedingly" means shining intensely through divine power.
"Appeared" means he became manifest; he showed himself before the king. "I am a yakkha."
“Freed from my former human existence, I have been born as a *yakkha* and have attained the state of a god.
‘There are no humans equal or like me’—there are no humans who are my equals in the perfection of my power or my perfection of wealth.
256. ‘Behold my immeasurable power!’—‘Behold this immeasurable divine power of mine.’”
He speaks while showing the king his own prosperity from direct experience:
"Having given an incomparable gift to the Saṅgha" means having given an incomparable, sublime gift to the Noble Saṅgha; "out of compassion for me, that which was approved by you";
"having constantly and always satisfied [them] with many things" means by satisfying the Noble Saṅgha with many gifts such as food, drink, clothing, and so forth.
"By her, throughout all time, as long as I lived— even there— was I constantly and uninterruptedly satisfied and nourished.
Therefore, O Great King, being happy as a human and a deva, I am now departing for whatever place I desire," he said,
taking leave of the king.
When the deceased had thus departed after taking leave, King Ajātasattu reported this matter to the monks.
The monks approached the Blessed One and reported it to him. Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
Having heard it, the great multitude abandoned the stain of stinginess and became devoted to meritorious deeds such as giving.
The commentary on the Cūḷāseṭṭhi Petavatthu is finished.
9. The commentary on the Aṅkura Petavatthu:
"For whose sake we go"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning the Aṅkura peta.
In this case, although the sprout itself was not a peta, because its history was connected with a peta, it is therefore called the "Aṅkurapeta-vatthu" (The Story of the Sprout-Peta).
Herein is the brief account: those who [were the subjects] of King Uttaramadhurādhipati, the son of Mahāsāgara...
In the city of Asitajjana in the region of Kaṃsabhoga, in the northern province bordering the ocean, there were eleven kṣatriyas:
Añjanadevī, who was born from the womb of Devagabbhā, the daughter of Mahākaṃsa;
and the ten brothers beginning with Vāsudeva—namely, Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Candadeva, Sūriyadeva, Aggideva, Varuṇadeva, Ajjuna, Pajjuna, Ghaṭapaṇḍita, and Aṅkura.

Among them, the brothers headed by Vāsudeva, beginning from the city of Asitajanana and ending at Dvāravatī, brought all the kings throughout the sixty-three thousand cities of the entire Jambudīpa to their end with the discus.
Residing in Dvāravatī, they divided the kingdom into ten portions. However, as for their sister, Añjanadevī—
They did not remember. When they remembered again and it was said, "Let us divide [the inheritance] into eleven portions," their youngest brother, Aṅkura, said:
"Give my portion to her; I shall live by conducting trade. You yourselves should remit the customs duties in your respective districts to me.
They agreed, saying, "Very well," and gave his portion to his sister.
Having given [the kingdom], the nine kings resided in Dvāravatī.
Aṅkura, however, while engaging in trade, constantly gave great alms. He had a single slave who was the treasurer and was well-disposed toward him.
With a clear and faithful mind, Aṅkura took a daughter from a noble family and gave her to him. He [the slave] had sons...
He died while still in the womb. When Aṅkura was born, his father gave him the food allowance and wages that had been assigned to him.
Later, when the boy reached maturity, a legal dispute arose at the royal court as to whether he was a slave or not.
Hearing of this, Añjanadevī compared him to a cow and declared, "The son of a mother who is free is himself free," and thus she released him from slavery.
But the boy, unable to endure living there due to his sense of shame, went to the city of Roruva;
having taken a daughter of a certain tailor there, he made his living by the craft of tailoring.
At that time, there was in the city of Roruva a great merchant named Asayha, who gave a great alms-offering to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the needy, mendicants, and beggars.

He gave it. That tailor, filled with joy and gladness because he did not know the house of the treasurer, extended his right arm toward the residence of the merchant Asayha and pointed it out, saying, "Let them go there and receive what they are to obtain.
His deed is recorded in the Pāḷi itself.
Then, at a later time, having passed away, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity in a certain banyan tree in the desert region; his right hand became a granter of all desires.

And in that very Roruva hell, there was a certain man who had been occupied with the almsgiving of the merchant Asayha, yet he was faithless, lacking confidence, and held wrong views regarding the performance of meritorious deeds.
Having died with disrespect, he was reborn as a peta not far from the dwelling place of that son of the gods.
The deed he committed is recorded in the Pāḷi itself. However, the merchant Asayha, having died, attained companionship with Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Then, at a later time, Aṅkura set out on the road through the desert wilderness with five hundred carts, and a certain brahmin likewise set out with five hundred carts;

thus both men, taking their goods with a thousand carts, became lost on the way and wandered there for many days until their grass, water, and food were completely exhausted. Then Aṅkura sent horse-messengers...

He had drinking water brought along the four directions. Then that *yakkha*, who could grant all desires, seeing their misfortune and reflecting on the assistance previously rendered to him by Aṅkura, thought, "Come now, I must become his support," and showed them the *vaṭa* tree where he dwelt.
That *vaṭa* tree, it is said, was fully endowed with branches and spreading boughs.
It was a dense-leaved tree with spreading shade, possessing many thousands of branches, and it measured one *yojana* in length, breadth, and height.
Seeing this, Aṅkura was delighted and joyful; he had his army encamp beneath it.
The yakkha extended his right hand and first satisfied all the people with water.
Then, whatever anyone desired, he gave that very thing to each of them.

Thus, when that great multitude had been satisfied according to their wishes with various kinds of food, drink, and other provisions, and the fatigue of the journey had subsequently subsided, that brahmin merchant, reflecting improperly, thought thus: "For the sake of acquiring wealth..."

“What shall we do by going from here to Kamboja? Rather, having captured this very *yakkha* by whatever means possible and placed him upon a vehicle, we shall go back to our own city. Having thought thus, they spoke of this matter to Aṅkura:
“For what purpose we are going to Kamboja, as carriers of wealth;”
“This yakkha is a granter of desires; let us lead this yakkha away.
“Having seized this yakkha, either by force or with kindness, and having placed him upon the vehicle, let us go quickly to Dvārakā.”
He spoke two verses. Therein, "for whose sake" means for what purpose. "Kamboja" refers to the kingdom of Kamboja.

"Carriers of wealth" means those who take away the wealth obtained through the sale of goods. "Giver of desires" means one who grants whatever is wished for. "Yakkha" means a son of the gods (*devaputta*).
"We shall lead" means we will carry [him] away. "With kindness" means by means of a request. "Having overcome" means having conquered by force; "vehicle" means—
A comfortable vehicle. "Dvāraka" refers to the city of Dvāravatī. This is the underlying intention:
whatever purpose we desire to achieve by going from here to Kamboja, that purpose can be accomplished right here. For this yakṣa is a granter of desires;
therefore, having requested this yakṣa, either with his permission, or if he does not comply, [one should proceed].
"Or else, having forcibly placed him on a vehicle and bound his arms behind his back while he is on the vehicle,
let us take him and go quickly from right here to the city of Dvāravatī.
But when the brahmin had spoken thus, Aṅkura, standing firm in the dhamma of a true noble man, rejected his words:
“Under the shade of whose tree one might sit or lie down, one should not break its branch;
for treacherous toward friends is an evil person.
Thus he spoke this verse. In that context, “one should not break” means one should not cut it. “Treacherous toward friends” refers to being malicious toward those who are friends.

The production of harm. "Evil" means unwholesome and treacherous toward friends. For even in the case of a tree that provides cool shade and dispels the fatigue of a person scorched by the heat, one should not think ill of it; how much less so, then, toward those who have become sentient beings?
This son of the gods is a virtuous person, one who has acted kindly toward us, a dispeller of our suffering, and of great benefit; nothing [evil] should be done to him.
He shows that one should not think of harm, but rather that he alone is to be honored.
Having heard this, the brahmins—relying on the path of policy according to the maxim, "The root of prosperity is conciliation"—took the side of Aṅkura and said:
"Under the shade of whose tree one might sit or lie down..."
“He would even cut off its trunk if there were need for such [wood],” he said in this verse.

Regarding that, “if there were need for such”: if there were a purpose for such timber-material, one would cut even the trunk of that tree; what need then to mention the branches and so forth? This was the intention.
When the brahmin had spoken thus, Aṅkura, upholding the very Dhamma of the virtuous person—
“Under the shade of whose tree one might sit or lie down, one should not break even a single leaf of that tree;
for a betrayer of friends is an evil person.”—this verse he spoke.

Therein, “one should not break even a single leaf of that tree” means that one should not cause even a single leaf of that tree to fall, let alone its branches and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the brahmin, asserting his own position,
said: "If there were such a purpose, one might uproot even that tree in whose shade one sits or lies down."
He spoke this verse. In that context, "he pulls it out by the roots" means he would uproot it there along with its very root; he would extract it—that is the meaning.
When the brahmin had spoken thus, the sprout, wishing to render that logic useless, said:
"In whose house a man might dwell for even a single night, and where he obtains food and drink;"
One should not even think of evil toward him in one’s mind; gratitude is praised by the virtuous.

“Even for one who might stay in one’s house for but a single night, provided with food and drink—one should not even think of evil toward him in one’s mind. One whose hand does no harm burns the betrayer of friends.”
“He who, having previously done what is wholesome, later harms with evil— such a person,
struck down by his own hand, shall not behold auspicious things.
Thus he spoke these three verses.
263. Therein, “of whom” means of whichever person. “Even for a single night” means that he might dwell in the house for even just one night alone.
“Where a man might obtain food and drink” means in whose presence some man might obtain food and drink, or whatever kind of nourishment.
“One should not think evil of him even in the mind” refers to that person.
One should not even mentally contemplate or long for what is unwholesome or harmful, much less express it through body or speech. Why is that?
Because gratitude is praised by the True Persons (*sappurisa*); that is to say, gratitude is commended by the Supreme Persons such as the Buddha and others.
"Attended" means waited upon; one is attended with food, drink, and so forth, [with the words] "Take this, eat this."
"Adubbhapāṇī" means one whose hand is non-violent, restrained in hand. "He burns the betrayer of friends":

he burns—that is, destroys—that person who betrays friends. An offense committed against another by someone else brings harm specifically to that very person who is not corrupt and who is endowed with a disposition toward welfare;
thus, in effect, the person who is not corrupt "burns" him. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who offends an unoffending man, a pure person free from blemish—the evil returns to that fool alone, like fine dust thrown against the wind.
(265) “He who has previously performed good deeds” refers to a person by whom some virtuous act was done, who has been made fortunate or to whom benefit was rendered. Afterwards...
"By evil he harms": this means that the one who performed the initial service is later afflicted by that evil, which is inauspicious and harmful.

"A person struck by a wet hand": he is struck—that is, afflicted—by a wet-hand performer of a beneficial act, namely by one who has washed his hands with water, acting as a benefactor in the manner described above;
or, he is "struck by a wet-hand" in the sense of being harmed by the affliction of that benefactor.

"Indeed, he is a person ungrateful. 'He does not see auspicious things' means that such a person as described does not see, find, or obtain desirable things in this world and the world beyond; this is the meaning.
Having thus spoken, having overcome him by means of the sprout that upholds the dharma of the virtuous, that Brahmin was left without reply.
He remained silent. But the yakkha, having heard the exchange of words between those two, although he was angry with the brahmin, thought:
"Let it be; we shall know later what must be done with this wicked brahmin. First, however, wishing to show that he could not be overcome by anyone, he said:
"I am not easily subdued by a god or a human, nor even by sovereign power."
“I am a *yakkha*, one who has attained supreme psychic power (*iddhi*), far-reaching, endowed with beauty and strength.
Thus he spoke this verse. Therein, “by whatever deity” means by any deity whatsoever. “By a human” follows the same principle here as well.
“By sovereignty” means either by divine sovereignty or by human sovereignty. In that context, what is called divine sovereignty is...

The divine power (*deviddhi*) belongs to the Catumahārājikas, Sakka, Suyāma, and others; what is called human sovereignty (*manussissariya*) is the merit-power (*puññiddhi*) of universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*) and the like.
Therefore, by the mention of "sovereignty," he includes gods and humans of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
For even gods of great majesty cannot overcome humans—even when those humans lack the support of the fruits of their own merit—if there is a failure in their own application.
Not to mention the others. *Asahane* is a particle meaning "in the face of non-endurance. *Na suppasayho* means "not easily assailed" or "unassailable.
"I am a *yakkha* who has attained supreme success (*paramiddhipatto*)"—by virtue of my own merit, I have entered the state of a *yakkha*. Being such a *yakkha*, I am not just anyone;
rather, I am one who has attained supreme success, endowed with the highest and most excellent *yakkha*-power. "Far-reaching" (*dūraṅgamo*)...
He is capable of traveling even a great distance in an instant. Regarding the phrase "endowed with beauty and strength":

it means he is "endowed" (*upapanna*) or possessed of excellence of form and physical power. By these three terms, he demonstrates that he cannot be overcome by others through the employment of mantras or similar means.
For one endowed with beauty is highly esteemed by others; and relying on that excellence of form, even when faced with an unwholesome object...
"Unassailable" means that the perfection of his complexion is a cause that cannot be overcome.
From here on follows the dialogue of questions and answers between the sprout and the young deity:
"Your hand is entirely golden, and from it flows a fivefold stream of honey."
“Various juices are dripping down; I think you must be Purindada.
“I am neither a deva nor a gandhabba, nor am I Sakka Purindada.
Know me, Aṅkura, as a peta who has come here from Roruva.”
“What was your character and what was your conduct in the city of Roruva?
By what holy life (*brahmacariya*) does merit arise in your hand?
“In the past, I was a weaver in the city of Roruva; at that time, I was there.”
“I am a miserable man with a difficult livelihood; I have nothing left to give.
Yet, near Asayha, I once had a residence belonging to one who was faithful, a master of generosity, a doer of merit, and modest.”
“There, to those who came as supplicants—mendicants of various clans—they asked me about the abode of the Unconquerable:
‘Where shall we go, may you be blessed? Where is alms being given?’”
Being asked by them, I declared the abode of the Unconquerable:
"Stretching forth your right arm, go there—may it be well with you!
There alms are given in the abode of the Unconquerable."
“That hand which gave away desires, that hand which poured forth honey—
by that holy life of mine, merit succeeds in my hand.
It is said that you never gave a gift from your own hands to anyone.”
Rejoicing in another’s gift, he raises his hand and proclaims:
“That hand is the giver of desires; that hand is a festival of honey.
Through that holy life of yours, merit succeeds in the hand.”
“Venerable sir, that one who gave gifts with his own hands,
full of faith— having cast off the human body, where indeed has he gone?
“I do not know the destination or the coming of Aṅgīrasa, the conqueror of the unconquerable.”
And I have heard from Vessavaṇa that Asayha has gone to the companionship of Sakka:
“It is indeed enough to do what is wholesome, to give gifts as is fitting;
seeing one whose hand grants all desires, who would not perform merit?”
“Indeed, having gone from here and reached Dvārakā,
I shall establish a gift that will bring me happiness.
I will give food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings.”
“The water-pot, the well, and the narrow passages on difficult terrain”—these are fifteen verses of questions and answers. 267.
Therein, “pāṇi te” means “your right hand. “Sabbasovaṇṇo” means entirely the color of gold. “Pañcadhāro” means...
It is called *pañcadhāra* because it possesses streams (*dhārā*) of desirable objects provided by others through its five fingers.
*Madhussava* means that which overflows with sweet flavor. Therefore he said, "various flavors flow forth" (*nānārasā paggharanti*);

the meaning is that various kinds of flavors—distinguished as sweet, bitter, astringent, and so on—overflow. For in the case of a *yakkha* who grants desires, [there are fruits] endowed with sweet and other such flavors.
It is said that as various kinds of solid and soft foods were released into his hands, sweet and other flavors flowed forth.
"I think him Purindada" means: "I think of that Purindada Sakka; I consider him to be Sakka, the king of the devas, one of such great majesty"—this is the meaning.
268. "I am not a *deva*": I am not a manifest deity such as Vessavaṇa and others. "Nor a *gandhabba*": I am also not a deity belonging to the *gandhabba* host. "Nor even Sakka Purindada":
I am not even Sakka, the king of the gods, who received the name "Purindada" (Giver of Cities) because he established [the practice of] giving in a previous existence.
To answer the question "But who was I?", he said: "O Aṅkura, know me to be a *peta*," and so forth.
“Know me as one reborn among the Aṅkurapetas; consider me as ‘a certain peta of great psychic power.
I have come here from Roruva”—that is, having passed away from the city of Roruva, I have come here by way of being reborn in this banyan tree in the Maru desert;
the meaning is that I have been born here.

269. "Of what character and of what conduct were you when you dwelt in the city of Roruva?"—referring to your former existence, while living in the city of Roruva, what was your character (*kiṃsīlo*) and what was your conduct (*kiṃsamācāro*)?

Having undertaken what kind of virtue (*sīla*) characterized by turning away from evil, and what was your conduct (*kiṃsamācāro*) characterized by the performance of meritorious deeds, such as the wholesome practices of giving (*dāna*) and so forth?
The meaning is: "What was his conduct like? Regarding the phrase "By what holy life (*brahmacariya*) does merit (*puñña*) succeed in your hand?":
the meaning is, "Tell me by what kind of supreme conduct this fruit of merit of yours—being of such a nature—is now succeeding and coming to fruition in your hands.
For here, by the elision of the latter member of the compound, "merit" (*puñña*) is intended to mean "the fruit of merit" (*puññaphala*). In that regard:
For it is said to be "merit" in such passages as: "Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states that merit increases in this way.
270. *Tunnavāyo* means a tailor. *Sukicchavutti* means one whose livelihood is very difficult; he is extremely hard-pressed to make a living. *Kapaṇo* means wretched; the meaning is "miserable.
*Na me vijjati dātabbaṃ* refers to [the thought] regarding travelers, recluses, and brahmins: "There is nothing for me to give."
"I have nothing suitable to give as a gift," [he thought], "but my intention is that a gift has been given.
271. *Nivesanaṃ* means a house or a workshop for laborers. *Asayhassa upantike* means in the vicinity of the home of the great merchant Asayha.
*Saddhassa* means one endowed with faith in the results of kamma. *Dānapatino* means in the act of giving.
Because he was overcome by the perfection of his continuous practice of generosity and by the suppression of greed;
"one who has performed merit" means one who has previously performed deeds of good conduct;

"the modest one" means one whose nature is to feel disgust toward evil. 272. "Therein" means in that dwelling of mine; "suppliants come" means that people seeking alms came to the merchant Asayha for something.
"They come desiring to beg. "Of various clans" means those who designate themselves as belonging to different lineages.
"Beggars" (vanibbaka) are those who proclaim their own excellence; they wander about making known their state of need to the donor by way of praising the fruits of merit and extolling his virtues.
"And they ask me there"—here, "there" (tattha) is a mere particle; it means those beggars and others ask me.
They inquire about the residence of the merchant Asayha. For grammarians maintain that in such instances two actions are intended.
(Verse 273: "Where shall we go? May it be well with you! Where is alms being given?"—this demonstrates the manner of their inquiry.
And here the meaning is this: "May it be well with you; [we have heard] that alms are being given by the great merchant Asayha."
"Having heard [of this], they have come, wondering: 'Where is alms being given? Where should we go?
Where can alms be obtained by going? When questioned by those travelers, I explained:
'Because I failed to perform merit in the past, I have now become incapable of giving anything to those such as you; the pinnacle of giving..."
But showing these [benefits] and generating joy by explaining the means for obtaining gain, he thought, "Even by this much I produce abundant merit," and having thus inspired reverence,
he extended his right arm and described to them the residence of Asayha the merchant.
Therefore he said, "Extending his right arm," and so forth.

274. "Therefore this hand is a granter of desires": by that aforementioned manifestation of giving to others—merely through the act of respectfully rejoicing (*anumodana*) in the gift given by another—my hand has now become a granter of desires (*kāmadada*), yielding whatever is wished for like a *kappa*-tree or a *santānaka* creeper.
And being a granter of desires, therefore this hand is a festival of honey.
He became one who bestows desirable objects. 276.
“It is said you did not give a gift”—*kira* is a particle used in the sense of hearsay;
it is said that you did not relinquish what was your own, nor did you with your own hands and by your own effort give anything to any ascetic or brahmin whatsoever.
He did not give a gift himself. "Rejoicing in the gift of another" means that he lived merely rejoicing in the gift given by another, thinking, "Oh, how you have set forth this gift!
(277) "Therefore your hand is a granter of desires" means: therefore your very hand is thus a granter of desires; the intention is, "Oh, how wonderful indeed is the course of meritorious deeds!"
278. "He who gave that gift with his own hands out of faith," the son of a god addressed him with reverence, "O Venerable One,
if such is the fruit and such is the power for you who merely rejoiced in a gift given by another,
then what must be the case for that merchant Asayha, the Great Merchant, who gave a great gift with his own hands, having become full of faith?"
He set [the wheel] in motion. "Having abandoned the human body" means having relinquished his human existence here.
"What indeed?"—*nu* and *so* are merely particles. "Gone to a direction" means gone to a place;
[the king] asked about the future destiny (*abhisamparāya*) of that merchant Asayha, wondering what the outcome of his departure was like.

279. "Asayhasāhino" means one who endures—that is, one who bears—the burden of the noble ones, such as the distribution of gifts and so forth, which cannot be borne or carried by other stingy people overcome by greed.
"Aṅgīrasassa" means of him whose radiance (rasa) issues from his limbs (aṅga).
For "rasa" is a designation for radiance. It is said that when he saw supplicants approaching, [he would give them what they desired].
A sublime joy and gladness arise, and the complexion of his face becomes serene; having made this evident to himself, he spoke thus:

"As for his going and coming—I do not know his destination, such that 'he has gone from here to a certain realm,' nor do I know his arrival, such that 'he will come back here from there at a certain time. This is beyond my range."
"And I have heard it from Vessavaṇa": moreover, this was heard by me while I had gone to attend upon the Great King Vessavaṇa.
"He went to the companionship of Sakka, the Unconquerable": the merchant Asayha went to the companionship of Sakka, the Lord of the Devas;
the meaning is that he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
280. "It is indeed fitting to do what is good" means that it is appropriate and proper to perform whatever is good, wholesome, and meritorious.
In this regard, in order to show that which is most excellent and common to all, it is said: "to give gifts as is fitting.
It is indeed fitting to give gifts according to the extent of one's own wealth and power. Regarding this, he states the reason: "the hand that grants desires."

"Having seen"— meaning, having seen this hand that grants all desires merely by pointing out the path to the donor's residence preceded by the rejoicing in the merit performed by others. "Who would not perform merit?"— meaning,
who like me would not perform the merit that serves as one's own foundation?

281. Having thus demonstrated his zeal for the performance of meritorious deeds by way of non-restriction, he now speaks the pair of verses beginning with "So hi nūna," showing that same zeal as restricted within himself.
Therein, *so* means "I, that [person]. *Hi* is a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
*Nūna* expresses reflection (*parivitakka*). *Ito gantvā* means "having departed from here," that is, from this desert region. *Anuppatvāna dvārakaṃ* means "having arrived at Dvārakā."
"Having reached the city of Dvāravatī, I shall establish [the festival]—that is, I shall set it in motion.
Thus, when Aṅkura had made his promise, "I will give a gift," the Yakkha, with a joyful mind, said:
"My dear sir, give the gift with confidence; as for me, I shall perform the task of assisting you, so that your property to be given away..."

“It will come to an end; I shall act in such a way that it does. Having thus encouraged him toward the act of giving, [Aṅkura] thought, “Brāhmaṇa merchant, you who wish to take me away by force against one such as I do not know your own limits.
He caused the merchant’s goods to vanish and terrified him, frightening him with the terrifying appearance of a *yakkha*. Then Aṅkura made various kinds of requests to him.
Having asked the brahmin for forgiveness and appeased him, and having had all his goods restored to their original state,
he released the yakkha as night approached. As he was departing, seeing a certain preta of extremely hideous appearance not far off,
he asked him about the deed he had committed:
“Why are your fingers crooked? Why is your face contorted? And why do your eyes stream?
What evil deed have you committed?”—thus he spoke this verse.

In this context, *kuṇāti* means crooked; *kuṇikā* and *paṭikuṇikā* mean being bent or distorted. *Kuṇalīkataṃ* means made distorted or contracted by a facial expression. *Paggharanti* means trickling out impurity.
Then the peta said:
“I was preeminent in the distribution of gifts at the giving of alms by that householder Aṅgīrasa, who was endowed with faith and sought the welfare of his household.”
“Seeing there those who were begging, those who had come seeking food,
I stepped aside to one side and made my mouth into a snout.
Because of that, my fingers became crooked and my mouth was made into a snout.”
“My eyes are streaming; that evil was committed by me.”—with these words he spoke three verses. 284.
Therein, with the words “Of Aṅgīrasa,” etc., he praises the merchant Asayha. “Gharamesino” means of one who dwells in a house.

Of a householder. "In the distribution of gifts" means at the place of relinquishment in the midst of giving. "I was preeminent in giving" means that I was established as preeminent in the office of giving, in the act of relinquishing the objects to be given. 285.
"Having stepped aside to one side": having seen beggars seeking food arrive, while occupied with the task of giving, [he moved] from the place of distribution.
Without moving away, but remaining right where I was, with a face serene from the joy and gladness that had arisen,
I should have given the gift with my own hand or caused it to be given by others who were suitable;
however, instead of doing so, when the beggars came, seeing them from afar, I did not show myself, but moved aside to one side, and having moved aside, I acted [in that manner].
"Kuṇaliṃ mukhaṃ ti vikuṇitaṃ": I made my face contorted and contracted. 286.

"Tenā" means: because at that time, while I was appointed by my master to the duty of giving, when the occasion for giving had arrived, being overcome by stinginess and departing from the place of giving, I resorted to contraction with my feet;
and instead of acting thus when it was to be given with one's own hands, I resorted to contraction of the hands.
I committed an offense; when one ought to have a serene face, I contracted my face;
when one ought to look with loving eyes, I produced turbidity in my gaze.
Therefore, my fingers and toes became crooked, my face became distorted, misshapen, and shriveled, and my eyes became impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome, with tears trickling down.
This is the meaning. Therefore it was said:
“Because of that, my fingers are crooked and my face is distorted;
my eyes are streaming with tears—such is the evil deed I have committed.”
Having heard that, Aṅkura, censuring him,
said: "O base man, because of the gift you gave to another, your mouth has been distorted and your eyes are streaming with tears."
"‘He made a snout for his face’—this is the verse he spoke.
Therein, ‘by dhamma’ means by a proper reason. ‘Tet’ means yours. ‘Kāpurisa’ means a base person. ‘Yaṃ’ means because. ‘Parassa dānassa’ means regarding the gift of another;
or rather, this is the reading: *parassa dāne*. Again, reproaching that donor, the merchant, [he said]:”
“How indeed could one giving a gift commit the offense of another—food, drink, hard food, and [provisions for] clothing and lodging? Thus he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is: how indeed could a person giving a gift cause that gift to become the offense of another, by means of another?
He would accomplish what ought to be accomplished and bring it to fulfillment; he would give with his own hand, having made it a matter of personal witness,
or he himself would be occupied therein, lest his own gift be wasted in an improper place and the recipients of offerings be deprived of their due.
Having thus rebuked him, he now shows the method by which he himself should proceed:
“Indeed, having gone from here and reached the gateway,
I shall establish a gift that will bring me happiness.”
“Food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings;
a pond and a well, and bridges across difficult terrain”—
he spoke these two verses, the meaning of which is exactly as stated.
“Then, having turned back and reached the gateway,
Aṅkura established a gift that brings him happiness hereafter.
He gave food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings.”
With a mind that was serene, he saw the well and the pool:
“Who is hungry? Who is thirsty? Who shall put on a garment?
Whose are these draft-animals? Let them yoke the carriage from here.”
“Who wants a sunshade and perfume? Who wants a garland? Who wants sandals?
Thus did the barbers and cooks proclaim there daily, evening and morning, at the residence of Aṅgula.
The four verses were placed by the compilers of the collection to demonstrate the conduct of Aṅgula. 291.
In that context, *tato* means from the desert wilderness (*marukantāra*). *Nivattitvā* means having turned back. *Anuppatvāna dvārakaṃ* means having reached the city of Dvāravatī.
*Dānaṃ paṭṭhapayi aṅguro* means that Aṅgula established a distribution of alms, his entire storehouse having been replenished by the *yakkha*.

Aṅgula established that great gift of provisions for all travelers. "Whatever brings him happiness" means whatever produces happiness both for himself in the present and in the future. 293. "Who is hungry?
means "who is famished?"; the intention is: "let him come and eat according to his desire. It is just this...
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Thirsty" means parched with thirst. "He will wrap himself" means he will dress and put on an upper garment;
such is the meaning. "Exhausted" means having reached a state of fatigue. "Vehicles" refers to chariot-draught animals. "Let them harness vehicles from here" means:
let them take whatever vehicles they prefer from this collection of draft animals and yoke them.
294. "Who desires an umbrella? means: who indeed desires an umbrella, such as one made of palm-leaf and so forth?

The intention is: "Let him take it. The same method applies to the remaining items as well. "Fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to scents such as the fourfold types of perfumes. "Garland" (*māla*) refers to flowers distinguished as either strung together or unstrung.
"Sandals" (*upāhana*) refers to footwear distinguished as those bound with leather straps and so forth. "It is thus" (*iti ssu*): here, *su* is merely a particle.
Thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with “Who is hungry? Who is thirsty? is as follows. *Kappakā* means barbers. *Sūdā* means cooks. *Māgadhā* means perfumers.
*Sada* means always; the construction is that they proclaim and shout out there in the house of Aṅgula day after day, evening and morning.
As time passed while he was thus distributing such great alms, the ranks of those seeking gifts became sparse and thin due to the satiation of their needs.
Seeing this, Aṅkura, his mind unsatisfied because of his exalted aspiration for giving,
addressed a young man named Sindhaka who was appointed to his own distribution of gifts:
“‘Aṅkura sleeps happily,’ so people know me;
‘Sindhaka sleeps in misery because he does not see beggars,’ so people know me.
“Aṅkura sleeps happily,” so people know me.
“I sleep in comfort, Sindaka, though my gains are few,” he said, speaking these two verses.
Therein, with the words “Prince Aṅkura sleeps in comfort; thus do people know me,” he meant:
“Prince Aṅkura, endowed with glory and wealth, a lord of giving, sleeps in comfort by virtue of his own abundance of wealth and his perfection in generosity; indeed, he sleeps in peace.”
"People regard me thus: 'He approaches [his bed] with ease and wakes up in comfort.
But as for me, Sindhaka, I sleep in suffering—Sindhaka, I sleep in nothing but suffering. Why? 'Because I see no supplicants,' that is to say:
because I do not see many supplicants who can receive the gifts intended for my own aspiration; that is the meaning. In this small amount..."
The construction is: "When there have arisen only a few, a small number of beggars, I sleep in suffering.
Here, *su* is merely an expletive particle; the meaning is "when there are only a few beggars.
Having heard this, Sindhaka, wishing to make his noble inclination toward giving even more manifest, said:
“If Sakka, the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, were to grant you a boon, what boon would you choose from among all that exists in the world?”—thus he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is as follows: Sakka, the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa gods and of the entire world, [offered] a boon...
"Choose whatever you desire, Aṅkura"—if he were to grant you a boon, should he indeed give it, what kind of boon would you choose, being one who desires and yearns for it? This is the meaning.
Then Aṅkura, making known his own aspiration exactly as it was, said:
“If Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-three, were to grant me a boon:
while I am still in the night, as the sun is rising,
may celestial foods appear before me, and may virtuous people come as supplicants.”
“May my giving not be exhausted; having given, may I have no regret;
while giving, may I gladden my mind—this is the boon I choose, O Sakka. Thus he spoke these two verses.
Regarding that, “of me who has risen at the proper time” means of one who has risen early in the morning for those worthy of offerings who are in need.
"While I am endowed with the energy of exertion by way of honoring and serving [the Teacher],
may the rising of the sun occur— that is, at the time of sunrise— may divine foods appear,
meaning that sustenances belonging to the world of the gods should arise; and may there be virtuous beggars, meaning that the beggars should be virtuous and of noble character."

299. "May it not be exhausted for me while giving": as I give gifts to those who come one after another, may my property to be given not be exhausted, may it not reach depletion. "Having given, may I have no regret":
having given that gift, even upon seeing something that causes displeasure, may I have no subsequent regret. "While giving, may I gladden the mind": while giving, may I gladden the mind.
“Having become one whose mind is indeed serene, I would give. This is the boon I choose from Sakka,” he said, addressing Sakka, the lord of the devas.

He would choose this fivefold boon: perfection of health, perfection of the object to be given, perfection of the recipient, perfection of the immeasurable quality of the object to be given, and perfection of the donor.
And herein, by the phrase “when I have arisen at the proper time,” perfection of health is indicated.
By the phrase “divine foods may appear,” the perfection of the gift (deyyadhamma-sampadā) is shown; by “the supplicants are virtuous,” the perfection of the recipient (dakkhiṇeyya-sampadā);
by “may my gift not be exhausted as I give,” the perfection of the immeasurable nature of the gift (deyyadhamma-aparimita-sampadā);
and by “having given, may I have no regret, and while giving, may my mind be serene,” the perfection of the donor (dāyaka-sampadā)—these are the five.
These goals are desired by means of excellence. Furthermore, it should be understood that these are for the sake of the loftiness of merit consisting in giving alone.
When Aṅkura had thus made known his own aspiration, a certain man named Soṇaka—who was seated there and was well-versed in the science of policy—desiring to restrain him from excessive giving, said:
"One should not bestow all one's wealth upon others; one should give gifts while protecting both wealth and property."
Therefore, wealth indeed is better than giving; through excessive giving, families cease to exist.
"The wise do not praise neither non-giving nor excessive giving;
therefore, wealth indeed is better than giving."
“He should conduct himself with equanimity;
that is the way of the wise”—thus he spoke these two verses. Others say that Sindhaka, wishing to test him once more, said, “Not all forms of wealth,” and so forth.
In this context, “all forms of wealth” refers to all the various requisites of wealth, distinguished as those with consciousness and those without consciousness.
“Riches” means wealth. “To others” means for another person; “to another” is the meaning. “Should not bestow” means he should not give;

the meaning is that one should not practice the relinquishing of all one’s property without leaving anything behind, thinking, “I have obtained those worthy of offerings. “And should give a gift” means that the duty of giving should not be performed in every single instance [without restraint];
rather, one should know one’s own income and expenditure.

One should give gifts in accordance with one's means. One should protect wealth by means of guarding what has not been acquired, preserving what has been acquired, and safeguarding what is already in possession.
As it is said: “One should enjoy wealth with one part, employ two parts in work, and set aside a fourth part as a reserve for times of misfortune.”

Or one should protect wealth according to the prescribed method, because giving has that as its basis. For those who contemplate policy maintain that all three paths should be practiced by purifying one another.

Therefore—meaning, because one who protects wealth and practices giving is engaged in what is beneficial for both worlds, and because giving is rooted in wealth—it is better to have wealth than to give.
“Excessively generous” means that one should not practice extreme giving; this is the intended meaning. Therefore he said, “Through excessive giving, families do not endure.
The meaning is that by failing to know the proper measure of wealth, through the consequence of such excessive giving, families do not endure, they do not continue, and they are cut off.
301. Now, establishing this very matter praised by the wise, he spoke the verse beginning with “Non-giving and over-giving.

Therein, “non-giving and over-giving” refers to the wise—those who are intelligent and of a discerning nature—who understand non-giving as the total failure to give even a spoonful of alms or a handful of rice, and over-giving as the relinquishment that exceeds the proper measure.
They do not praise it; they do not extol it. For by giving nothing at all, one is excluded from the benefits pertaining to the future life.

By excessive giving, the established order of this present world does not continue. "One should act with impartiality" means one should proceed without partiality, in accordance with worldly custom, with composure, and by the middle way of the right method. "That is the conduct of the wise" refers to the aforementioned practice regarding giving and non-giving.
This shows that it is the Dhamma of the wise who are endowed with steadfastness and skilled in the methods of policy, and that it is the path trodden by them.
Having heard this, Aṅkura, shifting his intention, thought:
"Oh, if only I myself were the one to give, and if the virtuous and true men were to associate with me!"
Like a cloud filling the lowlands, may he satisfy all those who live as forest-dwellers.
"For one whose facial expression brightens upon seeing a petitioner,
and who becomes joyful after giving— that house brings happiness to its dweller."
“When one sees a petitioner, their facial expression brightens;
having given, they are glad at heart—this is the perfection of sacrifice.
Before giving, one is joyful; while giving, one clarifies the mind.”
“Having given, he becomes joyful; this is the perfection of sacrifice.
With these four verses, he explained the method of practice to be followed by himself.
302. Therein, *aho vata* means “how excellent! *Reti* is a form of address. *Ahaṃ eva dajjaṃ* means “I myself would surely give.”
This is the summary of the meaning here: "Young man, if this doctrine of those skilled in policy—that 'wealth alone is better than giving'—is yours, then by all means let me give.

And may virtuous, true men associate with me"—that is, may virtuous, noble persons, whose conduct of body, speech, and mind is calm and tranquil, associate with and approach me regarding that act of giving.

"Like a cloud filling the valleys": this means that, raining down like a great rain-cloud, I shall fulfill the intentions of all those seeking alms in their low-lying places—that is, in the depths of their needs—thinking, "O, may I satisfy them! 303.
"When one sees supplicants at whose house... refers to when a person, seeing supplicants seeking food at their home, [thinks] first...
"The field of merit has indeed presented itself to me!"—thus the facial complexion of one who has conceived faith becomes serene;
and having given them gifts according to his means, he becomes joyful, his mind seized by rapture and gladness.
"That" refers here to the sight of the beggars, the serenity of the mind upon seeing them, and the state of being joyful after giving gifts as is appropriate.
304. "This is the perfection of the sacrifice"—this means the success, the fulfillment, and the accomplishment of the sacrifice.

305. "Even before the giving, he is glad"—this refers to being joyful and filled with gladness from the very moment one begins preparing the requisites for the gift, through the volition of relinquishment, thinking: "I shall store away this cause for success, this enduring treasure."

It should be so. "Giving, one should gladden the mind" means that while giving the object of charity and placing it into the hands of those worthy of offerings, one should gladden one's own mind by thinking, "I am taking what is essential from wealth which is without essence.
"Having given, one is glad" means that after having relinquished the object of charity to those worthy of offerings, one thinks, "I have performed what is prescribed by the wise."
"Aho! Well done, very well done!"—thus he becomes satisfied, gladdened in mind, and filled with joy and happiness.

"This is the perfection of the sacrifice" means that this—the fulfillment of these three volitions, namely the prior volition, the volition of the act itself, and the subsequent volition—which are accompanied by faith in the results of karma and embraced by happiness—is the perfection of the sacrifice, the success of the gift; the intention is that it is not otherwise than this.
Thus, after the sprout had demonstrated his own method of practice, his inclination toward giving increased even further,
and day by day he distributed great alms. Consequently, at that time, when all the kingdoms were made free of ploughing as the great alms were being given,
people who had obtained all their necessary requisites abandoned their respective labors and went about as they pleased.
They wandered about, and because of that, the treasuries of the kings went to ruin.
Then the kings sent a messenger to Aṅkura, saying: "Because of your giving, our income has been destroyed and our treasuries have gone to ruin;
therefore, you should know the proper measure."
Having heard that, Aṅkura went to the Southern Region (Dakkhiṇāpatha) and, in the Damila country, at a place not far from the ocean, had many great halls for giving constructed.
While distributing great gifts, he lived out his full lifespan; then, with the breaking up of the body after death, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
To demonstrate both the splendor of his generosity and his attainment of heaven, the compilers of the collection [said]:
“Sixty thousand cartloads of food were constantly given in the house of Aṅkura, for that person who was seeking merit.
Indeed, there were three thousand cooks adorned with jeweled earrings.”
“They subsist on the sprout, busy with giving and sacrifice.
“Sixty thousand young men, adorned with jeweled earrings,
were clearing the wood for Aṅkura’s great sacrifice.”
“Sixteen thousand women, adorned with every ornament,
gathered the offerings at Aṅkura’s great almsgiving.
Sixteen thousand women, adorned with every ornament...”
At the great almsgiving of Aṅkura, vessels of sour gruel were presented.
"The Kṣatriya gave much to many; he gave for a long time, with respect, with his own hands, having honored it again and again."
“For many months and fortnights, for seasons and years,
Aṅkura bestowed great gifts over a long period.
Having thus given and sacrificed over such a long time, Aṅkura— ”
"Thus, having cast off his human body, he went to the realm of the Thirty-three," they said in verse.

306. "Likewise, sixty thousand wagons"—that is, sixty thousand wagons filled with fragrant rice, husked rice, and so forth—at the residence of Aṅkura, who was seeking merit, whose inclination was toward giving, and who was devoted to charity.
The construction is: "Food for the seven-fold body of a living being is given constantly, day after day.
(307–8) Regarding the phrase "three thousand cooks": there are approximately three thousand cooks, that is, meal-preparers.

Furthermore, it should be understood that those who are primarily intended are the principal ones, while for each of them, there are many attendants who carry out their instructions. Thus, [it says] "three thousand cooks."
And they recite [the verse]: "Wearing earrings of set jewels" means wearing earrings variegated with various gems. This is merely by way of illustration;
they were also adorned with other ornaments such as bracelets and waist-bands. "Living off the sprouts" means they live depending on them;
the sense is that their livelihood was tied to those [sprouts]. "Engaged in giving or sacrifice" refers to what is known as a great offering (*mahāyāga*).
Those occupied with the giving or the performance of the sacrifice have applied themselves with zeal.
"The young men split wood" means that the youths, adorned and prepared, split and cleave wood for the purpose of cooking various kinds of food, such as hard and soft edibles.
(309) "Spices" (*vidhā*) refers to pungent condiments that ought to be prepared for the meal. "They grind" means they employ them by way of grinding.
310. *Dabbigāhā* means those who take with ladles. *Upaṭṭhitā* means they stood having approached the place of distribution.
311. *Bahuṃ* means great and abundant. *Bahūnaṃ* means for many. *Pādāsī* means he gave in various ways. *Ciraṃ* means for a long time;
for he appeared among humans whose lifespan was twenty thousand years. *Bahuṃ bahūnaṃ cirakālañca* [means] much, for many, and for a long time.
In order to show how he gave, the passage beginning with “sakkaccañca” was spoken. Therein, “sakkaccaṃ” means respectfully;
that is, having acted without casting it aside or treating it with contempt. “Sahatthā” means with one’s own hand, not merely by giving an order.
“Cittīkatvā” means having performed it with a mind endowed with reverence and great esteem, having honored it. “Punappunaṃ” means many times, not just once, nor only a few times.
Or, the construction is: "having performed it many times without having done [it before]. 312.
Now, in order to further clarify that very act of repeated performance, they recited the verse beginning with "and for many months.
Therein, "for many months" means for many, numerous months, such as the month of Citta and so forth. "In many fortnights" means in many fortnights, distinguished as dark and bright.
“Seasons and years”: many seasons, such as spring and summer, and many years; in all these cases, the accusative case is used for continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

“A long interval”: an interval of a long duration. And here, having stated that the giving occurred for a long time with the words “you gave for a long time,” he speaks again of its occurrence as being without interruption: “many...”
It should be understood that the passage beginning with "māse" (in a month) has been stated.
313. "In this way" means by the manner just described. "Having given and having sacrificed" is one and the same in meaning;
it refers to giving by way of relinquishing a certain gift to certain persons worthy of offerings, and then again, according to the method stated in the phrase, "He gave much to many."
Having performed a great sacrifice by giving to all who desired it according to their wishes, he— having abandoned his human body—
went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Thus, at the end of his lifespan, that Aṅkura, having relinquished his human existence, went to the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world by way of taking rebirth.
Thus, while he was enjoying celestial prosperity after being reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas,
during the time of our Blessed One, a young brahmin named Indaka, with a mind full of faith, had a ladleful of alms-food given to the Venerable Anuruddha Thera as he was walking for alms.
At a later time, having passed away, by the power of that merit acquired in the field [of giving], he...

Having been reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods as a son of the gods of great psychic power and great majesty, he outshines the deva-son Aṅkura by means of the ten divine attributes, such as form and so forth, and shines resplendently. Therefore it was said:
“Having given a spoonful of alms-food to Anuruddha, Indaka—”
Thus, having abandoned the human body, he went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
In ten respects, Indaka outshines Aṅkura:
in forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful tactile objects.
“By life-span and by fame, and by beauty and by happiness, and by sovereignty, Indaka outshines Aṅkura.
(314–5) In this context, *rūpe* means “on account of form”; the meaning is “by reason of his own excellence of physical form. The same applies to *sadde* and the other terms.
The same method applies here. "Ayu" means by means of life. But has it not been stated that the lifespan of the devas is of a limited measure?

True, it has been so stated, but that was by way of the majority. For indeed, some devas do experience premature death due to the failure of their meditative practice (*yogavipatti*) and other causes.
However, Indaka fulfills his full lifespan of three hundred and sixty million years.
Therefore it was said: “He outshines [others] by his lifespan. By “fame” (yasasā) is meant the excellence of a great retinue.

By “beauty” (vaṇṇena) is meant the excellence of physical form. The perfection of the elements of beauty (vaṇṇadhātu), however, is already expressed by the word “form” (rūpa). By “sovereignty” (ādhipaccena) is meant lordship.
Thus, while Aṅkura and Indaka were being reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods and enjoying divine prosperity, for us...
In the seventh year after his full enlightenment, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree by the gate of the city of Sāvatthī.
Proceeding gradually by three steps, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
there, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree upon the yellow sandalwood stone (paṇḍukambala-silā) on Mount Yugandhara, he shone like the rising sun, visible across ten world-systems.
Overpowering with the radiance of his own body the splendor of the assembly of devas and brahmas gathered there,
he sat down to teach the Abhidhamma; and seeing Indaka seated nearby and Aṅkura seated twelve yojanas away,
he spoke for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of those worthy of offerings:
“Great alms have been given by you, Aṅkura, for a long time;
you are sitting too far away, come near me.
Having heard this verse, Aṅkura thought, “The Blessed One has, for a long time, renounced much wealth that was worthy of being given by me...”
"Even though a great gift was distributed, because it lacked the excellence of a worthy recipient, it did not yield a magnificent fruit—like seed sown in a non-field.
But even Indaka’s gift of a single spoonful of alms-food, due to the excellence of the worthy recipient, produced an exceedingly magnificent fruit—like seed sown in a fertile field," he said.
To demonstrate this point, the compilers of the collection [said]:
“When the Buddha, the Supreme among Men, was dwelling at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree upon the yellow sandstone slab in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,
the deities from ten world-systems gathered together.”
They wait upon the Perfectly Awakened One as he dwells on the mountain peak.
No deity whatsoever excels the Perfectly Awakened One in beauty;
surpassing all deities, the Perfectly Awakened One alone shines forth.
“At that time, this sprout was twelve yojanas in height;
though not far from the Buddha, Indaka outshone him.
Having gazed upon both the sprout and Indaka, the Perfectly Awakened One—”
Honoring him as one worthy of offerings, he spoke these words:
“A great gift was given by you—a sprout with a long interval [before fruition].
You are sitting too far away; come into my presence.”
“Rebuked by the one of developed self, the sprout spoke thus:
‘What have I to do with that gift, which is empty of a worthy recipient?
This was Indaka the yakkha, who gave a meager gift.”
"He outshines us, like the moon among the hosts of stars.
"Just as when much seed is sown in a field that is parched and barren,
it does not yield an abundant harvest, nor does it satisfy the farmer."
“Even so, a gift established among those who are immoral, though it be abundant,
does not yield a vast fruit, nor does it satisfy the donor.
Just as when even a small seed is sown in a fertile field...”
“Just as the rain that falls properly brings satisfaction to the farmer with its fruit,
even so, toward those who are virtuous and endowed with such qualities,
even a small deed performed becomes merit of great fruit. Thus they spoke these verses.

317. "There, in Tāvatiṃsa" means in the Tāvatiṃsa abode. "Upon the stone, the Yellow Blanket" is to be construed as: when the Buddha, the Supreme among Men, dwelt upon the stone seat named Paṇḍukambala.

318. "The deities, having assembled from the ten world-systems"—that is, from the ten thousand world-spheres known as his birthplace and field, both the deities of the sense realm and the Brahmā deities, for the purpose of attending upon the Blessed Buddha and hearing the Dhamma.
Having gathered together from one side, he said: "They attend upon the Perfectly Enlightened One as he dwells on the mountain peak. The meaning is:

"on the peak of Sineru. "Then this sprout was twelve yojanas [in height]"—this sprout, whose conduct has been described as above, at that time when it was in the presence of the Teacher, stood at a distance of twelve yojanas;
that is, at a distance of twelve yojanas from the place where the Teacher was seated.
The meaning is: "He was seated in his proper place.
(323) "Urged by the One whose self is developed" means urged by the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose self is developed through the cultivation of the Noble Path and the perfection of the Pāramīs.
The verses spoken by Aṅkura in response to the Teacher’s reply, beginning with "What have I to do with him," [were spoken] because he was worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
"Empty" (*suññata*) means that which is empty, void, and devoid of one worthy of offerings; thus, my gift [is empty].
Therefore, saying "What have I to do with him?", he speaks while disparaging his own merit from giving.
(324) "Yakkha" means a son of the gods (*devaputta*). "Dajja" means having given. "He outshines us" means he greatly surpasses those like myself.
It shines. *Hi* is merely a particle; the meaning is that it shines having surpassed and overcome us. To the question "In what way?", he says:
"As the moon among the hosts of stars. 325–6. *Ujjaṅgale*:
on a ground portion that is exceedingly hard. Some say it means "in saline soil" (*ūsara*). It is said to be "planted."
"Having sown or having uprooted, it is sown again. "It does not satisfy" means it does not gladden, or it does not produce satisfaction because of its meager fruit.

"In the same way" means just as when much seed is sown in a field of barren soil, there is no abundant fruit or magnificent fruit, and thus it does not satisfy the farmer; even so, [among] those who are immoral, those devoid of virtue...
Even a vast gift established does not yield abundant or great fruit; the meaning is that for that very reason it does not satisfy the donor.
Regarding the two verses beginning with *Yathāpi bhaddako*, the application of the meaning should be understood through the reversal of the sequence of the words.
Therein, *sammā dhāraṃ pavecchanto* means "bestowing the rain properly," that is, causing the rain to fall correctly every half-month.
"Every ten days, every five days, while the rain falls"—this is the meaning. "Among those possessing virtues" means among those endowed with qualities such as *jhāna* and so forth.

"In such [persons]" means in those who have attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādi-lakkhaṇa*) regarding desirable things and the like. The word "benefit" (*kāraṃ*) is stated with a change of grammatical gender;
the meaning is "assistance. To the question "What kind of assistance? he says: "Merit" (*puññaṃ*).
“Having discerned, one should give a gift where what is given bears great fruit;
having given a gift after discerning, the donors go to heaven.
Having discerned, one should give a gift praised by the Sugata—those who are worthy of offerings here in the world of the living.”
"Gifts given to these [fields] yield great fruit, like seeds sown in a fertile field."—This verse was established by the compilers of the Council. 329.
Therein, "having discerned" means having investigated; having examined the field of merit with wisdom. The rest is entirely plain in every respect.
The *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu* was originated by the Teacher himself in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven before the devas of ten thousand world-systems,
for the purpose of illustrating the excellence of those worthy of offerings, beginning with the words, "A great gift was given by you.
After teaching the Abhidhamma there for three months, on the occasion of the Great Pavāraṇā, the God of Gods, surrounded by the hosts of devas, departed from the world of the gods.
Having descended to the city of Saṅkassa and traveling by stages until he reached Sāvatthī, while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove,

he took up the pinnacle of his teaching through a discourse on the Four Noble Truths, having taught in detail for the purpose of elucidating the excellence of those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya-sampatti) with the words,
"For whose sake we go," and so forth. At the conclusion of that teaching, for many thousands of millions of living beings...
"There was a realization of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the *Aṅkura-petavatthu* is finished.
10. The commentary on the *Uttara-mātā-petivatthu*.
"A bhikkhunī who had gone for her midday rest"—this refers to the story of the mother Uttara. Herein is the explanation of the meaning:

After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, when the First Great Council had been convened, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana dwelt in a certain forest grove not far from Kosambī together with twelve bhikkhus. At that time, the king’s...
A certain minister of Udena passed away, and it was he who had previously established the various works in the city.
Thereupon the king summoned the youth named Uttara, his son, and having instructed him, saying,
"You shall supervise the works established by your father," he appointed him to his father's position.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," one day he took carpenters and went to the forest for the sake of timber for the city's repairs.
There, having approached the dwelling place of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera, he saw the Elder sitting in seclusion there, wearing robes made of discarded rags; and even by his mere deportment—
Having gained confidence and exchanged greetings, he paid homage and sat down to one side. The elder preached the Dhamma to him.
Having heard the Dhamma, he conceived faith in the Triple Gem; having established himself in the refuges, he invited the elder, saying:
"Venerable sir, out of compassion, please accept my meal tomorrow together with the community of bhikkhus."
The Elder consented by remaining silent. Having departed from there and gone to the city, he informed the other lay devotees:
"I have invited the Elder for tomorrow; you too should come to my place of giving.
On the following day, having had excellent food, both hard and soft, prepared at an early hour, he had the time announced.
Having gone out to meet the Elder as he approached together with the monks, he paid homage to him and, escorting him, led him into his home.

Then, when the Elder and the monks were seated upon costly and suitable mats spread out for them, he made an offering of perfumes, flowers, and incense; having satisfied them with excellent food and drink, he was filled with faith.
With palms joined in reverence, having heard the expression of appreciation for the meal, he took the elder’s bowl and followed him as he departed.

After leaving the city and turning back, he requested, "Venerable sir, you should always enter my home," and having perceived the elder’s consent, he returned. Thus, while attending upon the elder, following his instruction—

Having established himself [in the faith], he attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and built a monastery; furthermore, he caused all his kinsmen to become deeply devoted to the Teaching (sāsana).
His mother, however, her mind overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess (macchera-mala), reviled him thus:
"Since you give food and drink to the recluses even though I do not desire it, may that turn into blood for you in the next world!"
However, she permitted the gift of a single peacock-feather fan to be given on the festival day of the monastery. Having passed away, she was reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts;
yet, by virtue of her rejoicing in the gift of the peacock-feather fan, her hair became blue, glossy, with curled tips, fine, and long.
Whenever she would descend into the river Gaṅgā thinking, "I shall drink water," the river would then be filled with blood.
There was a woman who, having wandered for fifty-five years overcome by hunger and thirst, one day saw the Elder Kaṅkhārevata sitting for his midday rest on the bank of the Ganges.
Concealing herself with her own hair, she approached him and asked for water. It is with reference to her that it was said:
A female ghost, ill-favored and terrifying to behold, approached a monk who had gone for his midday rest and was sitting on the bank of the Ganges.
Her hair was exceedingly long, hanging down as far as the ground.
“Covered with hair, she spoke thus to the ascetic.
These two verses were placed here at the beginning by the compilers of the collection.
In this context, *bhīrudassanā* means “of terrifying appearance. Alternatively, there is the reading *ruddadassanā*, meaning “of hideous and heavy appearance.”
The meaning is as follows. "Hanging down as far as the ground" means they hang down as far as the earth.
The earlier mention of "monk" (*bhikkhu*) and the later mention of "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) were both spoken specifically with reference to the Elder Kaṅkhārevata.
That female spirit (*petī*), having approached the Elder and requested water, said:
“For fifty-five years, since I passed away, I do not recall having eaten anything, nor even having drunk water.
Give me some water, venerable sir; I am thirsty for water. Thus she spoke this verse.
333. Regarding the phrase “therein I do not recall having eaten,” this means that over such a long interval of time, I do not recall having eaten food or drunk water;
the sense is that I am neither one who has eaten nor one who has drunk. “Thirsty” means parched with thirst.
“For the sake of water” is to be construed as: “Give me water, O Bhante, for me who am wandering about for the purpose of obtaining water.”
From here on:
"This cool-watered Ganges flows from the Himalayas;
drink from it after taking some—why do you beg me for water?"
“If, venerable sir, I myself draw drinking water from the Ganges, my blood turns red; therefore I beg for drinking water.
What evil deed have I committed with body, speech, or mind?”
“By the karmic result of my kissing, the Ganges becomes blood for you.
My son, named Uttara, was a faithful lay follower;
yet even against my will, he gave alms to the ascetics.”
“Robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings—
these I reproach, being afflicted by stinginess.
That which you bestow upon the recluses against my will,”
“May your robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings—
may these become blood for you in the next world, O Uttara!
By the ripening of that kamma, may the Ganges be blood for me.”
These are the verses of the Elder’s reply and the reply of the peta.
334. Therein, "from Himavanta" means from the king of mountains known as Himavā because of its possession of great snow.
"Flows" means proceeds. "From here" means from this Mahāgaṅgā. "Why do you ask me for water? [refers to] the river Gaṅgā.
"Having descended, she drinks as she pleases" is what this shows.
"My blood turns" means that by the fruit of my evil karma, the flowing water turns and transforms into blood for me; as soon as it is taken by her, the water becomes blood.
"Against my will" means while I am unwilling. "She offers" means she gives. "Requisite" means a requisite for the sick.
"Whatever requisites such as robes and so forth you bestow and give to the recluses—may this become blood for you in the world beyond," he said;
this refers to an evil deed committed by way of a curse. The construction is: "by the ripening of that [deed].
Then the Venerable Revata gave drinking water to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on behalf of that peta, and after wandering for alms...

Having taken almsfood, she gave it to the monks; having taken discarded rags from rubbish heaps and the like, she washed them and made them into mats and pillows, which she gave to the monks. Because of that, that female spirit (petī) attained divine splendors.
She went into the presence of the Elder and displayed to him the divine splendors she had obtained. The Elder [addressed] her—
Having related his own experience, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to the four assemblies who had approached him.

Consequently, the great multitude, moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*sañjātasaṃvega*), became free from the stains of stinginess and devoted themselves to wholesome qualities such as generosity and virtue.
It should be understood that this *Petavatthu* was included in the Second Council (*Dutiyasaṅgīti*).
The commentary on the story of Uttaramātā’s peta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Suttapeta Story:
“In the past, I was a bhikkhunī who had gone forth”—this is the Suttapeta story. What is its origin? It took place at Sāvatthī.
It is said that long ago, not far from here in a certain village, even before our Teacher had appeared, a certain boy attended upon a certain Paccekabuddha for more than seven hundred years.
When he reached maturity, his mother brought a daughter from a family of equal standing to be his wife. And on the very day of their wedding, that youth—
Having gone with his companions to bathe, he was bitten by a snake and died—some say he was seized by a *yakkha*.
Although he had performed much wholesome karma through his service to a *paccekabuddha*, because his mind remained attached to that girl, he was reborn as a *vimānapeta*;
nevertheless, he possessed great psychic power and great majesty.

Then, desiring to lead that maiden to his own celestial mansion, he wondered, "By what means might she perform an action whose result is to be experienced in this very life, so that she may enjoy herself here with me?
While investigating the cause for her enjoyment of divine wealth and prosperity, he saw a Paccekabuddha performing work on a robe; he went before him in human form and paid homage.
“Venerable sir, is there any need for thread? he asked. “I am making robes, lay follower,” [the Paccekabuddha] replied.
“In that case, venerable sir, go and collect alms of thread from such-and-such a place,” he said, and pointed out the house of that girl.
The Paccekabuddha went there and stood at the door of the house. Then, seeing the Paccekabuddha standing there—
Seeing her with a mind full of faith, and perceiving that "the noble one needs thread," she gave him a ball of thread.
Then that non-human being, assuming human form, went to the girl's house, requested [her hand] from her mother, and stayed there for several days with her.
Out of favor toward her mother, he filled all the vessels in that house with gold and bullion.
Having filled [the chest] and written her name everywhere upon it, saying, "This wealth belongs to Devadattā;
it must not be taken by anyone," he took the girl and went to his own celestial mansion.
Her mother, having obtained abundant wealth, gave it to her relatives, to the poor, the destitute, and others, and after enjoying it herself, was passing away.
Having told her kinsmen, "If my daughter comes, you must show this wealth," she passed away.
Then, after the lapse of seven hundred years, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and set the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he was staying in due course at Sāvatthī;
meanwhile, that woman continued to live together with that non-human being.
Longing arose within her. Saying, "It would be well, noble son, if you would take me back to my own home," she spoke thus:
"In the past, when you had gone forth as a monk, I approached you and, having requested it, gave you a thread."
The ripening of that deed is found as a vast fruit:
many millions of garments have arisen for me.
My celestial mansion is strewn with flowers, delightful, manifold, and frequented by men and women.
“I eat and I wear [robes], and my abundant wealth does not yet diminish.
Following the ripening of that very same karma, happiness and pleasure are obtained here in this world.
Having returned once more to the human realm, I shall perform meritorious deeds, O son of a noble man.”
He spoke these verses.
341. Regarding the phrase "of the bhikkhu who has gone forth" (*pabbajitassa bhikkhuno*), this is said with reference to the Paccekabuddha.
For he is, in the ultimate sense, "one who has gone forth" because he has completely and entirely expelled and abandoned the stains of sensual desire and the like from his own continuum.
Because his defilements have been shattered, he is worthy of being called a "bhikkhu. "Sutta" refers to the Kappāsīya-sutta.

"Having approached" means having approached my house. "Requested" means requested by way of the practice of begging for alms—defined as the employment of bodily intimation—as it is said: "The Noble Ones stand depending [on others]; this is the request of the Noble Ones. "Of that" refers to that gift of cloth.

"Vipāka" means that a result with abundant fruit is found; thus, the ripening (*vipāka*)—which has abundant fruit, a sublime arising, and a great arising—is found and experienced at this present time.
"Many" (*bahuka*) means numerous. "Cotton-cloth ends" (*vatthakoṭiyo*) means the ends of cotton cloths; the meaning is that there are hundreds of thousands of different varieties of cotton cloths.
"Multicolored" (*anekacitta*) refers to various kinds of textile work, or a form variegated by many jewels such as pearls, gems, and so forth.
"Served by men and women" means attended by men and women acting as attendants.
"I enjoy that" means I experience that celestial mansion. "I wear" means I both dress in and clothe myself with whatever is desired from among many millions of garments.
"Possessing abundant wealth" means having great riches and vast possessions, with an abundance of wealth and requisites.
"And it does not yet come to an end" means that this wealth does not diminish; it does not reach exhaustion or depletion.

"Following on from the ripening of that very karma" means that, as a result, condition, and cause of that very meritorious deed consisting of the gift of a thread, there arises here in this celestial mansion happiness—which is the fruition—consisting of the pleasant and the sweet, known as *sāta*.
"He is perceived. "Having gone back again to the human state" means having returned once more to the world of men (*manussaloka*).

"I shall perform meritorious deeds" means I shall perform those meritorious deeds that produce my particular happiness, or rather, the intention is: "those by which this prosperity was obtained by me.
"Lead me, noble son," means: "O noble son, lead me to the world of men; take me there"—this is the meaning.
Having heard this, that non-human being, out of compassion for her because his heart was bound to her and unwilling to let her go, said:
"You have come here seven hundred years ago;
there you shall become old and decrepit."
