"All those kinsmen of yours have passed away;
what will you do there by going from here?"—thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, "satta" is an expression formed by the elision of a case ending, or it is a nominative plural used in the sense of the ablative.

"From a hundred years" means from beyond seven hundred years; "you have come here" means you have come to this celestial mansion (*vimāna*), and the sense is that for you who have come here, seven hundred years have passed.

"And there you will be old and aged" means that although your physical being has been sustained here by divine climate and food, through the power of karma you have remained in the form of a youth for so long.

They remain here. But having departed from here, because their karma is exhausted and because they have become worn out by old age and advanced in years through the influence of human climate and food, you will exist there in that world of humans. How so?
Because "all those relatives of yours have passed away"—since a long period of time has elapsed, even all your relatives have died; therefore, from this heavenly world, go there.
"What will you do by going to the world of men? Spend whatever remaining lifespan you have right here; dwell here"—this was his intention.
Thus addressed by him, she, not believing his words, spoke again:
"Only seven years have passed since I came here, and I am endowed with divine happiness."
"Having returned once more to the human world, I shall perform meritorious deeds, O son of a noble family," she said, reciting this verse.
Therein, "seven years have passed since I came here" means, O son of a noble family, it seems to me that seven years have elapsed since I arrived here;
yet for one endowed with divine happiness, even seven hundred years pass as but a short time.
Not perceiving that he had departed, she spoke thus.
When addressed in this way by her, that being of the celestial mansion (vimānapeta) instructed him in various ways and said: "Now, for more than seven days you will not live there;
there is wealth deposited by your mother which has been given by me; [give it] to the recluses and brahmins."
Having said, "Give this and aspire for rebirth right here," he took her by the arm, placed her in the middle of the village, and said, "When others come here, you should advise them:
'Perform meritorious deeds according to your strength. Having spoken thus, he departed. As it is said:
"Taking her by force by the arm, he led back the very frail elder nun; having brought her back, he instructed her."
“Invite other people who have come here as well; perform meritorious deeds, for happiness is easily obtained.
Therein, *so* refers to that ghost of a celestial mansion (*vimānapeta*). *Taṃ* refers to that woman.

“Having seized by the arm with force” means having taken her by the arm like one leading her away by force. “Having brought back” means having brought her again to the village where she was born and raised.
"Having brought her. *Therim* means "an old woman"; the meaning is "one who is aged and advanced in years. *Sudubbalaṃ* means "very weak" precisely because of being worn out by old age.

It is said that immediately upon departing from that celestial mansion, she became aged, elderly, advanced in years, and had reached the final stage of life. *Vajjeyyāsi* means "you should say. And in order to show the manner of the words to be spoken:
“‘And other people as well,’ and so forth, was said. Its meaning is this: ‘O Bhaddā, you too should perform meritorious deeds;

and to other people who have come here for the sake of seeing you, you should say: “Noble sirs, even disregarding your burning heads or garments, perform meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtuous conduct.
And when merit has been performed, its fruit, which is happiness, will certainly come to them.’”
"It is perceived; no doubt should be made in this matter"—thus you should say, thus you should advise.

Having spoken thus, when he had departed, that woman went to the dwelling place of her own kinsmen, identified herself to them, and having received the wealth bestowed by them, she gave gifts to recluses and brahmins, [saying] to those who came to her:
“I have seen that both ghosts and likewise humans are tormented because they did not perform wholesome deeds;
but having performed karma to be experienced as happiness, gods and humans abide in happiness.
With this verse he gave him instruction.
Therein, "by what is unmade" means by that which has not been produced and has not been accumulated by oneself. "By the good" means by wholesome kamma;

the instrumental case is used here in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). "They are afflicted" means they undergo distress. "To be experienced as pleasure" refers to meritorious kamma that has a pleasant ripening.
"Established in pleasure" means firmly grounded in pleasure. Alternatively, the reading is "sukhedhitā," meaning flourished and increased by pleasure.

The meaning. This is the intended sense here: Just as the departed spirits (petas), so too have I seen human beings being tormented by unperformed wholesome deeds and by performed unwholesome deeds, falling into distress through hunger, thirst, and the like, and experiencing great suffering.
However, having performed karma to be experienced as pleasant, by that performed wholesome karma—and by [the non-performance of] unwholesome karma—...
"And by unwholesome karma, I have seen beings included among gods and humans established in happiness;
this is my own direct experience. Therefore, avoiding evil from afar, be intent and devoted to the performance of merit.
Having thus given this exhortation, she held a great almsgiving for seven days for ascetics, brahmins, and others, and on the seventh day—
Having passed away during the day, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The bhikkhus reported this occurrence to the Blessed One.

Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude, specifically proclaiming the great fruitfulness and great benefit of giving made to paccekabuddhas. Having heard this—
The great multitude became free from stain and avarice, and delighted in the merit of giving and other virtues.
The commentary on the *Sutta-peta-vatthu* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Kaṇṇamuṇḍa-peta-vatthu*.
"Golden stair-treads": this was spoken while the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa well.

It is said that in the past, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, a certain lay follower who was a stream-enterer, being of like purpose with five hundred other lay followers, engaged in such activities as planting groves, building bridges, and constructing walkways in the city of Kimila.
Being devoted to meritorious deeds, he lived while having a monastery built for the Saṅgha, and from time to time he went to that monastery together with them.

Their wives also became lay female devotees (upāsikā), and being in harmony with one another, they would go from time to time to the monastery with garlands, perfumes, ointments, and other offerings in their hands;
on the way, they would rest in parks, assembly halls, and similar places before continuing on.
Then one day, several rogues were seated together in a certain hall.

When those women had rested there and departed, the men, having observed their physical beauty, became infatuated with them; and perceiving that they were endowed with virtue, good conduct, and excellent qualities, they initiated this conversation:
"Who among these would be capable of breaking even a single one of their moral precepts? Thereupon, a certain one [among them]...
“I am capable,” he said. They performed a miracle with him for a thousand [pieces of gold], saying, “Let us perform a miracle.
While he was striving by many means, as those women had entered the assembly hall, he played the lute *sumuñcita* with its seventy strings, producing a sweet sound;
and singing songs connected with sensual desire in that very sweet voice, he [captivated] them with the sound of his song.
Causing a certain woman to break her virtue and making her an adulteress, he defeated those rogues for a thousand [pieces of money].
Having been defeated for that thousand, they reported it to her husband. Her husband asked her:
"Are you such a person as those men have described? She denied it, saying, "I do not know anything of the sort," but when he did not believe her—
Having pointed out a dog standing nearby, she made this oath:
"If I have committed such an evil deed, let this black dog with severed ears devour me in whatever state of existence I am born.
The other five hundred women, knowing that woman to be an adulteress, wondered: "Did she actually commit such an evil act, or did she not?"
Being questioned, they spoke falsely, saying, "We do not know such a thing," and then made this oath: "If we knew, may we become her very slaves in birth after birth!
Then that unchaste woman, her heart burning with remorse for that very act, withered away and did not survive for long.
Having passed away, she was reborn as a *vimāna*-petī on the shore of one of the seven great lakes, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa-daha, in Himavat, the king of mountains.
And adjacent to her *vimāna*, a lotus pond appeared, suitable for her to experience the ripening of her karma.
The other five hundred women also, having passed away, by virtue of their mutual oath...

They were reborn as female slaves. There, having enjoyed celestial splendor for part of the day as the fruit of merit performed in the past, she would rise from her bed at midnight, impelled by the force of her evil karma, and go to the edge of the lotus pond.
Upon arriving there, a single black dog, terrifying in appearance and the size of a young elephant, [attacked her].
With its ears severed, its fangs sharp, long, and hard, its eyes resembling a mass of glowing khadira charcoal,
its tongue like a continuous flash of lightning, its claws hard and sharp, and its coarse, long, and discolored hair, it came from there, threw him down upon the ground, and—
overcome as if by extreme hunger— seized him with its teeth, reducing him to a mere skeleton while devouring him by force, and then cast him into the lotus pond.

It disappears. And as soon as she is placed there, she resumes her natural form, ascends the celestial mansion, and lies down upon the couch. But the other experiences only the suffering of servitude.
Thus, while they dwell there, more than five hundred and fifty years pass by.
Then, as they were experiencing divine splendor without men, they became weary of it.
In that region, there was a river flowing from Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, which had come down through a mountain cleft and entered the Ganges River.
And near their dwelling place stood a celestial mango grove, filled with mango trees and other fruits such as breadfruit and jackfruit.
There was a forest region, adorned and resembling a pleasure grove. They thought to themselves:
"Come now, let us throw these mango fruits into this river; perhaps some man, seeing these fruits and longing for them, might come here, and we shall delight with him. So they did. But by them...
Some of the mango fruits that were cast in were taken by ascetics, some by forest-dwellers, some were scattered by crows, and some remained stuck on the bank.
However, one fruit, having entered the current of the Ganges, eventually reached Bārāṇasī.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was bathing in the waters of the Ganges, which were enclosed by a net of iron. Then that fruit—
Carried along by the current of the river, it gradually drifted down and became snagged in a net of iron.
When the king’s men saw that great celestial mango fruit, endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor, they presented it to the king.
The king took a portion of it and, for the sake of testing its quality, gave it to a condemned thief held in prison to eat. He ate it...
Having eaten it, he said, "Your Majesty, I have never before eaten such a thing;
I imagine this is a divine mango fruit. The king gave him another piece.

Having eaten that, his wrinkles and grey hair vanished, and he became exceedingly beautiful in form, appearing as if established in the prime of youth. Seeing this, the king was filled with wonder and amazement at that mango fruit.
Having eaten it and experienced a special excellence within his body, he asked the people, "Where do such divine mango fruits exist?
The people replied, "It is said, Your Majesty, that they are found in the Himavat, the king of mountains.
"Is it possible to bring them here? "The forest-dwellers know, Your Majesty."

The king summoned the forest-dwellers, explained the matter to them, and after they had deliberated, he gave a thousand [kahāpaṇas] to one forest-dweller who had agreed to go and dismissed him, saying: "Go, bring me that mango fruit quickly.
He gave those thousand kahāpaṇas to his wife and children, took provisions for the journey, and set out along the river.
Having gone toward the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake and passed beyond the path of men, he saw an ascetic in a region measuring sixty yojanas on this side of the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake;
traveling by the path indicated by him, he again saw an ascetic in a region measuring thirty yojanas;
traveling by the path indicated by him, he again [saw one] in a region measuring fifteen yojanas.
Seeing another ascetic in that place, he told him the reason for his coming. The ascetic instructed him:
"From now on, leaving this Great Gaṅgā and relying on this small river, you should go against the current.
When you see a mountain cleft, you should enter it at night, taking a torch. And as for this river—"
"It does not move during the night; therefore, you will be fit for travel by it. After crossing several yojanas, you will see the mango trees.

Having done so, at sunrise he saw [the place] where the ground was illuminated by a network of rays from various jewels, adorned with groves of trees whose canopies of branches were bent down by the weight of their fruit, and resounded with the warbling of various kinds of birds—exceedingly...
He arrived at the enchanting mango grove.
Then, seeing him approaching from afar, those non-human women ran toward him, each crying out, "He is mine!
He is mine! However, he was there to enjoy celestial splendor together with them.
Because he had not performed meritorious deeds, he was terrified upon seeing them; crying out, he fled and eventually reached Bārāṇasī, where he reported the matter to the king.
Having heard this, the king developed a desire to see those women and to eat the mango fruits;
consequently, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his ministers, he set out under the pretext of a hunt, equipped with bow and quiver.
Having fastened his sword and accompanied by a few attendants, he traveled along the path shown by that forest-dweller.
After leaving his men at a place some leagues away, he took only the forest-dweller and proceeded gradually.
Having made even that man turn back from there, he entered an mango grove as the sun was rising. Then those women [beheld him] as if he were newly arisen...
Seeing the young god, they went out to meet him; recognizing him as a "king," they conceived feelings of affection and great respect.
Having bathed him with care, they adorned and decorated him with celestial garments, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
Then, having placed him upon a celestial mansion and fed him various kinds of exquisite divine food, they waited upon him according to his every wish.
Then, when one hundred and fifty years had passed, the king rose and sat up at the time of midnight;
seeing that unchaste female peta going toward the edge of the lotus pond, he thought, "Why indeed is she going at this hour?
and, desiring to investigate, followed her. Then, seeing her there being devoured by a dog, he wondered, "What is this?"
Not knowing [the truth], and having observed him for three days, he thought,
"This man must be her enemy," and having pierced him with a sharpened arrow and deprived him of life, he beat that woman, cast her into the lotus pond, and seeing her restored to her former beauty,
said: "With steps made of golden planks, strewn with golden sand;"
There, the groves are fragrant, lovely, sweet-scented, and delightful.
They are covered with various kinds of trees, stirred by various scents,
strewn with various lotuses, and overspread with white water-lilies.
“A fragrant breeze, delightful and stirred by the wind, blows there;
it resounds with the cries of swans and cranes, and is filled with the warbling of ruddy geese.
It is crowded with flocks of various birds and abounds with diverse groups of lakes.”
The trees bear various fruits, and the forests hold various flowers.
"Among humans, there is no city such as this one;
you have many palaces made of gold and silver."
Shining brightly, they illuminate the four directions all around:
"The five hundred slave-girls who serve you as attendants here,
wearing shell-bracelets and armlets, adorned with golden earrings."
“Many are your couches, made of gold and silver;
covered with kadali-deer skins, they are spread with woolen rugs.
Wherever you have taken up residence, you are provided with every object of desire.”
When half the night had passed, you rose from there and went away.
Having gone to the grounds of the pleasure garden,
you stood upon its bank all around a lotus pond, on the lush and beautiful green grass.
“Then that dog Kaṇṇamuṇḍa devours your limbs one by one.
And when you have been devoured until you are but a skeleton,
you plunge into the lotus pond, and your body becomes as it was before.”
“Then you, with all your limbs and members, so beautiful and lovely to behold,
having clothed yourself in a garment, came into my presence.
What evil deed have you committed by body, speech, or mind?”
"By the karmic result of kissing, this dog with cropped ears is devouring your limbs one by one.
With these twelve verses, he questioned him regarding his past conduct.
348. "With steps and planks of gold" means having steps and planks made of gold.
"Spread with golden sand" means strewn all around with sand made of gold. "Therein" refers to the lotus pond. "Sogandhiya" means *sogandhika* (fragrant) lotuses.
"Vaggū" means beautiful and lovely. "Sucigandhā" means possessing a pleasing fragrance.
349. "Stirred by various fragrances" means stirred on all sides by a scented wind consisting of various kinds of sweet-smelling perfumes.
"Covered with various lotuses" means the surface of the water is covered by various kinds of red lotuses (*paduma*).
"Spread with white lotuses" means strewn with white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).

350. "Surabhiṃ sampavāyantī" means it wafts forth a truly fragrant scent; this is the intended meaning of "pokkharaṇī" (lotus pond). "Haṃsakoñcābhirudāti" means it resounds with the cries of swans and cranes.
351. "Nānādijagaṇākiṇṇāti" means crowded with various flocks of birds. "Nānāsaragaṇāyutāti" means endowed with throngs of various kinds of winged creatures.
"Nānāphaladharāti" means bearing various kinds of fruits, because their branches are perpetually bent down by the weight of diverse fruits.
"Forests bearing various flowers" means forests that provide all kinds of fragrant blossoms; for the word "forests" (*vanā*) is used here with a change of gender.
(352) "Among humans there is no city such as this" means that there is no city like this one of yours among humans;
it is not found in the human world. "Made of silver" means made of silver (*rajatamaya*). "Shining brightly" means exceedingly...
Radiant. "Ābhenti" means they beautify. "Samantā caturo disā" means all around the four directions.
353. "Yā te mā" means those which belong to you. "Paricārikā" means female attendants who perform services. "Tā" refers to those female attendants.
"Kambukāyūradharā" means adorned with shell bracelets and golden armlets. "Kañcanāveḷabhūsitā" means their hair-locks are decorated with golden ear-ornaments.

354. "Covered with kadali-deer skins" means spread with a bed-covering made of kadali-deer hides. "Ready" means prepared, fit for lying down. "Spread with *gonaka* wool" means covered with a long-haired woolen rug (*kojava*). 355. "Wherein" means on which couch.
"Having gone to rest" means having entered into rest; the meaning is "having lain down. "When half the night had arrived" means when the middle watch of the night had come.
"From there" means from the couch. 356. "From the lotus pond" means from a lotus pool. "Green" means blue. "With young grass" means covered with tender grass. "Beautiful."

"Suddhe" (O pure one) is an address to her. "Bhadde," meaning "O auspicious one," the construction is: "Having gone to the bank of that lotus pond, which was green with grass on all sides, you stood—there you remain.

"Kaṇṇamuṇḍo" means one whose ears were cut off, one whose ears were severed. "Khāyitā āsi" means she had been devoured. "Aṭṭhisaṅkhalikā katā" means she was reduced to nothing more than a skeleton. "Yathā pure" means just as before, as she was prior to being devoured by the dog.

358. *Tato* means after descending into the lotus pond. *Aṅgapaccaṅgī* means possessing all limbs and members in their entirety. *Sucārū* means very beautiful and delightful. *Piyadassanā* means lovely to behold. *Āyāsī* means you have come.
Thus questioned by the king, that female spirit (petī), explaining her own history to him from the beginning, said:
"In Kimilā there was a householder, a faithful lay follower (*upāsaka*);"
I was his wife, unvirtuous and unfaithful.
As I was being unfaithful, my husband said this to me:
"This conduct of yours is neither hidden nor fitting—that you should be unfaithful to me."
“I uttered a terrible oath and spoke a falsehood:
‘I shall not transgress against you, whether by body or by mind.
If I should transgress against you, whether by body or by mind—’”
“May this dog Kaṇṇamuṇḍa devour my limbs one by one!
“Because of the ripening of that deed, and of both [that deed] and the false speech,
for seven hundred years I have indeed experienced [this].”
“Kaṇṇamuṇḍa the dog devours my limbs one by one”—with these words he spoke five verses.
(360–1) Therein, *kimilāyaṃ* means in the city of that name. *Aticārinī*: for a wife is called “unfaithful” (*aticārinī*) because she wanders beyond her husband.
The construction is: “While I was being unfaithful, that husband said this to me.”
“*Netaṃ channaṃ*” and so forth is a demonstration of the manner in which it was spoken. Therein, “*netaṃ channaṃ*” means this is not fitting; “*na paṭirūpaṃ*” is a synonym for that very same thing.

“*Yaṃ*” is a reference to the action. “*Aticarāsī*” means you transgress; or rather, this is the reading itself. “*Yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ aticarasi*”: regarding that which you transgress against me, the meaning is: “this transgression is not hidden, nor is it fitting.”
362–4. *Ghoranti* means terrible. *Sapathanti* means an oath. *Bhāsisanti* means I spoke.
*Sacāhanti* means if I. *Tanti* means you. *Tassa kammassāti* means of that evil deed, of that deed of immorality.
*Musāvādassa cāti* means and of the false speech [spoken when saying] "I do not transgress against you. *Ubhayanti* means the result of both. *Anubhūtantī* means experienced.
The meaning is: "experienced by me. "From which" means from which evil kamma.
Having spoken thus, she praised the benefit he had rendered her:
"And you, O Lord, are my great benefactor; you have come here for my sake."
“I am liberated from Kaṇṇamuṇḍa; I am free from sorrow and have no fear from any quarter.
Therefore, O Lord, I pay homage to you; with palms joined in reverence, I entreat you:
‘Enjoy superhuman pleasures; O Lord, take delight with me.’”
He spoke two verses. Therein, "O King" (*deva*) is an address to the monarch. "From Kaṇṇamuṇḍa" (*kaṇṇamuṇḍassa*):
this is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative. Then the king, his mind weary of dwelling there, manifested his intention to depart.
Hearing that, the female spirit (petī), her heart bound to the king, requested him to remain right there and spoke the verse: "Therefore, O King, I shall pay homage to you."
Then the king, desiring nothing more than to go to the city with absolute resolve, made known his own intention, saying:
“I have enjoyed superhuman pleasures; I have delighted together with you.
Therefore, O fortunate one, I entreat you: quickly take me back.”

He spoke the concluding verse. Therein, *tāhaṃ* means "I, that [person]. *Subhage* means "O fortunate one. *Paṭinayāhi maṃ* means "Give me back my city; give me back to me. The rest is clear everywhere.

Then that *vimāna*-petī, having heard the king’s words, unable to endure separation, her heart agitated by the intensity of her grief, her body trembling, and although she entreated him with various means, being unable to make him stay there, [she spoke] with many...
Having escorted the king to the city with costly jewels and having led him up to the palace, she wept and lamented, then returned to her own dwelling place.
But the king, seeing her, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for heaven.
Then, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma...
In due course, while staying at Sāvatthī, on one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering among the mountains, saw that woman together with her retinue.
He asked her about the deed she had committed, and she told the Elder everything from the beginning.
The Elder taught them the Dhamma. The Elder then reported this matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for his discourse, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. The great multitude, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency, turned away from evil;
performing meritorious deeds such as giving, they became destined for heaven.
Thus ends the commentary on the story of the petī Kaṇṇamuṇḍā.
13. The Commentary on the Story of the Ubbarī Ghost.
"There was a king named Brahmadatta"—this story of the Ubbarī ghost was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain laywoman.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, the husband of a certain laywoman passed away.
Afflicted by the suffering of separation from her husband and grieving, she went to the cremation ground and wept.

The Blessed One, seeing that she possessed the necessary spiritual maturity (*upanissaya*) for the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), his mind stirred by compassion, went to her house and sat down on the prepared seat.
The female lay devotee approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Then he—

The Teacher asked, "What is it, laywoman, that you are grieving? When she replied, "Yes, Blessed One, I am grieving because of separation from what is dear," he wished to dispel her sorrow and related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Pañcāla, in the city of Kapila, there was a king named Cūḷanī Brahmadatta. He [fell into] a wrong course...
Having abandoned [his former life] and being devoted to bringing welfare to his people within his own realm, he ruled the kingdom without violating the ten duties of a king.
At one time, desiring to hear what was being said about his own reign, he assumed the guise of a weaver and, alone and without a companion, departed from the city.
Wandering from village to village and from district to district, he found that the entire kingdom was free from thorns and free from oppression.
Seeing people greeting one another and living as if their houses were open, he was filled with joy;
turning back and heading toward the city, he entered the house of a certain poor widow in a village.
Seeing him, she said, "Who are you, noble sir, and from where have you come? "I am a weaver, lady, working for wages."
“I wander about performing the work of a tailor. If you have any tailoring work, give me food and wages, and I will do the work for you as well. “We have no work, nor do we have food or wages;
go and work for others, noble sir. Having stayed there for a few days, he [saw] one endowed with the marks of grain and merit...
Seeing his daughter, he said to his mother: "Is this girl already claimed by someone, or is she unclaimed?
If she is unclaimed by anyone, give her to me; I am capable of providing for your livelihood with ease.
"Very well, noble sir," she replied, and gave her to him.
Thus, having stayed with her for a few days and given her a thousand kahāpaṇas, he said, "I shall return in just a few days.
My dear lady, do not be distressed," and went to his own city.
There, between that city and the village, he had the road leveled and decorated, and set out with great royal splendor.
Having gone there, he placed the girl upon a heap of kahāpaṇa coins, bathed her in golden and silver jars,
had her given the name “Ubbarī,” and established her in the position of chief queen.
Having bestowed that village upon her kinsmen and brought her to the city with great royal splendor, he took his pleasure with her and enjoyed the bliss of sovereignty for the rest of his life.
Having experienced [the fruits of her deeds], she passed away at the end of her lifespan.
When he had died and the funeral rites for his body had been performed, Ubbarī—her heart pierced by the arrow of grief due to separation from her husband—went to the cremation ground.

After worshipping with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings for many days and extolling the virtues of the king, she circumambulated the cremation ground while weeping and lamenting as if she had gone mad.

And at that time, our Blessed One, having become a Bodhisatta and gone forth as an ascetic, having attained meditative absorption and supernormal knowledge, was dwelling in a certain forest region in the vicinity of the Himalayas.
Seeing with his divine eye Ubbarī, who was pierced by the arrow of grief, he came through the air; appearing in visible form, he stood in the sky and [addressed] the people standing there.
He asked: “Whose funeral pyre is this, and for whose sake is this woman wailing and lamenting, crying out ‘Brahmadatta!
Brahmadatta!’? Hearing this, the people said: “The king of the Pañcālas named Brahmadatta has passed away at the end of his life;
this is his funeral pyre, and this is his chief queen, named Ubbarī, who cries out ‘Brahmadatta! Brahmadatta!’”
“Calling his name, she wept and lamented,” they said. To illustrate this matter, the compilers of the collection said:
“There was a king named Brahmadatta, the bull among charioteers of the Pañcālas;
with the passing of days and nights, the king passed away.”
“Having gone to the cremation ground, his wife Ubbarī wept;
not seeing Brahmadatta, she cried out, ‘Brahmadatta!
Then a sage, a muni perfected in conduct, arrived there.”
And there he asked those who had gathered together: "Whose cremation ground is this, filled with various fragrant scents?
Whose wife is this weeping for her husband who has gone far away?"
Not seeing Brahmadatta, she cried out, "Brahmadatta!
Then those who were gathered there gave their explanation concerning Brahmadatta’s welfare, O Blessed One;
concerning Brahmadatta’s welfare, O dear sir.
“This is his funeral pyre, perfumed with various scents;
his wife is weeping for her husband who has gone far from here.
Not seeing Brahmadatta, she cries out, ‘Brahmadatta!’”—thus they recited these six verses.
368–9. *Tattha ahū* means "there was. *Pañcālānaṃ* refers to the inhabitants of the kingdom of Pañcāla, or to the kingdom of Pañcāla itself.
For even a single province may, by conventional usage based on its princes, be designated by the plural term "the Pañcālas.
*Rathesabho* means "a bull among chariot-warriors," that is, a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*). *Tassa āḷāhanaṃ* means "his cremation ground."
The place where that king’s body was cremated. 370. *Isi*:
one who seeks (*esi*) qualities such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and so forth; thus, he is an *isi*. *Tattha*: in that place where Ubbarī stood;
the meaning is "in the cemetery. *Āgacchi*: he went. *Sampannacaraṇo*: one whose conduct is perfected, [meaning] perfection in virtue (*sīla*) and guardedness of the sense doors.

One who is endowed with and possessed of these fifteen qualities reckoned as "conduct"—namely, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven true qualities beginning with faith, and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas—is "perfected in conduct" (*caraṇasampanna*); this is the meaning.
A "sage" (*muni*) is so called because he "measures" (*munāti*) or knows both his own welfare and the welfare of others. And it was he who there asked [the question].
He questioned the people standing in that place. "Those who had gathered there" means those persons who had assembled at that charnel ground (*susāna*).
*Su* is merely a particle. Alternatively, the reading is "ye tatthāsuṃ samāgatā. *Āsuṃ* means "were" or "had been. 371.
"Perfumed with various scents" means thoroughly scented and infused on all sides by various kinds of fragrances. *Itoti*...
"From the human world. "Gone far away" means he says this because he has gone to the other world (*paraloka*).
"'Brahmadatta,' he cries out"—having thus uttered his name, he calls out by way of lamentation.
"O dear Brahmadatta! O venerable Brahmadatta!"—"Venerable" (*mārisa*) refers to one whose body and mind are free from affliction (*nirāmaya*).
"O Great Sage, this is the cremation ground of King Brahmadatta; this is the wife of that very King Brahmadatta.

May it be well with him, King Brahmadatta, and may it be well with her. The intention is that by thinking of the welfare of such great queens, even when they have passed away to the next world, there is indeed benefit and happiness."
Then that ascetic, having heard their words and moved by compassion, went into the presence of Ubbarī; and for the sake of dispelling her grief, he said:
"Eighty-six thousand men named Brahmadatta have been burned here in this funeral pyre; whom among them do you mourn?"
He spoke this verse. In it, "eighty-six thousand" means a number consisting of eighty thousand plus six thousand. "Named Brahmadatta" means those whose names were indeed "Brahmadatta.
"Whom among them do you mourn?"—he asked, "Among those numbered at eighty-six thousand Brahmadattas, which Brahmadatta do you mourn? With respect to which one has your sorrow arisen?"
Thus questioned by that seer, Ubbarī, explaining the Brahmadatta she herself desired,
said: "The king who is the son of Cūḷanī, the bull among chariot-warriors of the Pañcālas—
him, O Venerable One, I grieve for, my husband who grants all desires."
He spoke this verse. In it, "the son of Cūḷanī" refers to the son of the king named thus. "Sabbakāmadada" means one who gives everything desired by me, or one who gives what is desired by all beings.
When Ubbarī had spoken thus, the ascetic said again:
"They were all kings named Brahmadatta."
"All the sons of Cūḷanī, the bull-like chariot-warriors of the Pañcālas—
In due order, she made them all great queens. Why,
having left behind those who came before, do you grieve for the last?"— thus he spoke these two verses.

376. *Tattha sabbevāhesun* means that all those eighty-six thousand kings named Brahmadatta, sons of Cūḷanī, became elephant-riders (*rathesabha*) for the Pañcālas. None of them possessed these specific distinctions, such as the status of being a king. 377.
*Mahesittamakārayī* means that she, in turn, made herself the chief queen (*aggamahesī*) among all of them in succession.

The meaning is "not attained. He asked: "Why? Among all these people who are indistinguishable in terms of their virtues and their status as lords, why and for what reason do you grieve over only one, the last king, having abandoned the previous ones?
Having heard that, Ubbarī was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and spoke again to the ascetic:
“O Noble One, for a long time I have been a woman within myself;
you have spoken much concerning me, who am a woman in this cycle of existence”—thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, *ātume* means “within myself. *Itthibhūtāya* means “having entered into the state of being a woman. *Dīgharattāya* means...
For a long time. This is the intended meaning here: while existing as a woman, am I always only a woman within myself, or do I also attain the state of a man? "Of me who has become a woman" means:
of me, who has become a woman, you, O Great Sage, speak and declare such a state of being a great seer (*maheṣi*) throughout many cycles of existence (*saṃsāra*). "They said to me... [and so forth].
Or there is the reading “itthibhūtāya. In that context, *ā* is a particle used in the sense of recollection (*anussaraṇatthe*). “*Āhu me*”: this was personally recollected by me;
it was not known [previously] by me that, having been a woman—having attained the state of a woman—such was my successive rebirth for so long a time.
Why? Because for me, while being a woman, he caused all [men] to make me their chief queen (*mahesitti*) in succession.
"O Great Sage, why do you speak so much about *saṃsāra*?"—this is the construction [of the question].
Having heard that, the ascetic, demonstrating that there is no such fixed rule in *saṃsāra* as "a woman remains only a woman, and a man remains only a man," said:
"She was a woman, she was a man, and she even entered the womb of a beast."
"Thus it is for those of the past; no end is seen"—this verse he spoke.
Therein, "there was a woman, there was a man" means that you were sometimes a woman and sometimes a man.
Not only did you have the state of being a woman or a man, but you also entered the womb of an animal; at times you even had the state of an animal.
She came [into this world], and she even entered the womb of an animal. Thus, regarding those of the past, no end is seen;

that is to say, for those who have undergone such states as womanhood, manhood, and the state of animals as described above, no limit to their past existences is seen even by one looking with the eye of knowledge and great effort. Not...
It is not only yours alone; rather, for all beings wandering in saṃsāra, the limit of their individual existence is neither seen nor known. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not known of beings who, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, run on and wander through it."
Having thus heard the Dhamma taught by that ascetic— who was elucidating the boundlessness of *saṃsāra* and the fact that one's own actions are one's own property—
they became deeply stirred regarding *saṃsāra*, their minds were filled with confidence in the Dhamma,
and the thorn of sorrow having been removed, they expressed their own faith and the departure of their grief:
“While I was burning, like a fire drenched with ghee,
you have sprinkled me with water as it were and extinguished every dart.
You have indeed pulled out the arrow, the sorrow residing within my heart.”
“He who dispelled my sorrow when I was overcome by grief—
having heard you, O Great Sage, I have extracted the arrow, I have become cool, and I am extinguished; I do not grieve, nor do I weep.”
He recited three verses. Their meaning has already been explained above.
Now, the Teacher, demonstrating the conduct of Ubbarī, whose heart was filled with agitation, said:
“Having heard those well-spoken words of the ascetic...”
Taking her bowl and robes, she went forth into the homeless life.
Having gone forth from the home to the homeless state,
she cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of rebirth in the Brahma-world.
“Wandering from village to village, through market towns and royal capitals,
there was a village named Uruvelā where you passed away.
Having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of rebirth in the Brahma-world,”
“Having dispassionately abandoned the female mind, they have gone to the Brahma-world”—thus he spoke these four verses.
(383–4) Therein, *tassa* means “of that ascetic. *Subhāsitaṃ* means well-spoken; the meaning is “the Dhamma.
*Pabbajitā santā* means having entered the homeless life, or being those who, having gone forth, possess peace in body and speech. *Mettacittaṃ* means...
"A mind accompanied by loving-kindness. He speaks of the jhāna of loving-kindness under the heading of "mind.
Regarding "for rebirth in the Brahma-world": she developed that mind of loving-kindness for the sake of rebirth in the Brahma-world, not for the purpose of attaining insight (vipassanā) or the like.
For when no Buddha has appeared, ascetics and wanderers who develop the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and so forth do so solely for the sake of success within existence (bhava).
385–6. *Gāmā gāman* means from one village to another village. *Ābhāvetvā* means having developed or increased.
Some read *abhāvetvā*; for them, the vowel *a-* is merely a particle. *Virājetvā itthicittaṃ* means having dispelled the mind’s inclination, intention, and delight toward the female state;
that is, having become one whose mind is dispassionate toward the female state. *Brahmalokūpagā* refers to those who have reached the Brahma-world by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
She was one destined for rebirth in the Brahma-world. The rest is clear, as it follows the method already explained below.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher dispelled the grief of that female lay follower and gave a further discourse on the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, that female lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. And so it was for the assembled assembly.
"The teaching was fruitful.
The commentary on the story of the Ubbarī peta is finished.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Petavatthu* of the *Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*.
The commentary on the meaning of the second sub-section, the Ubbarivagga, adorned with thirteen bases, is completed. 3.
The Cūḷavagga (Minor Section).
1. Commentary on the Story of the Insubmersible Petas (*Abhijjamānapetavatthu-vaṇṇanā*).
"In water that does not submerge" was spoken concerning a certain hunter-peta while the Teacher was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*).
It is said that in Benares, on the opposite side of the Ganges in a western direction, beyond the village of Vāsabha, there was a place named Cundaṭṭhila.
In a certain village there was a hunter. Having killed deer in the forest, he would roast the choice meat over coals, eat it himself, and then bind the remainder in leaf-wraps;
carrying these on a shoulder-pole, he would return to the village.
When the village children saw him at the village gate, they ran toward him with outstretched hands, crying, "Give us meat! Give us meat! He gave them a little...

He gave him a small amount of meat. Then one day, having failed to obtain any meat, he adorned himself with an *uddālaka* flower, took a large quantity in his hand, and was walking toward the village.
Seeing him at the village gate, the children ran toward him, stretching out their hands and crying, "Give me meat!
Give me meat! He gave each of them a single cluster of flowers.
Then, at a later time, having passed away, he was reborn among the *petas*. Naked, deformed in appearance, and terrifying to behold,
not knowing food or drink even in his dreams, with a wreath of *uddālaka* flowers bound upon his head,
he went on foot against the current of the Ganges, thinking, "I shall receive something from my kinsmen at Cunda’s pillar."

He was going along. At that time, a high minister of King Bimbisāra named Koliya, having pacified a rebellious border region and returning, had sent his force of elephants, horses, and so forth by land route, while he himself was coming down the river Gaṅgā by boat with the current.
Seeing that peta going in such a manner, he asked:
“While the waters of the Ganges are flowing here,
you go across them naked like a hungry ghost from the previous existence, yet wearing garlands and adorned.
Where will you go, O ghost, and where will your dwelling be?”

He spoke this verse. Therein, "abhijjamāne" means in the water of the river Gaṅgā, which is not broken by the placing of footsteps—that is, in the current of the river Gaṅgā. "Idha" means in this place.

"Pubbaddhapetova" means like a deceased one from the first half of his body, like a son of the gods who has departed from his womb. How so? "Wearing a garland, adorned"—having been decked out with garlands.
The meaning is "with a decorated head. "Where will your dwelling be? means: "In which village or region will your residence be? Tell us that"—this is the sense.
Now, in order to show what was said at that time by that peta and by the Koliyan, the compilers [of the Canon] say:
“I shall go to Cundaṭṭhila; he says that he is a peta.
He is between Vāsabhagāma and the vicinity of Bārāṇasī.
And having seen him, the high official known as Koliya—
She gave roasted flour, a meal, and a pair of yellow garments to the peta.
While the boat was still standing, she had them given to the barber;
what was given to the barber appeared to the peta in that very place.
“Then, one who is well-dressed, wearing garlands, and adorned, the offering benefits the peta standing at that place.
Therefore, out of compassion, you should give to the petas again and again. Thus they spoke these verses.

388. *Tattha Cundaṭṭhila* refers to a village of that name. *Antare Vāsabhagāmaṃ Bārāṇasiñca santike* means "between Vāsabhagāma and in the vicinity of Bārāṇasī," that is, in the middle of Vāsabhagāma and Bārāṇasī.
Because of its connection with the word *antare*, this is the accusative case used in the sense of "between.
For that village was indeed near Bārāṇasī. This is the meaning here: between Vāsabhagāma and Bārāṇasī.
And [he thought], "I shall go to that village named Caṇḍaṭṭhila, which is not far from Bārāṇasī.

(389) "Renowned as a Koliyan" means his name was proclaimed as "Koliyan. "Flour and rice" means both flour and cooked rice. "He gave a pair of yellow garments" means he gave a pair of garments, one of which was yellow, the color of gold.
(390) If one asks, "When did he give them? it says: "While the ship was standing still. "He had the barber give [them]" refers to the departing ship.

Setting aside [the rest], he caused a pair of garments to be given there to a single lay devotee (upāsaka) who was a barber; the construction is that this was done when the pair of garments had been given.
"In that place" means at once, at that very moment. "Appeared to the peta" means it became manifest upon the peta’s body;
the cloth for his lower and upper garments was provided. Therefore he said: "Then, well-robed and well-clad, wearing garlands and adorned."

“Dressed in fine garments and well-adorned with garlands and ornaments—since this offering, when presented by one standing in the position of a worthy recipient (*dakkhiṇeyya*), is of benefit to that peta who stands in that place, it has reached its intended purpose.
Therefore, out of compassion for the petas, you should give again and again. This means: out of compassion for the petas.
The meaning is: "One should repeatedly give an offering dedicated to that deceased being.
Then, out of compassion for that deceased being, the Koliyan minister completed the ritual of giving and, returning downstream, reached Bārāṇasī as the sun was rising.
And the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring them, arrived through the air.
He stood on the bank of the Ganges. The chief minister of the Koliyans also stepped down from his boat and, with a joyful heart, invited the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal today out of compassion.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Having understood the Blessed One’s consent, he immediately [prepared] a delightful spot of ground.

Having caused a great pavilion of branches to be constructed, adorned above and on all four sides with various garments of many colors and diverse hues, he prepared a seat for the Blessed One there and offered it.
The Blessed One sat down upon the prepared seat.
Then that high official approached the Blessed One, honored him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having paid homage, stood to one side.
Seated there, he reported to the Blessed One his own previous words and the reply given by the peta.
Immediately upon the Blessed One’s thought, "Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus come," the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
urged by the power of the Buddha like a flock of golden swans surrounding the king of swans, Dhataraṭṭha— surrounded the King of Dhamma.
At that very moment, a great multitude gathered, thinking, "A sublime teaching of the Dhamma will take place.
Seeing this, the high minister, with a mind full of faith, satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, out of compassion for the great multitude, he said, "Let those who dwell in the villages near Bārāṇasī assemble!"
He made a formal resolve. Then, by the power of his supernormal success (*iddhi*), all those great crowds gathered together, and he made those spirits manifest in their true grandeur.
Among them, some wore rags of tattered and torn cloth; some had covered their nakedness with their own hair;
some were naked, like newborn infants, overcome by hunger and thirst, their bodies merely skin-covered skeletons. From there...
And as they were wandering about, they became visible to the great multitude.

Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi*) that they gathered together in one place and confessed to the great multitude the evil deeds they had committed. To illustrate this matter, the compilers of the collection [said]:
“Some were dressed in fresh bark garments, others were clothed in matted hair;”
The hungry ghosts go out for food, departing in every direction.
Some run a great distance and turn back even before finding anything;
famished, bewildered, and reeling, they collapse upon the ground.
“Some, having fallen there, were dashed against the ground;
having failed to perform wholesome deeds in the past, they were like those scorched by fire in the heat.
‘In the past we were of evil character, householders and mothers of families;’”
While there were worthy things to be given, we did not make an island for ourselves.
Although abundant food and drink were scattered about,
we gave nothing at all to the monks who had set out upon the right path.
“Desiring work yet lazy, craving comfort yet eating extravagantly,
we used to revile the recipients while giving them morsels of food from our own portions.
Those were our houses, those were our female slaves, and those were our very ornaments.”
“They serve others, while we are partakers of suffering.
“Women of the Veṇī caste are held in contempt, as are the Rathakāra women and those of ill-repute;
the Caṇḍālī women are wretched, and so too are the Kappaka women again and again.”
“Whatever families are lowly and destitute,
it is into those very ones that they are born— this is the destiny of the miserly.
But those who have performed good deeds in the past, who are generous and free from stinginess,”
They fill the heavens and illuminate the Nandana grove.
Having enjoyed themselves in the Vejayanta palace according to their desires,
they are born into high-ranking families when they pass away from those realms of enjoyment.
“In gabled halls and palaces, upon couches spread with woolen rugs,
their limbs fanned by peacock-feather whisks— women of noble birth and great renown,
wearing garlands and adorned with ornaments, pass from lap to lap.”
Nurses attend upon them, seeking their comfort morning and evening.
"This is not for those who have performed no merit;
this belongs only to those who have performed merit—the sorrowless, delightful, and charming Great Forest of the Thirty-Three."
“Happiness is not for those who have performed no merit, neither in this world nor in the next;
but happiness belongs to those who have performed merit, both in this world and in the next.
For those who desire such companionship, much wholesome merit must be done.”
“They who have performed merit rejoice in heaven, endowed with enjoyments”—thus they spoke these verses.
392. Therein, “wearing rags from a dust-heap” means wearing garments made of torn and tattered pieces of cloth. “Some” means certain individuals.
“Wearing their hair” means those who conceal their nakedness with their own hair. “Going for food” means thinking, “Perhaps having gone from here to wherever...”
Thinking, "In that place, may we find some leftover food, or vomited food, or the impurities of the womb,
and so forth," they do not remain in one spot but go about for the sake of food; they depart from place to place,
traveling many yojanas away from one location to another.
393. "Far away" means at a very distant place. "Some" refers to certain *petas*. "Having run forth" means having rushed forward for the sake of food.
"Turning back without obtaining" means they turn back without having obtained even a little food or drink.
"Fainting" means having fainted due to the delusion produced by the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth. "Wandering about" means moving restlessly. "Striking against the ground" means...
Remaining in that very state of fainting, they withered away like clods of clay thrown down and fell to the ground. (394) "There" means in the place where they had gone.
"They were dashed against the ground" means they fell to the earth because they were unable to remain due to the suffering of hunger and thirst, as if falling over a precipice;
or else, it means that in the place where they had gone, they fell there due to the lack of food and such.
The meaning is that, having had their hopes severed, they fall to the ground as if struck or beaten by someone from the front.
"Having previously performed no merit" means they did not perform wholesome deeds in former existences.

"As if burned by fire in the heat" means that, like those burned by fire in a place of intense sunlight during the summer season, they experience great suffering while being scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst.
395. *Pubbe* means in a previous existence. *Pāpadhammā* means those whose nature is base due to being envious, stingy, and so forth.
*Gharaṇī* means mistresses of the household. *Kulamātaro* means mothers of the children of the family, or mothers of the men of the family.
*Dīpa* means a support; the meaning is "merit. For that is called a "support" because it serves as the basis for beings to be established in the happy realms (*sugatī*).
*Nākamhā* means "we did not do.
396. *Pahūtaṃ* means "much. *Anna-pānaṃ pi* means "both food and drink. *Api ssu avakirīyati*: here *api* is merely a particle;
it means "is also strewn" or "is scattered. *Sammaggate* means "having gone rightly," "one who has entered upon the right path," or "to one who has practiced rightly."
"Pabbajite" means "to one who has gone forth. This is a locative expression used in the sense of the dative.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "when a person who has gone forth has arrived properly. "And we did not give anything" means they say this while overcome by remorse, thinking, "We did not give even the slightest thing that ought to be given."

397. *Akammakāmā*: they desire what should not be done; because they desire unwholesome action (*akusala-kamma*) which ought not to be performed, they are "those who desire non-action" (*akammakāmā*).

Alternatively, those who desire wholesome action (*kusala-kamma*) which ought to be performed by the virtuous are "those who desire action" (*kammakāmā*); those who do not desire action are "those who desire non-action.
The meaning is that they lack desire for wholesome states (*dhamma*). *Alasā*: lazy, lacking vigor in performing wholesome action. *Sādukāmā*: fond of things that are pleasant and sweet.

"Mahagghasāti" means "great eaters. This shows that even after obtaining food that was both excellent and sweet in both respects, they ate it themselves without giving anything to those who needed it. "Ālopapiṇḍadātāro" means givers of even a mere morsel-sized lump of food.
"Paṭiggahe" means to the one receiving it. "Paribhāsimhase" means we spoke while treating them with contempt.
The meaning is: "We despised them; we mocked them.
(398) "Those houses" refers to those dwellings where we formerly felt possessiveness, thinking, "This is our home";
the intention is that those houses remain exactly as they were, yet now nothing of ours serves any purpose there. And those female slaves, and those very ornaments...
The same principle applies here as well. In that context, "noti" means "to us. "Tet" means "those [things]," such as the house and so forth.
"Aññe paricārenti" means that others enjoy them; the sense is that they make use of them by way of consumption and so on. "Mayaṃ dukkhassa bhāginoti" means:
"But we, having previously been solely intent on play, did not know how to abandon our wealth and make it something to be taken away and followed after [in the next life]."
"Now we shall be partakers of the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth," they say, reproaching themselves.

399. Now, since beings who have passed away from the realm of hungry ghosts (*petayoni*) and are reborn among humans generally become those of low birth and a miserable livelihood due to the remaining ripening of that very same karma, [the text] states the following to demonstrate this point:
With the words “*veṇivā*,” etc., two verses are spoken. Therein, “*veṇivā*” means those of the *veṇi* caste;

the meaning is that they are basket-makers or reed-workers. The word “*vā*” has the sense of indefiniteness. “*Avaññā*” means those who are to be despised; what is meant is that they are to be looked down upon.
Alternatively, the reading is “*vambhanā*,” meaning they are to be oppressed by others. “*Rathakārī*” refers to leather-workers. “*Dubbhikā*” means...

"Betrayers of friends" means those who harm their friends. "Caṇḍālīs" means those of the caṇḍāla caste. "Miserable ones" (kapaṇā) refers to beggars who have fallen into a state of extreme pitifulness.

"Barbers" (kappakā) means those of the barber caste; in all instances, the phrase "they arise again and again" is to be connected [to each], meaning that they are reborn repeatedly even within these low-born families.

400. "They are born among those very [beings]" means that they are born among those very low-born families—such as the Nesaḍas, Pukkusas, and others—who are wretched, exceedingly contemptible, and extremely miserable;
having been reborn among the hungry ghosts (petas) through the stain of stinginess, and passing away from there, they are reborn [again]. Therefore he said: "This is the destination of the stingy."

401. Having thus shown the destiny of beings who have not performed merit, [the Buddha] now spoke seven verses beginning with “Those who formerly performed what is beautiful,” in order to show the destiny of those who have performed merit. Therein, “they fill the heavens”:
those who in a former birth performed what is beautiful—givers, delighting in the merit of giving, free from the stain of stinginess—they, by means of their own perfection of form...
And by means of their retinues and their excellence, they fill and complete the heavenly world of the devas. They illuminate Nandana;

for they do not merely fill it, but moreover, having overwhelmed even the Nandana Grove—which already shines by its own nature with the radiance of the *kappa*-trees and other such wonders—with the brilliance of their own garments and ornaments and the luster of their bodies, [they cause it to shine].
And having illuminated, they shine.

(402) *Kāmakāmī* means those who possess the enjoyment of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) according to their desire and as they wish. *Uccākulesu* means in high families, such as those of the Khattiyas. *Sabhogesū* means in those possessing great wealth. *Tato cutā* means fallen from that world of the gods.

(403) *Kūṭāgāre ca pāsāde* means in gabled houses and palaces. *Bījitaṅgā* means with their bodies being fanned. *Morahatthehi* means with fans whose handles are adorned with peacock feathers. *Yasassino* means possessed of retinues; the intention is that they take delight.
"Moving from lap to lap" means that even during childhood, they go from one lap—the place where relatives or nurses hold them—to another lap;
the intention is that they do not go to the ground. "They attend upon" means they provide service. "Seeking comfort" means desiring happiness;
the intention is that they attend upon [the parents] while avoiding even slight suffering, thinking, "May there be no cold or heat."

405. "This is not for those who have not performed merit": because it is free from the grounds for sorrow, this delightful, charming, and beautiful Great Forest of the Thirty-three gods—the Nandana, which serves as a great pleasure grove for the Tāvatiṃsa deities—is not for those who have not performed merit;
the meaning is that it cannot be obtained by them.

406. "Here" (idha) refers specifically to this human world where merit is performed; it is with reference to this that he says "here. Alternatively, "here" means in the present life (diṭṭhadhamme), and "in the other world" (parattha) means in the future life (samparāye).
407. "Of them" (tesaṃ) means by those aforementioned deities. "Desiring companionship" (sahabyakāmānaṃ) means desiring coexistence.

"Possessors of enjoyments" (bhogasamaṅgino) means endowed with enjoyments; the meaning is that they rejoice, being fully provided with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure. The rest is self-evident.
When the departed spirits had thus explained in common the destiny resulting from their own past actions and the destiny resulting from meritorious deeds,
the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the great assembly gathered there— headed by the Koliyan minister— who were moved with spiritual urgency, according to their individual inclinations.
At the conclusion of that teaching, for eighty-four thousand [beings]...
There was a realization of the Dhamma by thousands of beings.
The commentary on the *Abhijjamāna-peta-vatthu* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Sāṇavāsi-thera-peta-vatthu*.
"Thera Kuṇḍināgariya": this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning the deceased relatives of the Venerable Sāṇavāsi Thera.

It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, the son of King Kitava, while returning from a pleasure excursion in the park, saw the Paccekabuddha named Sunetta emerging from the city after wandering for alms.
Seeing him, the king became intoxicated with the pride of his sovereignty and thought, "How can this shaveling pass by without paying me homage?

With a corrupted mind, he descended from the back of the elephant and, while addressing him with the words, "Have you obtained alms-food?", he seized the bowl from his hand, threw it to the ground, and broke it.
Yet, because he had attained the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) in all circumstances, the monk remained without any change of expression.

As he gazed with a mind serene through the descent of joy born from the expansion of compassion, [the other]—his heart defiled by resentment at that improper situation—said, "Do you not know me, the son of King Kitava? What will you do to me just by looking?
and having spoken thus, he departed with a mocking laugh. As soon as he had departed, a feverish heat like the burning of the fires of hell arose in his body.
He was born there. Overwhelmed by that great torment and struck by exceedingly intense painful sensations, he died and was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.
There, he rolled about in many ways—on his right side, on his left side, face up, and face down.
After being boiled for eighty-four thousand years, he passed away from there and experienced the suffering of hunger, thirst, and the like among the *petas* for an immeasurable period of time.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the village of Keṇiya near the city of Kuṇḍina during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Knowledge of his former births arose within him, and by means of that, he recollected the suffering he had previously experienced.
Although he had reached maturity, out of fear of evil he did not go with his kinsmen for the purpose of fishing.
While they were going, he hid himself, being unwilling to kill fish;

and having gone [with them], he would break the net, or having caught the fish alive, he would release them back into the water. His kinsmen, not informing him of that deed, [sent him] from their home...
They carried him away. However, one of his brothers had a heart bound with affection for him.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling on Mount Sāṇa in dependence upon the city of Kuṇḍina.
Then that son of a fisherman, having been abandoned by his kinsmen, wandered here and there until he reached that region.
At the time for the meal, he approached the Elder. Having questioned him and learned that he was in need of food, the Elder gave him a meal.

When the Elder had finished his meal and learned of the entire situation, and having perceived that the man’s mind was gladdened by the discourse on the Dhamma, he asked, "Friend, will you go forth? "Yes, venerable sir, I shall go forth. The Elder—
Having ordained him, he went together with him into the presence of the Blessed One. Then the Teacher said to him, “Ānanda, you should show compassion toward this novice.
Because he had not performed meritorious deeds, he was one who received little.
Then the Teacher, wishing to favor him, directed him to fill the water-jars for the use of the monks. Seeing this, [the other novices...]
The lay devotees established many regular meals for him.
At a later time, having received full ordination and attained arahantship, he became an elder and lived on Sāṇapabbata together with twelve monks.
His relatives, numbering about five hundred, had not accumulated wholesome kamma and were possessed of evil qualities such as stinginess.
Having passed away, they were reborn among the *peta*s. However, his parents, fearing that "he was previously driven out from our home by us," did not approach him themselves;
instead, they sent a brother who was bound to him by affection. At the moment the Elder entered the village for alms, he placed his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined in reverence, said:
Having revealed himself, he spoke the verses beginning with, "Your mother and father, Bhante.
As for the first five verses beginning with "The Elder Kuṇḍināgariya," these were placed by the compilers of the Dhamma (the Dhammasaṅgāhakas) in order to show the connection between them:
"The Elder Kuṇḍināgariya, A resident of Sāṇavāsika..."
The ascetic named Poṭṭhapāda had developed his faculties.
His mother, father, and brother had fallen into a miserable state in the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, they had gone from here to the realm of the departed spirits.
“Those wretched ones, pierced by needles, exhausted, naked, and emaciated—
though filled with great longing and trembling, those cruel men do not show themselves.
His brother, having crossed over, was naked and alone on the path.”
Having assumed the form of a catukuṇḍika, he showed himself to the elder.
But the elder, paying him no heed, passed by in silence.
He then made himself known to the elder, saying, "I am your brother, who has gone to the realm of the departed."
“Venerable sir, your mother and father have fared ill in the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, they have gone from here to the realm of the departed spirits (petas).
Because of that, they are wretched, pierced by needles, exhausted, naked, and emaciated.”
Trembling with great fear, those cruel men did not give anything. [The Buddha said:
"O compassionate one, have pity! Having given, dedicate it to us;
by the gift you have given, the cruel men shall sustain themselves."
408–9. *Tattha kuṇḍināgariyo thero*: a senior elder born and raised in a city of that name;
there is also a reading, "the elder of Kuṇḍika-nagara," which has the same meaning. *Sāṇavāsinivāsiko*: a resident of Mount Sāṇa.
*Poṭṭhapādo ti nāmena*: by name, one named Poṭṭhapāda. *Samaṇo*: one who has stilled evil. *Bhāvitindriyo*: through the cultivation of the noble path.

"One whose faculties, such as faith, have been cultivated" means one who is worthy of the state of an Arahant. "His" refers to that Elder Sāṇavāsi. "Wretched" means those who have gone to an unhappy destination.
(410) "Afflicted by needles" means those who are tormented and oppressed by hunger and thirst, which is given the name "needles," and whose limbs are withered and putrid;
some read "sūcikaṇṭhā," meaning those whose mouth-openings are like the eye of a needle. "Exhausted" means...
With body and mind exhausted; "naked ones" means those with a naked form, wearing no clothes. "Emaciated" means having a lean body due to their bodies consisting of nothing but skin and bone.
"Trembling" means falling into a state of fear through a sense of moral dread (*ottappa*), thinking, "This ascetic is our son.

"Out of great fear" means having become terrified on account of the great danger arising from the kamma they themselves previously committed. "They do not show themselves" means they do not reveal themselves.
They do not come into manifestation. "Kurūri" means those of cruel deeds.
"His brother" refers to the brother of the Elder Sāṇavāsi. "Having crossed over" means having become one who has crossed; the meaning is that he was free from shame, anxiety, and fear.
Alternatively, the reading is "vituritvā," which means having hurried, that is to say, being in a state of haste. "On the single path."
On a narrow path. "Alone" means solitary, without a companion. "Having become one who squats on four limbs" (*catukuṇḍika*):
he is called *catukuṇḍika* because he "squats" (*kuṇḍeti*)—that is, maintains his physical form—with four limbs; the meaning is that he moves and stands with both knees and both hands.
For he acted in that way so as to conceal his private parts from those in front.
"Thinking to show himself to the Elder," he designated himself to the Elder and revealed himself. 412.
"Without taking it to mind" means without attending to it or reflecting upon it by thinking, "This is such-and-such a person.
"And he" refers to that peta. "'I was your brother in a past existence, and now, having become a peta, I have come here,'" [he said].
The construction is: "Having spoken thus, he made his request to the Elder.
To show how he made that request, three verses beginning with “Mother and father” were spoken.
Therein, “your mother and father” means both your mother and your father. “Be compassionate” means: favor them; have mercy upon them.
"Anvādisāhi" means "instruct. "No" means "to us. "Tayā dinnena" means "by what was given by you.
To show how the Elder acted upon hearing that, [the text says]:
"The Elder, having wandered for alms, [along with] twelve other monks..."
They gathered together at one time for the purpose of breaking their fast.
The Elder said to them all: "Give me whatever you have received;
I shall prepare a meal for the Sangha out of compassion for my kinsmen."
“They presented [the offering] to the Elder; the Elder invited the Saṅgha.
Having given it, the Elder dedicated the merit for his mother, father, and brother, saying:
‘May this be for my relatives; may my relatives be happy.’”
“Immediately after it was announced, food appeared—
pure, exquisite, abundant, with many kinds of sauces and condiments.
Then my brother emerged, handsome, strong, and happy.”
“Venerable sir, there is abundant food; see, we are naked.
Therefore, venerable sir, exert yourself so that we may obtain clothing.
The elder, having picked up some rags from a heap of refuse, said:
Having made a cloth banner, he gave it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
Having given it, the elder dedicated the merit for his mother, father, and brother, saying:
"May this be for my relatives; may my relatives be happy."
“Immediately after the instruction was given, garments appeared; then, clothed in fine raiment, he presented them to the Elder.
‘As many as there were coverings within the realm conquered by King Nanda,’”
“Venerable sir, we have even more garments for clothing:
silken ones, woolen ones, and those made of linen and cotton;
they are abundant and of great value, and they hang suspended in the air.”
“We shall burn you away, whatever is dear to your mind;
therefore, venerable sir, strive so that we may obtain a home.
The Elder, having constructed a leaf-hut, gave it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
Having given [the gift], the Elder dedicated it for his mother, father, and brother, saying:
"May this be for my kinsmen; may my kinsmen be happy.
Immediately after the dedication was made, houses appeared.
Our dwellings here are gabled houses, partitioned and measured out in parts.
"Among humans there are none such as these, our homes here;
even among the gods, there are none like our homes here."
“Shining brightly, they illuminate the four directions all around;
O Venerable Sir, exert yourself so that we may obtain water.
Having completed his task, the Elder gave [the water] to the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
Having given it, the Elder dedicated it for his mother, father, and brother, saying:
"May this be for my relatives; may my relatives be happy.
Immediately after the dedication was made, drinking water appeared.
The lotus ponds were deep and square, beautifully constructed. They possessed cool water,
were well-situated on firm ground, were cool and free from foul odors,
covered with pink and blue lotuses, and filled with water and pollen.
“Having bathed and drunk there, they presented themselves before the Elder, saying:
‘Venerable sir, there is abundant drinking water, but our feet are sore and smarting.
As we wandered about, we stumbled over pebbles, husks, and thorns.’”
“Venerable sir, exert yourself so that we may obtain a vehicle.
Having obtained a *sipāṭika* box, the Elder gave it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters;
having given it, the Elder made a dedication for his mother, father, and brother.
“May this belong to my relatives; may my relatives be happy.
Immediately after it was dedicated, the departed ones arrived by chariot:
“We have been shown compassion, O Blessed One, by means of food and clothing.”
“By our gift of water at home, and by our gift of vehicles—both of these—we have come, venerable sir, to pay homage to the Sage, the compassionate one in the world. Thus they spoke in verses.
(416–7) Therein, “the elder went for alms” means the elder went on his alms-round. The other monks...
And twelve other bhikkhus, together with the Elder, were staying there; they all gathered together in one place at the same time. Why?
"For the purpose of dismissing the meal," that is, for the sake of the meal-duty, for the purpose of eating. "They" refers to those bhikkhus.
"As obtained" means whatever was obtained. "Give" means give it.
418. *Niyyādayiṃsu* means they gave. *Saṅghaṃ nimantayi* means he invited those same twelve bhikkhus to give that meal on behalf of the Saṅgha.
*Anvādisi* means he assigned it. To show those for whom he assigned it, it is said:
“May this be for my mother, father, and brother; may my kinsmen be happy.”
419. *Samanantarānuddiṭṭhe* means immediately after it was recited. *Bhojanaṃ udapajjatha* means food arose for those hungry ghosts (*petas*).
To explain what kind [of food], he says "pure," and so forth. In that context, *anekarasabyañjanaṃ* means provided with various flavored condiments;
or alternatively, it means having many flavors and many condiments. *Tato* means after obtaining the food.
420. "The brother has appeared," said the deceased spirit who had been his brother, showing himself to the Elder.
"Handsome, strong, and happy"—by means of that gain of food, he had at that very moment become endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, and truly happy.
"Abundant food, Bhante," [he said]; "Venerable Sir, through the power of your generosity, abundant—that is, not meager—food has been obtained by us."
"It has been obtained. Look, we are naked"—that is, "observe that we are indeed naked; therefore, venerable sir, exert yourself and apply effort in such a way that we may all obtain clothes.
The meaning is: "Strive by whatever means or through whatever method it may be so that we all might receive garments."
421. "From a heap of refuse" means from various places where rubbish is gathered.
"Having picked up" means having taken them by way of searching. "Rags" refers to pieces of discarded cloth with torn edges.
Since those pieces of cloth are called *pilotikā* because they are in fragments, and since the Elder made a robe from them and gave it to the Saṅgha, he said: "A *pilotikā*..."

"Having made a cloth, he gave it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters. In this context, "gave to the Saṅgha of the four quarters" means he gave it to the community of monks who had arrived from all four directions;
for this locative expression is used in the sense of the dative.

"Wearing well-made garments" (*suvatthavāsano*) means wearing beautiful clothes. "He showed himself to the Elder" (*therassa dassayītuṃ*) means he showed himself to the Elder, he made himself manifest. "Paṭicchadā" means that which covers or conceals there.
428–9. *Kūṭāgāranivesanā* means houses consisting of gabled mansions (*kūṭāgāra*) and those designated as other types of dwellings.
This is stated by way of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). *Vibhattā* means divided according to shapes such as square, rectangular, circular, and so forth.
*Bhāgaso mitā* means measured out by parts. *No* means "our. *Idha* means "in this world of ghosts (*petaloka*). *Api dibbesu* means "even among the divine [realms]."
*Api* is merely a particle; the meaning is "in the worlds of the devas. 431.
*Karaṇaṃ* refers to a water-vessel (*dhammakaraṇa*). *Pūretvā* means having filled it with water.
*Vārikiñjakkhapūritā* means filled by being covered here and there on the surface of the water with the masses of filaments of lotuses, blue lilies, and so forth. *Phalanti* means...
They blossom; in the case of *paṇhikapariyanta* and so forth, the meaning is "they tear open.
435–6. *Āhiṇḍamānā*: wandering about. *Khañjāmā*: we go by means of limping. *Sakkhare kusakaṇṭake*:
on ground that is full of gravel and full of grass-thorns; the meaning is "treading upon gravel and grass-thorns."
"Vehicles" (*yāna*) refers to any kind of vehicle, such as chariots, ox-carts, and so forth. "A single-layered sandal" (*sipāṭika*) refers to a sandal made of a single piece of leather.
(437–8) "They came by means of a chariot" (*rathena māgamuṃ*): the letter *m* is used here for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*);

thus, it means they came by means of a chariot (*rathena āgamuṃ*). "Both" (*ubhaya*) means by both kinds of giving: namely, by the gift of vehicles and by the gift of the four requisites, such as food and so forth. Here, by the gift of drinking water, the gift of medicine is also included.
It is included [in the previous account]. The remainder is self-evident because it follows the method already explained below.
The Elder reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One said:
"Just as these people are now, so you too, in the immediately preceding past existence, having become a peta, experienced great suffering."
