Having spoken thus, when requested by the Elder, he recounted the *Petavatthu* story and taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude.
Having heard it, the great crowd was moved with spiritual urgency (*sañjātasaṃvega*) and became devoted to meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtue.
The commentary on the *Sāṇavāsīthera-petavatthu* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Story of the Charioteer’s Ghost (*Rathakārapetivatthu*).
The passage beginning “The beautiful, radiant pillar of beryl” was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a certain ghost.
It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was a certain woman who was endowed with virtue and good conduct.

Relying upon a spiritual friend, she developed deep faith in the Teaching; she constructed a residence that was exceedingly beautiful to behold, with well-proportioned and variegated walls, pillars, stairs, and floor-surfaces.
Having seated the monks there and served them with excellent food, she dedicated it to the Saṅgha of monks. Later, having passed away, due to another evil deed...
By virtue of that [merit], she was reborn as a *vimāna-petī* in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, dwelling near Rathakāradaha.
Through the power of her merit from giving a dwelling to the Saṅgha, there arose for her a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) made entirely of all kinds of gems—
exalted, exceedingly beautiful on all sides, heart-stealing, delightful, and adorned with a lotus pond like the Nandana Grove.
She herself was golden-hued, beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring.

There she dwelt, experiencing celestial splendor even without men. As she lived there for a long time without a man, dissatisfaction arose within her. Becoming weary, she thought, "There is this means."
He threw divine mango fruits into the river. Everything should be understood according to the method already given in the story of the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa peta.
Here, however, a certain young brahmin living in Bārāṇasī, having seen one of those mango fruits in the Gaṅgā and seeking its origin, eventually reached that place; seeing the river, he followed it.
He went to her dwelling place. Seeing him, she led him to her own quarters and sat down, offering him hospitality. Observing the excellence of her dwelling, he asked:
"Having ascended this many-colored, radiant, and beautiful mansion with its pillars of beryl—"
"There you sit, O goddess of great majesty, like the full moon on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Your complexion is like refined gold, radiant and exceedingly beautiful to behold;
seated upon that peerless, excellent couch, you are alone, for there is no husband for you."
“Moreover, these lotus ponds surrounding you are abundant with garlands and many white lotuses;
they are strewn all over with golden dust, and therein no mud or moss is found.
And these swans, beautiful and delightful to behold, are constantly moving about in the water.”
All the vowels and consonants resounded together like the booming of kettledrums.
"Radiant with glory, O glorious one, you stand leaning upon a boat;
with your long-lashed, lotus-like smile and sweet speech, O lady beautiful in every limb, you shine forth intensely."
“This celestial mansion is stainless and stands level, possessing gardens that increase the joy and delight of those who love it.
O woman, O Anomadassī, I desire to rejoice here with you in this Nandana grove.
Thus he spoke these verses.
439. "There, there" means in that celestial mansion (*vimāna*). "You sit" means you remain seated whenever you so desire. "O Goddess" is how he addresses her.
"Of great power" means endowed with great divine majesty. "On the road, on the journey" means on the path that is one's own way;
the meaning is "on the course through the expanse of the sky. "Like the moon on the fifteenth day" refers to the full moon on the full-moon night, its orb perfectly complete.
The meaning is: "shining like the moon. 440.
"And your complexion is like gold" means that your complexion is similar to refined *siṅgī* gold, exceedingly captivating to the mind.
Therefore he said: "Of radiant form, truly beautiful to behold. "Incomparable" (*atule*) means very costly. "Incomparable" (*atule*)... [end of fragment]
Or it means addressing a deity; that is, "of incomparable form. "And there is no husband for you" means that you have no husband. 441.
"Abounding with garlands" means possessing many kinds of flowers such as lotuses and water lilies. "With golden dust" means with golden sand.
"Covered all around" means strewn on every side. "Therein" means in those lotus ponds. "Mud and moss" means...
There is neither mud nor slippery water. 442.
"These swans are beautiful and delightful"—these swans are pleasant to behold and charming. "Wandering about" means they move hither and thither.
"At all times" means during all seasons. "Having gathered together" means having come together. "Melodious" means sweet. "Singing" means...
They cry out. "With the sound of drops" means with sounds that are not dispersed, but concentrated.
"Like the roar of kettledrums" means, by virtue of having a charming, drop-like sound, it is like the cry of swans in your lotus pond;
this is the meaning. 443. "Shining brightly" means gleaming exceedingly. "By glory" means by divine majesty (*deviddhi*). "In the boat" means in the wooden trough (*doṇī*); for in the lotus pond—
Having seen a female spirit playing in the water while seated upon a costly couch in a golden boat on the lotus pond, he spoke thus:
"Avalamba" means having leaned against a support. "Tiṭṭhasi" (you stand) is a word expressing the negation of motion, because the meaning of the root *ṭhā* is the cessation of movement.
Alternatively, the reading is "nisajjasi," which means "you sit."
The meaning should be understood as follows: “Āḷārapamha” means one whose eyelashes are curled, long, and dark blue. “Hasita” refers to one whose face is smiling or laughing.
“Piyavadā” means one who speaks kindly. “Sabbangakalyāṇī” means beautiful in all her limbs; the sense is that she possesses lovely major and minor limbs.
“Virocasi” means you shine forth.
444. *Virājanti* means they shine forth, being free from dust (*vigataraja*) and faultless (*niddosa*). *Same ṭhitaṃ* means situated on level ground;
or, because of its beauty, it is situated in equal parts, meaning it is auspicious on all sides (*samantabhaddaka*). *Uyyānavantaṃ* means accompanied by a Nandana grove.
*Ratinandivaḍḍhanaṃ* means that which increases both delight (*rati*) and joy (*nandi*); and of happiness...
"And the increase of rapture" is the meaning. "O woman" (*nārī*) is an address to her. "O Anomadassī" refers to one whose appearance is beyond reproach due to the perfection of all limbs and members.
"O Nandana" means O you who cause delight. "Here" refers to the Nandana Grove or the celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
The construction is: "I wish to rejoice" (*modituṃ*), that is, to take pleasure.
When the young brahmin had spoken thus, that deity of the Vimāna-peta realm gave him this reply:
"Perform deeds to be experienced here, and let your mind be fixed upon this place;
having performed deeds to be experienced here, you shall obtain me, O seeker of desire."
He spoke this verse. Regarding that: "Perform here an action to be experienced here" means:
perform—that is, produce—a wholesome action (*kusala-kamma*) that ripens and yields its fruit in this divine state. "Laid down here" means brought here;
or alternatively, the reading is "inclined here," meaning let your mind be inclined, bent, and leaning toward this place.
"Mamanti maṃ" means "they support me. "Lacchasīti" means "you will obtain.
Having heard those words of that *vimāna-peti*, the young man went from there to the human realm;
having directed his mind toward that [realm] and performed the corresponding meritorious deed, he passed away not long after and was reborn there with her.
“To companionship with the Petas. To clarify this matter, the compilers of the Council said:
“Having assented to her with ‘So be it,’ he performed there an action to be experienced [in that state].”
"Having performed an action there to be experienced [in that state], that young man was reborn into her companionship. Thus they spoke this concluding verse.
In that context, "sādhu" is a particle used for acceptance. "Tassa" means "of her," referring to that *vimāna*-petī.
"Having assented" means having accepted her words. "To be experienced there" refers to wholesome karma whose pleasant ripening is to be felt together with her in that celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
"Companionship" means co-existence. The construction is: "That young man was reborn into companionship with her. The rest is self-evident.
Thus, while they were enjoying celestial prosperity there for a long time, the man passed away due to the exhaustion of his karma;
the woman, however, having fulfilled her existence there for the duration of an entire interval between Buddhas by virtue of her own meritorious deeds having reached their full fruition, remained.
Then, when our Blessed One had appeared in the world and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma...
While staying in succession at Jetavana, on one occasion the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering among the mountains, saw that celestial mansion and its inhabitant;

having seen them, he questioned her with verses beginning, "O beautiful, radiant mansion with pillars of beryl," and she related to him her entire history from the very beginning. Having heard this, [he...]
The Elder returned to Sāvatthī and reported this to the Blessed One. Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
Having heard it, the great multitude became devoted to meritorious deeds such as giving.
Thus ends the commentary on the Story of the Cartwright Peta.
4. Commentary on the Story of Bhusa.
The verse beginning "One [man] repeatedly fills his cart with rice" was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning four *peta*s (hungry ghosts).
It is said that not far from Sāvatthī, in a certain village, there lived a fraudulent merchant who made his living through false measures and other such dishonest means.
He did so. Taking rice stalks, he soaked them in red clay, made them heavy, mixed them with red rice, and sold them.

His son, angry that his mother did not show proper respect to his friends and companions who came to the house, took a yoke-skin and struck her on the head. His daughter-in-law [did the same] for all of them...
Having stolen and eaten meat that had been set aside for a purpose, when questioned by those very people again, she made this oath:
"If I have eaten that meat, may I, in birth after birth, have the flesh carved from my own back and eat it.
His wife, however, when asking for some small household utensil and being told "there is none," and being pressed by them, said: "If..."
"I say that there is no such thing as 'peace'; wherever one is born, one must become a consumer of excrement," he said, swearing this oath with false speech.
After some time, all four of them passed away and were reborn as hungry ghosts (*peta*) in the Vindhya forest.
There, by the fruit of his own karma, the fraudulent merchant had to take burning chaff in both hands and [apply it] to himself...
Having poured [molten metal] upon his head, he experiences great suffering; his son likewise, having split open his own head with iron clubs, undergoes no small measure of pain.
His daughter-in-law, as the fruit of her karma, tears the flesh from her own back with extremely long and sharp claws and eats it, experiencing immeasurable [suffering].
He experiences suffering; as soon as his wife is served fragrant, perfectly pure rice cooked with black grains,
it turns into excrement, teeming with various kinds of worms and utterly foul-smelling and loathsome,
and she, grasping it with both hands, experiences great suffering while eating it.

Thus, while those four people were reborn as hungry ghosts (petas) and experiencing great suffering, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a mountain journey, arrived at that place one day. Seeing those ghosts, he asked:
"One person is eating rice; another is eating earth; this woman is eating her own flesh and blood;
and you are eating excrement—impure and loathsome. What is the result of this?"
With this verse, he asked about the deed they had committed. In that context, *bhusāni* means chaff. *Eko* means alone. *Sāliṃ* refers to rice;
here it is used in the accusative case in the sense of the genitive, meaning "the chaff of the rice. The intention is: "He scatters the blazing chaff of the rice over his own head.
*Punāparo* means "again another. For he who struck his mother’s head [was struck] with iron clubs.
He strikes his own head and reaches the state of having the skull shattered; it is with reference to this that he speaks.
"One's own flesh and blood" is to be construed as: one consumes one's own back-flesh and blood.
"Unwanted" means unpleasant and loathsome. "What is the result of this? means: what is the fruit of which evil deed is this, which you are now experiencing?
When the Elder had thus questioned them about the deed they had committed, the wife of the fraudulent merchant, explaining the entire deed performed by them all, said:
“This one formerly harmed his mother, and this one is a fraudulent merchant;
this one, having eaten meat, deceives others with false speech.”
“Among humans, having become human myself, I was a housewife, the mistress of the entire household.
While wealth existed, I concealed it and gave nothing from here.
I covered it over with lies, saying: ‘This is not in my house.’”
“If I conceal what is true, may excrement be my food.
By the ripening of that karma, and of both [the truth and the lie],
the fragrant rice meal turns for me into excrement.”
“Actions are never barren, for action does not perish;
I eat and I drink foul-smelling, worm-infested filth.”—thus he spoke this verse.
448. Therein, “she comes” means she shows her son. “She harms” means she oppresses with force, with a club.
The meaning is "he watches over. A "fraudulent merchant" (*kūṭavaṇijjo*) is a grain merchant; the meaning is one who practices trade through deception.
"Having eaten meat" means that after eating meat shared with others, he deceives them with a lie, saying, "I did not eat it.
449–50. An "agārinī" is a mistress of the house. "While they exist" means while the requisites requested by others are indeed available.
“I concealed,” meaning I hid it. This was said by way of a reversal of time.
“And I did not give anything from here”—that is, I did not give even the slightest thing from what belonged to me to another who needed it.
“I covered up,” meaning I concealed it with a lie, saying, “This is not in my house.”
"451-2. 'Feces turn for me': by the power of my karma, fragrant rice-meat turns and transforms into the state of feces.

'Not barren' means they are not fruitless or without result. 'For karma does not perish' means that karma accumulated in such a way does not perish without yielding its fruit. 'Infested with worms' means full of worms, having become a breeding ground for swarms of worms."
They "mow" (mīḷhanti) means they eat excrement. The rest is self-evident because it follows the method already explained below.

Thus, having heard the words of that peta woman, the Elder reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that event as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Bhusa-peta-vatthu* is concluded.
5. The Commentary on the Story of the Young Pet (Kumārapetavatthu) "The knowledge of the Sugata is wonderful to behold"—this is the story of the young pet. How did it originate?
It is said that in Sāvatthī, many lay devotees (upāsakas), having formed religious groups, had a great pavilion constructed in the city and [decorated] it with various colors...

Having adorned themselves with garments and invited the Teacher and the community of monks at an early hour, they had the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, sit upon seats spread with costly and excellent coverings; having honored them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they distributed a great almsgiving.
Seeing this, a certain man whose mind was overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess [reflected on] that hospitality...
Unable to endure this, he said: "It would have been better for all of this to be thrown into a heap of refuse than to have given it to these shavelings.
Hearing that, the lay devotees were deeply moved in their hearts and thought:
"Alas, a grievous evil has been committed by this man, in that he has thus offended against the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having reported the matter to his mother, they...
“Go, and ask the Blessed One together with his community of disciples for forgiveness,” they said. She consented, saying, “Very well.
Having rebuked and admonished her son, she approached the Blessed One and the community of monks;
confessing the transgression committed by her son, she asked for forgiveness and offered a gift of rice gruel to the Blessed One and the community of monks for seven days.
She performed an offering. Not long after, her son passed away and was reborn in the womb of a courtesan who lived off the proceeds of her impure trade.
As soon as he was born, she recognized him as a "child" and cast him away in a charnel ground.
There, by the power of his own merit, he was protected from anyone and remained unharmed, dwelling in happiness as if in his mother's lap.
He fell asleep. It is said that the deities took charge of his protection.

Then, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One arose from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw that the boy had been abandoned in the charnel ground; he went to the charnel ground at the hour of sunrise. "The Teacher..."
"He has come here; there must be a reason for his presence here," the great multitude gathered.
To the assembled company, the Blessed One said, "This child is not to be despised, even though he now stands abandoned and without protector in the charnel ground;
yet in the future, both in this very life and in the lives to come, he shall attain sublime prosperity. When those people asked, "What..."
When asked, "Venerable sir, was this deed performed by him in a previous birth?", he replied:
"The people made a magnificent offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha;
yet there, his mind underwent a change, and he spoke harsh and unseemly words."
Having illustrated the deed performed by the boy and the prosperity he would attain in the future according to this method,
he preached the Dhamma to the assembled assembly in accordance with their inclinations, and then delivered a further exalted discourse on the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the Truths, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma, and as for that boy—
A certain householder, possessing a wealth of eight hundred million, took [the boy] before the Blessed One, saying, "He is my son.
The Blessed One went to the monastery, thinking, "By this much this child has been protected, and a favor has been done for the great multitude.
Later, when that householder had passed away, he took possession of the wealth entrusted to him by him.
Establishing his family, he became a householder of great wealth in that very city and was devoted to giving and other virtues.
Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Oh, how compassionate the Teacher is toward sentient beings!
Even that boy who was then left without a protector now enjoys such great prosperity."
"And he performs sublime meritorious deeds. Having heard this, the Teacher declared: "Monks, his excellence does not end there;

rather, at the conclusion of his life, he will be reborn as a son of Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and he will attain great divine prosperity. Having heard this, the monks and the great multitude—
And having praised the Teacher’s extraordinary knowledge, saying, “It is said that seeing this reason,

the long-sighted Blessed One went there and showed compassion for him as soon as he was born and had been cast away in the raw charnel ground,” the compilers of the collection spoke of his conduct during that existence.
Illuminating that matter, they [said]:
“Wondrous is the knowledge of the Sugata, just as the Teacher has declared regarding this person:
some indeed possess abundant merit, while others possess but little merit.
This boy, though abandoned in the charnel ground, survives the night on the moisture from his own toe.”
Neither spirits, nor ghosts, nor reptiles would harm the prince who has performed meritorious deeds.
"Even dogs licked his feet; vultures and jackals rolled about them.
Flocks of birds carried away the contents of his bowels, while crows carried away the impurities from his eyes."
“No one provided protection for him, neither medicine nor mustard-seed fumigation;
they did not observe the conjunction of the constellations, nor did they scatter all kinds of grain [over him].
Thus he had fallen into the highest misery, red with blood, cast away in the charnel ground.”
“Trembling like a ball of meat thrown into a fire, full of doubt, with but a remnant of life left—him the one honored by gods and men beheld. Having seen him, the one of vast wisdom prophesied:
‘This prince shall become the foremost of the clans in this city, both in terms of lineage and wealth.’”
“What was his vow? What was his holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?
Having met with such a calamity, he will experience a corresponding success?”—thus they spoke these six verses.
453. Therein, "of a wonderful nature" means having a marvelous essence. "The knowledge of the Sugata" refers to the knowledge of the Perfectly Enlightened One that is not shared by others;
this is said specifically with reference to the knowledge of omniscience, such as the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*).
To the question, "How is this knowledge [possible], since it is outside the domain of others? he says: "Just as the Teacher declared regarding the individual. By this—
He shows that it is through the Teacher’s teaching alone that the marvelous nature of knowledge is understood.
Now, demonstrating the explanation, he said: "Some here have abundant merit; some here have limited merit.
The meaning of this is: even some individuals here who possess abundant wholesome states (kusala-dhamma), having obtained the necessary conditions...
By way of demerit, beings become inferior through birth and so forth;

yet even those with limited merit, or even those possessing very little meritorious dhamma, may become exalted by the great radiance of that merit through such factors as the excellence of their field.
454. *Sīvathikāya* means in a charnel ground. *Aṅguṭṭhasnehenā* means by the moisture flowing from the thumb, [referring to] the deity.

The meaning is: "with milk trickling from the thumb. "Neither *yakkhas*, *bhūtas*, nor reptiles" means that no *pisācas*, *yakkhas*, *bhūtas*, or reptiles—whether crawling or moving about—should harass or afflict them.
"They licked their feet" means they licked their own feet with their tongues. "Dhaṅkas" refers to crows. "Turning over" means...
Thinking, “May no one harm this prince,” they turned him back and forth while guarding him in order to ascertain his state of health.
*Gabbhāsaya* means the impurity of the womb. *Pakkhigaṇā* refers to flocks of birds such as vultures, hawks, and the like. *Haranti* means they carry away or remove.
*Akkhimala* means eye-secretion (eye-dirt).
456. "Some" refers to certain humans, while others—non-humans—provided protection. "Medicine" refers to an antidote that brings about health both then and in the future.

Regarding "the fumigation with mustard seeds": they indicate that even when people perform the fumigation with mustard seeds for the sake of protecting a newborn child, they did not do so [in this case].
They also did not take account of the conjunctions of the constellations (*nakkhattayoga*).

They did not even record the conjunction of the constellations; the meaning is that no one performed the birth ceremony for him by saying, "He was born under such-and-such a constellation, on such-and-such a lunar day, at such-and-such a moment.

Nor did they scatter all kinds of grain; the meaning is that when performing auspicious rites, they do not scatter rice and other grains mixed with mustard oil as a protective charm (agada), and they did not do so for him either.
457. *Etādisaṃ* means of such a kind. *Uttamakicchapattaṃ* means having fallen into the highest distress, having reached an extreme state of suffering.
*Rattābhataṃ* means brought during the night. *Nonītapiṇḍaṃ viya* means like a lump of fresh butter; it is described thus because it is merely a piece of flesh.
*Pavedhamānaṃ* means trembling due to its weakness. *Sasaṃsayaṃ* means "does he live?"—[possessing doubt].
"Is he indeed still living?"—thus, one who possesses doubt due to such uncertainty.
"With only life remaining" means that, due to the absence of the requisites which serve as the causes for the persistence of life, there remains only the mere state of being alive.
"He will become a member of a pre-eminent family by way of wealth" means that, on account of his wealth, he will become a member of a pre-eminent or most excellent family; this is the meaning.
459. “*Kissavatan*”—this verse was spoken by the lay followers standing in the presence of the Teacher as a means of inquiring about the deed he had performed.
Furthermore, it should be understood that they spoke it while assembled at the charnel ground (*sivathikā*). In this context, *kissa* means “of what”;
*vata* refers to the undertaking of a vow (*vatasamādāna*). Again, *kissa* (in the phrase *kissavata*) means “of what kind” [referring to] the well-practiced vow or holy life (*brahmacariya*).

The construction [of the sentence] is made by changing the case ending to the accusative (*cāti*). "Such as this" (*etādisaṃ*) means being born from the womb of a courtesan and being cast away in a charnel ground—of such a kind.

"Calamity" (*byasanaṃ*) means misfortune. "Of that sort" (*tādisaṃ*) means of that same nature, as in the passage beginning, "He subsists on the grease from his thumb for a night," and as in the passage beginning, "This boy will become the head of the leading family in this city."
And the meaning is "of the kind already described. "Iddhi" means divine power (*deviddhi*); what is meant is "divine attainment.
Now, showing how the Blessed One answered when questioned by those lay followers, the compilers [of the canon] say:
"The people performed a magnificent offering for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha."
Therein, his mind underwent a change, and he spoke harsh and unseemly words.
Having dispelled that thought and subsequently regained joy and confidence,
he attended upon the Tathāgata dwelling in Jeta’s Grove with rice porridge for seven nights.
“Indeed, that was his holy life, and this is the result of that well-practiced conduct.
Having encountered such a calamity, he will experience a corresponding success.
Having remained right here for a hundred years, fully endowed with all sensual pleasures;”
"With the breakup of the body, in the life hereafter, he goes to the companionship of Vāsava."—Thus they spoke these four verses. 460.
Therein, "the people" (janatā) means a multitude of people; the intended meaning is a group of lay followers (upāsaka). "Therein" (tatra) refers to that act of worship.
"Assa" means of that boy. "Cittassahu aññathattaṃ" means that in his previous existence there was a change of mind:
a lack of heedfulness, disrespect, and lack of reverence. "Asabbaṃ" means he spoke harsh words, which were unfit to be uttered even among the company of the virtuous.
"So" refers to this very person. "Taṃ vitakkaṃ" means that evil thought. "Pavinodayitvā" means having dispelled it by the mother’s [action].
"Having pacified him through conciliation": having obtained and generated joy and confidence.
"He attended with rice-gruel": he served him by giving a gift of rice-gruel. "For seven nights": for seven days. (462) "His vow and that holy life":
the meaning is that the pacification of his own mind and the act of giving described by me above constitute this person's vow and his holy life; there is nothing else.
463. “Having stood” means having remained right here in the human world until the end of one’s lifespan. “In the future life” means in a subsequent existence.
“He shall go to companionship with Vāsava” means he will attain a state of being together with Sakka, the lord of the gods, by becoming his son;
for this expression in the present tense refers to a future matter. Everywhere else, the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Kumārapeta-vatthu* is finished.
6. The commentary on the *Seriṇīpeta-vatthu*:
"Naked and of ugly form"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana, concerning the female ghost Seriṇī.
It is said that in the kingdom of Kuru, at Hatthinipura, there was a courtesan named Seriṇī.
There, monks gathered from various directions for the purpose of observing the Uposatha. On another occasion, there was a great assembly of monks.
Seeing this, the people prepared many offerings for alms, such as sesame seeds, rice, ghee, fresh butter, honey, and so forth, and they distributed a great gift.
And at that time, that courtesan was faithless, lacking confidence, and her mind was overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess;
although she was urged by those people, "Come now, give thanks for this gift," she only spread her lack of faith toward them,
saying, "What is the use of giving to these shaven-headed recluses?"— how much less could there be the renunciation of even a small amount?
At a later time, having passed away, she was reborn as a female peta on the embankment of a certain frontier city’s moat.

Then, a certain lay follower living in Hatthinipura went to that city for trade and, at the time of dawn during the night, went to the embankment of the moat for a similar purpose. There, she saw him.
Having recognized him, she stood not far away, naked, her body reduced to mere bones and skin, most loathsome to behold, and showed herself.
Seeing her, he said:
“Naked and foul of form you are, emaciated, with veins showing all over you;”
“O you with the protruding belly, so emaciated! Who are you standing here?
he asked in verse. She replied to him:
“I am a peta, O venerable sir, miserable, belonging to the world of Yama.”
“Having committed an evil deed, I have gone from here to the world of the departed,” she declared of herself with this verse.
Then he asked: “What evil has been done by body, speech, or mind?”
“By the ripening of the karma of kissing, I have gone from here to the world of the petas.
Thus questioned regarding the deed she had committed, she said:
“At unsheltered fords, I gathered half a māsaka coin;”
While there were gifts to be given among the virtuous, I did not make an island for myself.
"Thirsty, I approach a river, but it turns out empty;
in the heat, I approach the shade, but it turns into sunlight."
“A wind like the color of fire blows upon me, burning as it passes;
for this, O Venerable One, I deserve punishment, and even more than that, some evil deed.
Having gone to the city of Hatthinī, he rebuked my mother.”
“I have seen your daughter, fallen into misfortune in the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, she has gone from here to the realm of the departed.
There is something entrusted to me there, which has not yet been told by me.”
"Four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] shall be beneath my throne.
Let them give that as a gift for me, and let it be her livelihood.
Having given the gift, may my mother dedicate the merit to me."
"Then I shall be happy, with all my desires fulfilled.
With these six verses, she explained both the deed she herself had committed and the purpose that must now be accomplished by her.
(467) Therein, "at unbarred fords" means at the bathing places of rivers, ponds, and so forth, which are not obstructed by anyone.
In such places where people bathe and perform their water-rites;
there, overcome by greed, thinking, "Perhaps I might find even something left behind by people after they have set it down," I searched for and sought out even as much as half a māsaka coin.
Or else, "at unenclosed bathing places" means at those places where no one prevents beings from approaching.

While there were ascetics and brahmins who served as true refuges by virtue of being pure in their conduct and inner disposition, I—my mind overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess and giving nothing to anyone—specially selected even half a māsaka coin;
I did not accumulate merit. Therefore he said: "Though the things to be given were present, I made no island for myself."

“Thirsty” means parched with thirst. “Empty” means that even though the river was flowing and could have been drunk from by crows, through my evil karma it has become empty and void of water, turning over as nothing more than sand. “In the heats” means during the hot seasons.
“The heat prevails” means that when I approach a place of shade, heat takes its place.
469–70. *Aggivaṇṇo* means "like fire" by way of its touch. Therefore it is said: "It blows burning.
Regarding the phrase *etañca, bhante, arahāmi*: the word *bhante* is used out of respect for that lay follower.
*Bhante*, I am worthy to experience this aforementioned suffering of thirst and so forth, as well as other evil and dreadful sufferings corresponding to that [kamma].
The intention is: "because of having committed evil. "Vajjesī" means "you would say. 471–72.
Here, "placed, but not declared" means it has not been stated, "this much was placed here.
Now, showing its measure and the place where it was established, [she says]: "Four hundred thousand [of them], for the couch..."
"And from below," he said. Therein, "of the couch" means of his own former bed-couch.
"From there" means having taken a portion from where the wealth was deposited, let him give a gift in my name.

"Of her" means of my mother. When that peta woman had spoken thus, the lay follower accepted her words, completed his business there, went to Hatthinipura, and reported that matter to his mother. To show that matter—
Having agreed, saying "So be it," he went to the city where the female elephant was and said to her mother:
"I have seen your daughter; she has fallen into misfortune in the world of Yama."
Having committed evil deeds, she has gone from here to the world of the departed.
There, she incited me and reproached my mother, saying:
"I have seen your daughter, fallen into misfortune in the realm of Yama."
Having committed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of the departed (peta).
"And there is something deposited by me here, which has not been told to me:
four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] beneath the couch."
“‘Therefore, let her give alms to me, and let that be her livelihood;
having given the gift, may my mother dedicate the merit to me;
then I shall be happy, with all my desires fulfilled.’”
“Therefore she gave that gift, and she dedicated the merit to her;
the female spirit became happy, and she had a good livelihood,” said the Reciters of the Council.
These [verses] are indeed easy to understand.
Having heard this, her mother gave an alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and instructed her.

Consequently, she, established in the excellence of having obtained requisites, showed herself to her mother and explained the reason for it. The mother reported this to the bhikkhus, and the bhikkhus reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, taking that event as the occasion, [spoke] to the assembled assembly...
He taught the Dhamma. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the Seriṇīpetivatthu.
7. Commentary on the Migaluddakapetavatthu.
“Surrounded by men and women, young... This was spoken concerning the ghost of a deer-hunter while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove.
It is said that in Rājagaha, a certain hunter made his living by killing deer day and night.
He had a lay follower friend who, being unable to turn him away from evil at all times, said to him: “Come, [my friend].”
"Friend, refrain from taking life at night," he exhorted him toward merit during the night.
Having refrained at night, he nevertheless committed the taking of life during the day.
At a later time, having passed away, he was reborn as a *vemānika* peta near Rājagaha; for the duration of the day...
Having experienced great suffering, he now spent the night provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Seeing him, the Venerable Nārada said:
“Youthful, surrounded by men and women, you shine with these delightful strands of sensual pleasure.”
"You enjoy this cause during the day; what did you do in a previous birth?"—with this verse he questioned him.
Therein, "surrounded by men and women" means attended and waited upon by male and female deities who serve as attendants.
"Young" means youthful. "By things that provoke passion" means by desirable objects that serve as causes for the arising of lust.
“By the strands of sensual pleasure” means by the components of sensual desire. “You shine” means you radiate through the state of being endowed with them; this is the intended meaning.
Therefore he said, “You experienced the cause during the day,” meaning that during the daytime portion, you underwent various kinds of causes for slaughter.
Or, “in the nights” (*rajanī*) refers to among the nights. “By which” (*yehi*) is merely a particle. “What did you do in a previous birth? [is the question.]
The meaning is: "Tell me what kind of karma, leading to such pleasure and pain, you performed in a previous birth prior to this one.
Having heard that, the peta, explaining the deed he himself had committed to the Elder, said:
"In the delightful city of Rājagaha, in the charming Giribbaja..."
In the past, I was a deer-hunter, cruel and with blood-stained hands.
With a mind full of malice toward many beings who caused me no offense,
I wandered about always most cruelly, delighting in harming others and unrestrained.
“I had a companion, a kind-hearted, faithful lay follower;
out of compassion for me, he also repeatedly tried to restrain me:
‘Do not commit an evil deed, my dear; do not go to a state of misery.’”
“If you desire happiness after death, refrain from the lack of restraint that is the killing of living beings.
Having heard those words of one who desired my welfare and was compassionate for my benefit, I—
foolish and long delighted in evil— did not carry out his entire instruction.
“Thus, out of compassion for me, the one of vast wisdom established me in self-restraint:
‘If you kill living beings by day, then let there be restraint for you at night.
So, having killed living beings by day, I became abstinent and self-controlled at night.”
"At night I enjoy my pleasures, but by day I am devoured, wretched.
Because of that wholesome deed, I experience non-human delights at night;
but by day, dogs, being repelled [by me], run from all sides to devour me."
“And those who are constantly devoted, always applied to the teaching of the Sugata—
I consider that they attain only the Deathless, the unconditioned state.
Thus he spoke these verses.
479–80. Therein, *luddo* means cruel. *Lohitapāṇī* means one whose hands are constantly smeared with blood due to the frequent killing of living beings.
*Dāruṇo* means harsh; the meaning is one who harms sentient beings. *Avirodhakaresu* refers to deer, birds, and so forth, which do not create hostility toward anyone.

482–83. *Asaṃyamā* means lacking restraint, being immoral. *Sakalānusāsaniṃ* means the entire instruction; the meaning is that he abstained from taking life at all times. *Cirapāpābhirato* means one who has long delighted in evil.

484. *Saṃyameti* means "in good conduct. *Nivesayīhi* means "he caused him to settle. "If you kill living beings by day, then let there be restraint for you at night"—this is a demonstration of the manner in which he was settled [in his duties].
It is said that he was formerly addicted to killing living beings even at night by means of spears, snares, and other such devices.
485. *Divā khajjāmi duggato*: "Now, having fallen into a miserable state and reached great suffering, I am devoured during the daytime."
It is said that because he had dogs devour the deer during the day, the fruit corresponds to that action:
during the daytime, large dogs run at him and reduce his body to nothing but a heap of bones;
but when night arrives, it returns to its natural state, and he enjoys celestial splendor. Therefore it was said:
“Because of that wholesome deed, I experience a non-human being at night;
by day, dogs, as if their hearts were struck with enmity and filled with malice, run about from all sides to devour me.
In this context, “struck” means having their hearts struck, as if they were bound by hatred. “To devour from all sides” means [to devour] my body.
They run about from all sides to devour [the body]. This is said with reference to the time when they approach, which is extremely terrifying to them.
Having run up, they depart after leaving the body as nothing more than a skeleton.
487. As for the concluding verse, "And those who are constantly devoted," this is the summary of its meaning: "Even I, indeed, during the night..."
Having abstained from the taking of life, I experience such prosperity as this.
But those persons who are constantly engaged, firmly engaged, and perpetually devoted throughout all time to the higher virtue and other practices in the teaching of the Blessed One,
the Buddha, the Sugata— they, being possessed of merit, [attain] the "unconditioned state" which is entirely unmixed with worldly happiness.
"I believe they have attained nothing less than the Deathless itself; there is no obstacle whatsoever for them in its attainment.

When that peta had spoken thus, the Elder reported the matter to the Teacher. Taking that event as the occasion, the Teacher taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude. Everything else was exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the story of the deer-hunter peta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Second Story of the Deer-Hunter Ghost (*Migaluddaka-peta*).
The passage beginning with "In gabled halls and palaces" was spoken by the Blessed One while residing at Veḷuvana concerning another deer-hunter ghost.
It is said that in Rājagaha, a certain young brahmin hunter, although possessed of great wealth, [did not enjoy] the pleasure of riches...
Having abandoned [other pursuits], he wandered about day and night killing deer. A certain lay follower who was his companion, out of compassion, gave him this advice:
"It would be well, friend, if you were to abstain from taking life; let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
He did not heed it. Then that lay follower approached a certain elder (*thera*) whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), whom he held dear to his heart.
He requested: "It would be well, venerable sir, if you would teach the Dhamma to such-and-such a man in such a way that he might abstain from taking life.
Then one day, while wandering for alms in Rājagaha, that elder stood at the door of his house.
Seeing him, the hunter, filled with great reverence, went out to meet him, led him into the house, prepared a seat, and offered it to him.
The Elder sat down on the prepared seat, and he too, having approached the Elder, sat down.
The Elder explained to him the danger in the destruction of living beings and the benefit in abstaining from it. Although he heard this, he did not wish to abstain from it.
Then the Elder said to him: "Friend, if you are unable to abstain from it entirely, [then at least] even during the night..."
“Rest for now,” he said; and he replied, “Very well, venerable sir, I shall rest tonight,” and from that point he abstained. The remainder is similar to the immediately preceding account.
As for the verses: “In gabled houses and palaces, on couches spread with woolen blankets, you delight in the fivefold music, so beautifully played.”
“Then, at the end of the night, as the sun was rising,
you were cast away in a charnel ground and underwent great suffering.
What evil deed have you committed by body, speech, or mind?”
“Because of the karmic result of your kissing, you have come to this suffering.
With these three verses, the Elder Nārada questioned him. Then the peta replied:
“In the delightful city of Rājagaha, on the beautiful Mount Vebhāra;”
In the past, I was a deer-hunter, a cruel man who lacked self-restraint.
I had a friend who was kind-hearted, a faithful lay follower (upāsaka).
A monk, a disciple of Gotama, used to visit his family home.
Out of compassion for me, he also restrained me again and again:
"Do not commit an evil deed; do not go to a state of misery, my dear.
If you desire happiness after death, desist from the unrestrained killing of living beings."
“Having heard his words, he who desired my happiness and was compassionate for my welfare,
I— foolish and long delighted in evil— did not follow his entire instruction.
Then that one of vast and excellent wisdom, out of compassion, established me once more in self-restraint.”
“If you kill living beings by day, then let there be restraint for you at night.
“Having killed living beings by day, I am restrained and self-controlled at night;
I indulge myself at night, but by day I am devoured, miserable.”
“Because of that wholesome deed, I experience a non-human state by night;
by day, dogs indeed attack me and run at me from all sides to devour me.
But those who are constantly devoted, always applied to the teaching of the Sugata...”
“I believe that you alone shall attain the deathless, the unconditioned state.
Thus he explained the matter. The meaning of this is exactly as stated above.
The commentary on the second story of the hunter-peta is finished.
9. Explanation of the Story of the *Kūṭavinicchayika* Peta:
"Wearing garlands, wearing a crown, and adorned with armlets"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning the *kūṭavinicchayika* peta.
At that time, King Bimbisāra observed the Uposatha on six days of each month; following his example, [the people]...
Many people observe the Uposatha. The king asks the people who come into his presence:

“Have you observed the Uposatha, or have you not? Thereupon, a certain official appointed to a judicial office, being a backbiter, a deceiver, and a taker of bribes, unable to say “We have not observed it,” says, “We have observed it.”
“Devas,” he said. Then, as he was departing from the king’s presence, a friend said to him: “Friend, what have you been observing today?
“Out of fear, friend, I spoke thus in the presence of the king;
I am not one who observes the Uposatha. Then his friend said to him: “If that is so, let there be at least half an Uposatha for you today; [observe] the factors of the Uposatha.”
"Please undertake it. Having accepted his words with "Very well," he went home;
without eating, he rinsed his mouth, resolved upon the Uposatha, and retired for the night.

While there, due to a sharp pain caused by a violent wind arising from an empty stomach, his life-faculty was cut short, and immediately after passing away, he was reborn as a *vemānika* peta in the interior of a mountain.
For by merely observing the Uposatha for a single night, he obtained a celestial mansion accompanied by ten thousand maidens and great divine prosperity.
However, because of his former practice as a fraudulent judge and his habit of slandering others, his own back flesh falls away and is eaten by him of its own accord.
As the Venerable Nārada was descending from Gijjhakūṭa, he saw this and said:
“Wearing garlands, a crown, and armlets, your limbs are anointed with sandalwood;
your facial complexion is serene, and you shine like the sun.
Your attendants are non-human beings who serve you.”
Ten thousand maidens who were her attendants followed her,
wearing shell-bracelets and armlets, adorned with golden earrings.
"You possess great majesty, O one of hair-raising form!"
"You are tearing out and eating your own back-flesh.
What evil deed have you committed by body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what action do you eat your own back-flesh?"
"You eat what you have snatched up yourself":
"I have acted for my own harm in this world of the living,
through slander and lying, and through guile and deception."
“Having gone there to the assembly, when the time for truth has arrived,
I reject the goal and the Dhamma, and follow what is contrary to the Dhamma.
Thus does he devour himself who is a backbiter.”
“As I am eating my own back-flesh today, this was seen by you yourself, Nārada. Those who are compassionate and skilled would say:
‘Do not speak slander, do not speak falsehood; may you not be a back-biter.’”
The Elder questioned him with four verses, and he too answered that matter to him with four verses.
499. Therein, *mālī* means "wearing a garland"; the intention is that he is adorned with celestial flowers.

*Kiriṭī* means "one whose head is bound [with a crown]. *Kāyūrī* means "possessing armlets"; the meaning is that he is adorned with ornaments for the arms. *Gatta* refers to the limbs of the body. *Candanussada* means...
“Anointed with the essence of sandalwood. “You shine like the color of the sun”: you radiate having become like the color of the rising sun.

There is also a reading, “araṇavaṇṇī pabhāsasī,” which means: “araṇa” refers to the gods of the Araṇa realm; thus, it means you shine with a complexion similar to theirs, the domain of the Noble Ones (ariya).
500. “Pārisajjā” means those included in the assembly; the meaning is “attendants. “Tuvam” means “you. “Lomahaṃsanarūpavā” means possessing a form that causes the hair to stand on end.
It is endowed with a form that causes the hair of those passing by to stand on end. This was said because he possesses great majesty (*mahānubhāvatā*).
"Having cut off" (*ukkacca*) means having cut away; the meaning is "having severed.

(503) "I practiced" (*acāriṃ*) means I engaged in [the path]. "By means of slander and lying" (*pesuññamusāvādena*) means by both slander and false speech. "And by guile and deception" (*nikativañcanāya*) means by guile, by deception through showing a semblance of things, and by deceiving others through the display of altered behavior.
504. *Saccakāle*: at the time when it is appropriate to speak the truth. *Atthaṃ*: benefit categorized as pertaining to this life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and so forth.
*Dhammaṃ*: the cause, the principle (*ñāya*). *Nirākatvā*: having discarded or abandoned. *So*: that being who practices slander and so forth.
All the rest is exactly according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the *Kūṭavinicchayika-peta-vatthu* is finished.
10. The commentary on the *Dhātuvivaṇṇa-peta-vatthu*:
"Standing in the sky"—this is the *Dhātuvivaṇṇa-peta-vatthu*. [It was spoken] by the Blessed One at Upavattana in Kusinārā.
When the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna between the twin *sāla* trees in the *sāla* grove of the Mallas, and the distribution of the relics had been performed,
King Ajātasattu took the portion of relics he had received and, for seven years, seven months, and seven days,
maintained a sublime offering while recollecting the virtues of the Buddha. Therein, incalculable and immeasurable people set their minds at peace.

They attained rebirth in heaven; however, eighty-six thousand men, their minds distorted by long-standing lack of faith and wrong view, became corrupted even toward objects worthy of confidence and were reborn among the hungry ghosts (petas).
In that very city of Rājagaha, there was the wife of a certain wealthy householder.

The daughter and the daughter-in-law, their hearts full of faith, took scents, flowers, and other offerings, intending to perform a relic worship (*dhātupūjā*), and set out for the site of the relics.
That householder, however, reviled them, saying, "What is the use of worshipping bones?
and disparaged the relic worship. Yet, disregarding his words, they went there, performed the relic worship, and returned home.
Overcome by such a disease, they passed away before long and were reborn in the world of the devas.
But he, overcome by anger, passed away before long and was reborn among the *petas* due to that evil deed.
Then one day, out of compassion for sentient beings, the Venerable Mahākassapa performed a corresponding feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*).
He made a resolution such that humans could see those hungry ghosts and those deities.
Having done so, standing on the courtyard of the shrine, he questioned that discolored hungry ghost with three verses. That hungry ghost answered him:
“Standing in the sky, you emit a foul, putrid stench.”
And worms devour your mouth, which reeks with a foul stench; what deed did you do in the past?
Then, taking up a blade, they plunge it in again and again;
having sprinkled [the wound] with caustic acid, they plunge it in again and again.
“What evil have you done by body, speech, or mind?
Through the ripening of what action do you undergo this suffering?
“In the delightful city of Rājagaha, in the charming Giribbaja;”
“I am the master, dear sir, of abundant wealth and grain.
This woman here is my wife, my daughter, and my daughter-in-law;
she [offers] this garland, blue lotuses, and costly ointment.”
I forbade those who were carrying the stupa; that evil was committed by me.
"Eighty-six thousand of us, experiencing individual retribution, having disparaged the worship of the stupa, we are suffering intensely in hell."
“And those who point out the danger while the stupa-worship, the great festival for the Arahant, is underway— you should separate them from that.
And look at these women approaching, wearing garlands and adorned.”
Experiencing the ripening of their garlands, they are successful and renowned.
Having seen that marvel, so extraordinary and hair-raising,
the wise pay homage and revere that Great Sage.
“Surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, I shall perform worship at the stupa again and again, being diligent.
(507–8) Therein, “foul-smelling” (*duggandha*) means an undesirable odor; the sense is that it smells like a corpse. Therefore he said: “putrid” (*pūti*).
"Vāyasī" means from that point above, where there is a foul-smelling flow and where it is to be devoured by worms.
"Having seized a being, they cut again and again" means that beings impelled by karma seize a sharp-edged blade and repeatedly cut that opening of the wound.
"Having sprinkled with caustic, they cut again and again" refers to the place where they have been cut.
Having sprinkled it with alkaline water, they scratch it again and again.
510. “A lord of wealth and grain, of what is well-accumulated”: he is the lord and master of exceedingly abundant wealth and grain; the meaning is that he is rich and possesses great riches. 511.
“And this wife of mine, and daughter, and daughter-in-law”: these [belonged] to him, to me, in my previous existence.
"Wife," "this daughter," "this daughter-in-law"—he speaks thus, showing that they have become deities and are standing in the sky.
"Paccaggha" means fresh. "Vāresiṃ thūpaṃ harantiyo" means while they were bringing [the relics] to worship the stupa, I rebuked them, disparaging the relics.
"Taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā" means that evil act of disparaging the relics was committed and performed by me.
He speaks having fallen into remorse.
"Eighty-six thousand" means a measure of eighty thousand plus six thousand. "May I" refers to him speaking while including those hungry ghosts (petas) together with himself.
"Individual sensations" refers to the painful sensations being experienced separately by each one.
Regarding "Niraya": because of the suffering [there] being so intense, he spoke of the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) as being like hell.

513. And those who, while the great offering to the stupa of the Arahant—the Perfectly Enlightened One—is taking place, proclaim the disadvantage and fault of such stupa-worship, just as I have done; they...
"He would separate that person from their merit, cause them to be separated, and cast them out"—by this indirect expression, he reveals his own great lack of discernment. 514.

"Coming" means arriving through the air. "The ripening of garlands" refers to the fruit or result of performing garland-offerings at a stupa. "Prosperous" means endowed with divine excellence. "Those illustrious ones" means those possessed of a retinue.
515. "And having seen that" means: having seen the wonderful, marvelous, hair-raising, and exceedingly exalted distinction of the result of that very small merit of worship;
"the wise pay homage" means, Venerable Kassapa, these women pay homage to, salute, and offer reverence to you, the Great Sage, who have become a supreme field of merit.
The meaning is: "and they pay homage.

Then that peta, with a heart full of agitation, spoke the verse beginning with "So may I... to show what he himself ought to do for the future in accordance with that agitation. That [verse] has a self-evident meaning.
Having been addressed thus by the peta, Mahākassapa took that as the occasion and taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
The commentary on the *Dhātuvivaṇṇa* and *Petavatthu* is finished.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā* concerning the *Petavatthu*,
which is adorned with ten stories.
The commentary on the meaning of the third Minor Chapter (Cūḷavagga) is finished.
4. The Great Chapter (Mahāvagga). 1. Commentary on the Story of the Ambasakkara Ghost (Ambasakkara-petavatthu).
"There is a city named Vesālī belonging to the Vajjis"—this is the *Ambasakkara-petavatthu*. What is its origin?
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Jetavana, a Licchavi king named Ambasakkara, who held wrong views and was a proponent of nihilism, ruled in Vesālī.
At that time, near the shop of a certain merchant in the city of Vesālī, there was a muddy puddle.
There, many people, having jumped up and crossed over, grew weary; some were smeared with mud.
Seeing this, the merchant had cow-head bone—free from foul odor and resembling the color of a conch shell—brought and placed there, thinking, "May these people not step on the mire.
By nature he was virtuous, free from anger, and gentle in speech.
He also proclaims the true virtues of others as they really are.
One day, while his companion was bathing and not looking out of negligence, he playfully removed the companion's lower garment;
having caused him distress by doing so, he gave it back. His nephew, however, [took it] from another's house by theft.
Having brought the goods, he deposited them in that very shop. While the owners of the goods were investigating, they showed the nephew along with the merchandise to the king.
The king commanded, "Cut off his head, but impale his nephew on a stake!
The king's men did exactly so. Having died, he was reborn among the earth-deities (bhummadeva).
He was reborn. Because he had constructed a bridge with cow-heads, he obtained a divine, swift, thoroughbred horse of white color;
because he had spoken in praise of those possessed of virtue, a divine fragrance wafted from his body; but because he had discarded his garment, he was naked.
Surveying the kamma he himself had previously performed, and following its sequence, [he saw] his own nephew...
Seeing him impaled on the stake, his mind moved by compassion, he mounted a horse swift as thought and went to the place where he was fixed upon the stake at the hour of midnight.
Standing not far off, he spoke day after day: "Live, sir! Life itself is better!
At that same time, King Ambasakkāra, seated upon the back of a noble elephant, was performing a circumambulation of the city.
Having seen a certain woman who, having opened a window in a particular house, was watching the royal splendor, he became infatuated with her.

Giving a signal to a man sitting behind him, saying, "Keep watch over this house and this woman," he eventually entered his own royal palace and dispatched that man, saying: "Go, my good man, to her..."
“Find out whether this woman has a husband or not. Having gone and learned that she had a husband, he reported it to the king.
The king, contemplating a means to take possession of the woman, summoned her husband and said, “Come, my man, attend upon me.
Although he was unwilling, [the king continued] because the king would not do as he was told...
Thinking, "The king shall inflict punishment upon me," he accepted the service of attending upon the king out of fear and went to attend upon him day after day.
The king, having caused his food and wages to be given to him, said this to him after several days had passed when he had come to the court early in the morning:
"Go, my man; there is a lotus pond in such-and-such a place; from there, [fetch] clay the color of the dawn."
"Bring red lotuses; if you do not return this very day, there shall be no life for you.
When he had departed, he said to the gatekeeper, "Today, before the sun has even set, all the gates must be closed.
And although that lotus pond was three *yojanas* away from Vesālī, nevertheless, that man was driven by the terror of death.

Driven by the force of the wind, he reached that lotus pond early in the morning. Because he had already heard beforehand that "this lotus pond is presided over by non-human beings," he was filled with fear and, wondering, "Is there perhaps some danger here? he walked all around it.
Seeing him, the non-human guardian of the lotus pond approached him in human form, appearing as if moved by compassion.
“Sir, for what purpose have you come here? he asked. He told him what had happened.
[The deity] said, “If that is so, take as much as you require,” and having shown his divine form, he vanished.
He took the dawn-colored clay and red lotuses from there, and while the sun had not yet set, he reached the city gate.
He arrived. Seeing him, the gatekeeper closed the door even as he was crying out.
When the door was closed and he could not gain entry, he saw a man impaled on a stake near the gate and thought:
"Even while the sun had not yet set and I was still crying out, they closed the door upon me. 'I have come at the very proper time; my slave..."
“‘It does not exist’—let this also be known by you,” he said, making him his witness. Having heard that, he replied, “I am impaled on a stake, condemned to death, and facing my end;
how can I be your witness? However, a certain powerful peta will come near me here;
make him your witness. [The other asked], “But how can he be seen by me? “Right here, you—”
“Wait; you shall see for yourself. Standing there, he saw that deceased person arrive during the middle watch of the night and bore witness to it.
When the night had dawned and the king said, “You have transgressed my command;
therefore, I shall inflict royal punishment upon you,” he replied, “Your Majesty, I did not transgress your command. For while the sun had not yet set, I—”
“‘He has come here. To that, [the king asked], ‘Who is your witness? He pointed to a naked ghost who was coming near that man impaled on a stake, saying, ‘This is my witness.
When the king said, ‘How are we to believe this?’, he replied, ‘Today at night, send a man with whom you can trust, along with me. Having heard this, the king—”
Having gone there himself with him and stood there, when the deceased had arrived and said, "Live, sir!
Life itself is better," he questioned him back with five verses beginning with, "Neither sleeping nor sitting is for him.
Now, however, the verse from the beginning, "There is a city named Vesālī belonging to the Vajjīs," is for the purpose of showing the connection between them.
The compilers of the collection recorded it thus:
"There was a city named Vesālī belonging to the Vajjis; there lived a Licchavi named Ambasakkhara.
Having seen this [tree] outside the city, one who sought the reason for it questioned him right there."
“For him there is no bed nor sitting, no advancing and no retreating;
eating, drinking, chewing, and the enjoyment of clothing—even that pleasure he has not.
Those kinsmen and dear friends who were once compassionate toward him, whom he had seen and heard of in the past—”
Now they do not even wish to see you, for you have been shunned by that people.
Friends do not remain with one who has fallen low; seeing him impaired, friends abandon him.
But when they perceive his welfare, they surround him; many friends belong to one who has risen high.
“Brought low by all his wealth, miserable, smeared with filth, and with limbs broken apart;
like drops of dew falling away, today or tomorrow there will be an end to his life.
To one who has reached such a state of supreme misery—”
You have been impaled on a stake of *pucimanda* wood;
now, for what reason, O Yakkha, do you say:
“Live, sir! Life itself is better”?
517. *Tattha tattha* means "in that [city] of Vesālī. *Nagarassa bāhiraṃ* means existing outside the city;
it refers to what was born, occurred, or connected specifically outside the city of Vesālī. *Tattheva* means in that very place where he saw him.
*Taṃ* refers to that deceased person (*peta*). *Kāraṇatthiko* refers to the meaning stated as: "Live, sir! Life itself is better."
Being in need of a cause [for his suffering].

518. "There is for him neither lying down nor sitting": lying down (*seyyā*) is characterized by the stretching out of the back, and sitting (*nisajjā*) is characterized by folding the legs in a cross-legged posture;
these two do not exist for this person who has been impaled on a stake. "There is no advancing and no retreating."

He has not even the slightest movement characterized by approaching and so forth. "That service [of the senses] also" means that the service of the sense-faculties (*indriya-paricāraṇā*), which is characterized by the enjoyment of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, as well as clothing, that too is absent in him.

Alternatively, the reading is “*pariharaṇā sāpī*,” meaning that the maintenance of the sense-faculties (*indriya-pariharaṇā*) through the enjoyment of food and so forth—that too is absent in him because his life-force has departed. Some read “*paricāraṇā sāpī*.”
519. "Those dear friends who were compassionate to him in the past" refers to those friends—both those seen in person and those not seen—who were full of kindness toward him previously.

"Not even to see" means they do not obtain the opportunity to behold him, much less to dwell with him; this is the meaning. "One whose nature is devoid of lust" means one whose inherent character has been relinquished. "By that people" means by that group of kinsmen and others.

520. "There are no friends for one who has sunk into the depths": for one who has passed away and is devoid of consciousness, there are no such things as friends, because the duties that must be performed by friends have already elapsed. "Friends abandon one when they perceive him to be destitute":
let alone the case of one who is dead; even while living, when they perceive a person to be destitute of wealth, [thinking], "Nothing more can be taken from him," [they desert him].

"Friends abandon him. And "seeing his wealth, they surround him": seeing his wealth—that is, his property—those who speak kindly and look to his face surround him. "Many friends belong to one who has risen high":
for one whose nature has risen high through the attainment of prosperity, many—that is, numerous—friends exist; this is the nature of the world, such is the meaning.
521. "Deprived of all enjoyments" means deprived of all things for use and enjoyment.
"Distressed" means suffering. "Smeared" means his body is smeared with blood. "With limbs shattered" means his internal organs have been torn apart by the spear.
"Dripping like a dewdrop" means resembling a drop of dew trickling down the tip of a blade of grass. Today...
"Tomorrow" (*suve*) means either today or tomorrow; the meaning is that the obstruction and cessation of this person's life will occur, and from that point on it shall not proceed.
(522) "Terrified" (*uttāsita*) means bound or impaled. "On a stake of the *pucimanda*" means on a stake made from the staff of a *nimba* tree.
"By what praise? means "for what reason. "Live, sir! Life itself is better," [the Buddha said]. "Sir, man, live. Why?
Because even for you who have been impaled on a stake, life here is a hundredfold and a thousandfold better—more excellent—than the life of one who has passed away from here."
Thus questioned by the king, that peta, making known his own intention, said:
"He was my own kinsman; I remember him from a previous birth.
And upon seeing him, O King, compassion arose within me: 'May this one of evil character not fall into hell!'"
“Passing away from here, this man, a Licchavi, shall go to the Satthūsada hell, which is terrible in form;
having performed evil deeds, he will be reborn there—intensely hot, bitter, and fearsome.
This very stake is many times better than that hell.”
“Exclusively painful, bitter, and terrifying, it leads one to fall into the exclusively intense hell.
“Having heard these words of mine, he might, overcome by suffering, give up his life;
therefore, I do not speak in his presence, lest there be a cessation of my own life from this very moment.”
He spoke four verses.
523. In this context, *sālohita* means one who shares the same blood; it refers to a relative by birth, meaning a kinsman. *Purimāya jātiyā* means in a previous existence.
“May this man of evil character not fall into hell”—this [verse] concerns a person of evil character falling into hell.
The construction is: "Seeing this, I felt compassion [thinking], 'May he not fall, may he not be reborn in hell.
(524) *Sattussadaṃ* means crowded with beings who have committed evil deeds; or alternatively, it refers to the fivefold torment:
the pouring of molten copper into the mouth, the casting onto mountains of glowing coals, the throwing into cauldrons of molten iron, and the entry into the forest of sword-leaves.
"Crossing into the Vettaraṇī River" means being cast into the Great Hell.
"Abounding with" these seven kinds of cruel tortures, such as the fivefold binding, means that they are heaped up one upon another. "Great torment" means great suffering, or the heat of a great fire.
"Bitter" means undesirable. "Terrifying" means producing fear.
525. *Anekabhāgena guṇena* means by many portions or advantages. *Ayameva sūlo nirayena tena*:
compared to that very hell which is his place of rebirth, this stake itself is better;
for here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*). *Ekantatibbaṃ* means exclusively sharp suffering, that is to say, certain great suffering.
526. Having heard these words of mine—having heard my words spoken as "fallen from here," and so forth—this person, brought to suffering, would be as if led to the suffering of hell by my word.
"He might abandon his life" means he might relinquish his own existence. "Therefore" means for that reason. "May [it] not be with me alone" means [may it not be] with me in this regard.
"I do not speak these words in the presence of this person with the intention that there be an end to a man's life;
rather, my intention is simply this: 'Live, sir! Life itself is better.
When the peta had thus revealed his own intention, the king spoke this verse, creating an opportunity to ask further about the peta's condition:
“This matter of the man has been understood; we wish to ask you something else as well.
If you will grant us the opportunity, let us ask you this, and you should not be angry.
“Surely I gave my promise then; it is not right for one who lacks faith to fail to speak.”
"Since he is one whose word is to be trusted even against his will, ask me whatever you desire, as much as you can bear.
These are the verses of exchange between the king and the deceased. 527.

In this context, *aññāto* means "understood. *Icchāmasa* means "we wish. *No* means "to us. *Na ca kujjhitabbaṃ* means that anger should not be felt, thinking, "These people are asking all sorts of things."
"528. *Addhā* means certainly. By way of knowledge, [the thought] "I have given my consent" is the consent [given by saying] "Ask," which means granting an opportunity.
*Tadā ahū* means it occurred at that time, during the first seeing. *Nācikkhaṇā appasannassa hoti* means there is no speaking to one who has no faith;
for only one who has faith speaks something to another who has faith. But you, at that time—"
Because you lacked confidence in me and I lacked confidence in you, you were unwilling to speak even after having promised to do so.

But now, since I have no desire for your word to be trusted and your word must be accepted against my own will—for this reason—you may ask me whatever you wish, according to your inclination; ask me about that matter as you see fit. As for me, however—
The intention is: "I shall speak in accordance with my own power of knowledge, in such a way that it is bearable and possible for me to endure.
When the peta had thus created an opportunity for questioning, the King said:
"Whatever I see with my eye..."
"I would believe all of that from you; even if,
upon seeing it myself, I were not to believe it,
you should perform the act of subordination against me, O Yakkha."
He spoke this verse. Its meaning is as follows: "Whatever I might see with my eye, I would believe all of that to be exactly so;
yet even after seeing it, I might not believe those words.
O Yakkha, you should perform the act of subduing and the act of restraint against me. Alternatively: "Whatever I shall see with my eye..."

"Whatever I might see with my eye, because of not seeing that which is beyond the range of the eye"—"all that I would place my full confidence in" means that all that has been seen, heard, or otherwise known by you, I would place my full confidence in.
For such is my deep conviction regarding you; this is the intended meaning. As for the final phrase, its meaning is exactly as previously stated.
Having heard that, the peta said:
“Let this be your promise of truth to me: having heard the Dhamma, may you attain great confidence;
seeking nothing else and with a mind free from malice, [teach] whatever Dhamma you have heard and even what you have not heard.”
“I shall tell you everything just as I know it,” he said, and recited this verse. Following this:
“With a white horse, beautifully adorned, you approached the one impaled on a stake.
This vehicle is wonderful and beautiful to behold; of what karma is this the fruit?”
“In the middle of the city of Vesālī, on a muddy road, there was a pit.
With a mind full of faith, I took a piece of white gośīrṣa sandalwood and placed it in that pit.
Having stepped upon it with my feet, both I and others passed over it.”
“This vehicle is wonderful and beautiful to behold; it is the fruition of that very deed.
“Your complexion illuminates all directions, and your fragrance wafts through all directions.
You have attained the psychic power of a yakkha and possess great majesty; yet you are naked—what is the fruition of this?”
“Free from anger, with a mind always serene, I approach people with gentle words.
This is the ripening of that very deed: my divine complexion shines forth constantly.
Having seen those established in the Dhamma, possessing fame and renown, I speak to them with a serene heart.”
“This is the ripening of that very same kamma: a divine fragrance wafts from me constantly.
‘While my companions were bathing at the ford, I took their clothes on shore and hid them;
though seeking amusement, I was not ill-intentioned. Because of that, I am naked and my livelihood is difficult.’”
“Whoever commits an evil deed while playing, they say such is the ripening of that karma;
but as for one who commits it without playing, what do they say is the ripening of that karma?
“Those people who are of wicked intention and mind, defiled in body and speech...”
“With the breakup of the body, after passing away, they will undoubtedly go to hell. But others,
aspiring for a happy destination, delighting in giving and having cultivated their own being,
with the breakup of the body, after passing away, will undoubtedly go to a happy destination.”
These are the verses of question and answer between the two of them.
530. Regarding that: “Let this promise of yours be true for me,” means:
“Let this promise of yours—that ‘I shall have faith in everything’—be true for me. “Having heard the Dhamma, receive full confidence” means: [this is said] by me as I speak.
Having heard the beautiful Dhamma, may you obtain serene confidence (*pasāda*).
"One who seeks for something else" (*aññatthiko*) means one who seeks for knowledge (*ājānanatthiko*). "Just as they understand"—that is, just as another person who understands understands;

or the meaning is: "just as it was known by me," i.e., "as it has been known by me. 531. "Of what is this the result? (*kissetaṃ kammassa ayaṃ vipāko*)—of what? Of what indeed is this? Of what action is this the maturation (*vipāka*)? Or, *etaṃ* is merely a particle; the construction is "of what action? Some read it as "kissa te."
532–33. "On a muddy road" means on a path possessed of mud. "A pit" means a hollow. "For one day" means for a single day.
"I placed it in the pit" means I set it down in that muddy hollow in such a way that the mud would not be stepped upon.
"Of that" refers to that making of a bridge with the head of the ox.
"536–7. 'Those established in the Dhamma' means those who practice the Dhamma, those who act with equanimity. 'I speak' means I tell, I praise.
'Desiring sport' means having laughter as one's purpose. 'And not with a corrupt mind' means that toward the owner of the goods, his mind is not defiled;
the meaning is that he neither intends to steal nor intends to destroy."

538. *Akīḷamāno* means one who does not intend playfulness, whose mind is defiled by greed and other such passions. "What do the wise say is the ripening of that deed?"—they ask how bitter the painful result of that evil deed thus committed is said to be by the wise.
539–40. *Duṭṭhasaṅkappamano* refers to mental thoughts defiled by sensual intentions and so forth; by this, he speaks of misconduct of the mind.
*Kāyena vācāya ca saṃkiliṭṭhā* means stained by body and speech through acts such as killing living beings and so forth. *Āsamānā* means hoping, longing, or aspiring.
When the peta had thus explained the fruits of kamma in brief, the king, not believing it, said:
“How may I know this for certain—that this is the ripening of good and evil?
Or what must I see to believe it? Or who might make me believe this?”

He spoke this verse. Regarding that, as for the phrase "How could I know that with absolute certainty?"—this refers to what was stated by you through the analysis of the ripening of both wholesome and unwholesome karma, beginning with:
"Those people who have evil intentions and are defiled in body and speech," and continuing with:
"But others, aspiring to a happy destination. For what reason [could I know that with certainty]?
