"I would believe through direct personal realization, independent of others. Or, having seen what, would I believe?
What kind of directly perceived illustration (*nidassana*) would I see that I might then believe in accordance with it?
Or who could make me believe this? What wise and learned person could make me believe in this matter? Tell me that. This is the meaning.
Having heard that, the peta explained the matter to him by way of its cause:
“Having seen and having heard, believe this: such is the ripening of the good and the evil.
If both the good and the evil were non-existent, could beings possibly be well-fated or ill-fated?”
“If mortals did not perform deeds here in the world of men— both good and evil—
there would be no beings in the world of men who are well-faring or ill-faring, nor any who are base or sublime.
But because mortals do perform deeds here in the world of men— both good and evil— ”
"Therefore, beings in the world of humans—whether well-faring or ill-faring, low or exalted—are said to experience the ripening of two kinds of kamma:
that which is to be felt as pleasure and that which is to be felt as pain.
Those foolish people who do not see this duality indulge with those goddesses; they are reborn [there], being blind to the twofold nature."
He spoke this verse:

542. Therein, "having seen" (*disvā*) means even having seen directly before one's eyes. "Having heard" (*sutvā*) means having heard the Dhamma and, by following its guidance, drawing out the underlying principle through inference.
Regarding "the beautiful and the evil" (*kalyāṇa-pāpassa*), this refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma; [he understands] "this is pleasant, this..."
“Believe that the result is suffering. Regarding the phrase “both being non-existent”: this refers to the two kinds of karma, namely the wholesome and the unwholesome, being absent.

“Could there be beings who are well-faring or ill-faring? means: could it be possible, how could it be conceivable, that “these beings have gone to a good destination or a bad destination, or that they are wealthy in a good destination or poor in a bad destination”? This is the meaning.

543–4. Now, he elucidates the aforementioned meaning through both negative (vyatireka) and positive (anvaya) reasoning by means of the two verses beginning with "No cettha kammāni" and "Yasmā ca kammāni.
In this context, "inferior and superior" refers to those who are lowly or exalted in terms of lineage, physical form, health, retinue, and so forth. 545.
"They say there is today a twofold ripening of kamma" means that there is now, at present, a twofold [result] of kamma—namely, well-performed and ill-performed.
They speak of and explain the *vipāka* (resultant fruit). What is it? He says:
"to be experienced as pleasure and pain," meaning that which is fit to be experienced as both the desirable and the undesirable. Regarding the phrase "those deities enjoy themselves":
those who obtain a resultant fruit to be experienced as pleasure in its highest degree, having become deities in the world of the gods, enjoy their sense faculties while endowed with divine bliss.
"Fools burn because they do not see duality" means that those fools who, failing to see and lacking faith in the duality of both action and the fruit of action,
are intent upon evil and experience the ripening that is to be felt as suffering; they are "burned" by their karma in the hells and other realms,
reaching a state of misery.
Addressing the inquiry, "Since you thus believe in the fruit of karma, why do you experience such suffering?", he said:
"There are no deeds performed by oneself; even after giving, there is none who can assign [the result] to me.
Because of that—clothing, bedding, food, and drink—I am naked and my livelihood is difficult."

He spoke this verse. In that regard, "there are no deeds done by oneself" means: because there are no meritorious deeds (*puññakamma*) previously performed by myself, which I might now receive as clothing and other such things;

and even though I have given gifts, "there is no one who can dedicate them," meaning there is no one who, having given a gift to ascetics and brahmins, [can direct it] saying, "May this be for such-and-such a peta."

"He might assign it to me or designate it for me; that does not exist. Therefore, I am naked and my livelihood is difficult"—by these two reasons, he thought, "I am now naked and without a loincloth, and my livelihood and way of life are difficult and painful.
Having heard this, the king, desiring to provide him with clothing and other necessities—
“Could there perhaps be some reason, O Yakkha, by which you might obtain clothing?
Tell me what the cause is; we wish to hear a convincing word of reason.

Thus he spoke this verse. Therein, *yena* means “by which reason”; *tvaṃ acchādanaṃ labhetha* means “you might obtain clothing”; *kiñci taṃ kāraṇaṃ siyā nu kho* means “could there perhaps be some such reason?”; *yad-atthi* means “if it exists.”
Then the peta, explaining the reason for this, said:
“There is here a monk named Kappitaka, a meditator of virtuous conduct, an arahant, liberated;
one whose faculties are guarded, whose *pātimokkha* is restrained, who has become cool and attained the supreme vision.”
“Gentle, generous, well-spoken, pleasant-faced, easy to approach, and easy to converse with;
a field for merit, dwelling in a state free from conflict, he is worthy of offerings from gods and humans.
Peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, without longing, liberated, free from the arrow of pain, selfless, and without crookedness.”
Free from acquisitions, with all conceptual proliferation exhausted, he has attained the three knowledges and is radiant.
Though not well-known and difficult to understand even when seen, people address him as a "Muni";
yet the *yakkhas* and spirits know him—the unshakable one of noble qualities—as he wanders through the world.
“If you should give even one pair or two to me, designating them for my sake,
they would be accepted as such, and you would see me wearing the cloth.
Thus he spoke this verse.
548. Therein, “one who has attained [the goal]” (*kappitaka*) refers to the venerable Elder Upāli’s preceptor among the thousand matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*).
“Here” (*idha*) means in the vicinity of this Vesālī.

“A meditator” (*jhāyī*) is one who meditates with the meditation of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-jhāna*). “One who has become cool” (*sītibhūta*) is one who has reached a state of coolness through the subsiding of all the distress and fever of the defilements (*kilesa*). “One who has attained the supreme vision” (*uttamadiṭṭhipatta*)—
He has attained right view, the supreme and highest fruit. 549. *Sakhila* means gentle. *Suvaca* means easy to speak to.

*Svāgama* means one whose traditional knowledge (*āgama*) has been well-acquired. *Suppaṭimuttaka* means one whose speech is well-released; the meaning is that he speaks with liberation. *Araṇavihārī* means one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettā*). 550. *Santa* means one whose defilements (*kilesa*) have been stilled.
*Vidhūma* means one from whom the smoke of wrong thoughts (*micchā-vitakka*) has departed. *Anīgha* means free from suffering (*dukkha*).

“Free from longing” (*nirāsa*) means devoid of craving. “Liberated” (*mutta*) means released from all states of existence (*bhava*). “Thornless” (*visalla*) means free from the thorns of passion and so forth. “Without ‘mine’” (*amama*) means devoid of the sense of possessiveness (*mamaṃkāra*).

“Upright” (*avaṅka*) means free from crookedness such as bodily crookedness. “One who has abandoned the substrata” (*nirūpadhi*) means one who has cast off the substrata of defilements, volitional formations, and so on.

“One for whom all proliferations have ceased” (*sabbapapañcakhīṇa*) means one whose proliferations such as craving have been completely exhausted. “Radiant” (*jutimā*) means radiant with the unsurpassed radiance of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
"Unknown" means he is not well-known because his virtues are concealed by supreme fewness-of-wishes (appicchatā).
"And even having seen him, he is not easily known" means that because of his profundity, even after seeing him, it is not easy to discern: "He is of such virtue, such nature, and such wisdom.
"Yakṣas and bhūtas know him as unshaken" means that yakṣas and bhūtas know the unshaken one, free from craving, as an "Arahant."
They know him as one of "virtuous nature," meaning one possessing qualities such as beautiful virtue (*sīla*).
552. "Of him" means of that Mahāthera Kappitaka. "A pair" means a single pair of garments;
"two or" means two pairs of garments. "Having dedicated them to me" means having dedicated them for my sake. And they were accepted.
Those pairs of garments would have been accepted by him. "Sannaddhadussa" means armor made of cloth;
the meaning is that he obtained the cloth and wore it as an upper and lower garment.
Then the king—

“In which place does the ascetic dwell, that we might go and see him now—he who would dispel today our doubt, our perplexity, and the thorns of wrong views?”—thus he asked about the elder’s dwelling place.
In this context, *kasmiṃ padese* means “in which place”; *yo majja* means “who [will] today,” the syllable *ma-* being used for the purpose of metrical conjunction (*padasandhi*).
Then the peta said:
"There sits Kapinaccanā, surrounded by many deities;
he of true name speaks a discourse on the Dhamma, being diligent toward his own teacher."
He spoke this verse. In that context, "at Kapinaccanā" means at the place known by the designation "Kapinaccanā" because of the dancing of the *kapi*s, that is, the monkeys.
"Truly named" (*saccanāmo*) means one who is truly named according to his actual qualities—such as "meditator," "virtuous," "arahant," or "liberated"—and thus possesses an unerring name.
When this was said by the peta, the king immediately desired to go into the presence of the elder.
“‘In that case, I shall go now and provide the ascetic with a pair of garments;
let them be accepted, and we two may see you dressed in fine cloth,’ he said in this verse.
In it, ‘I shall provide’ (kassāmi) means ‘I will do.’”
Then the peta, showing that "the Elder is teaching the Dhamma to the deities, therefore this is not the time to approach him," said:
"Do not approach the one gone forth at an inopportune moment; excellent, O Licchavis, is this practice of yours.

means who indeed would say "do not release him" regarding one who is performing such a legitimate legal act (*dhammiyakamma*) within this realm of faults? The meaning is that no one at all is permitted to speak in such a manner.

This is its name. As for that which is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparapariyāyavedanīya*), the meaning is that its fruit is to be experienced in a subsequent life, provided that the process of saṃsāra continues.

“Of happy result” (*sukhudraya*) means having a pleasant maturation. “Merit always increases”: having performed merit even once, one is not satisfied, thinking, “That much is enough.”
For one who offers oblations and fulfills successive courses of good conduct, merit increases at all times;
or rather, for one fulfilling successive courses of good conduct, the fruit of merit—designated as "merit"—increases further and further and becomes fully perfected; such is the meaning.

"King named Piṅgalaka"—this is the *Nandaka-petavatthu*. What is its origin? Two hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Teacher, there was a king named Piṅgala in the province of Surāṣṭra.
His general, named Nandaka, was of wrong view and perverted vision; having adopted the false conviction that "there is no giving," and so forth, he—
He wandered about. His daughter, a female lay follower named Uttarā, had been given in marriage into a suitable family.
But after Nandaka passed away, he was reborn as a *vemānika* spirit in a great banyan tree in the Viñjhā forest.

When he had died, Uttarā [prepared] a water-pot filled with pure, cool, fragrant water, along with [food] consisting of boiled rice mixed with [ingredients] endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.

go for refuge to that Dhamma, O subduer of enemies, together with your sons and wife.”
“There are four who have entered the path and four who abide in the fruit;
this is the Saṅgha, upright, established in wisdom and virtue.
Go for refuge to that Saṅgha, O Arindama, together with your sons and wife.”
“Quickly refrain from taking life; avoid what is not given in the world;
do not drink intoxicants, nor speak falsehoods, and be content with your own wife.
“O Yakkha, you desire my welfare; O deity, you desire my benefit.”
“I shall do your bidding; you are my teacher.
I go for refuge to the Buddha, and to the Dhamma which is unsurpassed;
and to the Saṅgha of the God among Men—I go for refuge.”
“I quickly abstain from taking life; I avoid what is not given in the world;
I do not drink intoxicants nor speak falsehoods; I am content with my own wife.
I wash away [my sins] in a great wind or in a swiftly flowing river.”
“I renounce evil views, delighting in the teaching of the Buddhas.
Having said this, Soraṭṭha, having desisted from his wicked perspective and paid homage to the Blessed One, mounted the chariot as its leader— thus they spoke in verse.

658–9. Therein, "the king named Piṅgalaka" refers to the lord of the Surāṣṭra region; because of his tawny eyes, he was known by the well-known name "Piṅgala," and he was the sovereign king of the Surāṣṭra country. "Of the Moriyas" means of the Moriya kings;
this is said with reference to Dhammāsoka. "He returned again to Surāṣṭra" means toward the territory of Surāṣṭra, [taking] the road leading to Surāṣṭra.
He returned. "Mudbhūmi" means a marshy ground. "Vaṇṇupatha" means a path through a forested wilderness created by a *peta*. 660. "Khemam" means free from fear.

"Sovatthikam" means bringing about a state of safety. "Sivam" means free from calamity. By the phrase "near the region of Suratta," he means: "We are indeed in the vicinity of the territory of Suratta as we travel by this road.

661–2. "Soraṭṭho" means the ruler of Suratta. "Ubbiggarūpo" means one whose nature is agitated. "Bhiṃsanam" means causing fear. "Lomahaṃsanam" means the bristling of the hair due to the quality of being terrifying.
"663. 'In the presence of the messengers of Yama' means in the vicinity of the *petas*.

'A superhuman odor wafts' means the stench of the *peta* bodies wafts. 'A dreadful sound is heard' means the most terrifying noise of beings undergoing punishment in the individual hells (*paccekaniraya*) is heard."
666. A "tree" (*pādapa*) is so named because it drinks water by means of root-branches that are like feet.
"Endowed with shade" (*chāyāsampanna*) means possessing abundant shade. "Resembling the color of a dark cloud" means being like a blue cloud in its hue.
"Appearing with the splendor of the color of a cloud" means appearing while having the shape and color of a cloud.

670. “*Pūraṃ pānīyasarakanti*” means a water-vessel full of water. “*Pūve ti khajjaketi*”: regarding “*pūva*,” it refers to sweet, delicious cakes that produce wealth; he saw them placed there, having filled various bowls with them. 672. Regarding “*atho te adurāgatan*”:
here, *atha* is merely a particle, or it has the sense of emphasis. “O Great King, your arrival is not a bad arrival (*durāgata*);
rather, it is indeed a welcome arrival (*svāgata*)”—this is what we accept. This is the meaning.
*Arindama*: one whose nature is to subdue enemies. 677. *Amaccā pārisajjā*:
the ministers and the assembly members; the construction is: "Let the ministers and the assembly members hear the words, and let the brahmin who is your domestic priest also hear them.
678. *Suraṭṭhasmiṃ aham*: "In Suraṭṭha, I [am]"—meaning in the country of Suraṭṭha. *Devā*: he addresses the king as "O Lord. *Micchādiṭṭhī*: one of wrong view.
One who has a perverted view due to the nihilistic view (*natthikadiṭṭhi*). "Immoral" (*dussīla*) means devoid of virtue (*nissīla*). "Miserly" (*kadariya*) means one who is stubbornly stingy.
"Abusive" (*paribhāsaka*) means one who reviles ascetics and brahmins.
679. "They will ward off" (*vārayissanti*) means they have warded off. "I am an obstacle-maker" means [an obstacle] for those giving gifts and those performing acts of assistance.

"Having become an obstacle-maker, I shall prevent many people, or cause them to be prevented, from the merit consisting of giving when others are bestowing gifts"—this is the construction [of the sentence].
"There is no fruition for giving," and so forth, is the demonstration of the manner in which they were prevented. In that context, "there is no fruition for giving" means:
"Of one giving a gift, there is no ripening (vipāka) or fruit to be attained in the future"—thus he denies the ripening.
"Whence can there be a fruit for self-restraint?"—the intention is that there is simply no fruit for moral conduct (sīla) whatsoever.
"There is no such thing as a teacher"—there is no one at all who is called a teacher who instructs in proper conduct and discipline. [This is] by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāvato).
The intended meaning is that beings are indeed either tamed or untamed. Therefore he said, "Who will tame the untamed? (681).
"Beings are equal" means that all these beings are exactly the same as one another; therefore, there is no such thing as an elder, so how could there be one who honors an elder?
The sense is that there is no such merit as honoring an elder. "There is no power."

It rejects that power of energy by which beings, established in their own strength and exerting effort, attain success ranging from human prosperity up to Arhatship. Or, the statement "there is no energy; how could there be initiative or manly effort?
is spoken by way of rejecting those who maintain such views as "we proceed by means of manly energy and manly action."
682. "There is no fruit of giving" means that there is indeed no fruit whatsoever for giving;
the meaning is that the relinquishing of the object to be given is as fruitless as ashes cast into the fire. "It does not purify one who has enemies":

here, "one who has enemies" refers to a person who possesses enmity and has committed evil through acts such as killing and so forth; [giving] does not purify such a person from their enmity or from the evil deeds committed by way of those enmities, nor does it purify them through the practice of giving, virtue, and so on.

Sometimes one does not even perform what is pure. It should be understood that the previous passage, beginning with “there is no result of giving,” shows how one has prevented oneself and others from engaging in giving and so forth;
however, the passage beginning with “there is no such thing as the fruit of giving” shows one’s own false adherence.
“Laddheyyaṃ” means that which is to be obtained. To the question “How is it to be obtained? he says: “born of the transformation of destiny.”

The intention is that when this being experiences pleasure or pain, he experiences it solely through the power of fixed transformation (niyati-vipariṇāma), and not because of the performance of karma, nor by means of a Lord (Issara) or other such causes. 683.
"There is no mother, father, or brother" refers to the absence of any fruit for either right or wrong conduct toward mothers and others.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "There is no world beyond this" means that from this world here, there is no so-called "other world" at all;
the intention is that beings are annihilated right there and then. "What is given" refers to a great gift (*mahādāna*). "What is offered" refers to hospitality consisting of messengers;
he rejects both of these as "non-existent," intending that they bear no fruit. "Well-stored" means well-deposited.
"It does not exist" means that what those ascetics and brahmins call "a following treasure" in regard to giving—that does not exist.
The intention is that for them, it is merely a matter of words. 684.
"No one kills anyone" means that even if a man were to kill another man, [the head of] that other man—
One might cut [them], yet in the ultimate sense (paramatthato) no one kills anyone there; it is as if one were killing because of the state of being pierced among the seven elements (kāya).
To the question, "How is there the stroke of a blade? he says: "In the interval between the openings of the seven.
The blade enters into the opening, the interval, which is the space between the seven elements such as earth and the rest; by that means, beings [are struck] with swords and so forth.
They appear as if struck down; however, because the remaining parts of the body also possess a permanent nature (*niccasabhāva*), they do not actually break apart—this is the intended meaning.

685. "The life-principle (*jīva*) is indeed indestructible and indivisible": this life-principle of sentient beings cannot be cut by weapons or the like, nor can it be broken, because of its permanent nature.
"Eightfold and round like a lump of sugar": furthermore, that life-principle is sometimes eightfold and sometimes [round].
It is round like a ball of sugar. Having attained the state of a "complete one" (kevalī), it is five hundred yojanas in height.
"Who is worthy to cut the soul?"—who indeed is capable of cutting the eternal and unchanging soul with weapons and the like?
He says that it cannot be disturbed by anything.
686. "In a ball of thread" means in a ball of thread that has been made by winding it up. "Thrown" means thrown by way of being unwound.
"It runs away as it is being unwound" means that when a ball of thread is thrown while standing on a mountain or at the top of a tree, it goes along only as long as it is being unwound;
once the thread is exhausted, it does not go further. "In the same way" means just as that ball of thread [goes] while being unwound...

When the thread is exhausted, it no longer goes; in the same way, that soul (*jīva*), unwinding the ball of its own personal existence (*attabhāva*) for the duration of the time specified as "eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons" (*mahākappa*), flees and continues on, but beyond that point it does not continue.
And in this very way, that soul—just as if some man were to depart from his own village of residence and [proceed from there]...

Just as one enters another village for some particular business, even so that living being (jīva), having departed from this body, enters another subsequent body by way of necessity—this is the intended meaning. *Bondi* means the body. 689.
*Cullāsīti* means eighty-four. *Mahākappino* means of great aeons (*mahākappa*). In that regard: "From one great lake..."
"By this method—removing a single drop of water from the Anotatta lake with the tip of a blade of kusa grass every hundred years—it takes seven such attempts for that lake to become devoid of water;
this constitutes what is called one 'great aeon' (mahākappa). Having said this, they further state:
"The measure of saṃsāra is eight million four hundred thousand such great aeons. Those who are fools...

"And both the wise and the foolish" refers to all those who are blind fools as well as those who possess wisdom. "Having exhausted saṃsāra" means having exhausted saṃsāra—defined by the aforementioned time-limit—by way of successive rebirths.
"They will make an end of suffering" means they will bring about the limit, the conclusion, of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Even the wise are not able to attain purification prematurely, nor are the fools.
His tenet is that [suffering] does not proceed beyond that point.
(690) "Pleasures and pains are measured by *doṇas* and *piṭakas*" means that the pleasures and pains of sentient beings are, as it were, measured by *doṇas*, *piṭakas*, and other measuring vessels;
they are individually limited precisely by the aforementioned temporal boundaries.
For each of those beings, those [karmic results] produced by the transformation of destiny are limited. The Victor, standing on the ground of victory, understands all this;
he understands it solely because he has transcended *saṃsāra*. But the rest of the world, wandering in *saṃsāra*, remains deluded.
691. "I had such a view previously" means that formerly I was one who held the nihilistic view as described.
"Deluded, shrouded by delusion" means: deluded by the confusion that serves as the cause for the aforementioned view;
moreover, shrouded by the delusion co-arising with it—that is to say, the intention is that the seeds of the wholesome have been concealed.

692. Having thus shown the evil deed committed by virtue of the evil view that had previously arisen within himself, he now spoke the words beginning with “In less than six months for me,” showing the fruit of that deed which he himself must experience in the future.
695–7. Therein, “a hundred thousand years” (*vassāni satasahassāni*) means a hundred thousand years; “having passed” (*atikkamitvā*) is the ellipsis of the verb.
Alternatively, this is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is “when a hundred thousand years have elapsed. Ghoso.

"It is heard thus" means that when such a length of time has elapsed, at that very moment, a sound is heard in that hell: "O sirs, here for you border-dwellers, a period measuring one hundred thousand years has passed.
This is a metaphorical expression, O Great King; "a hundredth part of ten million years" refers to a hundred parts, that is, a hundred divisions of ten million years.
"Great King, this is the measure of the lifespan, this is the limit, for beings suffering in hell;
such is the meaning. This is what is meant: ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; ten times ten thousands make a hundred thousand;
a hundred times a hundred thousand makes a *koṭi*. By way of those *koṭis*, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of years."
Hundreds of millions of years. And this should be understood as the calculation of years specifically for those in hell, not for humans or devas.
The lifespan of those in hell consists of many hundreds of thousands of such millions of years. Therefore it was said:
"People are cooked in hell for hundreds of thousands of millions. By whatever kind of evil deed beings [fall] thus into hells...
To show by way of conclusion that they are being cooked, it is said: "Those of wrong view and immoral conduct, and those who revile the Noble Ones.
*Vedissanti* means "I shall experience.
(698–706) Having thus shown the evil fruit to be experienced by oneself in the future, [the Blessed One now asks]: "By what holy life (*brahmacariya*)..."
Having explained the matter asked by the king—“This is your power”—and desiring to establish him in the refuges and the precepts, he said, “Listen to that, O Great King,” and so forth.
Therein, “delighting in the precepts and the Uposatha” means being devoted to both the regular precepts and the Uposatha precepts.
“Adā” means he gave. “That Dhamma” refers to that Eightfold Path and the state of the Deathless.
709–12. Thus exhorted by the peta regarding the refuges and the precepts, the king, with a mind full of faith, first extolled the benefit he had received from him;

then, establishing himself in the refuges and other virtues, he spoke three verses beginning with “One who desires his welfare,” and finally, declaring that he had relinquished the evil view he had previously held, he uttered the verse beginning with “I shake off.”

In this context, "I winnow it like chaff in a great wind" means that when a great wind blows, O Yakkha, I winnow—that is, I shake off—that evil view by means of the wind of your teaching of the Dhamma.
"Or in a swift-flowing river" means that I carry away that evil view like grass, wood, leaves, and husks in a great river with a rapid current; such is the intention. "I vomit it out."
"An evil view" means: "I cast off this evil view that has entered my mind. Regarding this, he states the reason:

"Delighting in the teaching of the Buddhas. Since I am resolutely and joyfully devoted to the teaching of the Blessed Buddhas, which brings the deathless, therefore I vomit out that poison known as [this] view—such is the construction.
713. These concluding verses were placed there by the compilers of the Saṅgīti. In that context, "standing at the head" means facing the eastern direction.
"He mounted the chariot" means the king mounted his own royal chariot prepared for departure;
having mounted it, through the power of the *yakkha*, he reached his own city on that very day and entered the royal palace. At a later time, he [recited] this...
He reported the matter to the bhikkhus; the bhikkhus reported it to the elders (theras); and the elders included it in the compilation during the Third Council.
The commentary on the *Nandaka-petavatthu* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Revatī-petavatthu*.
714–36. "Arise, Revatī, you of most evil character"—this is the *Revatī-petavatthu*.

Since it is indistinguishable from the *Revatī-vimānavatthu*, whatever needs to be said here regarding its origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and the verses should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the *Vimānavatthu* in the *Paramatthadīpanī*. For this [account] was told by way of the divine youth Nandiya.

It should be understood that although it was included in the *Vimānavatthu-pāḷi*, it was also included in the *Petavatthu-pāḷi* by way of the verse connected with Revatī, titled "The Story of the Petī Revatī.
The commentary on the "Story of the Petī Revatī" is finished.
5. Commentary on the Story of the Sugarcane Thief.
"This sugarcane field of mine is large"—this is the story of the sugarcane thief. What is its origin?
While the Blessed One was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, a certain man, having placed a bundle of sugarcane on his shoulder, was eating a stalk of sugarcane.
He was walking along. Then a certain lay follower, virtuous and of good character, was walking behind him with a young boy.
Seeing some sugarcane, the boy began to cry out, "Give it to me! When the lay follower saw the boy crying, he engaged the man in conversation in order to conciliate him. But that man, with him...
He did not say a word and gave the boy not even a piece of sugarcane. When the lay devotee pointed out the boy and said, “This boy is crying excessively;
give him a piece of sugarcane,” the man, unable to endure it, established a hostile attitude and, out of disregard, threw a stalk of sugarcane behind him.
Thus, at a later time, having passed away, he was reborn among the *petas* due to the long-accumulated influence of his greed.
For the fruit of one’s actions corresponds to the action itself, a vast sugarcane grove arose, eight *karīsa* in extent,
covered thickly with sugarcane stalks the size of pestle-handles and dark as collyrium, spreading over the entire area.
As soon as he approached with the desire to eat, thinking, "I will take some sugarcane," the sugarcane struck him;
questioned by that [ghost], he fell down.
Then one day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was going to Rājagaha for alms, he saw that peta on the way. Upon seeing the Elder, he asked him about the deed he had committed.
“This field of mine is vast, and it yields no small fruit of merit;
yet now it does not come to my enjoyment. Venerable sir, tell me, what is the result of this?
I am being struck, I am being devoured, and though I strive and exert myself, I cannot enjoy anything.”
"Alas, my strength is severed; I am a wretch and lament. Of what karma is this the result?
"Afflicted, I fall upon the ground;
I wallow like a water-dweller in the heat."
"And as I wept, tears flowed from my eyes.
Tell me, venerable sir, what is the result of this?
"Hungry, exhausted, and thirsty, agitated, he finds no pleasant happiness."
“I ask you this matter, O Blessed One: how indeed might I obtain the enjoyment of sugarcane?
“In a former life, when you were a human being, you yourself performed the deed.
And I shall tell you this matter; having heard it, you will understand.”
“You were walking along eating sugarcane when a man followed behind you.
As he called out to you from behind, you did not say anything to him.
He begged you as you remained silent, and you said to him, ‘Sugarcane, my dear sir.’”
"You gave sugarcane to him from behind his back; this is the result of that deed.
'Come now, go and take it from behind; having taken it, eat as much as you wish.
By that very act, you will become satisfied, joyful, elated, and gladdened.'"
“Having gone, he seized him from behind; having seized him, he ate him as much as he desired.
Because of that, he became satisfied, joyful, elated, and full of delight.
These verses of dialogue were spoken by the peta and the elder respectively.
737–8. Therein, "of what" means "of what kind"; the intention is "of what kind of action. "I am slain" means I am afflicted, I fall into distress.
Or, "I am harassed" means I am oppressed; the meaning is that I am especially tormented. "I am devoured" means I am eaten;
the meaning is that I am cut by the sugarcane blades which, like swords, are sharpened and devouring. "I am striving" means...
"I make an effort to eat sugarcane. "I move about" means I apply effort.
"To enjoy" means to enjoy the juice of sugarcane; the sense is "to eat sugarcane. "With severed sap" means with severed strength, with vitality cut off;
the sense is that one's power is completely exhausted. "Miserable" means wretched. "I lament" means, being tormented by suffering, I cry out excessively.
739. *Vighāto* means afflicted (*vighātavā*) or one whose strength is destroyed (*vihatabala*). "I fall to the ground" means that being unable to stand, I fall upon the earth.
"I roll about" means I wallow. "Like a water-dweller" means like a fish. "In the heat" means on land scorched by the heat. 740–4. *Santassito*:
thoroughly parched due to the drying up of the lips, throat, and palate. *Sātasukha*: that which has become pleasant.
"Sukham" means happiness. "Na vindati" means I do not find; "na labhāmi" means I do not obtain. "Tam" refers to you. "Vijānāti" means he knows;
"vijānāhi" means know [it]. "Payāto" means having set out to go. "Anvagacchi" means he followed after. "Paccāsanto" means hoping for or expecting.
"Tass' etaṃ kammassa": here, "etam" is merely a particle; the meaning is "of that action. "Piṭṭhito gaṇheyyāsi" means you would take [him] by your own back.
"You should take some sugarcane. "Pamodito" means "delighted.

Having taken it, he ate as much as he desired; that is, having taken the sugarcane according to the elder’s instruction and eating it to his heart's content, he took a large bundle of sugarcane and offered it to the elder. The elder, out of compassion for him, [accepted] by that very [means].
Having had that bundle of sugarcane taken, he went to Veḷuvana and gave it to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, consumed it and delivered a discourse of thanksgiving. With a mind full of faith, the peta paid homage and departed;
from that time forth, he enjoyed sugarcane as he pleased.
Thus, at a later time, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Furthermore, this account of the peta’s existence became well known in the human world. Then, people approached the Teacher and asked about that matter.
The Teacher explained the facts to them in detail and taught the Dhamma; having heard it, the people [were freed] from the stain of avarice.
"They became abstainers.
The commentary on the *Ucchu-peta-vatthu* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Kumāra-peta-vatthu*.
“Sāvatthī by name, a city”—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning two *petas*.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, two sons of the King of Kosala, who were handsome, in the prime of their youth, and intoxicated by the pride of their vigor, committed adultery with another man’s wife;
having died, they were reborn as *petas* on the bank of a moat. At night...
They wailed with a terrifying sound. When people heard it, they were struck with fear and trembling, thinking, "If this is done, this ill omen will be pacified.
They gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Lay followers, hearing that sound will not cause you any obstacle whatsoever," and so on.
Having explained the reason for this, in order to teach them the Dhamma, he said:
"There is a city named Sāvatthī, facing the Himalayas;
there were two young princes there, so I have heard."
“Addicted to things that provoke lust, delighting in the gratification of sensual desires,
and greedy for present pleasure, they did not see what was to come.
Having passed away from the human state, they have gone from here to the other world.”
Thus they cried out, seeing what they had previously done wrong:
"Alas! While many things worthy of being given were present, we were unable to provide even a small measure of protection that would bring us happiness."
"What evil could there be greater than this, that we, having passed away from a royal family,
have been reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, afflicted by hunger and thirst?
Having been masters here, we have become non-masters there."
People, high and low, wander about tormented by hunger and thirst.
Having understood this danger arising from the intoxication of power,
and having abandoned that pride of power, a person goes to heaven in the next existence.
“When the body breaks up, the wise one is reborn in heaven”—thus he spoke this verse.
(746) Therein, “Thus have I heard” means that it was not only seen by his own knowledge, but rather that it was heard by him in this way because it was well-known in the world.

(747) “Delighting in the gratification of sensual pleasures” means having a nature of rejoicing by way of the gratification found in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). In [the pursuit of] present happiness...
"Greedily" means being greedy and attached to the mere pleasure occurring in the present.

"They did not see what was to come" means that, having abandoned misconduct and practiced good conduct, they did not contemplate the future happiness to be obtained in the realms of gods and humans hereafter.

"They wail there, though they are not seen": those ghosts who were formerly princes wail and cry out here near Sāvatthī, their forms invisible. As to what they cry out, he says: "The evil deeds committed by ourselves in the past."
749. Now, in order to explain the cause and the fruit of their lamentation by way of analysis, it was said: “*Bahūsu vata santesū*,” and so forth.
Therein, “*bahūsu vata santesū*” means while many worthy recipients (*dakkhiṇeyya*) exist.

“*Deyyadhamme upaṭṭhite*” means when the gift to be given, belonging to oneself, is present nearby; the sense is that it is obtainable. “*Parittaṃ sukhāvahan*” means [a gift] that brings about limited happiness.
The construction is: "Alas, we were unable to make ourselves secure and free from calamity by performing even a small amount of merit that brings happiness in the future.
(750) What could be more evil than that? What else could there be that is more evil or base than this which happened to us?

"Having fallen from the royal family" means: by whatever evil deed we have fallen from the royal family and been reborn here in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), having taken birth among the ghosts, we wander afflicted by hunger and thirst—this is the meaning.
"Having been masters here" means: having previously been masters in this very place in this world.
They wander about; in that very place they remain without a master. "High and low" refers to humans:
having been masters during their human lifetime, once deceased, they wander about—lowly due to the power of karma—afflicted by hunger and thirst. This shows one to see the structure of saṃsāra. 752.
"Having known this danger, which arises from the intoxication of lordship": this [danger] has arisen through the power of the intoxication of sovereignty.
Having understood the danger and fault known as rebirth in the states of misery, and having abandoned the intoxication of power, he became devoted to merit.
"A man who has gone to heaven in existence" means that he would indeed have gone to the heavenly world of the devas.
Thus the Teacher, having related the history of those petas, [described] the gift made by those humans for the sake of those petas.
Having had it announced, he taught the Dhamma to the assembled company in accordance with their inclinations. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Kumāra-peta-vatthu* is finished.
7. The commentary on the *Rājaputta-peta-vatthu*.
"Of deeds done in the past": This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the peta who was once a prince.
In that regard, he was the son of a king named Kitava in the past;
having offended against a Paccekabuddha in the past, he suffered in hell for many thousands of years, and due to the remaining ripening of that very karma, he was reborn among the petas. He...
Here, the one intended is the "Prince-Peta. His story has already been related in detail below in the *Sāṇavāsi-petavatthu*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there. For at that time, when the Elder had spoken of the circumstances of his own kinsmen who had become petas, the Teacher said:
"It is not only your kinsmen, but you yourself as well, in the immediately preceding past..."
“Having become a peta in this very body, he experienced great suffering,” he said. When requested by him [to explain further], he spoke:
“The ripening of deeds performed in the past churns the mind, Regarding forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful tangibles.”
“Having thus enjoyed abundant song, delight, and play,
and having wandered about in the pleasure grove, as I was entering Giribbaja,
I beheld the seer Sunetta— self-tamed and concentrated.”
“He who has few desires, is endowed with moral shame, and delights in the alms collected in his bowl”—
having descended from the back of the elephant, the Khattiya cried out,
“O Wandering One, you have been found! Having taken his bowl, the nobleman held it up high.
“Having broken my bowl on the bare ground, he departed laughing:
‘I am the son of a gambling king; what can you do to me, monk?
Because of that harsh deed, its ripening was bitter.”
What the prince experienced while cast into hell:
For sixty-four million and eighty-four thousand years,
you underwent intense suffering in hell, having committed evil deeds.
“Upside down he was roasted, face down on his left and right;
with feet held upward, the fool suffered for a long time.
For many thousands of years, and many tens of millions, he burned.”
"You have fallen into great suffering, having committed a transgression in hell.
Indeed, such bitter retribution for those who harbor malice toward the innocent comes upon evildoers who have assailed a sage of virtuous conduct."
“Thus, having experienced much suffering there for many years,
he passed away from that state and became a preta known as ‘Afflicted by Hunger and Thirst.
Having understood this danger, which arises from the intoxication of power;”
Having abandoned the intoxication of lordship, one should live in accordance with those who are free from passion.
"One who has respect for the Buddhas is praised even in this very life;
at the breaking up of the body, that wise person is reborn in heaven."
He related this story of a peta. 753.
Regarding the phrase "the ripening of deeds done in the past churns the mind":
the fruit of unwholesome kamma performed in previous births, when it arises as something immense, would churn—that is, overwhelm—the minds of the blind and foolish.
The intention is that one should produce one’s own welfare by way of not causing harm to others.
Now, in order to show that mental cultivation together with its object, it is said: “In forms, in sounds,” and so forth.
Therein, “in forms” means for the sake of form; the meaning is: as a cause for obtaining a desirable and pleasing objective support (ārammaṇa) of form according to one’s wish.
The same method applies to the terms *saddā* and so forth.

Having thus explained the meaning stated in common terms, [the author] speaks the passage beginning with “dancing and singing” in order to define it specifically. Therein, *rati* means sensual delight; *khiḍḍā* means play with companions and the like; *Giribbaja* means Rājagaha. 755.
*Isi* means a sage (*isi*) in the sense of seeking the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (*asekkha*). *Sunetta* is the name of one such [sage].
To the Paccekabuddha. "Self-tamed" means one whose mind has been tamed by the supreme discipline.

"Concentrated" means concentrated by the concentration of the fruit of Arahatship. "Delighting in alms gathered in the bowl" means delighted and content with the food obtained through the practice of alms-round that has come into the bowl and is contained within it.

756. “‘I have received [alms], venerable sir,’ he said; ‘Have you, venerable sir, received alms?’—he spoke thus for the sake of generating confidence. ‘Lifting it high’ means having raised the bowl, making it higher. 757.
‘Breaking the bowl on the bare ground’ means breaking the bowl while throwing it onto a rough and hard patch of earth.
‘He stepped back’ means he withdrew a short distance. And as he was stepping back, thinking, ‘For no reason at all, this blind fool has brought about great harm...’”
As the Paccekabuddha gazed upon him with compassion, thinking, "He has done this to himself," the prince said to him, "I am the son of a gambling king;
what can you do to me, monk? (Verse 758) *Pharusassa*:
of the harsh one, meaning the cruel one. *Kaṭuko*: disagreeable. *Yaṃ*: that which, namely the result (*vipāka*). *Samappito*: attached or joined.

759. “Six times eighty-four, and ninety million years”—that is, lying on his back for eighty-four thousand years, face down, on his left side, on his right side, with his feet upwards, hanging head-downwards, and remaining as he was;
thus there are six periods of eighty-four thousand years. Therefore he said:
“Upside down he was boiled, face down on his left and right;
with feet held upwards, the fool suffered for a long time.
Since those years amounted to many tens of millions (*nahuta*), it is said “tens of millions. “He underwent intense suffering” means he reached a state of extreme misery.
761. *Pūgāni* means a collection of years; here, in connection with the preceding verse, the accusative case should be understood as expressing absolute conjunction (*accantasamyoga*).

762. *Etādisaṃ* means of such a kind. *Kaṭukaṃ* means extremely painful; this is a description using a term of reproach (*bhāvanapaṃsaka*), similar to [the usage of] "sat down to one side" (*ekamantaṃ nisīdi*) and so forth.
Having assailed—that is, having harmed—the sage who was free from malice, possessed of no ill-will, and of virtuous conduct, those of evil deeds...
The construction is: "Persons experience such bitter and exceedingly painful [retribution].

(763) *So* refers to that ghost of the prince. *Tattha* means in hell. *Vedayitvā* means having experienced. *Nāma* indicates by way of being well-known and famous. *Tato cuto* means passed away from hell. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Thus the Blessed One, having inspired a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the great multitude gathered there through the story of the ghost of the prince, proclaimed the Truths (*sacca*) above. At the conclusion of the Truths, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and other stages.
The commentary on the *Rājaputta-petavatthu* is finished.
8. The commentary on the *Gūthakhādaka-petavatthu*:
"Having emerged from a pit of dung"—this was told concerning a dung-eating peta while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana.
It was said. It appears that in a certain village not far from Sāvatthī, a householder had a monastery built for the sake of a particular bhikkhu who was his personal attendant.
Bhikkhus came from various districts and resided there.
Seeing them, the people, with hearts full of faith, served them with excellent requisites. That bhikkhu, his personal attendant—
Unable to endure it, he became filled with envy and, speaking ill of those bhikkhus, incited the householder against them.
The householder, in turn, reviled those bhikkhus and held them in contempt.
Then, after his death, the one who had been the family attendant was reborn as a peta in a latrine within that very monastery; the householder, however, after his death, was reborn upon him.
Having become a peta, he was reborn there. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, seeing him, asked:
"Who are you that, having emerged from a pit of excrement, do not fall back into it dejected?
Without doubt you must have committed evil deeds; what indeed do you believe?"
He spoke this verse. Having heard it, the peta said:
"I am a peta, O venerable sir, miserable and belonging to the world of Yama;
having performed evil deeds, I have gone from here to the world of petas."
He declared himself by means of a verse. Then the Elder asked him:
"What evil deed was committed by body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what action do you undergo this suffering?"
He asked him about the deed he had performed in that verse. That peta replied:
"There was a resident in my dwelling, envious and stingy toward families;
he dwelt in my house, miserly and abusive."
“Having heard her words, O monks, I rebuked her;
by the ripening of that kamma, I have gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts.
With these two verses, he recounted the deed he himself had committed.
769. “There was one who lived there as my resident” means that in my own residence, the monastery built by me, there was a single monk who was a resident, staying there permanently.
“He dwelt in my house” means he was settled in my home through his status as a family attendant (*kulūpaka*), due to an adherence rooted in craving.

770. “Of him” means of that family-attendant monk. “Monks” refers to the monks. “I reviled” means I abused them. “Gone from here to the world of the departed” means having entered the animal womb of the departed (*petayoni*) in this manner, he became a departed spirit (*peta*).
Having heard that, the elder, inquiring after the other’s destination,
asked: “That friendless one who, in the guise of a friend, was your family associate—
upon the breakup of the body, what destination did that witless man go to after passing away?”
He spoke this verse. Therein, "in the guise of a friend" means in the semblance of a friend, by way of appearing like a friend.
Again, the peta, explaining that matter to the elder, said:
"I stand upon the very head, at the summit of that same evil deed."
And having reached another realm, he said these two verses:
“Whatever others eat, O Venerable One, that is my food; and whatever I eat, upon that he subsists.”
772. "Therein, 'of him alone' means of me alone, who was formerly a peta who had been a bhikkhu supporting a family (*kulūpaka*).
'Of evil karma' means of one whose conduct was wicked. 'I stand upon his head, on the crown' means I stand upon the head;
and while standing, I stand specifically on the crown, not in space merely the size of the head—this is the meaning. 'Having reached another realm' refers to [having departed] from the human world."
He arrived at the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), which had become his own domain. "Mameva" means "he became my very own attendant"—this is the completion of the sentence.

773. "Yaṃ bhadante hadantaññe": O Venerable One, O Noble Mahāmoggallāna, whatever others were throwing away—that is, voiding excrement—in that privy, "etaṃ me hoti bhojanaṃ" means that this excrement was my food for the day.
There is food during the day. Regarding the phrase "that which I give," it means that after he has eaten my excrement, whatever excrement I myself produce—that is what he subsists upon;
the meaning is that this spirit who frequents my family subsists by eating it day after day, thereby sustaining his own body.
Among them, the householder reviled the well-behaved bhikkhus, saying, "It would be better for you to eat excrement than to consume food in this manner.
But the family-attendant bhikkhu, having incited the householder to speak likewise, reviled him in that same way himself;
consequently, his livelihood became even more despised than before. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported this matter to the Blessed One.
He reported this. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, demonstrated the danger in reviling others and taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the Story of the Feces-Eating Petas.
9. The Exposition of the Story of the Dung-Eating Petas (Gūthakhādakapetavatthuvaṇṇanā) [774–81].
“Having emerged from a dung-pit” was said concerning a certain dung-eating peta while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana.
The story of that peta is similar to the immediately preceding story. In that case, a monastery was built by a lay follower.
This [story] was related by way of a male lay follower (*upāsaka*), whereas here it is by way of a female lay follower (*upāsikā*); this alone is the distinction.
There is nothing new in the remainder of the narrative or in the verses.
The exposition of the story of the dung-eating *peta* is concluded.

10. The Commentary on the Story of the Group of Petas (*Gaṇapetavatthu-vaṇṇanā*) "‘Naked, of ugly form...’"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a large number of petas.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, there were many people living in groups who lacked faith, were without confidence, and whose minds were obsessed with the stain of stinginess.
Having turned away from good conduct such as giving and having lived for a long time, upon the breakup of the body, they were reborn in a state of existence as hungry ghosts near the city.
Then one day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was going for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw those ghosts along the way and said:
“Naked, of hideous appearance, emaciated, with veins showing all over;”
“O you who are like withered stalks, emaciated, who indeed are you here, dear sirs?”—thus he asked in verse.

In that context, “of ugly appearance” means you have bodies of an unsightly form. “Who indeed are you here? means who exactly are you? He addresses them as “dear sirs” (mārisā) in accordance with his own status.
Having heard this, the petas—
“Venerable sir, we are ghosts, miserable beings belonging to the world of Yama;
having committed evil deeds, we have gone from here to the realm of ghosts.
Having thus declared their state as ghosts with this verse, the Elder spoke again:
“What evil deed was committed by body, speech, or mind?
By the ripening of what action have you gone from here to the world of the hungry ghosts?”—
thus she was questioned regarding the deed she had committed in verse.
“In open fords we searched for even a half-penny;
though there were things to be given, we did not provide for ourselves an island of safety.
Thirsty, we approach a river, but it flows back empty.”
We approach the shade during the heats, and the sunlight shifts away.
But the wind, with the color of fire, blows upon us, burning us.
Venerable sir, we deserve this and other evils even worse than that.
“We would travel for leagues, hungry and greedy for food;
yet we turn back without having found any—alas for our meager merit!
Hungry, fainting, and staggering, we have collapsed upon the ground.”
“Lying face up, we were repelled; turning face down, we fell.
Having fallen right there, dashed against the ground, we struck our chests and heads—alas for our meager merit!”
“Venerable sir, we deserve this and even more than that evil deed:
while there were things worthy of being given, we did not make an island for ourselves.
For surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth...”
“Generous and endowed with virtue, we shall perform much wholesome merit”—thus they spoke of the deeds they had performed themselves.
(788) Therein, “we shall go even for many leagues” means we shall go for many leagues indeed. How so? “Hungry and seeking food.”
For a long time we have been tormented by hunger; being greedy and covetous for food, even though we go out [in search], we return without having obtained any food at all.
"Appapuññatā" means a lack of merit, a state of not having performed wholesome deeds.
"Uttānā paṭikirāma" means that sometimes, with our limbs and members scattered about as if we were lying on our backs, we move along. "Avakujjā patāmase" means that sometimes we fall down face-down.

790. "Te ca" means "those very ones. "We shall strike our chests and heads" means that, having fallen face down and being unable to rise, we shall rub our own chests and heads while writhing in agony and overcome by pain.

The rest is exactly as explained below. The Elder reported this occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. Having heard it, the great multitude abandoned the stain of stinginess and became devoted to good conduct such as giving.
The commentary on the *Gaṇapeta-vatthu* is finished.
11. The Commentary on the Story of the Ghost of Pāṭaliputta.
"You have seen the hells and the animal womb"—this was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain ghost in a celestial mansion (vimāna-peta).
It is said that many merchants from Sāvatthī and from Pāṭaliputta were traveling by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
They arrived there. Among them, a certain lay follower who was afflicted by illness and whose mind was bound to a woman passed away.
Although he had performed wholesome deeds, because his mind was bound to that woman, instead of being reborn in the world of the devas, he was reborn as a *vimāna-peta* in the midst of the ocean.
Meanwhile, the woman to whom he was attached boarded a ship bound for the Land of Gold.
He was departing. Then that peta, desiring to seize that woman, obstructed the journey by boat.
Thereupon, the merchants, wondering, "For what reason does this boat not move?", began to distribute lots for ill omen (*kāḷakaṇṇisalāka*).
Due to the influence of a non-human being (*amanussa*), the lot fell to that very woman three times in succession—the woman to whom his heart was bound. That...
Having seen this, the merchants lowered a bundle of bamboo into the ocean and lowered the woman upon it.
As soon as the woman was lowered, the ship set out with great speed toward Suvaṇṇabhūmi. A non-human being placed the woman in his own celestial mansion and took his pleasure with her.
After one year had passed, she became weary of the world and, entreating that ghost, said:
"While living here, I am unable to accomplish my welfare for the life to come; it would be well, dear sir, if you would take me back to Pāṭaliputta.
Thus he was entreated by her.
“You have seen the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, the asuras, and likewise humans and gods;
you yourself have witnessed the ripening of your own karma. I shall lead you to Pāṭaliputta unharmed;
having gone there, perform wholesome deeds.”
He spoke this verse. In that regard, "the hells were seen by you" means that some individual hells (*paccekaniraya*) were also seen by you.

"The animal realm" (*tiracchānayoni*) is to be construed as meaning that even animals of great power, such as *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas*, were seen by you. "Pretas" refers to *pretas* distinguished by hunger, thirst, and so forth.
"Asuras" refers to *asuras* distinguished by Kālakañcika and others. "Devas" refers to certain deities of the Four Great Kings (*cātumahārājika*). It is said that he...
By her own supernatural power, she wandered about from time to time, seizing him and showing him the various individual hells and other realms;

therefore, she spoke thus. "She saw for herself the ripening of her own karma" means that, having gone specifically to the hells and other realms, she herself directly perceived and beheld the ripening of the karmas she had committed. "I shall not send you to Pāṭaliputta" means... [text fragment].
"Now I shall lead you, unharmed and uninjured by anyone, in human form itself, to Pāṭaliputta.
But once you have gone there, perform wholesome deeds; the meaning is that since the ripening of kamma is seen directly, you should be devoted to merit and intent upon it."
Then that woman, having heard his words, was delighted and said:
"You desire my welfare, O Yakkha; you desire my benefit, O Devatā.
I shall do your bidding; you are my teacher."
“I have seen the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghosts, the asuras, and also humans and gods;
I myself have witnessed the ripening of my own karma. Therefore, I shall perform no small amount of meritorious deeds.
Thus he spoke this verse.
Then that peta, taking the woman, traveled through the air and, having set her down in the middle of the city of Pāṭaliputta, departed.
When her relatives, friends, and others saw her, they rejoiced, saying, "We thought we had been cast into the ocean and were dead;
look, she has been seen! Oh, she has returned safely! Thus they gathered together and [inquired] about her condition.
They questioned her. She related to them everything she had seen and experienced from the very beginning.
When those merchants residing in Sāvatthī eventually arrived at Sāvatthī, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side;
they then reported that incident to the Blessed One. The Blessed One [used] that matter as the occasion for the discourse.

Having done so, he taught the Dhamma to the four assemblies. Upon hearing it, the great multitude was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and became devoted to wholesome deeds such as giving.
The commentary on the *Pāṭaliputta-peta* story is concluded.
12. The commentary on the *Ambavana-peta* story.
"And this lotus pond of yours is so delightful"—this was spoken concerning Ambapālī while the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain householder whose wealth had been exhausted. His wife passed away, and he had only one daughter.
Having placed her in the house of a friend, he [was burdened] with a hundred kahāpaṇas borrowed on loan.
Taking his merchandise, he set out on a trading journey with a caravan.
Before long, having obtained five hundred kahāpaṇas in profit along with his original capital, he was returning together with the caravan. On the way, bandits attacked and fell upon the caravan;
the members of the caravan fled hither and thither, but that householder remained in one place.
Having deposited the kahāpaṇas in the shop, he hid himself nearby. The thieves seized him and took his life.
Out of greed for wealth, he was reborn right there as a peta.
The merchants went to Sāvatthī and reported that news to his daughter. Due to her father’s death and the fear for her livelihood, she...
And being overcome with extreme dejection, she lamented bitterly. Then her father’s friend, the householder, said to her:
“Just as all pottery vessels end in breaking, even so does the life of sentient beings end in destruction.
Death is common to all and cannot be averted; therefore, do not grieve excessively for your father.”
"Do not lament; I am your father, you are my daughter. I shall perform for you the duties of a father;
remain without dejection and take delight in this house as if it were your father's home," he said, and thus comforted her.
By his words, her grief was allayed; she conceived toward him a sense of reverence and esteem as if toward her own father, yet out of her own wretched state—
Acting as his attendant and desiring to perform the funeral rites for her father,
she cooked rice gruel and placed well-ripened, sweet mango fruits, the color of red arsenic, in a bronze bowl.
Having the maidservant take both the gruel and the mango fruits, she went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and spoke thus:
“May the Blessed One favor me by accepting my offering. With his mind stirred by great compassion, the Teacher, fulfilling her wish, signaled for her to provide a seat.
Delighted and joyful, she spread out the very pure cloth she had brought upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared and offered it; the Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Then she offered rice gruel to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One accepted the rice gruel.
Then, having given rice gruel to the monks for the sake of the Saṅgha, she again, with washed hands, offered mango fruits to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One consumed them.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she spoke thus: "Venerable sir, by virtue of my gift of the bedspread, the rice gruel, and the mango fruits..."
“May this gift that has been offered reach my father. The Blessed One said, “So be it,” and gave the blessing of thanksgiving.
She paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
As soon as that gift was dedicated, the peta obtained mango groves, pleasure gardens, celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, lotus ponds, and great divine prosperity.
Then, at a later time, those merchants, while traveling for trade, set out upon that very same road and stayed for one night at the place where they had previously dwelt.
Seeing them, that ghost of a celestial mansion revealed himself to them along with his garden, mansion, and other splendors.
When the merchants saw him, they asked about the prosperity he had attained:
“This lotus pond of yours is so delightful, level, with excellent bathing places and abundant water;
well-flowered and swarming with flocks of bees—how was this charming place obtained by you?
And this mango grove of yours is so delightful, bearing fruit throughout all seasons.”
“Blossoming and crowded with swarms of bees, how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?”—these two verses they spoke. Regarding those [verses]:
*suramma* means very delightful; *sama* means level; *sutittha* means having beautiful bathing-places due to its stairs made of jewels; *mahodaka* means possessing abundant water.

797. *Sabbautukaṃ* means bringing happiness in all seasons through trees and other plants that bear flowers and fruits at various times. Therefore, he said: "It bears fruits. *Supupphitaṃ* means always in full bloom.
Having heard this, the peta, explaining the cause for obtaining lotus ponds and such things, said:
"Ripe mangoes, water, rice-gruel, and delightful cool shade;"
“By the gift given by my daughter, it is for that reason that I receive this here,” she said in verse.

Regarding that, “it is for that reason that I receive this here” means: because of the gift given by my daughter—who gave mangoes, water, and rice porridge to the Blessed One and the monks specifically for my sake—it is by virtue of that gift of my daughter that [I receive this].
By the gift of alms given here in this divine mango grove, the mangoes ripen in all seasons;

by the gift of rice gruel and a spread of cloth, one obtains here the cool shade and delightful beauty found in pleasure gardens, celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth— the meaning is that these things are successfully attained.
Having spoken thus, that peta led the merchants [to his home], showed them those five hundred kahāpaṇas, and said:
"Take half of this; as for the other half, give it to my daughter so that, having cleared the debt, she may live in comfort.
The merchants, arriving in Sāvatthī in due course, told her about it, and by him...

They gave even their own allotted shares to her alone. She paid a hundred kahāpaṇas to her creditors and gave the remainder to her father’s friend, that householder; she herself remained living there, performing domestic chores.
He, saying, "Let all this be yours alone," returned it to her and made her the mistress of his eldest son's household.
In the course of time, having obtained a son and nurturing him, she said:
“Behold this visible fruit of action—the result of generosity, self-control, and restraint!
Having been a slave in noble families, I have now become a daughter-in-law who is the mistress of the household.”
She spoke this verse.
Then one day, the Teacher, observing the ripening of her knowledge, manifested himself by pervading her with radiance as if standing before her and said:
"What is unpleasant appears in the form of the pleasant; what is unlovely appears in the form of the lovely."
“Suffering, in the guise of pleasure, overcomes the heedless”—this verse he spoke.
At the conclusion of that verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

On the following day, having given an alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, she reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One [took] that matter as the occasion for a discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Having done so, he taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Ambavana-peta-vatthu* is finished.
13. The commentary on the *Akkharukkha-peta-vatthu*.
"That which one gives does not belong to oneself"—this is the story of the *peta* who gave dice. What is its origin?
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī filled his carts with goods and went abroad for trade.
Having sold his own goods there and loaded the goods in exchange onto the carts, he returned to Sāvatthī.
He set out on the road. As he was traveling along that path, an axle of a cart broke in a forest.

Then a certain man, having taken an axe and a hatchet for the purpose of felling trees, left his own village and, wandering in the wilderness, reached that spot and saw the lay follower overcome with grief because of the broken axle.
Seeing him and thinking, "This merchant is suffering in the forest because his axle has broken," he felt compassion;
he cut down a tree trunk, fashioned a sturdy axle, fitted it onto the cart, and gave it to him.

Later, having passed away, he was reborn as a terrestrial deity in that very same forest region. Reflecting upon his own deed, he went to the house of that lay follower during the night and stood at the door of the house, saying:
“What one gives does not remain with that [giver]; indeed, by giving a gift while it is being given, one crosses over both worlds.
By means of that gift, one goes to both. Be vigilant; do not be negligent. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “what one gives does not remain with that”: whatever object of generosity (*deyyadhamma*) the donor gives, that very thing [does not remain].
In the next world, there is indeed the fruit of that gift; moreover, there is another, abundant, desirable, and pleasing fruit.
Therefore, "one should surely give gifts"—give gifts in whatever manner possible. Regarding this, he states the reason: "Having given, one crosses over both.
Having given a gift, one crosses over suffering and misfortune pertaining both to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and to the future life (*samparāyika*).

It transcends [the world]. "Both go by means of that gift" means that both kinds of happiness—both pertaining to this life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*)—approach and are attained through that gift;
this meaning should also be applied in terms of the welfare and happiness of oneself and others.
"Be awake, do not be negligent"—thus, there is the warding off of both kinds of misfortune and the accomplishment of both kinds of benefit.
The meaning is: "Be vigilant to accomplish the act of giving; having prepared the requisites for giving, be heedful therein.
This is stated here in a reduplicated form (*āmeḍita*) for the purpose of showing respect.
Having completed his own business, the merchant turned back and, arriving at Sāvatthī by stages, on the second day—
Having approached the Teacher and paid homage, he sat down to one side and reported that occurrence to the Blessed One.
The Teacher, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Akkharu*-tree *petavatthu*.
14. Commentary on the Story of the Petas Who Were Deprived of Their Wealth.
“We have been deprived of our wealth”—this is the story of the petas who were deprived of their wealth. How did its origin come about?

While the Blessed One was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha, it is said that four women, by means of false weights and other such frauds, [deceived others regarding] ghee, honey, oil, grain, and so forth.
Having engaged in worldly transactions and amassed wealth through improper means, they lived their lives.
Upon the dissolution of the body after death, they were reborn as female spirits (petīs) on the bank of a moat outside the city. Overwhelmed by suffering during the night, they cried out:
"We amassed wealth, both fairly and unfairly..."
"Others enjoy those [possessions], while we are partakers of suffering.
Wailing thus, they cried out with a terrifying, great sound. Hearing this, the people were struck with fear and terror;
when the night had turned to dawn, they prepared a great almsgiving for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and [invited] the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Having invited [the Blessed One] and served him with excellent hard and soft foods, they sat down beside the Blessed One when he had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, and reported the matter to him.
The Blessed One said, "Lay followers, there is no obstacle for you because of that noise;
however, four female spirits (petīs), overwhelmed by suffering, have been lamenting after confessing their own evil deeds."
They cried out with loud voices:
“We have accumulated wealth by both fair and foul means,
yet others enjoy it while we are the ones who share in suffering.”
"I have spoken this verse," he said.
Therein, "possessions" (*bhoga*) refers to specific types of wealth and requisites, such as clothing and ornaments, which receive that name in the sense of being objects to be enjoyed.
"We accumulated" means that with minds overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, we gathered [wealth] without giving anything to anyone. By "fairly" (*samena*),...
"And by unjust means"—that is, by improper methods and contrary to the right way, or by a semblance of the right way that is actually contrary to it—those enjoyments were accumulated by us;
now others enjoy them. "We are partakers of suffering" means:
because we have not performed any good conduct and have instead committed misconduct, we have now fallen into this great state of existence as hungry ghosts (petas).
"We have become sharers in suffering; we experience great suffering"—this is the meaning.
Thus the Blessed One, having spoken the verse uttered by those female spirits (petīs) and having explained their history, made that the occasion for a teaching.
He taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude and subsequently proclaimed the Truths (saccāni). At the conclusion of the Truths, many...
They attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.
The commentary on the story of the ghost who was deprived of his wealth is finished.
15. Commentary on the Story of the Merchant’s Son Ghost.
"Sixty thousand years"—this is the *Petavatthu* of the merchant’s son. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, fully adorned and arrayed, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, was wandering through the city with great royal majesty and great royal power.
In a certain house, while looking out from an upper chamber through an open window at that royal splendor,
he saw a woman whose beauty was like that of a celestial nymph; his mind was suddenly overwhelmed by the arising of defilements toward this unprecedented object,
even though there were people in the inner apartments who were endowed with excellence in lineage, physical form, conduct, and other virtues.
However, under the influence of his own naturally light and difficult-to-tame mind, he became mentally attached to that woman;
having given the signal to a man sitting behind him, saying, "Keep watch over this palace and this woman," he entered the royal palace.
All other details are to be understood according to the method already set forth in the Ambasakkara Petavatthu.

But this is the distinction: here, a certain man came while the sun had not yet set, and when the city gates were closed, he fastened the dawn-colored clay and the blue lotuses he had brought to the panels of the city gate, and then went to Jetavana to lie down.
Meanwhile, the king, having retired to his bed of honor, was in the middle watch of the night [considering] "sa," "iti," "na," "iti," "du"—and so forth.
And he heard these four syllables—"So" (so)—uttered as if with a loud voice, yet through the force of a cry of distress.
It is said that in the past, four sons of wealthy merchants living in Sāvatthī, intoxicated by the pride of their riches, had accumulated much demerit during their youth through the act of adultery;
subsequently, having passed away, [they were reborn] in that very city...
Having been reborn nearby in a copper cauldron and being cooked there, they reached the rim of the copper cauldron;
having uttered only the initial syllable of each verse recited by those seeking sensual pleasures,
they fell into the suffering of intense pain and descended into the copper cauldron.
But the king, having heard that sound, became terrified, agitated, and his hair stood on end; he passed the remainder of the night in distress.
When the night had dawned, he summoned the court chaplain and told him what had happened.
Knowing the king was terrified and agitated, the chaplain—being greedy for gain—thought, "This is a means for me to produce profit for myself and for the brahmins."
Having reflected, he said, "Great King, a truly great calamity has arisen; you must perform the 'All-Fourfold' sacrifice.
When the king heard his words, he commanded his ministers, "Prepare the requisites for the All-Fourfold Sacrifice.
Upon hearing this, Queen Mallikā spoke thus to the king: "Great King, why, having heard the word of the brahmin..."
"You wish to perform a task involving the slaughter and killing of many living beings; surely you should consult the Blessed One, whose range of knowledge is unimpeded in all respects?
You should act exactly as the Blessed One explains it to you.
Having heard her words, the king went into the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "No..."

"Great King, because of that, will there be any obstacle for you? Having said this, he related from the beginning the history of those beings reborn in the Lohakumbhī hell, and began to recite the verses uttered by each of them:
"For sixty thousand years, in their entirety..."
For those being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?
“There is no end; from where could there be an end? No end is in sight;
for thus was evil committed by you and by me, O dear ones.”
“We lived a life ill-lived, we who, though possessing means, did not give;
while there were things worthy of being given, we failed to make an island for ourselves.
