“Surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, I shall [act accordingly].”
“Generous and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit.
Thus he spoke, having completed his account.
Therein, “sixty thousand years” means sixty thousand years of human reckoning. It is said that in that Lohakumbhi hell...
A being born there, descending downward, reaches the lower surface in thirty thousand years;
likewise, ascending upward from there, it reaches the region of the rim of the mouth in exactly thirty thousand years.
With that perception, desiring to utter the verse, "Sixty thousand years, in their entirety," he says *sa*.
Having spoken thus, he fell face down, overcome by extreme agony. But the Blessed One spoke to him, completing the king’s verse.
This same method applies to the remaining verses as well. In that context, "When will there be an end?
means: "When indeed will there be an end, a conclusion, to this suffering of ours who are being cooked in the Lohakumbhi hell?"
803. “Tathā hi” means: just as for you and me there is no end to this suffering, nor is an end perceived, so too has evil karma been performed by you and by me;
thus it should be stated, having shifted the grammatical case. 804.
“Dujīvitaṃ” means a life censured by the wise. “Ye santa” means we who exist, being present.
*Deyyadhamme*: "Na dadamhase" means we did not give. To make this same meaning clearer, it is said:
"While there were things to be given, we did not make an island for ourselves.
(805) *So haṃ*: "So" refers to "I. *Nūna* is a particle used in reflection. *Ito*: from this. *Gantvā*: having gone.
"Having departed. "Having obtained a human birth" means having attained a human womb, a human state of existence.
"Generous" (*vadaññū*) means one whose nature is renunciation, or one who understands the speech of supplicants. "Endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanno*) means endowed with virtuous conduct.
"I shall do much wholesome [deed]" means that, without falling into negligence as before, I will perform abundant and extensive wholesome meritorious action.
The meaning is: "I shall accumulate.
Having spoken these verses, the Teacher taught the Dhamma in detail.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the man who had been carrying the clay, the red lotuses, and the water-lilies was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). The king, having become deeply moved, abandoned covetousness for the possessions of others.
"He was content with his own wife.
The commentary on the *Setthiputta-petavatthu* is finished.
16. Commentary on the *Saṭṭhikūṭa-petavatthu*.
"Is he perhaps mad?"—this was said concerning a certain peta while the Teacher was dwelling in the Veḷuvana.
It is said that in the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a certain cripple who was skilled in the art of casting salt and had reached perfection in the craft of throwing pebbles.
Sitting at the foot of a banyan tree by the city gate, he would, with strokes of pebbles, create the forms of elephants, horses, men, chariots, gabled houses, banners, full water-jars, and so forth.

He showed [the paintings] on the leaves of the banyan tree. The city children, having given coins such as *māyakaḍḍha* and *māsaka* for their own amusement, had those crafts executed according to their desire.
Then one day, the King of Bārāṇasī, having departed from the city, approached the foot of that banyan tree and [saw] upon the banyan leaves...
Having seen various manifestations of forms conjured up by way of elephant-forms and so forth, he asked the people:
"By whom, indeed, were these various manifestations of forms created upon these banyan leaves? The people showed him the cripple, saying:
"Your Majesty, they were made by this man. The king had him summoned and spoke thus: "Is it possible, my man,..."
“Is it possible, O King, to fill the belly of a man whom I shall show you while he is speaking, without his even knowing it, with raw balls of dough?

“It is possible, Your Majesty. The king, having become weary of his many-talking court chaplain, led him to his own royal palace, summoned the chaplain, and in a secluded place enclosed by a screen of cloth, [spoke] together with him.
Having sat down and deliberating, he summoned the cripple. The cripple arrived carrying a measure of *ajalaṇḍikā* (a type of fish), and perceiving the king’s intention, sat facing the chaplain.

When the chaplain opened his mouth, the cripple, through an opening in the wall, placed one *ajalaṇḍikā* after another at the base of his throat. Unable to spit them out due to shame, he swallowed them all.
He swallowed it. Then the king dismissed him with his belly filled with *ajalaṇḍika* beans, saying: "Go, brahmin! You have obtained the fruit of your much talking;
drink this beverage prepared from *maddana* fruits, *piyaṅgu*, lac, and other ingredients, and vomit it up.
In this way, you will be safe. And that cripple was satisfied with that deed.

Having offered it, he gave fourteen villages. Having obtained these villages, while making himself happy and satisfied and making his dependents happy and satisfied, giving to recluses, brahmins, and others as was appropriate, and not neglecting welfare both in this world and the next, he lived in comfort.
He provided food and wages to those who came to him to learn a craft.
Then a certain man approached him and said, "It would be well, teacher, if you would teach me this craft as well;
as for me, food and wages are not necessary. He taught that man the craft.
Having mastered the craft and wishing to test it, he went to Sunetta by name, who was sitting on the bank of the Ganges.
He struck the head of the Paccekabuddha with a clod of earth, and the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna right there on the bank of the Ganges.
When people heard what had happened, they beat that man right there with clods, sticks, and other weapons, and took his life.
Having died, he was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell and remained in hell for many thousands of years.

Having been cooked there, due to the remaining residue of the ripening of that very karma, he was reborn as a hungry ghost (peta) not far from the city of Rājagaha during this current appearance of a Buddha. Because a ripening similar to that karma must occur,
sixty thousand iron spikes, propelled by the force of his karma, [pierced] his head at the time of morning, the time of midday, and the time of evening.
They fall down. With his head severed and split open, he falls to the ground, overcome by extreme agony.
But as soon as the iron spikes have withdrawn, his head stands restored to its original state.
Then one day, as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Mount Gijjhakūṭa, he saw him and—
"Why do you run about like one who is mad, like a bewildered deer?
Without doubt you are a doer of evil deeds; why indeed do you cry out?"—with this verse he questioned him.
Therein, "like one who is mad" means as if having the nature of a madman, having fallen into madness.
"Like a bewildered deer you run": like a bewildered deer, you run hither and thither.
For when those iron spikes fall, seeing no protection, he flees here and there, thinking, "Perhaps this blow will not strike me.
But those [spikes], flung by the force of karma, fall right upon the head of whoever stands anywhere. Why is that?
"Why do you cry out? Why indeed do you make this sound, wandering about with such excessive screaming?
Hearing that, the peta said:
"I am a peta, O venerable sir, miserable, belonging to the world of Yama."
“Having committed an evil deed, I have gone from here to the world of the departed (peta).
Sixty thousand peaks, complete in every respect,
fall upon my head and shatter my skull.”
He gave a reply with two verses. Therein, "sixty thousand peaks" means sixty thousand iron spikes.
"Full" means complete, without deficiency. "In every way" means from every part.
It is said that his head was produced as large as a mountain peak, capable of supporting the falling of sixty thousand iron spikes. Even the mere pricking of it with the tip of a hair—
Those peaks, falling without leaving any space, shatter his head; therefore, he utters a cry of distress.
Thus it was said: “They fall upon my head from every side, and they shatter my skull.
Then the Elder, inquiring as to what deed had been committed, said:
“What evil deed have you committed by body, speech, or mind,
through the ripening of which karma do you undergo this suffering?
Sixty thousand full crores [of gold pieces]— ”
“They fall upon your head and pierce your skull”—
thus he spoke these two verses.
Then the peta, explaining the deed he himself had committed, said:
“Then I saw the Fully Awakened One, the one with the beautiful eyes, whose faculties were cultivated;
sitting at the foot of a tree, meditating, free from fear from any quarter.
‘With the strike of my fist, I shall split his head!’”
“By the ripening of that kamma, I have come to this suffering:
sixty thousand full peaks fall upon my head from every side, and they shatter my skull.”
He spoke three verses. 811.

Therein, *sambuddha* refers to a Paccekabuddha. *Sunetta* is his name. *Bhāvitindriya* means one whose faculties, such as faith and the rest, have been developed through the cultivation of the Noble Path. 812–13. *Sālittakappahārena*:
*Sālittaka* is said to be the act of throwing pebbles with a bow or with the fingers themselves; for there is also a reading, "by the striking of a pebble. *Bhindissanti* means they broke [it].
Having heard this, the Elder, showing that "this is now the fruit obtained for his former karma, exactly in accordance with the deeds he himself committed," said:
"By right, you base man!
Sixty thousand fraudulent measures, complete in every respect..."
“They fall upon your head and shatter your skull”—this was the concluding verse he spoke.
Therein, “by means of the Dhamma” means by a corresponding cause. “These” refers to you;
this fruit has been brought to you that is entirely appropriate for the evil deed committed by you when you wronged that Paccekabuddha.
"Therefore, he shows that this cannot be obstructed by anyone—whether by a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or even by a Perfectly Enlightened One himself.

Having spoken thus, and having wandered for alms in the city and finished his meal, the Teacher approached the Blessed One in the evening and reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, said:
While teaching the Dhamma to the assembled company, he revealed the power of the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas and the infallibility of kamma;
the great multitude, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, abandoned evil and became devoted to merit such as giving.
The commentary on the *Saṭṭhikūṭa-peta-vatthu* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the fourth Great Section, adorned with sixteen stories, within the *Petavatthu* of the *Khuddaka-ṭṭhakathā*.
The Conclusion:
And so far— those beings who,
having performed evil deeds, have been reborn among the hungry ghosts (petas);
By these deeds, that evil result was bitter for them.
Making this evident through direct experience as well as through questions and answers,
this teaching, according to its systematic order, increases spiritual urgency in the virtuous.
Those great seers, who were skilled in the subject matter of discourse and had thoroughly understood its basis,
compiled this work under the name *Petavatthu*.
To explain its meaning, following the method of the ancient commentaries:
The commentary on the meaning that I have undertaken by relying [on this work],
which elucidates the ultimate meanings therein as appropriate in each instance,
is known by the name *Paramatthadīpanī*.
Having reached completion with its orderly analysis,
this concludes the fifteenth section of the recitation from the Pāḷi text.
Thus, whatever has been attained by me while compiling it—
By the power of that merit, may all embodied beings,
having entered the teaching of the Lord of the World through the practice of purification beginning with virtue, partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world;
may all living beings always maintain reverence for it.
May the Lord of the World, the deity as well, send rain properly and in due season.
"May he, delighting in the true Dhamma, rule the world by means of the Dhamma alone.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the *Petavatthu*,
composed by the venerable teacher Dhammapāla, an eminent sage and ascetic dwelling at the Badaratittha Monastery.
The Commentary on the *Petavatthu* is completed.
